# Custom artifact

Source: `apps/docs/content/packaging/function/custom-artifact.mdx`
Route: `/packaging/function/custom-artifact`

Use `custom-artifact` when you build the Lambda deployment package yourself, for example with a custom compiler step, a monorepo build tool or a separate CI job. Point `packagePath` at a zip file, a directory or a single file; Stacktape zips directories and single files for you and deploys the result. It works for [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function), [deployment scripts](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) and [custom resources](/resources/advanced/custom-resources).

If you have no build step of your own, let Stacktape build: [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle) for JavaScript and TypeScript, [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) for Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET and Rust. With `custom-artifact`, source maps and code shared between functions are up to you.

## Basic example

Specify `packagePath` and `handler` in the packaging, and `runtime` on the Lambda resource:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging({
      packagePath: './dist/lambda.zip',
      handler: 'index.js:default'
    }),
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x'
  });

  return {
    resources: { api }
  };
});
```


## Configuration

`CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging` has two required properties, `packagePath` and `handler`; the function also needs a `runtime`. All other Lambda settings (`memory`, `timeout`, environment variables, etc.) are configured on the [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) resource itself, not on the packaging.

### packagePath

`packagePath` is the path to your deployment package. It can be:

| Input type | Behavior |
|------------|----------|
| A `.zip` file | Deployed directly |
| A directory | Automatically zipped before deployment |
| A non-zip file | Automatically zipped before deployment |

You don't need to zip your output manually if your build produces a directory. Point `packagePath` at the directory and Stacktape handles the zipping.

### handler

The `handler` property tells Lambda which function to invoke when the Lambda is triggered. The syntax is `filepath:functionName`.

For example, `index.js:default` invokes the `default` export from `index.js` at the artifact root, and `handlers/process.js:main` invokes `main` from `handlers/process.js`. Stacktape turns the path into Lambda's handler format by dropping the file extension: `handlers/process.main`.

Java and .NET artifacts use Lambda's own handler format, which Stacktape passes through as written: `com.example.Handler::handleRequest` for Java, `Assembly::Namespace.Class::Method` for .NET.

Set `handler` here and `runtime` on the Lambda resource: Stacktape does not infer them from the artifact.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging({
      packagePath: './build/output',
      handler: 'process.js:main'
    }),
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x',
    memory: 512,
    timeout: 60
  });

  return {
    resources: { processor }
  };
});
```


In this example, `packagePath` points to a directory. Stacktape zips it automatically, and Lambda invokes the `main` export from `process.js` at the root of the resulting package. The `memory` and `timeout` properties are [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) settings, not part of the packaging configuration.

## Using with a custom build step

Custom artifact packaging works well with an external build step in your CI pipeline or local workflow. Run your build tool to produce the artifact, then point `packagePath` at the output.

Make sure the build runs before `stacktape deploy` so that `packagePath` contains the artifact you intend to release.

A typical CI workflow:

```bash
npm run build
```

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage production
```

The build step is entirely decoupled from Stacktape: Stacktape reads the artifact at `packagePath` at deploy time.

## Directory packaging example

Custom artifact packaging accepts directories as input. When your build produces a directory, point `packagePath` at the directory root:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const fn = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging({
      packagePath: './lambda-build',
      handler: 'app.py:handler'
    }),
    runtime: 'python3.12',
    memory: 256,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return {
    resources: { fn }
  };
});
```


Stacktape zips the directory before deployment. Make sure the file referenced by `handler` is located at the expected path inside the package: in this case, `app.py` must be at the root of the `./lambda-build` directory. As with the previous example, `memory` and `timeout` are [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) settings configured alongside packaging.

## FAQ

### What value do I set for the handler property?

The `handler` property uses `filepath:functionName` syntax and points at the file *inside the deployment package*, not your source. For a TypeScript Lambda compiled to JavaScript, reference the output `.js`, not the source `.ts`: if your build emits `dist/index.js` with an exported `handler`, set `handler: 'index.js:handler'` and point `packagePath` at `dist`.

### Why does my custom artifact deploy but fail at runtime?

The most common cause is a `handler` path that doesn't match the file structure inside your zip. Unzip the artifact locally and confirm the handler file exists at the path Lambda will see: a mismatch typically surfaces as a module-not-found or handler-not-found error at invocation time. Use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) to view the error.


### Definition: `CustomArtifactLambdaPackagingProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/deployment-artifacts` with definition name `CustomArtifactLambdaPackagingProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `handler` | yes | `string` | - |
| `packagePath` | yes | `string` | - |

---

# JS bundle for Lambda

Source: `apps/docs/content/packaging/function/js-bundle.mdx`
Route: `/packaging/function/js-bundle`

The `js-bundle` packaging type (`JsBundleLambdaPackaging`) packages a JavaScript or TypeScript [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) from its entry file. Stacktape bundles the entry file and everything it imports into one minified file, installs the dependencies that cannot be bundled, and uploads the result. The bundle's source maps are stored in the stack's deployment bucket, outside the package.

`js-bundle` supports JavaScript and TypeScript only. For Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET and Rust functions, use [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack).

## When to use

Use `js-bundle` for every JavaScript or TypeScript Lambda function unless you already build the deployment package yourself: API handlers, event processors, scheduled tasks and webhooks.

Use [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) instead when:

- You have a pre-built zip from a separate CI pipeline or build tool.
- Your build needs steps that the bundler does not support.
- You need to include artifacts generated outside your project tree.

For container resources ([web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service), [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job)), see [container `js-bundle`](/packaging/containers/js-bundle).

## Basic example

`entryfilePath` is the only required property. It is relative to the Stacktape configuration file.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    })
  });

  return {
    resources: { api }
  };
});
```


The handler file exports a function that AWS Lambda invokes:

```typescript
export const handler = async (event: any) => {
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Hello from Lambda' })
  };
};
```

## Entry file

`entryfilePath` points to the file that contains the handler, relative to the Stacktape configuration file. Stacktape bundles the code starting from this file into one output file. Use `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` to keep selected packages out of the bundle. They are installed separately in the deployment package, which is often needed for packages with native binaries.

## Handler function

The `handlerFunction` property names the exported function to execute when the Lambda is invoked. Set it when your entry file exports a specifically named handler function.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const processOrder = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/orders.ts',
      handlerFunction: 'processOrder'
    }),
    memory: 512,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return {
    resources: { processOrder }
  };
});
```


The `memory` and `timeout` properties in these examples are [`LambdaFunction`](/resources/compute/lambda-function) settings, not packaging options: they are included here for realistic context.

The handler file would export the named function:

```typescript
export const processOrder = async (event: any) => {
  // process the order
  return { statusCode: 200, body: 'Order processed' };
};
```

## Including and excluding files

`includeFiles`, `excludeFiles` and `excludeDependencies` control what goes into the deployment package. Code is bundled starting from the entry file. Use `includeFiles` for runtime files that are not pulled in by the bundler, and `excludeFiles` to remove matched files from the deployment package. These options are useful when your function reads files at runtime that aren't statically imported (templates, configuration files, ML models, data files).

### Including additional files

The `includeFiles` property explicitly includes files matched by glob patterns in the deployment package. Paths are relative to your Stacktape config file. Use this for any file your handler reads at runtime via the filesystem (e.g., `fs.readFile`) rather than through an `import`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const emailSender = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/email-sender.ts',
      includeFiles: ['./templates/**/*.html', './config/email-config.json']
    }),
    memory: 256,
    timeout: 15
  });

  return {
    resources: { emailSender }
  };
});
```


### Excluding files

The `excludeFiles` property explicitly excludes files matched by glob patterns from the deployment package. This is useful when `includeFiles` globs are broader than intended, or when your project tree contains large files (test fixtures, documentation, local data) that would otherwise be included.

### Excluding dependencies

The `excludeDependencies` property lists dependencies to exclude from the deployment package. Use it when you know a dependency is not needed at runtime. Smaller packages can reduce cold start times, so exclude dependencies you do not need at runtime.

## Bundling options

All options are properties of `JsBundleLambdaPackaging` next to `entryfilePath`. See the [API reference](#api-reference) for the complete list.

### How the bundle is built

Stacktape bundles your code starting from the entry file into a single output file. The bundle is minified (whitespace and syntax only, so function names stay readable in stack traces), and on Node.js 18 and later, imports of `@aws-sdk/client-*` and `@aws-sdk/lib-*` are left out of the package because the Lambda runtime provides them. Source maps are generated automatically and kept outside the package; see [Source maps](#source-maps).

### Source maps

Each deployment stores the function's source maps in the stack's deployment bucket instead of the deployment package, so the package carries code only. The maps contain no source code. When the [Stacktape Console](/observability/error-tracking) first sees an error from the function, it uses the maps of the code that threw to show the stack trace with the original file, line and function. Stack traces in CloudWatch logs point into the bundled code.

The deployment bucket keeps a function's maps as long as it keeps a deployment package that uses them, so the maps of every release you can [roll back](/cli/rollback) to stay available.

- **`keepSourceMapsInPackage: true`** ships the maps in the package and turns on Node.js `--enable-source-maps`, so CloudWatch stack traces are mapped too. The package gets larger, and Node.js reads the maps on every cold start.
- **`outputSourceMapsTo`** also saves complete maps, original source included, to a local directory, for uploading to Sentry, Datadog or another tool.
- **`disableSourceMaps: true`** generates no maps; error locations then point into the bundled code everywhere.

Key options:

- **`nodeVersion`**: major Node.js version used to build the bundle. Supported: 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24. Default: `24`. This does not replace the Lambda resource's `runtime`; set both to matching versions when overriding the default.
- **`outputModuleFormat`**: `'cjs'` (CommonJS) or `'esm'` (ES Modules, enables top-level `await`). Node.js 24 and later use ESM output; with earlier Node.js versions the default is CommonJS. Edge functions remain CommonJS. Some npm packages don't support ESM, and ESM may produce less readable stack traces.
- **`tsConfigPath`**: path to your `tsconfig.json`, used to resolve path aliases during bundling.
- **`emitTsDecoratorMetadata`**: enable for frameworks that rely on TypeScript decorator metadata reflection (NestJS, TypeORM).
- **`dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle`**: packages treated as external (not bundled into the single output file). They're installed separately in the deployment package. Set the array to `['*']` to exclude all dependencies from the bundle.
- **`dependenciesToExcludeFromDeploymentPackage`**: removes non-bundled dependencies from the final package. Only applies to dependencies already excluded from the bundle. Set the array to `['*']` to exclude all non-bundled dependencies.
- **`disableSourceMaps`**: skips source map generation. Error locations then point into the bundled code.
- **`keepSourceMapsInPackage`**: keeps source maps in the deployment package and maps CloudWatch stack traces. Default: `false`. See [Source maps](#source-maps).
- **`outputSourceMapsTo`**: also saves complete source maps to a local directory. Useful for external error tracking tools like Sentry or Datadog.
- **`minify`**: minifies the bundle (whitespace and syntax). Local function and variable names are kept, so stack traces and error messages stay readable. Default: `true`.
- **`minifyIdentifiers`**: also shortens local variable and function names. Slightly smaller bundle, but the names disappear from stack traces and error messages and change with every build, so Stacktape Console cannot group the same error across deployments. Default: `false`.
- **`bundleAwsSdk`**: bundles `@aws-sdk/*` from your `node_modules` instead of using the copy the Lambda runtime provides. Enable it when you need a newer SDK than the runtime ships. Default: `false`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x',
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts',
      nodeVersion: 22,
      outputModuleFormat: 'esm',
      dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle: ['dd-trace'],
      tsConfigPath: './tsconfig.json'
    }),
    memory: 1024,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return {
    resources: { api }
  };
});
```


This example sets both `runtime: 'nodejs22.x'` on the Lambda function and `nodeVersion: 22` in its packaging config. The former selects the AWS Lambda runtime; the latter selects the Node.js version the bundle targets. Keep them aligned. Because Node.js 22 otherwise defaults to CommonJS, `outputModuleFormat: 'esm'` explicitly enables ES Module output. Use `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` for dependencies you do not want statically bundled: excluded dependencies are installed separately in the deployment package. An APM agent such as `dd-trace` needs this, because it instruments other modules as they load from `node_modules`. Setting `tsConfigPath` lets the bundler resolve TypeScript path aliases during bundling.


> **Info:** Use `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` for dependencies with native binaries. Excluded dependencies are installed separately in the deployment package rather than being statically bundled. This is the most common fix when a dependency works locally but fails in Lambda with a binary-related error.


## Build caching

Stacktape caches deployment packages based on a checksum, so unchanged code is not re-packaged. This makes iterative deployments faster when only some functions have changed. Caching works automatically with no configuration needed.

## Shared code between functions

When a stack has two or more JavaScript or TypeScript Lambda functions that can be packaged together, it builds them in a single pass and moves the npm dependencies they have in common into [Lambda layers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/chapter-layers.html) that those functions share. Your own shared modules stay in each function's package while they total 2 MB or less, so editing them deploys as a code update, as fast as editing a handler, without publishing a new layer version. When a shared module runs setup code as it loads (for example, it sets `process.env` or starts tracing) before packages load, the packages and your modules stay in the shared layers together, so they still load in the original order. Nothing needs to be configured, and your imports do not change.

The effect grows with the number of functions. Twenty-five functions that all import the same npm libraries (say, an ORM and a validation library) produce twenty-five small packages plus one layer, instead of twenty-five packages that each carry a full copy of those libraries. The AWS SDK is not part of this: the Lambda runtime provides it and Stacktape leaves it out of the package by default.

Stacktape creates at most three layers, leaving two of Lambda's five layer slots for layers you attach yourself. Code that only one function uses is never moved into a layer.

### When a function is packaged on its own

A function is packaged individually, without a shared layer, when it uses an option the shared build cannot honor:

- [tracing](/observability/tracing) is enabled for it (its handler is wrapped at the bundle entry)
- `outputModuleFormat: 'cjs'`
- `emitTsDecoratorMetadata: true`
- `outputSourceMapsTo`
- `dependenciesToExcludeFromDeploymentPackage`
- `includeFiles` or `excludeFiles`
- a `nodeVersion` other than 18, 20, 22 or 24

Functions also have to agree with each other to share a build. Architecture, `nodeVersion`, `tsConfigPath`, `disableSourceMaps`, `keepSourceMapsInPackage`, `minify`, `minifyIdentifiers`, `bundleAwsSdk`, `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` and `excludeDependencies` must match; functions that differ are grouped separately. The largest group shares a build and the rest are packaged individually, so one unusual function no longer costs the others their shared layer.


> **Info:** Changing your own shared code changes the package of every function that uses it, and the layers stay as they are. Changing one handler's own code changes only that one package. Changing a shared npm dependency publishes a new layer version.


## Processor architecture

`JsBundleLambdaPackaging` does not expose an architecture setting. Configure architecture on the [Lambda function resource](/resources/compute/lambda-function); see that page for details. If your function uses native binary dependencies, verify they ship builds compatible with your chosen architecture before switching.

## API reference


### Definition: `JsBundleLambdaPackagingProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/deployment-artifacts` with definition name `JsBundleLambdaPackagingProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `entryfilePath` | yes | `string` | - |
| `bundleAwsSdk` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `dependenciesToExcludeFromDeploymentPackage` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `disableSourceMaps` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `emitTsDecoratorMetadata` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `excludeDependencies` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `excludeFiles` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `handlerFunction` | no | `string` | - |
| `includeFiles` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `keepSourceMapsInPackage` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `minify` | no | `boolean` | `true` |
| `minifyIdentifiers` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `nodeVersion` | no | `number: 16 \| 17 \| 18 \| 19 \| 20 \| 21 \| 22 \| 23 \| 24` | - |
| `outputModuleFormat` | no | `string: "cjs" \| "esm"` | - |
| `outputSourceMapsTo` | no | `string` | - |
| `tsConfigPath` | no | `string` | - |


## FAQ

### Should I use `js-bundle` or a custom artifact?

Use `js-bundle` for most projects. It handles bundling and artifact creation with minimal configuration. Use [custom artifact packaging](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) when you already have a pre-built zip from an external build pipeline, need a custom toolchain the bundler doesn't support, or want full control over the deployment package contents.

### Can I use ES Modules (ESM)?

Yes. Node.js 24 and later use ES Module output automatically. With an earlier Node.js version, set `outputModuleFormat: 'esm'`; ESM also enables top-level `await`. Edge functions remain CommonJS. Some npm packages don't support ESM, and ESM can produce less readable stack traces: test your function after switching to catch compatibility issues.

### What is the maximum Lambda deployment package size?

AWS Lambda allows 250 MB unzipped for a function and all its layers together. Its 50 MB zipped limit applies only to direct uploads; Stacktape deploys code through S3, so it doesn't apply. `js-bundle` keeps packages small on its own: it bundles to a single minified file, leaves the runtime-provided AWS SDK out, and moves code shared between functions into [a shared layer](#shared-code-between-functions). `excludeFiles` and `excludeDependencies` trim further. If your dependencies still cannot fit, consider moving the workload to a container resource such as a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service), or [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

### How do I handle native binary dependencies like sharp or Prisma?

Usually you don't need to do anything. Stacktape detects packages that load native binaries or read their own files at run time, keeps them out of the bundle and installs them for the function's platform. Prisma's client is bundled, and the function gets the query engine for its architecture. With Prisma 5 or 6, add `rhel-openssl-3.0.x` (x86_64) or `linux-arm64-openssl-3.0.x` (arm64) to `binaryTargets` in `schema.prisma`; Prisma 7 needs no engine. If a dependency still works locally but fails in Lambda, add it to `dependenciesToExcludeFromBundle` to install it beside the bundle.

### My function runs an older AWS SDK than the one in my package.json: why?

On Node.js 18 and later, the Lambda runtime ships the AWS SDK v3, and `js-bundle` leaves `@aws-sdk/client-*` and `@aws-sdk/lib-*` imports out of the package so they resolve from the runtime. The runtime's copy can lag behind npm. If your code needs a newer SDK, set `bundleAwsSdk: true` to bundle the version from your `node_modules`.

### Why does my stack contain Lambda layers I did not configure?

When several functions can be packaged together, Stacktape moves the code they share into layers so each package carries only its own code. This is automatic. See [shared code between functions](#shared-code-between-functions) for what goes into a layer and which options keep a function off that path.

### How do I debug a function packaged with `js-bundle`?

The Stacktape Console shows each runtime error with the original file, line and function, read from the source maps the deployment stored in your deployment bucket. CloudWatch logs show positions in the bundled code; set `keepSourceMapsInPackage: true` to have Node.js map them as well. For rapid iteration without a full redeploy, use [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) with Lambda functions.

---

# Packaging overview

Source: `apps/docs/content/packaging/overview.mdx`
Route: `/packaging/overview`

Stacktape packaging turns your source code into a deployable artifact: a Lambda zip for functions or a container image for always-on services. Your [resource type](/configuration/resources) determines which category applies. The packaging type you choose controls how the artifact is built.

## Two packaging categories

Lambda functions and container workloads require a `packaging` configuration. The category is determined by your resource type, not chosen independently.

**Function packaging** produces a Lambda deployment zip. It applies to [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function), [deployment scripts](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts) and [custom resources](/resources/advanced/custom-resources).

**Container packaging** builds or references an OCI container image. The `js-bundle`, `buildpack` and `dockerfile` types build an image and upload it to a managed ECR repository. The `prebuilt-image` type references an existing image from Docker Hub, ECR or another registry. Container packaging applies to [web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [private services](/resources/compute/private-service), [worker services](/resources/compute/worker-service), [multi-container workloads](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload), [batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) and [AgentCore runtimes](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).


## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Function packaging | Container packaging |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Artifact produced | Lambda deployment zip | OCI container image (built or referenced) |
| Packaging types | js-bundle, buildpack, custom-artifact | js-bundle, buildpack, dockerfile, prebuilt-image |
| Build from source without extra config | yes | yes |
| Bring your own build | Pre-built zip, directory, or non-zip file | Dockerfile or prebuilt image |


## Function packaging

Function packaging bundles your code and dependencies into a Lambda deployment zip.

| Type | Use when |
|------|----------|
| [**`js-bundle`**](/packaging/function/js-bundle) | JavaScript or TypeScript. Point to the entry file. Stacktape bundles it into one minified file, keeps its source maps in the deployment bucket, leaves the AWS SDK to the Lambda runtime, moves code shared between functions into a shared layer, and installs dependencies with native binaries separately. |
| [**`buildpack`**](/packaging/function/buildpack) | Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET or Rust. Point to the entry file. Stacktape installs dependencies and compiles the code in Docker on the Lambda build image of the function's `runtime`. |
| [**`custom-artifact`**](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) | You build the deployment package yourself. Provide a zip, directory or other file. Stacktape zips directories and non-zip files automatically. |

Use `custom-artifact` only when your build can't be expressed through `js-bundle` or `buildpack`, for example a custom compiler step, a monorepo build tool, or an artifact produced by a separate CI job. It needs a `packagePath` and a `handler`, and the function needs a `runtime`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    })
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


`js-bundle` options such as `nodeVersion`, `outputModuleFormat` and `keepSourceMapsInPackage` are direct properties next to `entryfilePath`. See [JS Bundle for Lambda](/packaging/function/js-bundle). For other languages, the function's `runtime` selects the language version; see [Buildpack for Lambda](/packaging/function/buildpack).

## Container packaging

Container packaging builds or references an OCI container image. Four types cover the range from a bundled Node.js entry file to a fully custom build.

| Type | Use when |
|------|----------|
| [**`js-bundle`**](/packaging/containers/js-bundle) | A JavaScript or TypeScript service with one entry file, on Node.js, Bun or Deno. Stacktape bundles the code and builds a small image. |
| [**`buildpack`**](/packaging/containers/buildpack) | Any other project: Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, Ruby, .NET, Elixir, or a Node.js framework such as Next.js. Stacktape detects the language, framework and start command from the project files. No Dockerfile needed. |
| [**`dockerfile`**](/packaging/containers/dockerfile) | You need a specific base image, system setup, multi-stage builds or full control over the build. Stacktape builds the image from your Dockerfile. |
| [**`prebuilt-image`**](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image) | The image already exists in Docker Hub, ECR or a private registry. Stacktape does not build an image. |

### Choosing a container packaging type

Use **`js-bundle`** (`JsBundleImagePackaging`) for JavaScript and TypeScript services that start from one entry file, such as Express, Hono, Fastify or NestJS, on Node.js (the default), Bun or Deno (`runtime: 'bun'` or `'deno'`). Use **`buildpack`** (`BuildpackImagePackaging`) for every other language and for frameworks with their own build output. It works without configuration for projects that follow their ecosystem's conventions, and `startCommand`, `buildCommand` and the other overrides cover the rest. Use **`dockerfile`** (`DockerfilePackaging`) when you need a specific base image, GPU drivers or a custom entrypoint. Use **`prebuilt-image`** (`PrebuiltImagePackaging`) when your CI pipeline already produces images, or for third-party software such as Redis, Nginx or Prometheus.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebService, BuildpackImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new WebService({
    resources: { cpu: 0.5, memory: 1024 },
    packaging: new BuildpackImagePackaging({
      sourceDirectoryPath: './api'
    })
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


The `resources` property belongs to the web service, not to packaging. It sets CPU and memory for the container. See the [web service page](/resources/compute/web-service) for supported values and scaling options.

## Build caching

`js-bundle` and `buildpack` artifacts are cached by a checksum of their inputs. When the code, dependencies and options have not changed since the last deploy, the packaging step is skipped and the existing artifact is reused. For container `buildpack` images, dependency install layers are also cached by Docker BuildKit, so a code-only change does not reinstall dependencies. `prebuilt-image` uses the image you reference. `custom-artifact` uses the `packagePath` you provide and zips directories and non-zip files automatically.


> **Tip:** You can run packaging without deploying using [`stacktape package`](/cli/package). This is useful for testing your build configuration or for CI pipelines that separate the build and deploy steps.


## FAQ

### Which packaging type should I start with?

For JavaScript and TypeScript, start with `js-bundle`, either [for Lambda](/packaging/function/js-bundle) or [for containers](/packaging/containers/js-bundle). For other languages, start with `buildpack`, either [for Lambda](/packaging/function/buildpack) or [for containers](/packaging/containers/buildpack). Switch to [`dockerfile`](/packaging/containers/dockerfile), [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) or [`prebuilt-image`](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image) when you need full control or already have a build pipeline.

### Which languages are supported?

- **Lambda `js-bundle`:** JavaScript and TypeScript.
- **Lambda `buildpack`:** Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET and Rust.
- **Container `js-bundle`:** JavaScript and TypeScript, on Node.js, Bun or Deno.
- **Container `buildpack`:** Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Go, Rust, Java, .NET, Elixir, Deno, Gleam, C/C++, static sites and shell scripts.
- **`dockerfile` and `prebuilt-image`:** anything that runs in a container.

### Are the Lambda `buildpack` and the container `buildpack` the same?

No. Both build from source without a Dockerfile, but they are separate builders. The Lambda `buildpack` produces a zip on the Lambda build image of the function's `runtime` and uses keyed options (`python`, `java`, `dotnet`). The container `buildpack` detects the project with [Railpack](https://railpack.com) and produces a container image; its options are `startCommand`, `buildCommand`, `packages` and similar.

### How large can a Lambda deployment package be?

AWS Lambda allows 250 MB unzipped for a function and its layers. `js-bundle` keeps packages small by bundling into one minified file, leaving the runtime-provided AWS SDK out of the package, and moving code shared between functions into [a shared layer](/packaging/function/js-bundle#shared-code-between-functions). If a package still exceeds the limit, consider a container resource such as a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service); container images can be much larger.

### Where does Stacktape store container images?

The `js-bundle`, `buildpack` and `dockerfile` types upload the image to a managed ECR (Elastic Container Registry) repository. You don't need to create or configure it. With [`prebuilt-image`](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image), you provide the name or URL of an existing image, and Stacktape does not build or push anything.

### Does Stacktape rebuild my code on every deploy?

Not always. `js-bundle` and `buildpack` reuse the previous artifact when its inputs have not changed. `dockerfile` builds use Docker's layer cache.

### I'm upgrading from Stacktape v3. What changed?

Stacktape v4 has fewer packaging types with new names, and some options moved or were removed. See [Upgrading from v3](/getting-started/upgrading-from-v3) for a before-and-after example of each change.

---

# Resource catalog

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/index.mdx`
Route: `/resources`

A resource is one part of your stack: a service, a database, a bucket, a queue. You declare it in the `resources` of your configuration, and Stacktape creates the AWS services it needs in your AWS account. [Declaring resources](/configuration/resources) explains the syntax. This page helps you pick the right resource.


## Pick by what you are building


**Run code**

- [Web service](/resources/compute/web-service): An API or a web app in a container
- [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function): Code that runs per request or event
- [Worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service): A background worker that stays on
- [Private service](/resources/compute/private-service): A service only your other resources can call
- [Batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job): A job that runs to completion, with GPUs if needed
- [Triggers](/resources/triggers/overview): Code on a schedule, a file upload or a queue message

**Serve a frontend**

- [Framework pages](#frontend): A Next.js, Astro, Nuxt, SvelteKit, SolidStart, TanStack Start or Remix app
- [Static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting): A static site or a single-page app

**Store data**

- [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database): PostgreSQL or MySQL
- [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb): Key-value data with no servers to manage
- [Redis](/resources/databases/redis): A cache or user sessions
- [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis): A cache for Lambda-heavy apps, paid per request
- [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket): Files and uploads

**Connect and extend**

- [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue): A queue between services
- [Email sender](/resources/messaging/email-sender): Email from your app
- [User authentication pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool): Sign-up and sign-in for your users
- [Raw CloudFormation](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources): An AWS service with no resource here
- [AWS CDK constructs](/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs): An existing CDK construct


## All resources

### Compute

Compute resources run your code. Always-on resources bill by the hour even with no traffic; the others scale to zero.

| Resource | AWS service | How it runs | When idle |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Web service](/resources/compute/web-service) | ECS on Fargate or EC2 | Always on, in containers, with a public HTTPS URL | Bills hourly |
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | Lambda | Per event from a [trigger](/resources/triggers/overview), for up to 15 minutes | Scales to zero |
| [Private service](/resources/compute/private-service) | ECS on Fargate or EC2 | Always on, in containers that only the stack can call | Bills hourly |
| [Worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) | ECS on Fargate or EC2 | Always on, with no URL: it polls queues or runs loops | Bills hourly |
| [Batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) | AWS Batch | From a trigger until the job finishes, with CPUs, memory or GPUs | Scales to zero |
| [Multi-container workload](/resources/compute/multi-container-workload) | ECS on Fargate or EC2 | Always on, several containers in one task | Bills hourly |
| [Edge function](/resources/compute/edge-function) | Lambda@Edge | Per CloudFront request or response | Scales to zero |
| [Convex](/resources/compute/convex) | ECS, RDS, S3 and a load balancer | Always on, as a self-hosted Convex backend | Bills hourly |

Containers are packaged with [container packaging](/packaging/overview#container-packaging) and Lambda functions with [function packaging](/packaging/overview#function-packaging).

### Frontend

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [Static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) | S3 and CloudFront | Static sites, single-page apps and pre-rendered builds |
| [Next.js](/resources/frontend/nextjs) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | Next.js with server rendering |
| [Astro](/resources/frontend/astro) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | Astro with server-rendered routes |
| [Nuxt](/resources/frontend/nuxt) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | Nuxt with server rendering |
| [SvelteKit](/resources/frontend/sveltekit) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | SvelteKit with server rendering |
| [SolidStart](/resources/frontend/solidstart) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | SolidStart with server rendering |
| [TanStack Start](/resources/frontend/tanstack-start) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | TanStack Start with server rendering |
| [Remix](/resources/frontend/remix) | Lambda, S3 and CloudFront | Remix with server rendering |

### Databases

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | RDS or Aurora | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and other SQL engines |
| [Aurora DSQL](/resources/databases/dsql) | Aurora DSQL | Serverless SQL that works like PostgreSQL, with IAM sign-in |
| [DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb) | DynamoDB | Key-value and document data at any scale |
| [Redis](/resources/databases/redis) | ElastiCache | Caching, sessions, rate limits and pub/sub inside your VPC |
| [Upstash Redis](/resources/databases/upstash-redis) | Upstash (outside AWS) | Pay-per-request Redis for serverless apps |
| [MongoDB Atlas](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas) | MongoDB Atlas (outside AWS) | Document data with a flexible schema |
| [OpenSearch](/resources/databases/opensearch) | OpenSearch Service | Full-text search and log analytics |

### Storage

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) | S3 | Files, uploads, backups and other objects |
| [EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem) | EFS | A shared file system that containers mount |

### Networking

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | API Gateway (HTTP API) | Pay-per-request HTTP routing to functions and containers |
| [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway) | API Gateway (WebSocket API) | Persistent client connections handled by functions |
| [AppSync API](/resources/networking/appsync-api) | AppSync | A GraphQL API with Lambda resolvers |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | Elastic Load Balancing (ALB) | HTTP routing by path, host or header. Billed per hour plus usage (LCUs) |
| [Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer) | Elastic Load Balancing (NLB) | TCP and TLS traffic, such as gRPC or MQTT |
| [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) | CloudFront | Caching in front of a bucket, API, load balancer or function |
| [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains) | Route 53 and ACM | Serving a resource at your own domain |

### Messaging

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) | SQS | Queuing work between services |
| [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) | SNS | Sending one message to many subscribers |
| [Event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) | EventBridge | Routing events to targets by pattern |
| [Kinesis stream](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream) | Kinesis Data Streams | Ordered, replayable streams of records |
| [Kafka cluster](/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster) | MSK Serverless | Kafka topics for producers and consumers |
| [Email sender](/resources/messaging/email-sender) | SES | Sending email from a verified domain or address |

### Triggers

Triggers are not resources of their own. You add them to a Lambda function, and some also to a batch job or a container, so it runs when something happens. [Triggers overview](/resources/triggers/overview) compares them.

| Trigger | Runs your code when |
|---|---|
| [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) | A request reaches an HTTP API Gateway or a load balancer |
| [Schedule triggers](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers) | A rate or cron schedule fires |
| [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) | Messages arrive in a queue |
| [SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events) | A message is published to a topic |
| [S3 events](/resources/triggers/s3-events) | Objects are created, deleted or restored in a bucket |
| [DynamoDB streams](/resources/triggers/dynamodb-streams) | Items change in a table |
| [Kinesis events](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events) | Records arrive in a stream |
| [Kafka topic events](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics) | Records arrive in a Kafka topic |
| [Event bus events](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events) | An event on a bus matches a pattern |
| [CloudWatch Logs](/resources/triggers/cloudwatch-logs) | New records appear in a log group |
| [Alarms as triggers](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers) | An alarm goes into the `ALARM` state |

### Orchestration

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [State machine](/resources/orchestration/state-machine) | Step Functions | Multi-step workflows with branches, retries and parallel steps |

### Security

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| [User authentication pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) | Cognito | Sign-up, sign-in, MFA and social or enterprise login |
| [Web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) | WAF | Blocking common attacks before they reach APIs and load balancers |
| [Bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) | EC2 with Systems Manager | Reaching private databases and caches from your machine |

### AgentCore

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|

| [AgentCore Memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory) | Bedrock AgentCore | Memory an agent keeps across sessions |

### Advanced

| Resource | AWS service | Use it for |
|---|---|---|

| [Raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) | Any | Declaring any AWS resource directly |


## What else goes in a stack

[Uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests) are configured in the stack too, and [alarms](/observability/alarms) are set on the resource they watch. Their pages are under Observability.

## What resources cost

Always-on resources bill by the hour even with no traffic. These include web, private and worker services, multi-container workloads, relational databases, Redis, OpenSearch, load balancers, Kafka clusters, bastion hosts and Convex. Most other resources bill per request, per message or per GB stored. Each resource page has a pricing note, and [Managing costs](/managing-costs/overview) explains how to track the bill.

# AWS CDK constructs

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs.mdx`
Route: `/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs`

An `aws-cdk-construct` adds the resources of an AWS CDK construct to your stack. You write a construct class in
TypeScript or JavaScript, and Stacktape synthesizes it and deploys its resources with the rest of the stack. Use it for
AWS services that have no Stacktape resource, such as Cognito identity pools, IoT rules or MediaConvert, when the CDK's
higher-level constructs save you work.

Check the [resource catalog](/resources/) first; GraphQL APIs, for example, have a native
[AppSync API](/resources/networking/appsync-api) resource. For one or two plain resources,
[raw CloudFormation](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) needs no extra dependencies. To change a resource
Stacktape already creates, use [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

## Basic example

Install the CDK libraries in your project. Stacktape loads them from the `node_modules` next to the construct file:

```bash
npm install aws-cdk-lib constructs
```


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AwsCdkConstruct } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const alerts = new AwsCdkConstruct({
    entryfilePath: './cdk/alert-topic.ts'
  });

  return {
    resources: { alerts }
  };
});
```


```typescript
// cdk/alert-topic.ts
import { Construct } from 'constructs';
import { CfnOutput } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import * as sns from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns';
import * as subscriptions from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sns-subscriptions';

export default class AlertTopic extends Construct {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string) {
    super(scope, id);
    const topic = new sns.Topic(this, 'Topic', { displayName: 'Application alerts' });
    topic.addSubscription(new subscriptions.EmailSubscription('ops@example.com'));
    new CfnOutput(this, 'TopicArn', { value: topic.topicArn });
  }
}
```

The file must export a class that extends `Construct`. Stacktape uses the default export; for a named export, set
`exportName` to the class name. A class that extends `Stack` isn't accepted: move its resources into a `Construct`.
Stacktape creates the class twice during a deploy (once to check it), so keep the constructor free of side effects such
as API calls.

The construct's resources get logical IDs that start with the resource name in PascalCase (`AlertsTopic…`), and its
`CfnOutput`s become outputs of the stack.

## Pass values in

`constructProperties` is passed to the constructor as its third argument:

```typescript
new AwsCdkConstruct({
  entryfilePath: './cdk/data-access.ts',
  constructProperties: {
    retentionDays: 14,
    dataBucketArn: $ResourceParam('dataBucket', 'arn')
  }
})
```

```typescript
// cdk/data-access.ts
import { Construct } from 'constructs';
import { Duration } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import * as iam from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-iam';
import * as sqs from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-sqs';

export default class DataAccess extends Construct {
  constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props: { retentionDays: number; dataBucketArn: string }) {
    super(scope, id);
    new sqs.Queue(this, 'Jobs', { retentionPeriod: Duration.days(props.retentionDays) });
    new iam.ManagedPolicy(this, 'ListData', {
      statements: [new iam.PolicyStatement({ actions: ['s3:ListBucket'], resources: [props.dataBucketArn] })]
    });
  }
}
```

Plain values arrive as they are. A directive such as `$ResourceParam` arrives as its text while the construct runs,
and Stacktape replaces it with the real reference in the finished template. So use it only as a whole property value,
as above. Code that parses or builds on it, such as `Bucket.fromBucketArn()` or `` `${arn}/*` ``, gets the directive
text instead of an ARN.

## Use the construct's resources

A construct can't be a `connectTo` target, and it has no [referenceable parameters](/configuration/referenceable-parameters).
To use one of its resources from a Stacktape resource:

1. Run `stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1` and find the resource's logical ID in `compiled-template.yaml`.
2. Reference it with [`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives). For the topic in the basic example that is
   `$CfResourceParam('AlertsTopicCF7C81C9', 'TopicArn')`.
3. Grant access with `iamRoleStatements` on the workload.

The CDK keeps a logical ID stable as long as the construct's path doesn't change.

## Limits

- Stacktape deploys the synthesized template only. It doesn't publish CDK assets, so constructs that package local
  files or Docker images, such as `lambda.Code.fromAsset()` or `BucketDeployment`, don't work. Run code with Stacktape
  [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or containers instead.
- No `overrides` and no dev mode. Change the construct's code instead.
- The construct's resources count toward CloudFormation's 500-resource limit per stack. CDK constructs often create more
  resources than you expect.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AwsCdkConstructProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/aws-cdk-construct` with definition name `AwsCdkConstructProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `entryfilePath` | yes | `string` | - |
| `constructProperties` | no | `unknown` | - |
| `exportName` | no | `string` | `default` |


## Next steps

- [Raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources): add single resources without CDK.
- [Custom resources](/resources/advanced/custom-resources): manage things outside AWS during deploys.
- [Directives](/configuration/directives): `$ResourceParam` and `$CfResourceParam`.

# Custom resources

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/advanced/custom-resources.mdx`
Route: `/resources/advanced/custom-resources`

A custom resource runs your Lambda function when the stack creates, updates or deletes it. Use it to manage something
outside AWS together with the stack: a webhook in Stripe, a monitor in Datadog, a DNS record at another provider. It's
created on deploy, updated when its properties change and removed when you delete the stack.

It has two parts. A `custom-resource-definition` is the Lambda function with your code. A `custom-resource-instance`
is one managed thing: it names a definition and passes it properties. One definition can serve many instances.

For a step that just runs once per deploy, such as a migration, a [deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts)
is simpler: it doesn't need the response protocol below. For an AWS resource type Stacktape doesn't have, use
[raw CloudFormation](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  CustomResourceDefinition,
  CustomResourceInstance,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  $Secret
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const webhookProvider = new CustomResourceDefinition({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/webhook-provider.ts'
    }),
    timeout: 60,
    environment: { EXTERNAL_API_KEY: $Secret('external-api-key') }
  });

  const apiWebhook = new CustomResourceInstance({
    definitionName: 'webhookProvider',
    resourceProperties: {
      callbackUrl: 'https://myapp.example.com/webhook'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { webhookProvider, apiWebhook }
  };
});
```


The handler receives `resourceProperties` as `event.ResourceProperties`. The default `timeout` is 10 seconds, which is
short for calls to outside APIs; the maximum is 900.

## The handler

CloudFormation calls the function with a `RequestType` of `Create`, `Update` or `Delete`, then waits until the function
PUTs a result to the `ResponseURL` in the event. The function must report `FAILED` when the outside API refuses the
request; `fetch` doesn't throw on a 4xx or 5xx response, so check the status yourself:

```typescript
type Event = {
  RequestType: 'Create' | 'Update' | 'Delete';
  ResourceProperties: { callbackUrl: string };
  PhysicalResourceId?: string;
  ResponseURL: string;
  StackId: string;
  RequestId: string;
  LogicalResourceId: string;
};

const api = (path: string, init: RequestInit = {}) =>
  fetch(`https://api.example.com${path}`, {
    ...init,
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.EXTERNAL_API_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }
  });

export default async (event: Event) => {
  let physicalResourceId = event.PhysicalResourceId;
  let data: Record<string, string> = {};
  let status: 'SUCCESS' | 'FAILED' = 'SUCCESS';
  let reason = '';

  try {
    if (event.RequestType === 'Create') {
      const response = await api('/webhooks', {
        method: 'POST',
        body: JSON.stringify({ url: event.ResourceProperties.callbackUrl })
      });
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Create failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
      const webhook = await response.json();
      if (!webhook.id) throw new Error('Create response has no webhook id');
      physicalResourceId = webhook.id;
      data = { webhookId: webhook.id };
    }

    if (event.RequestType === 'Update') {
      const response = await api(`/webhooks/${physicalResourceId}`, {
        method: 'PUT',
        body: JSON.stringify({ url: event.ResourceProperties.callbackUrl })
      });
      if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Update failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
      data = { webhookId: physicalResourceId! };
    }

    if (event.RequestType === 'Delete' && physicalResourceId?.startsWith('wh_')) {
      const response = await api(`/webhooks/${physicalResourceId}`, { method: 'DELETE' });
      // Already gone counts as deleted.
      if (!response.ok && response.status !== 404) {
        throw new Error(`Delete failed: ${response.status} ${await response.text()}`);
      }
    }
  } catch (error) {
    status = 'FAILED';
    reason = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error);
  }

  const result = await fetch(event.ResponseURL, {
    method: 'PUT',
    body: JSON.stringify({
      Status: status,
      Reason: reason,
      // A failed Create has no id yet; reuse the request ID so CloudFormation gets a value.
      PhysicalResourceId: physicalResourceId ?? event.RequestId,
      StackId: event.StackId,
      RequestId: event.RequestId,
      LogicalResourceId: event.LogicalResourceId,
      Data: data
    })
  });
  if (!result.ok) throw new Error(`Could not send the response to CloudFormation: ${result.status}`);
};
```

`wh_` stands for the outside service's ID format. The check skips the API call when a failed Create never got a real
ID, for example during the rollback that follows it.

Rules that keep a stack out of trouble:

- **Always respond.** Without a response, CloudFormation waits about an hour and then fails the deploy.
- **Keep the physical ID stable on Update.** A different ID means "replaced": CloudFormation then sends a `Delete` for
  the old ID.
- **Make Delete tolerant.** It also runs during rollbacks, sometimes for something that was never created. A missing
  resource is a success. A Delete that fails leaves the resource in `DELETE_FAILED`.
- **Keep the response under 4 KB.** That limit covers the whole body, including `Data`.

| Event field | Contains |
|---|---|
| `RequestType` | `Create`, `Update` or `Delete` |
| `ResourceProperties` | The instance's `resourceProperties` |
| `OldResourceProperties` | The previous properties, on `Update` only |
| `PhysicalResourceId` | The ID your function returned last time; absent on `Create` |
| `ResponseURL` | Pre-signed URL for the result |
| `StackId`, `RequestId`, `LogicalResourceId` | Copy them into the result |

## Instances

Each instance is its own resource with its own lifecycle. Changing an instance's `resourceProperties` sends an `Update`
with the old and new properties; removing the instance from the config sends a `Delete`.

```typescript
const apiDns = new CustomResourceInstance({
  definitionName: 'dnsProvider',
  resourceProperties: { name: 'api.example.com', target: '203.0.113.10' }
});

const appDns = new CustomResourceInstance({
  definitionName: 'dnsProvider',
  resourceProperties: { name: 'app.example.com', target: '203.0.113.20' }
});
```

## Use the result elsewhere

Values in `Data` are attributes of the instance. Read them with
[`$CfResourceParam`](/configuration/directives) and the instance's logical ID, which is its name in PascalCase plus
`CustomResource`:

```typescript
environment: { WEBHOOK_ID: $CfResourceParam('ApiWebhookCustomResource', 'webhookId') }
```

`stacktape synth` writes the template to `compiled-template.yaml`, where you can confirm the logical ID.

## Packaging and access

The definition takes the same packaging as a Lambda function: [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle),
[`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) or [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) with a
`handler` in `file:function` format. `runtime` is detected from the entry file unless you set it.

`connectTo` gives the function access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters, for example
`STP_CONFIG_BUCKET_NAME`. For other AWS services, add `iamRoleStatements`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

The function runs only during deploys and deletes, so it costs a few Lambda invocations per deploy.

## Configuration reference

### Custom resource definition


### Definition: `CustomResourceDefinitionProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/custom-resource` with definition name `CustomResourceDefinitionProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `packaging` | yes | `js-bundle \| buildpack \| custom-artifact` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `memory` | no | `number` | - |
| `runtime` | no | `string: "dotnet10" \| "dotnet6" \| "dotnet7" \| "dotnet8" \| "java11" \| "java17" \| "java21" \| "java25" \| "java8" \| "java8.al2" \| "nodejs18.x" \| "nodejs20.x" \| "nodejs22.x" \| "nodejs24.x" \| "provided.al2" \| "provided.al2023" \| "python3.10" \| "python3.11" \| "python3.12" \| "python3.13" \| "python3.14" \| "python3.8" \| "python3.9" \| "ruby3.3" \| "ruby3.4" \| "ruby4.0"` | - |
| `timeout` | no | `number` | `10` |


### Custom resource instance


### Definition: `CustomResourceInstanceProps`

| Property | Required | Type | Default |

| `definitionName` | yes | `string` | - |
| `resourceProperties` | yes | `unknown` | - |

# Deployment scripts

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts.mdx`
Route: `/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts`

A `deployment-script` is a Lambda function that Stacktape runs during a deploy (`after:deploy`) or before a delete
(`before:delete`). Use it for work that must run inside AWS at that moment: database migrations, seed data, search
index mappings, cleanup before a stack is removed. With `connectTo` and `joinDefaultVpc` it can reach databases in the
stack's VPC.

Work that runs on your machine or CI runner, such as builds, belongs in [hooks](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts). Work
longer than 15 minutes needs a [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job). The
[lifecycle guide](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deployment-scripts-and-hooks) compares the options for migrations.

## Basic example

This script runs the database migrations after every deploy:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  DeploymentScript,
  RelationalDatabase,
  RdsEnginePostgres,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  $Secret
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('main-database-password') }
  });

  const migrate = new DeploymentScript({
    trigger: 'after:deploy',
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './scripts/migrate.ts' }),
    connectTo: ['mainDatabase'],
    joinDefaultVpc: true,
    timeout: 300
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, migrate }
  };
});
```


Create the password secret once per region before the first deploy:

```bash
stacktape secret set main-database-password --region eu-west-1
```

`connectTo` injects `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`; `joinDefaultVpc` puts the script in the VPC so it can reach
the database. Set `timeout` explicitly: the default is 10 seconds, and the maximum is 900.

The script must bring its migration code with it. The bundle contains only what `migrate.ts` imports, so a CLI such as
`prisma migrate` or a folder of `.sql` files isn't there unless you add it. This script keeps the migrations as imported
TypeScript and runs each one in a transaction with the `postgres` package, recording what ran:

```typescript
// scripts/migrations.ts
export const migrations = [
  { id: '001_create_users', sql: 'CREATE TABLE users (id uuid PRIMARY KEY, email text NOT NULL UNIQUE)' },
  { id: '002_add_user_name', sql: 'ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN name text' }
];
```

```typescript
// scripts/migrate.ts
import postgres from 'postgres';
import { migrations } from './migrations';

export default async () => {
  const sql = postgres(process.env.STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING!, { ssl: 'require' });
  try {
    await sql`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (id text PRIMARY KEY, applied_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now())`;
    for (const migration of migrations) {
      await sql.begin(async (tx) => {
        const [done] = await tx`SELECT 1 FROM schema_migrations WHERE id = ${migration.id}`;
        if (done) return;
        await tx.unsafe(migration.sql);
        await tx`INSERT INTO schema_migrations (id) VALUES (${migration.id})`;
      });
    }
  } finally {
    await sql.end();
  }
};
```

If a migration fails, its transaction rolls back and the earlier ones stay recorded, so the next run continues where
this one stopped. A migration tool that runs in-process, such as Drizzle's or Knex's migrator, works the same way; add
its migration files to the bundle with `includeFiles` on the packaging.

## When it runs and what a failure does

An `after:deploy` script runs on every deploy, after every other resource in the stack has been created or updated.
By then your new application code is already deployed and serving traffic, so for the length of the migration the new
code runs against the old schema.

If the script fails, the deploy fails:

- By default, the stack stays in `UPDATE_FAILED` with everything that already updated, including the new code. Fix the
  script and deploy again, or run [`stacktape stack recover`](/cli/cf-rollback) to return the stack to its previous
  version.
- With `deploymentConfig.autoRollback: true`, CloudFormation returns the infrastructure and the code to the previous
  version automatically.

Neither undoes what the script already wrote to the database. A rollback only means the old code runs against whatever
schema the script left behind. So:

- Make each migration work with both the old and the new code: add columns and tables, don't rename or drop them.
- Deploy the code that needs the new schema in the next release, after the migration is in.
- Drop old columns in a later release still, once no deployed code reads them.

### before:delete

A `before:delete` script runs at the start of [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete), before any resource is removed. Use it
to export data or unregister webhooks. If it fails, the stack ends in `DELETE_FAILED` with the script's error. Fix the
script, or catch the errors you can live with inside it, and run the delete again.

```typescript
new DeploymentScript({
  trigger: 'before:delete',
  packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './scripts/cleanup.ts' }),
  timeout: 300
})
```

## Run a script manually

```bash
stacktape deployment-script run migrate --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

The command rebuilds the script from your local code, **replaces the code of the deployed script Lambda** with it,
resolves `parameters` from your local config and invokes it. So it runs the code in your working directory, not the
last deployed version, and that code stays deployed afterwards. Changes to `environment`, `connectTo`, memory, timeout
or VPC settings still need a [`deploy`](/cli/deploy). See [`deployment-script run`](/cli/deployment-script-run).

## Packaging

| Type | When to use |
|------|-------------|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle) | JavaScript and TypeScript. Stacktape bundles the entry file and what it imports. |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) | Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET or Rust. |
| [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) | A zip or directory you built yourself, with `handler` in `file:function` format. |

Stacktape picks the Lambda runtime from the file extension unless you set `runtime`. `memory` takes 128 to 10,240 MB
(more memory also means more CPU), and `storage` sets the `/tmp` space from 512 MB (the default) to 10,240 MB.

## Connecting to resources

`connectTo` grants the script access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters as
`STP_<RESOURCE_NAME>_<PARAMETER>` variables, for example `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource provides.

Databases and Redis run in the VPC, so the script also needs `joinDefaultVpc: true`. A Lambda function in the VPC has
no internet access unless the VPC has NAT (see `stackConfig.nat`). If the script must call an outside API too, set up
NAT or split it into two scripts. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add `iamRoleStatements`.

## Environment and parameters

- `environment` sets environment variables. Put secrets here with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives).
- `parameters` is passed to the handler as its event. Don't put secrets in it: the values are stored in the stack
  template.

```typescript
new DeploymentScript({
  trigger: 'after:deploy',
  packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './scripts/seed.ts' }),
  environment: { ADMIN_EMAIL: $Secret('admin-email') },
  parameters: { seedCount: 100 },
  timeout: 60
})
```

```typescript
export default async (event: { seedCount: number }) => {
  console.info(`Seeding ${event.seedCount} rows for ${process.env.ADMIN_EMAIL}`);
};
```

Script logs are in CloudWatch like any function's. A deployment script runs on Lambda pricing; a 10-second migration at
512 MB costs a fraction of a cent.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `DeploymentScriptProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/deployment-script` with definition name `DeploymentScriptProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `packaging` | yes | `js-bundle \| buildpack \| custom-artifact` | - |
| `trigger` | yes | `string: "after:deploy" \| "before:delete"` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `joinDefaultVpc` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `memory` | no | `number` | - |
| `parameters` | no | `unknown` | - |
| `runtime` | no | `string: "dotnet10" \| "dotnet6" \| "dotnet7" \| "dotnet8" \| "java11" \| "java17" \| "java21" \| "java25" \| "java8" \| "java8.al2" \| "nodejs18.x" \| "nodejs20.x" \| "nodejs22.x" \| "nodejs24.x" \| "provided.al2" \| "provided.al2023" \| "python3.10" \| "python3.11" \| "python3.12" \| "python3.13" \| "python3.14" \| "python3.8" \| "python3.9" \| "ruby3.3" \| "ruby3.4" \| "ruby4.0"` | - |
| `storage` | no | `number` | `512` |
| `timeout` | no | `number` | `10` |


## Next steps

- [Deployment scripts and hooks](/deployment-and-lifecycle/deployment-scripts-and-hooks): pick where a deploy step runs.
- [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database): the database a migration script connects to.

# Raw CloudFormation resources

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources.mdx`
Route: `/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources`

`cloudformationResources` adds plain CloudFormation resources to your stack's template. Use it for an AWS service
that has no Stacktape resource, such as a CloudWatch dashboard, a Cognito identity pool or a Glue job. Stacktape
merges them into the template as written and deploys them with the rest of the stack.

Check the [resource catalog](/resources/) first: a Stacktape resource gives you `connectTo`, alarms, dev mode and the
Console views, which raw resources don't get. To change one property of a resource Stacktape already creates, use
[overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches). For several related resources with sensible defaults, an
[AWS CDK construct](/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs) saves you writing every property.

## Basic example

`cloudformationResources` sits next to `resources`. Each key is the resource's logical ID in the template, and each
value is ordinary CloudFormation with a `Type` and usually `Properties`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging, $CfResourceParam } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    environment: {
      FEATURE_FLAGS_PARAM: $CfResourceParam('FeatureFlags', 'Name')
    },
    iamRoleStatements: [
      {
        Effect: 'Allow',
        Action: ['ssm:GetParameter'],
        Resource: ['arn:aws:ssm:*:*:parameter/my-app/feature-flags']
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { api },
    cloudformationResources: {
      FeatureFlags: {
        Type: 'AWS::SSM::Parameter',
        Properties: {
          Name: '/my-app/feature-flags',
          Type: 'String',
          Value: '{"newCheckout":false}'
        }
      }
    }
  };
});
```


The function reads the parameter's name from `FEATURE_FLAGS_PARAM`. Raw resources don't work with `connectTo`, so the
function gets access through `iamRoleStatements`, which every compute resource accepts.

## Reference resources both ways

- From a Stacktape resource to a raw one: `$CfResourceParam('<logical ID>', '<attribute>')`, where the attribute is one
  that `Fn::GetAtt` returns, or `Ref`.
- From a raw resource to a Stacktape one: `$ResourceParam('<resource name>', '<parameter>')` with a
  [referenceable parameter](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) such as `arn` or `url`.
- Between raw resources: CloudFormation's own `{ Ref: 'LogicalId' }` and `{ 'Fn::GetAtt': ['LogicalId', 'Arn'] }`.

This subscribes an SQS queue from the stack to a raw SNS topic:

```typescript
cloudformationResources: {
  DeployAlerts: {
    Type: 'AWS::SNS::Topic'
  },
  DeployAlertsToQueue: {
    Type: 'AWS::SNS::Subscription',
    Properties: {
      TopicArn: { Ref: 'DeployAlerts' },
      Protocol: 'sqs',
      Endpoint: $ResourceParam('alertQueue', 'arn')
    }
  }
}
```

The queue also needs a policy that lets SNS send to it; the [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) page shows one.

In TypeScript, intrinsic functions are objects: `{ Ref: 'Id' }`, `{ 'Fn::GetAtt': ['Id', 'Arn'] }`,
`{ 'Fn::Sub': '…' }`, `{ 'Fn::Join': [',', […]] }`.

## Resource attributes

`DependsOn`, `DeletionPolicy`, `UpdateReplacePolicy`, `CreationPolicy`, `UpdatePolicy`, `Metadata` and `Condition`
pass through to the template. `DeletionPolicy: 'Retain'` keeps a resource, such as a log group with audit data, when
you delete the stack:

```typescript
cloudformationResources: {
  AuditLogGroup: {
    Type: 'AWS::Logs::LogGroup',
    DeletionPolicy: 'Retain',
    Properties: { LogGroupName: '/my-app/audit', RetentionInDays: 365 }
  }
}
```

Without it, deleting the stack deletes every raw resource with it.

## Check the template before you deploy

A logical ID that matches one Stacktape generates breaks the deploy. Give your keys a distinct prefix and look at the
final template:

```bash
stacktape synth --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

`synth` writes the template to `compiled-template.yaml` without deploying. Search its `Resources` for your keys and for
the logical IDs of Stacktape's resources. Stacktape's own logical IDs are internal and can change between versions, so
reference Stacktape resources with `$ResourceParam` instead of their logical IDs.

## Limits

A CloudFormation template holds at most 500 resources, raw ones included, and AWS doesn't raise this limit. One
Stacktape resource creates several CloudFormation resources, so a large stack reaches it sooner than the number of
entries in your config suggests. Stacktape warns from 470 resources and stops the deploy above 500. Error tracking
adds one log subscription per function and container; `deploymentConfig.errorTracking.enabled: false` frees them.
Beyond that, split the stack into several stacks.

CloudFormation itself is free. You pay for the AWS resources you add.

## Next steps

- [Overrides and escape hatches](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches): change resources Stacktape creates.
- [AWS CDK constructs](/resources/advanced/aws-cdk-constructs): higher-level building blocks for unsupported services.
- [Directives](/configuration/directives): `$ResourceParam`, `$CfResourceParam` and the others.

# AgentCore Browser

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/ai/agentcore-browser.mdx`
Route: `/resources/ai/agentcore-browser`

An `agentcore-browser` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser: a managed, isolated web browser your agent can drive to
read pages, fill in forms and click through sites. Use it with an [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime)
when the agent has to work with real web pages.

If the agent only calls APIs, it doesn't need a browser: call them from the agent's code, or expose them through an
[AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AgentCoreBrowser, AgentCoreRuntime, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const browser = new AgentCoreBrowser({});

  const researchAgent = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts' }),
    useBrowser: 'browser'
  });

  return {
    resources: { browser, researchAgent }
  };
});
```


`useBrowser` gives the runtime access to the browser and injects its ID as `STP_AGENTCORE_BROWSER_ID`. The agent starts a
browser session with that ID through the AgentCore SDK and drives it, for example with Playwright over the session's
automation endpoint:

```typescript
const browserId = process.env.STP_AGENTCORE_BROWSER_ID!;
```

The browser runs in AgentCore's public network mode, so it can open any site on the internet.

## Record sessions

`recording` saves browser sessions to an S3 bucket so you can replay what the agent did:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AgentCoreBrowser, Bucket, $ResourceParam } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const recordings = new Bucket({});

  const browser = new AgentCoreBrowser({
    recording: {
      enabled: true,
      bucketName: $ResourceParam('recordings', 'name'),
      prefix: 'sessions/'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { recordings, browser }
  };
});
```


Stacktape lets the browser write to that bucket and prefix. Recordings can contain whatever the agent saw, including
personal data, so set access and a lifecycle rule on the bucket to match your retention rules. For a bucket outside the
stack, pass its name as a string.

## Cost

AgentCore bills browser sessions per second for the CPU and memory they use. Recordings add S3 storage. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AgentCoreBrowserProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/agentcore` with definition name `AgentCoreBrowserProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | no | `string` | - |
| `recording` | no | `unknown` | - |
| `tags` | no | `Array<CloudformationTag>` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `id` | Browser ID |
| `arn` | Browser ARN |

## Next steps

- [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime): the agent that drives the browser.
- [AgentCore Code Interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter): let the agent run code instead.
