# AgentCore Code Interpreter

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter.mdx`
Route: `/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter`

An `agentcore-code-interpreter` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Code Interpreter: a managed sandbox where your agent runs
code it writes, for example to analyze a CSV file, do exact calculations or draw a chart. Use it with an
[AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).

An agent that only calls APIs or queries your databases doesn't need it; give the runtime access with `connectTo`
instead. Long-running jobs belong in a [batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AgentCoreCodeInterpreter, AgentCoreRuntime, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const codeInterpreter = new AgentCoreCodeInterpreter({});

  const analyst = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts' }),
    useCodeInterpreter: 'codeInterpreter'
  });

  return {
    resources: { codeInterpreter, analyst }
  };
});
```


`useCodeInterpreter` gives the runtime access to the interpreter and injects its ID as
`STP_AGENTCORE_CODE_INTERPRETER_ID`. The agent starts an interpreter session with that ID through the AgentCore SDK
and sends it code to run:

```typescript
const codeInterpreterId = process.env.STP_AGENTCORE_CODE_INTERPRETER_ID!;
```

The interpreter runs Python, JavaScript and TypeScript. The
[AgentCore documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/) lists the preinstalled
libraries and session limits.

## Network and permissions

The sandbox runs in AgentCore's public network mode, so the code it runs can reach the internet. Its role allows every
`bedrock:*` and `bedrock-agentcore:*` action on all resources. Code that a model generates from user input runs with
those permissions, so treat what users can make the agent run as untrusted.

## Cost

AgentCore bills interpreter sessions per second for the CPU and memory they use. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AgentCoreCodeInterpreterProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/agentcore` with definition name `AgentCoreCodeInterpreterProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | no | `string` | - |
| `tags` | no | `Array<CloudformationTag>` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `id` | Code interpreter ID |
| `arn` | Code interpreter ARN |

## Next steps

- [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime): the agent that sends the code.
- [AgentCore Browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser): let the agent use web pages.

# AgentCore Gateway

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway.mdx`
Route: `/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway`

An `agentcore-gateway` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway: one MCP endpoint that exposes your Lambda functions as
tools an agent can discover and call. Each tool declares its operations with a JSON schema, and the gateway invokes the
function behind it. Use it when an agent needs several tools, or when other MCP clients should use the same tools.

For one or two functions, an agent can invoke them directly with `connectTo` and skip the gateway. Tools behind a gateway
must be Lambda functions.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  AgentCoreGateway,
  AgentCoreRuntime,
  LambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  JsBundleImagePackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderLookup = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/order-lookup.ts' })
  });

  const tools = new AgentCoreGateway({
    authorizer: {
      type: 'jwt',
      properties: {
        discoveryUrl:
          'https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_ABC123/.well-known/openid-configuration',
        allowedAudience: ['my-app-client-id']
      }
    },
    tools: [
      {
        name: 'orders',
        function: 'orderLookup',
        toolSchema: [
          {
            name: 'lookupOrder',
            description: 'Find an order by its ID',
            inputSchema: {
              type: 'object',
              properties: { orderId: { type: 'string', description: 'The order ID' } },
              required: ['orderId']
            }
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  });

  const agent = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts' }),
    useGateway: 'tools'
  });

  return {
    resources: { orderLookup, tools, agent }
  };
});
```


`function` names a Lambda function in the stack; for a function elsewhere, use `lambdaArn`. Stacktape lets the gateway
invoke it. `useGateway` injects the gateway's MCP endpoint into the runtime as `STP_AGENTCORE_GATEWAY_URL`; connect an MCP
client to that URL.

## Write a tool function

The gateway invokes the function with the tool's arguments as the event. Which operation was called is in the Lambda
client context under `custom.bedrockAgentCoreToolName`, as `<target>___<operation>`; take the part after the last
`___`. The [AgentCore developer guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/) describes the
Lambda target format.

```typescript
import type { Context } from 'aws-lambda';

export default async (event: { orderId: string }, context: Context) => {
  const custom = (context.clientContext as { custom?: Record<string, string> } | undefined)?.custom;
  const operation = (custom?.bedrockAgentCoreToolName ?? '').split('___').pop();
  if (operation === 'lookupOrder') {
    return { orderId: event.orderId, status: 'shipped' };
  }
  throw new Error(`Unknown operation ${operation}`);
};
```

A tool can list several operations in `toolSchema`, all served by the same function. Each operation needs a `name` and
an `inputSchema`; `description` and `outputSchema` are optional. Keep schemas to plain JSON Schema (`type`,
`properties`, `required`, `items`, `description`). Stacktape passes them to AWS, which rejects what it doesn't support.

## Authorization

`authorizer` is required, because the gateway exposes every tool it lists:

- `type: 'jwt'` accepts only callers with a valid token from your identity provider. `discoveryUrl` points to the
  provider's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`; `allowedAudience`, `allowedClients` and `allowedScopes` narrow it
  down. For a [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool), the URL is
  `https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<user pool ID>/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
- `type: 'none'` lets anyone who reaches the endpoint call the tools. Use it only for tools that are safe in public.

With `jwt`, the agent must send a token with each request; `useGateway` doesn't give it one.

## Other settings

- `instructions` tells agents in plain language what the gateway is for and when to use which tool.
- `searchType: 'SEMANTIC'` lets agents search the tools by meaning, useful with many tools.
- `supportedVersions` limits the MCP protocol versions the gateway accepts.
- `exceptionLevel: 'DEBUG'` returns detailed errors. Turn it off in production, where the details can expose internals.

## Cost

AWS bills the gateway per tool call and per search, and the Lambda functions as usual. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AgentCoreGatewayProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/agentcore` with definition name `AgentCoreGatewayProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `authorizer` | yes | `jwt \| none` | - |
| `description` | no | `string` | - |
| `exceptionLevel` | no | `string = "DEBUG"` | - |
| `instructions` | no | `string` | - |
| `searchType` | no | `string = "SEMANTIC"` | - |
| `supportedVersions` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `tags` | no | `Array<CloudformationTag>` | - |
| `tools` | no | `Array<AgentCoreGatewayTool>` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| `id` | Gateway ID |
| `arn` | Gateway ARN |
| `url` | MCP endpoint URL |

## Next steps

- [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime): the agent that calls the tools.
- [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function): memory, timeout and logs of the tool functions.
- [User auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool): issue the tokens the JWT authorizer checks.

---

# AgentCore Memory

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/ai/agentcore-memory.mdx`
Route: `/resources/ai/agentcore-memory`

An `agentcore-memory` is an Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory store. An agent saves conversation events to it and recalls
them later, also in a new session: what a user asked last week, their preferences, facts the agent extracted. Use it
with an [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime).

For your application's own data, use a [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) or a
[relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database). An agent that only needs context within one session
doesn't need a memory resource.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AgentCoreMemory, AgentCoreRuntime, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const agentMemory = new AgentCoreMemory({});

  const agent = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts' }),
    useMemory: 'agentMemory'
  });

  return {
    resources: { agentMemory, agent }
  };
});
```


`useMemory` gives the runtime access to the memory and injects its ID as `STP_AGENTCORE_MEMORY_ID`. Pass it to the
AgentCore SDK when you save and read events:

```typescript
const memoryId = process.env.STP_AGENTCORE_MEMORY_ID!;
```

Another workload, such as a Lambda function, can use the memory through its `id` or `arn`
[parameter](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) with `$ResourceParam()`, plus `iamRoleStatements` for the
`bedrock-agentcore` actions it calls.

## Retention

`eventRetentionDays` sets how long AgentCore keeps raw events before deleting them: 30 days by default, 7 to 365 days
allowed. Keep it short for passing conversational context; make it longer for agents that build up knowledge about a
user over months.

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({ eventRetentionDays: 90 })
```

## Memory strategies

Without strategies, the memory stores raw events only. A strategy makes AgentCore extract long-term records from them,
for example facts, summaries or user preferences. `memoryStrategies` is passed to AWS as written, in the CloudFormation
[`MemoryStrategies`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/TemplateReference/aws-resource-bedrockagentcore-memory.html)
format:

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({
  memoryStrategies: [
    { SemanticMemoryStrategy: { Name: 'facts', Namespaces: ['/users/{actorId}/facts'] } },
    { UserPreferenceMemoryStrategy: { Name: 'preferences', Namespaces: ['/users/{actorId}/preferences'] } }
  ]
})
```

Stacktape doesn't check the shape; AWS rejects an invalid strategy during the deploy.

## Encryption

AgentCore encrypts the memory at rest. To use your own KMS key, set `encryptionKeyArn`:

```typescript
new AgentCoreMemory({ encryptionKeyArn: 'arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/your-key-id' })
```

## Cost

AgentCore Memory bills for events stored and for long-term records extracted and read. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AgentCoreMemoryProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/agentcore` with definition name `AgentCoreMemoryProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `description` | no | `string` | - |
| `encryptionKeyArn` | no | `string` | - |
| `eventRetentionDays` | no | `number` | `30` |
| `memoryStrategies` | no | `Array<unknown>` | - |
| `tags` | no | `Array<CloudformationTag>` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| `id` | Memory ID |
| `arn` | Memory ARN |

## Next steps

- [AgentCore Runtime](/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime): the agent that uses the memory.
- [AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway): give the agent tools.

# AgentCore Runtime

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime.mdx`
Route: `/resources/ai/agentcore-runtime`

An `agentcore-runtime` runs your AI agent as a container on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime. AWS starts an isolated
session per conversation, scales them and bills for the CPU and memory a session uses. Stacktape builds the image,
creates the runtime and its endpoints, and connects the agent to AgentCore [memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory), a
[gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway), a [browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser) and a
[code interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter).

For a service that calls a model and returns the answer, a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service) is simpler.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AgentCoreRuntime, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const agent = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
      entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts'
    }),
    protocol: 'HTTP'
  });

  return {
    resources: { agent }
  };
});
```


With the `HTTP` protocol, AgentCore expects the container to listen on `0.0.0.0:8080` and answer two routes:

- `POST /invocations` with the request payload. Return JSON, or stream with server-sent events.
- `GET /ping`, the health check. Return `{"status":"Healthy"}`.

```typescript
// agent/server.ts
import { createServer } from 'node:http';

createServer(async (req, res) => {
  if (req.method === 'GET' && req.url === '/ping') {
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }).end(JSON.stringify({ status: 'Healthy' }));
    return;
  }
  if (req.method === 'POST' && req.url === '/invocations') {
    let body = '';
    for await (const chunk of req) body += chunk;
    const { prompt } = JSON.parse(body || '{}');
    // Call your model here.
    res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }).end(JSON.stringify({ answer: `You asked: ${prompt}` }));
    return;
  }
  res.writeHead(404).end();
}).listen(8080, '0.0.0.0');
```

AgentCore runs `linux/arm64` images. Stacktape builds the image for arm64; a `prebuilt-image` must be arm64 too. The
[AWS HTTP contract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-http-protocol-contract.html)
has the details, including WebSocket support.

After `stacktape deploy`, get the runtime ARN and invoke it. The session ID groups requests of one conversation and must
be at least 33 characters:

```bash
stacktape param get agent arn --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

```bash
aws bedrock-agentcore invoke-agent-runtime --region eu-west-1 \
  --agent-runtime-arn <runtime-arn> --qualifier default \
  --runtime-session-id "session-$(uuidgen)" \
  --payload '{"prompt":"Hello"}' --cli-binary-format raw-in-base64-out response.json
```

`response.json` then holds the agent's answer.

## Protocols

| `protocol` | Use when the container |
|----------|-------------|
| `HTTP` (default) | Serves `/invocations` and `/ping` as above |
| `MCP` | Is an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server |
| `A2A` | Speaks the Agent-to-Agent protocol |
| `AGUI` | Implements the AG-UI protocol |

Each protocol has its own port and paths, described in the
[AgentCore developer guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/).

## Tools: memory, gateway, browser and code interpreter

Each tool is its own resource. Attach it by name, and Stacktape grants the runtime access and injects its identifier:

| Property | Resource | Injected variable |
|----------|----------|-------------------|
| `useMemory` | [AgentCore Memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory) | `STP_AGENTCORE_MEMORY_ID` |
| `useGateway` | [AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway) | `STP_AGENTCORE_GATEWAY_URL` |
| `useBrowser` | [AgentCore Browser](/resources/ai/agentcore-browser) | `STP_AGENTCORE_BROWSER_ID` |
| `useCodeInterpreter` | [AgentCore Code Interpreter](/resources/ai/agentcore-code-interpreter) | `STP_AGENTCORE_CODE_INTERPRETER_ID` |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  AgentCoreRuntime,
  AgentCoreMemory,
  AgentCoreBrowser,
  JsBundleImagePackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const agentMemory = new AgentCoreMemory({});
  const browser = new AgentCoreBrowser({});

  const agent = new AgentCoreRuntime({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './agent/server.ts' }),
    protocol: 'HTTP',
    useMemory: 'agentMemory',
    useBrowser: 'browser'
  });

  return {
    resources: { agentMemory, browser, agent }
  };
});
```


The agent reads `process.env.STP_AGENTCORE_MEMORY_ID` and `process.env.STP_AGENTCORE_BROWSER_ID` and passes them to the
AgentCore SDK. Attach only what the agent uses: a browser or code interpreter adds its own sessions and charges.

## Endpoints

An endpoint is the address callers use, passed as `--qualifier` when invoking. Without `endpoints`, Stacktape creates one
named `default`. List names, or objects with a `description` and a pinned `runtimeVersion`:

```typescript
endpoints: ['default', { name: 'beta', description: 'Preview of the next version' }]
```

The `endpointName` and `endpointArn` parameters point to the endpoint named `default`, or to the first one if none has
that name.

## Sessions and lifecycle

AWS keeps a session alive between requests with the same session ID. `lifecycle` limits how long:

- `idleTimeoutSeconds` ends a session after it has been idle this long. AWS's default is 15 minutes.
- `maxLifetimeSeconds` ends a session after this long even while it's active. AWS's default is 8 hours.

```typescript
lifecycle: { idleTimeoutSeconds: 300, maxLifetimeSeconds: 7200 }
```

A shorter idle timeout lowers cost for agents that answer quickly. Keep it longer when users pause mid-conversation and
the agent holds state in memory.

## Authentication

Without an `authorizer`, callers sign requests with AWS credentials that are allowed to invoke the runtime. To let users
call it with tokens from your identity provider, set a JWT authorizer:

```typescript
authorizer: {
  discoveryUrl: 'https://cognito-idp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/us-east-1_abc123/.well-known/openid-configuration',
  allowedAudience: ['my-app-client-id'],
  allowedClients: ['trusted-client'],
  allowedScopes: ['agent:invoke']
}
```

`discoveryUrl` is required; the other three are optional filters on the token's claims.

## Access to other resources

The runtime's role allows every `bedrock:*`, `bedrock-agentcore:*` and `bedrock-agentcore-control:*` action on all
resources, so the agent can call Bedrock models and AgentCore tools without extra permissions. Keep that in mind when
you review what the agent's code is allowed to do.

`connectTo` gives the agent access to resources in the stack and injects their parameters, for example
`STP_CONVERSATIONS_NAME` for a DynamoDB table named `conversations`. For other AWS services, add `iamRoleStatements`.

`environment` passes other settings; put secrets there with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives).
`requestHeaders` lists request headers, such as `X-Tenant-Id`, that AgentCore forwards to the container.

## Packaging

AgentCore Runtime takes the [container packaging](/packaging/overview) types: `js-bundle` (`JsBundleImagePackaging`) for
one TypeScript or JavaScript entry file, `buildpack` for Python and other languages without a Dockerfile, `dockerfile`
for full control, and `prebuilt-image` for an existing arm64 image.

## Cost

AgentCore Runtime bills per second for the CPU and memory a session actually uses, and doesn't charge CPU while the agent
waits for a model or a tool. Model calls, memory, gateway and browser are billed separately. See
[AgentCore pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/agentcore/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AgentCoreRuntimeProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/agentcore` with definition name `AgentCoreRuntimeProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `packaging` | yes | `js-bundle \| prebuilt-image \| dockerfile \| buildpack` | - |
| `authorizer` | no | `AgentCoreJwtAuthorizerConfig` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `description` | no | `string` | - |
| `endpoints` | no | `Array<AgentCoreRuntimeEndpoint \| option-2>` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `lifecycle` | no | `AgentCoreRuntimeLifecycleConfig` | - |
| `protocol` | no | `string: "A2A" \| "AGUI" \| "HTTP" \| "MCP"` | - |
| `requestHeaders` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `tags` | no | `Array<CloudformationTag>` | - |
| `useBrowser` | no | `string` | - |
| `useCodeInterpreter` | no | `string` | - |
| `useGateway` | no | `string` | - |
| `useMemory` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| `id` | Runtime ID |
| `arn` | Runtime ARN, used to invoke it |
| `endpointName` | Name of the referenced endpoint |
| `endpointArn` | ARN of the referenced endpoint |

## Next steps

- [AgentCore Memory](/resources/ai/agentcore-memory): keep context across sessions.
- [AgentCore Gateway](/resources/ai/agentcore-gateway): give the agent tools behind one MCP endpoint.
- [Secrets](/configuration/secrets): store model provider keys.

# Batch job

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/compute/batch-job.mdx`
Route: `/resources/compute/batch-job`

A batch job runs a container until it finishes: a nightly export, a video transcode, an import, a model training run.
A trigger starts it (a schedule, an HTTP request, a file upload, a queue message and others), and you declare the CPU,
memory and optional GPU it needs. It runs on AWS Batch, which starts EC2 instances for queued jobs and stops them when
the queue is empty.

You pay for the EC2 instances while jobs run, including their start-up time, and nothing between jobs. Spot capacity
costs up to 90% less if the job can be interrupted. For work under 15 minutes, a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) starts faster; for a process that never ends, use a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service).

## Basic example

A TypeScript job that runs every night at 02:00 UTC:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, BatchJob, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const nightlyReport = new BatchJob({
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/nightly-report.ts'
      }),
      environment: { REPORT_BUCKET_PREFIX: 'reports/nightly' }
    },
    resources: {
      cpu: 2,
      memory: 4096
    },
    timeout: 3600,
    events: [
      {
        type: 'schedule',
        properties: {
          scheduleRate: 'cron(0 2 * * ? *)'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { nightlyReport } };
});
```


`js-bundle` builds the image from `./src/jobs/nightly-report.ts`, `resources` asks for 2 vCPU and 4096 MB, and
`timeout` stops a run after one hour. Schedules use AWS cron or `rate(2 hours)` syntax in UTC; see
[Schedule triggers](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers). Each run's output appears in
`stacktape logs nightlyReport --stage dev`.

## Compute resources

`cpu` is a whole number of vCPUs and `memory` is in MB; AWS Batch picks instances that fit. Request a little less than a
power of two, for example `7680` instead of `8192` MB, because the instance keeps some memory for itself. Add `gpu` only
for GPU work such as training or rendering.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, BatchJob, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const trainingJob = new BatchJob({
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/train-model.ts'
      })
    },
    resources: {
      cpu: 8,
      memory: 30720,
      gpu: 1
    }
  });

  return { resources: { trainingJob } };
});
```


Jobs run on x86 instances with the Amazon ECS-optimized Amazon Linux 2023 image; GPU jobs use its NVIDIA variant on
`p4d` and `g5` instances. The instances require IMDSv2 and use cgroup v2, so software in your image that reads instance
metadata with IMDSv1, or memory limits only from cgroup v1 (such as Java before 8u372), needs a current version.

## Packaging

A batch job supports four container image packaging types. Start with `js-bundle` for JavaScript or TypeScript and `buildpack` for other languages, then switch only when the image needs precise runtime control.

| Type | When to use |
|------|-------------|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/containers/js-bundle) | A JavaScript or TypeScript job with one entry file. Stacktape bundles it into a small image. |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/containers/buildpack) | Build from source without a Dockerfile. Detects Python, Go, Rust, Java, PHP, Ruby, .NET, Node.js and more. |
| [`dockerfile`](/packaging/containers/dockerfile) | Control the Dockerfile, build context, build args and startup command |
| [`prebuilt-image`](/packaging/containers/prebuilt-image) | Run an image that already exists in a registry and optionally override its command |

Put the job's settings in `container.environment`, secrets in [`$Secret()`](/configuration/secrets).

## Triggers

Pick the trigger by where the work comes from. Sources that retry delivery can start the same job twice, so make the
job safe to repeat.

| Trigger type | Use it for |
|--------------|------------|
| `schedule` | Recurring jobs such as reports, cleanup, imports, and periodic syncs |
| `s3` | Object-created, object-removed, restore, or replication events from a bucket |
| `sqs` | Queue-backed jobs where each message or batch represents work to process |
| `sns` | Pub/sub fanout where a topic delivery should start the job |
| `kinesis-stream` | Stream records processed in batches |
| `dynamo-db-stream` | Table change records after DynamoDB streams are enabled |
| `http-api-gateway` | HTTP request starts a job through an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) |
| `application-load-balancer` | HTTP request starts a job through an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) rule |
| `cloudwatch-log` | Matching CloudWatch log records start the job |
| `event-bus` | EventBridge events matching a pattern start the job |

The [configuration reference](#configuration-reference) has each trigger's options, and the
[triggers overview](/resources/triggers/overview) compares them.

### Reading trigger data

The job is a process, not a handler: it gets the trigger event as JSON in `STP_TRIGGER_EVENT_DATA`, and the attempt
number in `STP_CURRENT_ATTEMPT` and `STP_MAXIMUM_ATTEMPTS`.

```typescript
const event = JSON.parse(process.env.STP_TRIGGER_EVENT_DATA ?? '{}');
const attempt = Number(process.env.STP_CURRENT_ATTEMPT ?? '1');
const maximumAttempts = Number(process.env.STP_MAXIMUM_ATTEMPTS ?? '1');
await processJob(event, { attempt, maximumAttempts });
```

## Retries and timeout

`timeout` (in seconds) stops a job that runs too long. `retryConfig` runs failed or timed-out jobs again.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, BatchJob, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const importJob = new BatchJob({
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/import-catalog.ts'
      })
    },
    resources: { cpu: 2, memory: 4096 },
    timeout: 7200,
    retryConfig: {
      attempts: 3,
      retryIntervalSeconds: 30,
      retryIntervalMultiplier: 2
    }
  });

  return { resources: { importJob } };
});
```


`attempts` counts the first run and defaults to 1. The wait before each retry is `retryIntervalSeconds` × the number of
failed attempts × `retryIntervalMultiplier`: with 3 attempts, interval 30 and multiplier 2, the job waits 60 seconds
before attempt 2 and 120 seconds before attempt 3.


> **Warning:** A retry runs the whole job again. Make writes, imports and notifications safe to repeat before you allow more
than one attempt.


## Spot capacity

`useSpotInstances: true` runs jobs on spare EC2 capacity for up to 90% less. AWS can take the instance back: the
container gets `SIGTERM` and 120 seconds to stop. Use Spot for restartable imports, image processing or training with
checkpoints, together with `retryConfig`, and keep on-demand capacity for deadlines and work that can't be repeated.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, BatchJob, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const thumbnailJob = new BatchJob({
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/thumbnails.ts'
      })
    },
    resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 },
    useSpotInstances: true,
    retryConfig: {
      attempts: 5,
      retryIntervalSeconds: 60
    }
  });

  return { resources: { thumbnailJob } };
});
```


## Connecting to resources

`connectTo` grants IAM permissions, opens the network path to databases and Redis, and injects
`STP_<RESOURCE>_<PARAM>` variables into the job.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  BatchJob,
  Bucket,
  RelationalDatabase,
  RdsEnginePostgres,
  $Secret,
  JsBundleImagePackaging
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const reports = new Bucket({});
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('database', 'password') }
  });

  const exportJob = new BatchJob({
    connectTo: [mainDatabase, reports],
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/export.ts'
      })
    },
    resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
  });

  return { resources: { reports, mainDatabase, exportJob } };
});
```


This job gets `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`, `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_HOST`, `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_PORT` and the other
database variables, plus `STP_REPORTS_NAME` and `STP_REPORTS_ARN`. For other AWS permissions, use `iamRoleStatements`.

## Logging

The job's output goes to CloudWatch Logs, kept for 90 days by default (`logging.retentionDays`). Log the input ID and
attempt number so you can follow one run across retries.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, BatchJob, JsBundleImagePackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const cleanupJob = new BatchJob({
    container: {
      packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({
        entryfilePath: './src/jobs/cleanup.ts'
      })
    },
    resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 },
    logging: {
      retentionDays: 30
    }
  });

  return { resources: { cleanupJob } };
});
```


## Dev mode

Batch jobs always run in AWS Batch, also in [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview): dev mode builds and
pushes their images at startup, so restart it after changing job code. `--resources` and `--skip-resources` don't apply
to them; use a dev-specific config to leave a job or its triggers out. A job reaches local databases through the
[dev network](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#the-dev-network), with its AWS costs and network round
trip.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `BatchJobProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/batch-job` with definition name `BatchJobProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `container` | yes | `BatchJobContainer` | - |
| `resources` | yes | `BatchJobResources` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `events` | no | `Array<application-load-balancer \| sns \| sqs \| kinesis-stream \| dynamo-db-stream \| s3 \| schedule \| cloudwatch-log \| http-api-gateway \| event-bus>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `logging` | no | `BatchJobLogging` | - |
| `retryConfig` | no | `BatchJobRetryConfiguration` | - |
| `timeout` | no | `number` | - |
| `useSpotInstances` | no | `boolean` | `false` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `batch-job`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jobDefinitionArn` | Arn of the job definition resource | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "jobDefinitionArn")` |
| `stateMachineArn` | Arn of the state machine controlling the execution flow of the batch job | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "stateMachineArn")` |
| `logGroupArn` | Arn of the log group aggregating logs from the batch job | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "logGroupArn")` |

# Convex

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/compute/convex.mdx`
Route: `/resources/compute/convex`

The Convex resource runs a self-hosted [Convex](https://www.convex.dev) backend in your AWS account: the Convex server
on ECS, a PostgreSQL database on RDS, five S3 buckets for its storage, an Application Load Balancer for HTTPS and
WebSocket traffic, and the admin dashboard. After each deploy, Stacktape pushes your Convex functions to it.

It runs all the time. With the defaults, an idle deployment costs about $60 a month in us-east-1:

| Part | Default size | Per month |
|---|---|---|
| Backend | 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB on Fargate | about $18 |
| Dashboard | 0.25 vCPU, 0.5 GB on Fargate | about $9 |
| Database | `db.t4g.micro`, 20 GB | about $14 |
| Load balancer | Application Load Balancer | about $16 plus traffic |

Each container and the load balancer also pay $3.65 a month per public IPv4 address. Prices are x86 Fargate, RDS and
ELB on-demand rates for 730 hours ([Fargate pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing/)).

Use it when your data must stay in your AWS account or you want Convex next to the rest of your stack. Otherwise
Convex's own cloud is cheaper to start with and runs the backend for you.

## Basic example

`appDirectory` points to your `convex/` directory, the one with `schema.ts` and your functions. It's the only required
property.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 0.5,
        memory: 1024
      }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 0.25,
        memory: 512
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


The deploy creates everything listed above, then runs `npx convex deploy` against `appDirectory` to push your functions.
Stacktape generates the admin key, stores it in AWS Secrets Manager and passes it to that command.

Without custom domains, the backend is served on a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain, on ports 3210 (client API), 3211
(HTTP actions) and 6791 (dashboard). That domain comes from the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console).
Without the Console connected, set [custom domains](#custom-domains) for all three origins, or the deploy stops and
asks for them.

## Custom domains

Convex serves three origins:

| Origin | Serves | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `cloud` | The API and WebSocket endpoint that `convex-js` clients connect to | `api.myapp.com` |
| `site` | Your `httpAction()` routes, such as webhooks and OAuth callbacks | `webhooks.myapp.com` |
| `dashboard` | The admin dashboard | `convex-admin.myapp.com` |

With `customDomains`, `cloud` and `site` are required, and `dashboard` is required while the dashboard is enabled.
[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add` before the
first deploy, so that issued certificates exist for these names.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 2,
        memory: 4096
      }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 0.25,
        memory: 512
      },
      allowedIpRanges: ['203.0.113.0/24']
    },
    customDomains: {
      cloud: { domainName: 'api.myapp.com' },
      site: { domainName: 'webhooks.myapp.com' },
      dashboard: { domainName: 'convex-admin.myapp.com' }
    },
    deletionProtection: true,
    storage: {
      versioning: true
    },
    database: {
      automatedBackupRetentionDays: 7
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


This production setup also turns on deletion protection, keeps old versions of stored files and allows the dashboard
only from one address range.

## Passing the Convex URL to other workloads

`$ResourceParam('myConvex', 'url')` is the `cloud` origin. Pass it to a frontend or another workload as an
environment variable for the `convex-js` client:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 1,
        memory: 2048
      }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 0.25,
        memory: 512
      }
    }
  });

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    }),
    environment: {
      CONVEX_URL: "$ResourceParam('myConvex', 'url')"
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex, api }
  };
});
```


## Functions deployment

After the infrastructure is up, Stacktape runs `npx convex deploy --codegen disable --typecheck try` in the parent
directory of `appDirectory`, with `CONVEX_SELF_HOSTED_URL` and `CONVEX_SELF_HOSTED_ADMIN_KEY` set. `functionsDeployment`
changes the command (for example to use `pnpm`), the directory (`workingDirectory`), or turns the step off
(`enabled: false`) when your CI deploys functions itself.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 }
    },
    functionsDeployment: {
      command: 'pnpm convex deploy --codegen disable'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


## Backend

The backend container runs the Convex server. All queries, mutations, actions and subscriptions go through it. Read
its logs with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs).

The open-source backend runs as a single process: two backends on one database would corrupt it. Stacktape runs
exactly one backend task, so you scale it up, not out. Sizes from Convex's self-hosting guidance:

| Use | CPU | Memory |
|---|---|---|
| Development, a few dozen users | 0.5 vCPU | 1024 MB (default) |
| Production, hundreds of subscribers | 1 vCPU | 2048 MB |
| Heavier production, vector search | 2 vCPU | 4096 MB |
| Upper end of one process | 4 vCPU | 8192 MB |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: {
        cpu: 2,
        memory: 4096
      }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


For EC2 instead of Fargate, set `instanceTypes` (Graviton types such as `c6g.large` cost the least per vCPU).
`enableWarmPool: true` keeps a pre-initialized instance ready for faster replacement and works with one instance type.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: {
        instanceTypes: ['c6g.large'],
        enableWarmPool: true
      }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


`backend.image` overrides the backend image (by default a tested release of `ghcr.io/get-convex/convex-backend`).


> **Warning:** A new backend image can run data migrations. Try an upgrade on a staging stage before production.


## Dashboard

The dashboard is the Convex admin UI: data browser, logs, function runner, environment variables and snapshot
export and import. It runs as its own container (0.25 vCPU and 512 MB by default, about $9 a month).

It has no sign-in of its own; the admin key you paste is the only protection. Restrict it to your office or VPN
addresses with `allowedIpRanges`, especially on production stages:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 },
      allowedIpRanges: ['203.0.113.0/24', '198.51.100.42/32']
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


`dashboard.enabled: false` removes the container and saves its cost. You then manage data and environment variables
with the `npx convex` CLI. `dashboard.image` pins the dashboard image.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
    },
    dashboard: {
      enabled: false
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


## Database

Convex stores its data in a PostgreSQL database that it owns: single-AZ RDS PostgreSQL 16 on `db.t4g.micro` by default,
with 20 GB of storage, one day of backups and access from the backend only. You can't point Convex at an existing
database.

`database.engine` takes the PostgreSQL engines of a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database):
RDS PostgreSQL (default), Aurora Serverless v2 or provisioned Aurora. Convex needs PostgreSQL 13 or later. The
`database` property also takes `automatedBackupRetentionDays` (default 1; raise it for production),
`preferredMaintenanceWindow` and `logging`. Leave `accessibility` as it is: only the backend needs the database.

## Storage

Convex keeps modules, files, search indexes, exports and snapshot imports in five private, encrypted S3 buckets.
`storage` applies to all five: `versioning` keeps old versions of overwritten or deleted objects, and `lifecycleRules`
can expire old exports.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 }
    },
    storage: {
      versioning: true
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


## Deletion protection

`deletionProtection: true` protects the database and the five buckets. A delete then stops until you deploy with
`deletionProtection: false`. It's off by default; turn it on for production stages.

## Backups

The database has daily automated backups (one day by default). For a portable copy of your data, use
`npx convex export`. `storage.versioning` lets you recover overwritten or deleted files.

## Alarms

Convex takes the [alarm](/observability/alarms) triggers of an Application Load Balancer and of a relational database.

## Dev mode

In [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), Convex runs locally in Docker with SQLite and local file
storage. Pushing functions is faster over your own machine, and no AWS resources run for it. Set `dev.remote: true` to
use the deployed backend instead, for example to work with real data; the stage must be deployed first.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Convex } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myConvex = new Convex({
    appDirectory: './convex',
    backend: {
      resources: { cpu: 1, memory: 2048 }
    },
    dashboard: {
      resources: { cpu: 0.25, memory: 512 }
    },
    dev: {
      remote: true
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myConvex }
  };
});
```


## Configuration reference


### Definition: `ConvexProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/convex` with definition name `ConvexProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `appDirectory` | yes | `string` | - |
| `alarms` | no | `Array<ApplicationLoadBalancerAlarm \| RelationalDatabaseAlarm>` | - |
| `backend` | no | `ConvexBackendConfig` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `ConvexCustomDomains` | - |
| `dashboard` | no | `ConvexDashboardConfig` | - |
| `database` | no | `ConvexDatabaseConfig` | - |

## Referenceable parameters

`url` is the `cloud` origin for the `convex-js` client. `adminKey` and `instanceSecret` resolve from AWS Secrets
Manager. Pass them to other workloads through `environment`.


## Referenceable Parameters: `convex`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | Cloud origin (CONVEX_CLOUD_ORIGIN) used by frontend clients. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "url")` |
| `siteUrl` | HTTP-actions origin (CONVEX_SITE_ORIGIN) where httpAction() routes live. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "siteUrl")` |
| `dashboardUrl` | Admin dashboard URL. Only available when the dashboard is enabled. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "dashboardUrl")` |
| `adminKey` | Sensitive root credentials for the deployment, resolved from AWS Secrets Manager. Reference explicitly with $ResourceParam; never auto-injected by connectTo. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "adminKey")` |
| `instanceSecret` | Sensitive boot secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Almost never needed by user code. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "instanceSecret")` |

# Edge function

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/compute/edge-function.mdx`
Route: `/resources/compute/edge-function`

An edge function is a Lambda@Edge function that CloudFront runs on requests and responses of a
[CDN](/resources/networking/cdn), at locations close to your users. Use it for small decisions before or after the
origin: redirects, URL rewrites, security headers, A/B routing or a quick token check.

It can't use environment variables or reach anything in your VPC, and a viewer-side function gets at most 128 MB and
5 seconds. Lambda@Edge costs $0.60 per million requests plus run time, with no free tier
([Lambda@Edge pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing/)). For rules a CDN can express without code, such as
caching or path routing, use the [CDN settings](/resources/networking/cdn); for application logic, a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function).

## Basic example

This edge function adds a security header to every response of a bucket's CDN:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket, EdgeLambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const securityHeaders = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge/security-headers.ts'
    })
  });

  const website = new Bucket({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      edgeFunctions: {
        onResponse: 'securityHeaders'
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { securityHeaders, website }
  };
});
```


The handler gets the CloudFront event and returns the changed response:

```ts
export const handler = async (event: any) => {
  const { response } = event.Records[0].cf;
  response.headers['x-frame-options'] = [{ key: 'X-Frame-Options', value: 'DENY' }];
  return response;
};
```

After the deploy, `curl -I` on the CDN URL of any file in the bucket shows `x-frame-options: DENY`. Stacktape deploys
edge functions to `us-east-1`, as CloudFront requires, whatever your stack's region.

## CDN attachment

A CDN's `edgeFunctions` names the function for one of four hooks: `onRequest` and `onResponse` run between the
viewer and CloudFront; `onOriginRequest` and `onOriginResponse` run between CloudFront and your origin, only on cache
misses. Route rewrites can attach their own functions. See [Edge functions on the CDN](/resources/networking/cdn#edge-functions).

## Runtime limits

`memory` defaults to 128 MB and `timeout` to 3 seconds. Viewer hooks (`onRequest`, `onResponse`) allow at most 128 MB
and 5 seconds; origin hooks allow up to 10,240 MB and 30 seconds. Raise them only for an origin hook that needs it.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EdgeLambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const edgeRewrite = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge-rewrite.ts',
      handlerFunction: 'handler'
    }),
    memory: 128,
    timeout: 3
  });

  return { resources: { edgeRewrite } };
});
```


`runtime` comes from the file extension. Edge functions run Node.js (`nodejs24.x`, `nodejs22.x`, `nodejs20.x`,
`nodejs18.x`) or Python (`python3.13` to `python3.8`).

## Packaging

Edge functions use Lambda packaging:

| Type | Use it for |
|---|---|
| [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle) | A JavaScript or TypeScript entry file (`handlerFunction` names the export) |
| [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) | A Python entry file and its dependencies |
| [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) | A package your own build produces (`packagePath`, `handler` as `file:function`) |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EdgeLambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const edgeRewrite = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge-rewrite.ts',
      handlerFunction: 'handler'
    })
  });

  return { resources: { edgeRewrite } };
});
```


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EdgeLambdaFunction, CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const edgeRewrite = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging({
      packagePath: './dist/edge-rewrite.zip',
      handler: 'index.js:handler'
    })
  });

  return { resources: { edgeRewrite } };
});
```


## Permissions

`connectTo` on an edge function grants IAM permissions only, for example to read a bucket. It injects no
variables, because edge functions can't have any. Add other AWS permissions with `iamRoleStatements`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  Bucket,
  EdgeLambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const assets = new Bucket({});

  const edgeRewrite = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge-rewrite.ts',
      handlerFunction: 'handler'
    }),
    connectTo: ['assets'],
    iamRoleStatements: [
      {
        Action: ['ses:SendEmail'],
        Resource: ['*']
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { assets, edgeRewrite } };
});
```


## Logging

Edge functions write their logs to CloudWatch in the region where CloudFront ran them, which is often not your stack's
region. Look for them in the region closest to the users who made the requests. `logging` sets retention and
forwarding.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `EdgeLambdaFunctionProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/edge-lambda-function` with definition name `EdgeLambdaFunctionProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `packaging` | yes | `js-bundle \| buildpack \| custom-artifact` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `logging` | no | `LambdaFunctionLogging` | - |
| `memory` | no | `number` | `128` |
| `runtime` | no | `string: "nodejs18.x" \| "nodejs20.x" \| "nodejs22.x" \| "nodejs24.x" \| "python3.10" \| "python3.11" \| "python3.12" \| "python3.13" \| "python3.14" \| "python3.8" \| "python3.9"` | - |
| `timeout` | no | `number` | `3` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `edge-lambda-function`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |

# Lambda function

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/compute/lambda-function.mdx`
Route: `/resources/compute/lambda-function`

A Lambda function runs your code on AWS Lambda each time an event arrives: an HTTP request, a queue message, a
schedule, a file upload. It scales from zero to thousands of parallel invocations, and you pay per request and per
millisecond of run time, so an idle function costs nothing. One invocation can run for at most 15 minutes.

For an always-on server or a long-running process, use a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) or a
[worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service). For jobs longer than 15 minutes, use a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job).

## Basic example

This function answers `GET /users/{id}` through an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway).
Stacktape bundles `./src/get-user.ts`, picks the Node.js runtime from the file extension and adds the permissions the
gateway needs to call the function.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiGateway,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const apiGateway = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const getUser = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/get-user.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'http-api-gateway',
        properties: {
          httpApiGatewayName: 'apiGateway',
          method: 'GET',
          path: '/users/{id}'
        }
      }
    ],
    memory: 1024,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return { resources: { apiGateway, getUser } };
});
```


`memory: 1024` gives the function 1,024 MB and a matching share of CPU. `timeout: 30` stops an invocation after 30
seconds (default 10, maximum 900).

The handler:

```ts
export async function handler(event: { pathParameters?: { id?: string } }) {
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    body: JSON.stringify({ id: event.pathParameters?.id })
  };
}
```

The deploy prints the gateway URL. Call `https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com/users/42` and you get
`{"id":"42"}` back. Read the function's logs with `stacktape logs getUser --stage dev`.

## Packaging

Stacktape supports three Lambda packaging types: [`js-bundle`](/packaging/function/js-bundle), [`buildpack`](/packaging/function/buildpack) and [`custom-artifact`](/packaging/function/custom-artifact).

| Type | Best for |
|---|---|
| **`js-bundle`** (JavaScript, TypeScript) | Point to a source file. Stacktape bundles, minifies and source-maps the code, moves code shared between functions into a shared layer, and uploads the package. |
| **`buildpack`** (Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET, Rust) | Point to a source file. Stacktape installs dependencies and compiles the code in Docker on the Lambda build image of the function's `runtime`. |
| **`custom-artifact`** | Provide a pre-built zip. Use when your CI already produces a deployment package or when you need a build step Stacktape does not support. |

`js-bundle` and `buildpack` are the better defaults: they detect the runtime from the file extension, build for the selected architecture and skip unchanged packages. Use [custom artifact](/packaging/function/custom-artifact) only when you own the build outside Stacktape.

### JS bundle

`JsBundleLambdaPackaging` options such as `nodeVersion`, `outputModuleFormat`, `disableSourceMaps` and `minify` are direct properties next to `entryfilePath`. See [JS Bundle for Lambda](/packaging/function/js-bundle) for all options.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts',
      nodeVersion: 22,
      outputModuleFormat: 'esm'
    })
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


`nodeVersion` selects the Node.js major version for the build; keep it aligned with the function's `runtime`. `outputModuleFormat` switches between `'cjs'` (CommonJS) and `'esm'` (ES Modules, enables top-level `await`). Node.js 24 and later use ESM output automatically; earlier versions default to CommonJS. Some npm packages do not support ESM.

### Buildpack

`BuildpackLambdaPackaging` builds Python, Java, Go, Ruby, .NET and Rust functions. The function's `runtime` selects the language version. Language options are grouped under `python`, `java` and `dotnet`. See [Buildpack for Lambda](/packaging/function/buildpack) for all options.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, BuildpackLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    runtime: 'python3.13',
    packaging: new BuildpackLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/process.py',
      python: { packageManagerFile: './pyproject.toml' }
    })
  });

  return { resources: { processor } };
});
```


### Custom artifact

The `CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging` class takes a `packagePath` pointing to a pre-built deployment package. If the path points to a directory or a non-zip file, Stacktape zips it before upload. With `custom-artifact`, there is no source file for runtime auto-detection, so you must set `runtime` on the resource and `handler` in the packaging. The handler file must be at the artifact root; see [custom-artifact limitations](/packaging/function/custom-artifact#handler). If you use `architecture: 'arm64'`, pre-compile any native dependencies for that architecture yourself.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new CustomArtifactLambdaPackaging({
      packagePath: './dist/processor.zip',
      handler: 'index.js:handler'
    }),
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x'
  });

  return { resources: { processor } };
});
```


`handler` follows the format `filepath:functionName` and tells Lambda which exported function to invoke.

## Triggers

A function receives work through its `events` list. Stacktape creates the event source and the permissions for each
entry.

| Trigger | `type` | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP API Gateway | `http-api-gateway` | [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) |
| Application Load Balancer | `application-load-balancer` | [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) |
| WebSocket API Gateway | `websocket-api-gateway` | [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway) |
| AppSync GraphQL resolver | `appsync-api` | [AppSync API](/resources/networking/appsync-api) |
| Schedule | `schedule` | [Schedule triggers](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers) |
| S3 | `s3` | [S3 events](/resources/triggers/s3-events) |
| SQS | `sqs` | [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) |
| SNS | `sns` | [SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events) |
| DynamoDB stream | `dynamo-db-stream` | [DynamoDB streams](/resources/triggers/dynamodb-streams) |
| Kinesis stream | `kinesis-stream` | [Kinesis events](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events) |
| EventBridge | `event-bus` | [EventBridge events](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events) |
| CloudWatch Logs | `cloudwatch-log` | [CloudWatch logs](/resources/triggers/cloudwatch-logs) |
| CloudWatch alarm | `cloudwatch-alarm` | [Alarms as triggers](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers) |
| Kafka topic | `kafka-topic` | [Kafka topics](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics) |

Queue and stream triggers (`sqs`, `kinesis-stream`, `dynamo-db-stream`, `kafka-topic`) deliver records in batches.
`batchSize` caps the records per invocation and `maxBatchWindowSeconds` (up to 300) waits to fill a batch. Defaults and
limits differ per source; each trigger guide lists them. When a handler throws, the whole batch is retried, including
the records that succeeded. Make handlers idempotent, or turn on `reportBatchItemFailures` and return the failed record
IDs in `batchItemFailures` so only those are retried.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  SqsQueue,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const jobs = new SqsQueue({});

  const worker = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/worker.ts' }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'sqs',
        properties: {
          sqsQueueName: 'jobs',
          batchSize: 10,
          maxBatchWindowSeconds: 30
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { jobs, worker } };
});
```


A `schedule` trigger takes a rate (`rate(5 minutes)`) or a six-field AWS cron expression in UTC
(`cron(0 18 ? * MON-FRI *)`). See [Schedule triggers](/resources/triggers/schedule-triggers).

## Function URLs

A function URL gives one function its own HTTPS endpoint (`https://<id>.lambda-url.<region>.on.aws`) with no API
gateway. It suits a webhook receiver or an app that does its own routing, such as Hono or Express behind `handle()`.
Use an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) when several functions share one API or you want
routing by method and path.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const webhook = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/webhook.ts' }),
    url: {
      enabled: true,
      authMode: 'NONE',
      cors: {
        enabled: true,
        allowedOrigins: ['https://app.example.com'],
        allowedMethods: ['POST']
      }
    }
  });

  return { resources: { webhook } };
});
```


`authMode` is `'NONE'` by default, so anyone can call the URL. `'AWS_IAM'` accepts only signed requests from AWS
identities with invoke permission. `cors.enabled: true` alone allows every origin and method; `allowedOrigins` and
`allowedMethods` narrow it. These CORS settings override CORS headers your code returns.

`responseStreamEnabled: true` sends the response as your handler writes it, instead of buffering it, and lifts the 6 MB
limit of buffered responses. The handler must use Lambda's streaming handler pattern.

## Runtime resources

`runtime`, `architecture`, `memory`, `timeout` and `storage` set the language version, CPU, time limit and scratch
disk of each invocation.

`runtime` comes from the file extension with `js-bundle` and `buildpack` packaging. Set it to pin a version, for Rust
(`provided.al2023`) and for `custom-artifact` packaging. The accepted values are listed in the
[configuration reference](#configuration-reference).

`memory` is 128 MB unless you set it, and accepts 128 to 10,240 MB. CPU grows with memory: 1,769 MB is one vCPU. For
CPU-bound code, more memory often costs less in total, because the function finishes sooner.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const imageProcessor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/image-processor.ts' }),
    runtime: 'nodejs22.x',
    architecture: 'arm64',
    memory: 2048,
    timeout: 120,
    storage: 2048
  });

  return { resources: { imageProcessor } };
});
```


`architecture: 'arm64'` (AWS Graviton) costs about 20% less per GB-second than the default `x86_64` and usually needs no
code changes. `js-bundle` and `buildpack` build for the architecture you pick; with a custom artifact, compile native
dependencies for it yourself.

`storage` sets the size of `/tmp`, from 512 MB (default) to 10,240 MB. It's scratch space: it isn't shared between
instances and can disappear between invocations.

## Concurrency

- **`reservedConcurrency`** caps how many instances of this function run at once and reserves that many from your
  account's limit. Use it when a database or a third-party API can't take unlimited parallel calls. It costs nothing.
- **`provisionedConcurrency`** keeps instances initialized so requests skip the cold start. You pay for them while they
  wait. Use it only on latency-sensitive paths.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const checkout = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/checkout.ts' }),
    reservedConcurrency: 25,
    provisionedConcurrency: 3
  });

  return { resources: { checkout } };
});
```


## Networking

A function runs outside your VPC by default and can reach the internet. Set `joinDefaultVpc: true` only when it must
reach something that accepts VPC connections only: a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database)
in a VPC access mode, a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) or an [EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem).

A function in the VPC loses internet access. S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints, but calls to payment
providers, AI APIs or webhooks fail. To keep them working, set `stackConfig.nat`: VPC functions then run in private
subnets and go out through NAT. The `ec2` NAT is one small instance managed by Stacktape (about $7 a month, no
failover), `ha-ec2` runs one per availability zone with failover, and `gateway` uses AWS NAT Gateways (about $32 a
month per zone plus $0.045 per GB). See [VPC and networking](/configuration/connecting-resources#vpc-and-networking).
Without NAT, `stacktape deploy` warns about every VPC function that has no internet access.

### Connecting to resources

`connectTo` grants IAM permissions, opens the network path to databases and Redis, and injects
`STP_<RESOURCE>_<PARAM>` environment variables. [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) lists the
variables per resource type. Put your own settings in `environment` and secrets in
[`$Secret()`](/configuration/secrets).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  RelationalDatabase,
  RdsEnginePostgres,
  $Secret,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const database = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' }
    }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('database', 'password') }
  });

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    connectTo: [database],
    joinDefaultVpc: true,
    environment: { LOG_LEVEL: 'info' },
    memory: 1024,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return { resources: { database, api } };
});
```


Here the function gets `STP_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`, `STP_DATABASE_HOST`, `STP_DATABASE_PORT` and the other
database variables next to `LOG_LEVEL`.

For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, such as Rekognition, Bedrock or Textract, add `iamRoleStatements`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const analyzer = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/analyzer.ts' }),
    iamRoleStatements: [
      {
        Effect: 'Allow',
        Action: ['rekognition:DetectLabels', 'rekognition:DetectText'],
        Resource: ['*']
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { analyzer } };
});
```


## Storage

For files that must outlive an invocation or be shared between functions, mount an
[EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem) with `volumeMounts`. Mounts need `joinDefaultVpc: true`, and
`mountPath` must start with `/mnt/`. The `s3files` mount type attaches an S3 Files access point you already manage. For
most data, an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) or a database is simpler than a file system.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  EfsFilesystem,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const sharedFiles = new EfsFilesystem({});

  const renderer = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/renderer.ts' }),
    joinDefaultVpc: true,
    storage: 2048,
    volumeMounts: [
      {
        type: 'efs',
        properties: {
          efsFilesystemName: 'sharedFiles',
          rootDirectory: '/renders',
          mountPath: '/mnt/renders'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { sharedFiles, renderer } };
});
```


`rootDirectory` limits the mount to a directory of the file system (default `/`).

## CDN

`cdn.enabled: true` puts a CloudFront distribution in front of the function's URL. Cacheable public responses, such as
a product catalog, are then served from CloudFront locations near your users without invoking the function. Leave it
off for personalized responses. See [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) for cache rules.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const catalog = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/catalog.ts' }),
    url: { enabled: true },
    cdn: {
      enabled: true
    }
  });

  return { resources: { catalog } };
});
```


## Deployments

`deployment.strategy` shifts traffic from the old version to the new one gradually, and rolls back if something fails.
Use it for production functions where a bad release would hurt users.

| Strategy | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `Canary10Percent5Minutes`, `…10Minutes`, `…15Minutes`, `…30Minutes` | 10% of traffic first, the rest after the wait |
| `Linear10PercentEvery1Minute`, `…2Minutes`, `…3Minutes`, `…10Minutes` | 10% more at each interval |
| `AllAtOnce` | Switch at once |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    deployment: {
      strategy: 'Canary10Percent5Minutes'
    }
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


`beforeAllowTrafficFunction` and `afterTrafficShiftFunction` name functions that check the release before and after the
shift. If one reports a failure, the deployment rolls back. See
[Gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments).

## Destinations

For asynchronous invocations (S3, SNS, EventBridge, or an `Event` invoke), `destinations` sends each result to an SQS
queue, SNS topic, event bus or another function: `onSuccess` for results, `onFailure` for errors after the retries.
They don't apply to synchronous callers like API gateways and load balancers. Stream triggers have their own
`onFailure` setting.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  SqsQueue,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const deadLetterQueue = new SqsQueue({});

  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/processor.ts' }),
    destinations: {
      onFailure: "$ResourceParam('deadLetterQueue', 'arn')"
    }
  });

  return { resources: { deadLetterQueue, processor } };
});
```


Both take an ARN. Use [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/directives) for a resource in the same config.

## Logs and alarms

Everything the function writes to stdout and stderr goes to CloudWatch Logs, kept for 90 days by default
(`logging.retentionDays`). Read it with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs). `logging.logForwarding` sends logs to an HTTP
endpoint, Datadog or Highlight.io; see [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding).

Function alarms use the `lambda-error-rate` and `lambda-duration` triggers. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) for
evaluation settings and notification channels.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    logging: {
      retentionDays: 30
    },
    alarms: [
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'lambda-error-rate',
          properties: { thresholdPercent: 5 }
        }
      },
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'lambda-duration',
          properties: { thresholdMilliseconds: 5000 }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { api } };
});
```


This alarm fires when more than 5% of invocations fail, or when an invocation runs longer than 5 seconds.

## Layers

`layers` attaches up to five Lambda layer ARNs: shared libraries, a custom runtime or data that several functions need.
You rarely need them, because `js-bundle` and `buildpack` package dependencies for you.

## Examples

### HTTP API with DynamoDB

A Hono API that reads and writes a [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb). `connectTo` grants the function
read and write access to the table and injects `STP_USERS_TABLE_NAME`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiGateway,
  DynamoDbTable,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const apiGateway = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const usersTable = new DynamoDbTable({
    primaryKey: { partitionKey: { name: 'userId', type: 'string' } }
  });

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'http-api-gateway',
        properties: {
          httpApiGatewayName: 'apiGateway',
          method: '*',
          path: '/{proxy+}'
        }
      }
    ],
    connectTo: [usersTable],
    memory: 512,
    timeout: 30
  });

  return { resources: { apiGateway, usersTable, api } };
});
```


The handler:

```ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { handle } from 'hono/aws-lambda';
import { DynamoDBClient, GetItemCommand, PutItemCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-dynamodb';

const app = new Hono();
const client = new DynamoDBClient({});
const tableName = process.env.STP_USERS_TABLE_NAME!;

app.get('/users/:id', async (c) => {
  const result = await client.send(new GetItemCommand({
    TableName: tableName,
    Key: { userId: { S: c.req.param('id') } }
  }));
  return c.json(result.Item ?? {});
});

app.post('/users', async (c) => {
  const body = await c.req.json();
  await client.send(new PutItemCommand({
    TableName: tableName,
    Item: {
      userId: { S: body.id },
      name: { S: body.name },
      email: { S: body.email }
    }
  }));
  return c.json({ success: true }, 201);
});

export const handler = handle(app);
```

### Scheduled job

A function that runs every night at 03:00 UTC:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const cleanup = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/cleanup.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'schedule',
        properties: { scheduleRate: 'cron(0 3 * * ? *)' }
      }
    ],
    timeout: 120
  });

  return { resources: { cleanup } };
});
```


To delete expired DynamoDB items, a [TTL attribute](/resources/databases/dynamodb) is cheaper than a scheduled scan.
