# Relational database

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/databases/relational-database.mdx`
Route: `/resources/databases/relational-database`

A relational database is a managed SQL database on Amazon RDS or Aurora. You pick the engine, and Stacktape creates the
database, its network access, its credentials and its backups in your AWS account.

Standard RDS and provisioned Aurora bill for every hour an instance runs, used or not. The smallest PostgreSQL
instance, `db.t4g.micro`, is about $12 a month in us-east-1 plus storage. Aurora Serverless v2 bills for the capacity it
uses and, by default, pauses when nobody connects. For key-value data with no idle cost, use
[DynamoDB](/resources/databases/dynamodb).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro'
      }
    })
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


The deploy creates a PostgreSQL 16 database on a `db.t4g.micro` instance with 20 GB of storage. It contains a database
named `defdb`, and you sign in as `db_master_user`. If the `database` secret doesn't exist yet, the deploy generates a
random password and stores it there. Creating a new database takes 10 to 15 minutes.

Check that it answers:

```bash
stacktape query sql mainDatabase "SELECT version()" --stage dev
```

Anyone who has the credentials can reach this database from the internet, because `internet` is the default
[access mode](#accessibility). Restrict it before you store real data.

## Engine types

| | Standard RDS | Aurora | Aurora Serverless v2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Engines | PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server | PostgreSQL, MySQL | PostgreSQL, MySQL |
| Compute | One instance of a size you pick | Instances of a size you pick | Scales between `minCapacity` and `maxCapacity` |
| Idle cost | Full instance price | Full instance price | Storage only while paused |
| High availability | `multiAz` standby (doubles the instance cost) | Add a second instance | Add a reader |

Start with standard RDS when you want one fixed monthly price, or with Aurora Serverless v2 when traffic is uneven or
the database sits idle for long periods (dev and preview stages). Provisioned Aurora suits large production databases
that need fast failover and several readers.

### Standard RDS

Engine types: `postgres`, `mysql`, `mariadb`, `oracle-se2`, `sqlserver-ee`, `sqlserver-ex`, `sqlserver-se` and
`sqlserver-web` (classes `RdsEnginePostgres`, `RdsEngineMysql`, `RdsEngineMariadb`, `RdsEngineOracleSE2` and the
`RdsEngineSqlServer*` classes). Oracle and SQL Server run with a license included in the instance price. The
`oracle-ee` type currently fails validation, so use `oracle-se2` for Oracle.

`instanceSize` sets CPU and memory. PostgreSQL prices in us-east-1, single-AZ, on-demand
([RDS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/postgresql/pricing/)):

| Instance | vCPU | RAM | Per month (730 hours) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `db.t4g.micro` | 2 | 1 GB | about $12 |
| `db.t4g.medium` | 2 | 4 GB | about $47 |
| `db.r6g.large` | 2 | 16 GB | about $164 |

The `t` family is burstable: it earns CPU credits while idle and slows down when it runs out under sustained load. It
suits development and small production apps. The `r` family gives steady performance and more memory. Move to it when
CPU stays above about 60% for long periods.

Storage is billed separately; see [Storage](#storage).

### Aurora

Aurora is a clustered PostgreSQL- or MySQL-compatible database. It keeps six copies of your data across three
availability zones. Engine types: `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` (classes `AuroraEnginePostgresql` and
`AuroraEngineMysql`).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, AuroraEnginePostgresql } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new AuroraEnginePostgresql({
      version: '16',
      instances: [{ instanceSize: 'db.r6g.large' }, { instanceSize: 'db.r6g.large' }]
    })
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


The first entry in `instances` is the writer, the others are readers. With two or more instances, AWS promotes a reader
if the writer fails, usually within a minute. Readers share read traffic through the reader endpoint; they don't add
write capacity. Each instance bills at its own hourly rate, plus storage at $0.10 per GB-month and $0.20 per million
I/O requests ([Aurora pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/rds/aurora/pricing/)).

### Aurora Serverless v2

Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute in Aurora capacity units (ACUs, about 2 GB of memory each) between `minCapacity`
and `maxCapacity`. Engine types: `aurora-postgresql-serverless-v2` and `aurora-mysql-serverless-v2` (classes
`AuroraServerlessV2EnginePostgresql` and `AuroraServerlessV2EngineMysql`). An ACU-hour costs $0.12 in us-east-1.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, AuroraServerlessV2EnginePostgresql } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new AuroraServerlessV2EnginePostgresql({
      version: '16',
      minCapacity: 0.5,
      maxCapacity: 16
    }),
    accessibility: {
      accessibilityMode: 'vpc'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


- **`minCapacity`**: when you leave it out, Stacktape sets 0. The database then pauses after about five minutes without
  connections and you pay only for storage while it's paused. The first connection after a pause waits about 15 seconds
  while it resumes. Set `0.5` or more to keep it running, which costs at least $44 a month at 0.5 ACU.
- **`maxCapacity`** (default 10) caps scaling and cost. 16 ACUs give about 32 GB of memory.
- **`serverlessReadersCount`** (default 0) adds readers. Each reader scales between the same bounds.

Pausing at 0 ACUs needs a recent engine version (for example PostgreSQL 16.3 or later). A major version such as `'16'`
always gets a current minor version.

AWS retired Aurora Serverless v1 on 31 March 2025, and Stacktape v4 rejects its engine types
(`aurora-postgresql-serverless`, `aurora-mysql-serverless`). To move a deployed v1 database, see
[Upgrading from v3](/getting-started/upgrading-from-v3/#aurora-serverless-v1).

## Database name, port and version

| Property | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `dbName` | `defdb` | The database created with the instance. For Oracle it's the SID (8 characters at most). SQL Server doesn't accept it. |
| `port` | 5432 PostgreSQL, 3306 MySQL and MariaDB, 1521 Oracle, 1433 SQL Server | Not configurable on Aurora Serverless v2. |
| `version` | Required | A release line (`'16'` for PostgreSQL, `'8.4'` for MySQL) or an exact version (`'16.9'`). |

With a release line, AWS runs a current minor version and applies new minor versions in the maintenance window.
Switching a deployed database from `'16.6'` to `'16'` doesn't change the running version. Oracle and SQL Server need an
exact version. Set `disableAutoMinorVersionUpgrade: true` on the engine to stop automatic minor upgrades.

## Accessibility

The access mode decides who can open a network connection to the database. The username and password are checked in
every mode.

| Mode | Who can connect |
|---|---|
| `internet` (default) | Anyone on the internet who has the credentials |
| `vpc` | Resources in the stack's VPC, plus `whitelistedIps` |
| `scoping-workloads-in-vpc` | Only workloads that list the database in `connectTo`, plus `whitelistedIps` |
| `whitelisted-ips-only` | Only the addresses in `whitelistedIps` |

Use `scoping-workloads-in-vpc` for production. It admits the workloads that declare the database in
[`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources), plus any `whitelistedIps`. The example below also admits one office
address; leave `whitelistedIps` out if only your workloads should connect.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro'
      }
    }),
    accessibility: {
      accessibilityMode: 'scoping-workloads-in-vpc',
      whitelistedIps: ['203.0.113.50/32']
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


`whitelistedIps` adds addresses, for example your office or a CI runner, and has no effect in `internet` mode. In the
VPC modes the database keeps a public IP address that only whitelisted addresses can reach. `forceDisablePublicIp: true`
removes it; set it, without `whitelistedIps`, for a database nothing outside the VPC can reach. On Aurora you can set it
only when you create the database.

To connect from your machine to a database that isn't open to the internet, use a
[bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host) and [`stacktape bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel), or pass
`--bastion-resource` to `stacktape query sql`.

## Credentials

`masterUserPassword` is required; `masterUserName` defaults to `db_master_user`. Keep the password in a
[secret](/configuration/secrets) with `$Secret()`, as in the examples.


> **Warning:** Changing `masterUserName` after the first deploy replaces the database and deletes all its data.


Avoid these characters in the username and password: `[]{}(),;?*=!@`. Many drivers and ORMs fail to parse connection
strings that contain them.

## High availability and read replicas

- **Standard RDS**: `multiAz: true` on the primary instance keeps a standby copy in a second availability zone. AWS fails
  over to it automatically and patches with less downtime. The standby serves no traffic and doubles the instance cost.
  `readReplicas` adds instances that serve reads, each with its own endpoint and asynchronous replication.
- **Aurora**: add instances to `instances`. Every extra instance is both a failover target and a reader.
- **Aurora Serverless v2**: set `serverlessReadersCount`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.r6g.large',
        multiAz: true
      },
      readReplicas: [{ instanceSize: 'db.r6g.large' }]
    })
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


## Connecting from workloads

List the database in a workload's [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources). Stacktape opens the network path
(in the VPC modes) and injects one environment variable per [referenceable parameter](#referenceable-parameters). For a
database named `mainDatabase` these include `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`, `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_HOST`,
`STP_MAIN_DATABASE_PORT`, `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_DB_NAME` and `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_JDBC_CONNECTION_STRING`. Aurora adds the
`READER_*` variants, and RDS read replicas add `READ_REPLICA_*` lists.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  RelationalDatabase,
  RdsEnginePostgres,
  LambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro'
      }
    })
  });
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts'
    }),
    memory: 1024,
    timeout: 30,
    connectTo: [mainDatabase]
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, api }
  };
});
```


The connection string includes the username, password, host, port and database name. Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM and most
drivers accept it as is:

```typescript
import { Client } from 'pg';

const client = new Client({
  connectionString: process.env.STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING
});
await client.connect();
```

A Lambda function opens a connection per concurrent execution. If a busy function exhausts the database's connection
limit, reuse the client across invocations (create it outside the handler) or move to a larger instance.

## Storage

Standard RDS starts with 20 GB of gp3 storage (`storage.initialSize`) and grows automatically up to 200 GB
(`storage.maxSize`) when free space runs low. You pay for the allocated size, not the maximum. Aurora manages storage
itself and grows up to 128 TB.

Raise `initialSize` for write-heavy workloads, because each automatic expansion can briefly slow I/O. Set `maxSize` to cap
storage cost if a bug starts writing data in a loop.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.medium'
      },
      storage: {
        initialSize: 50,
        maxSize: 500
      }
    })
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


## Backups and maintenance

AWS backs up the database every day. `automatedBackupRetentionDays` sets how long backups are kept (default 1 day):

- Standard RDS accepts 0 to 35. 0 turns automated backups off.
- Aurora accepts 1 to 35. Aurora backups can't be turned off.

Raise it to 7 or more for production. With one day of backups, you can't go back past yesterday when someone finds bad
data on Monday. A restore creates a new database from a backup; you do it in the AWS console and then point your config
or workloads at the restored database.

`preferredMaintenanceWindow` sets when AWS applies patches, in UTC (for example `Sun:02:00-Sun:04:00`). By default it's
Sunday 02:00–04:00 in the region's local standard time, and the daily backup runs an hour before it. The database can be
unavailable for a short time during maintenance; `multiAz` and Aurora readers shorten it.

Deleting the stack, or removing the database from the config, deletes the database without a final snapshot.
`deletionProtection: true` prevents that for production data. While it's on, `stacktape delete` lists the protected
databases and stops before deleting anything, and a deploy can't remove or replace the database. To remove it, deploy
with `deletionProtection: false` first.

## Logging

Database logs go to CloudWatch and are kept for 90 days (`logging.retentionDays`). The log types depend on the engine:

| Engine | Log types |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL | `postgresql` |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `audit`, `error`, `general`, `slowquery` |
| Oracle | `alert`, `audit`, `listener`, `trace` |
| SQL Server | `agent`, `error` |

`logging.engineSpecificOptions` tunes what gets logged:

- **PostgreSQL**: `log_min_duration_statement` logs queries slower than this many milliseconds (default 10000).
  `log_statement` picks the statements to log: `none`, `ddl` (default: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`), `mod` (also `INSERT`,
  `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) or `all`. `log_connections`, `log_disconnections` and `log_lock_waits` help with connection and
  locking problems.
- **MySQL**: `server_audit_events` (default `['QUERY_DDL']`) picks what the audit log records. `QUERY` and `QUERY_DML`
  log every data operation and produce a lot of output. `long_query_time` (default 10 seconds) sets the slow query
  threshold.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro'
      }
    }),
    logging: {
      retentionDays: 30,
      engineSpecificOptions: {
        log_min_duration_statement: 1000,
        log_statement: 'mod'
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


Read the logs with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs). `logging.disabled: true` turns CloudWatch logging off, and
[log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) sends the logs to another service.

## Alarms

Database alarms notify your [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels) when a metric crosses a threshold. See
[Alarms](/observability/alarms) for evaluation settings and channels.

| Trigger type | Threshold unit | Watches |
|---|---|---|
| `database-cpu-utilization` | Percent | CPU usage |
| `database-free-memory` | MB | Available memory |
| `database-free-storage` | MB | Free disk space |
| `database-connection-count` | Count | Open connections |
| `database-read-latency` | Seconds | Read I/O latency |
| `database-write-latency` | Seconds | Write I/O latency |

Set at least a `database-free-storage` alarm on every production database. A database that runs out of storage stops
accepting writes.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    credentials: {
      masterUserPassword: "$Secret('database', 'password')"
    },
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({
      version: '16',
      primaryInstance: {
        instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro'
      }
    }),
    alarms: [
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'database-cpu-utilization',
          properties: { thresholdPercent: 80 }
        }
      },
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'database-free-storage',
          properties: { thresholdMB: 1000 }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase }
  };
});
```


`disabledGlobalAlarms` excludes named legacy Console alarm rules while you
[export them into the config](/observability/alarms#migrating-legacy-console-alarm-rules).

## Dev mode

In [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview), PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB and Aurora databases run
locally in Docker with their own generated password. Oracle and SQL Server can't run locally. Set `dev.remote: true` to
use the deployed database instead. See [Local databases](/local-development/local-databases).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `RelationalDatabaseProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/relational-database` with definition name `RelationalDatabaseProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `credentials` | yes | `RelationalDatabaseCredentials` | - |
| `engine` | yes | `AuroraEngine \| AuroraServerlessV2Engine \| RdsEngine` | - |
| `accessibility` | no | `DatabaseAccessibility` | - |
| `alarms` | no | `Array<RelationalDatabaseAlarm>` | - |
| `automatedBackupRetentionDays` | no | `number` | `1` |
| `deletionProtection` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `dev` | no | `DevModeConfig` | - |
| `disabledGlobalAlarms` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `logging` | no | `RelationalDatabaseLogging` | - |
| `preferredMaintenanceWindow` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `relational-database`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `connectionString` | Fully-formed connection string that can be used to access the primary instance. For aurora databases, this is connectionString to cluster endpoint, which can be used for both reads and writes. Includes **host**, **port**, **username**, **password** and **dbName**. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "connectionString")` |
| `jdbcConnectionString` | Fully-formed connection string in JDBC form that can be used to access the primary instance. Includes **host**, **port**, **username**, **password** and **dbName**. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "jdbcConnectionString")` |
| `host` | Hostname (address) of the primary instance that can be used for both reads and writes. For aurora databases, this is hostname of a cluster endpoint, which can be used for both reads and writes. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "host")` |
| `port` | Port of the database. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "port")` |
| `dbName` | Name of the automatically created database (can be configured using the `dbName` property). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "dbName")` |
| `readerHost` | Hostname (address) used for reads only. (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). If you have multiple instances, it is advised to use readerHost for reads to offload the primary (read/write) host. ReaderHost automatically balances requests between available instances. Connections are auto-balanced among available reader hosts. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerHost")` |
| `readerConnectionString` | Same as **connectionString** but targets readerHosts (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). Connections are auto-balanced among available reader hosts. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerConnectionString")` |
| `readerJdbcConnectionString` | Same as **readerConnectionString** but in JDBC format (only available for `aurora-postgresql` and `aurora-mysql` engines). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readerJdbcConnectionString")` |
| `readReplicaHosts` | Comma-separated list of read replica hostnames (only available if read replicas are configured). Read replicas can only be used for read operations. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaHosts")` |
| `readReplicaConnectionStrings` | Comma-separated list of connection strings (URLs) used to connect to read replicas (only available when read replicas are configured). Read replicas can only be used for read operations. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaConnectionStrings")` |
| `readReplicaJdbcConnectionStrings` | Same as **readReplicaConnectionStrings** but in JDBC format (only available when read replicas are configured). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readReplicaJdbcConnectionStrings")` |


## FAQ

### How do I run database migrations?

Run them from a [hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) after each deploy. Define a `local-script` with
`connectTo: ['mainDatabase']`, which injects the same `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_*` variables, and call it from
`hooks.afterDeploy`. For a database that isn't open to the internet, use a `local-script-with-bastion-tunneling` script
and a [bastion host](/resources/security/bastion-host).

### Can I change the engine or instance size later?

Changing `instanceSize` or `multiAz` updates the instance in place, with a short interruption for a size change.
Changing the engine type, for example from RDS to Aurora, replaces the database: the deploy creates an empty new one and
deletes the old one with its data. Dump the data first and restore it into the new database, and keep
`deletionProtection` on so a deploy can't delete the old database by accident.

---

# Upstash Redis

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/databases/upstash-redis.mdx`
Route: `/resources/databases/upstash-redis`

Upstash Redis is a serverless Redis database run by Upstash, outside your AWS account. Your code reaches it over HTTPS
(the REST API) or the Redis protocol, so [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) need no VPC and no
connection pool. Stacktape creates the database through your Upstash account.

You pay Upstash, per command: $0.20 per 100,000 commands, plus $0.25 per GB-month of stored data after the first GB
([Upstash pricing](https://upstash.com/pricing/redis)). An idle database costs only its storage. For high, steady
traffic from containers, a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) in your VPC is faster and cheaper per request.

## Provider configuration

Stacktape needs your Upstash account email and an Upstash API key, created in the Upstash console under
**Account → Management API**. Store the key as a [secret](/configuration/secrets):

```bash
stacktape secret set upstash-api-key
```

Then reference it in `providerConfig.upstash`, once per stack, as in the example below. You can also save the
credentials once on the **Third-party providers** page of the [Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  UpstashRedis,
  LambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const cache = new UpstashRedis({});

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    }),
    connectTo: [cache]
  });

  return {
    providerConfig: {
      upstash: {
        accountEmail: 'you@company.com',
        apiKey: "$Secret('upstash-api-key')"
      }
    },
    resources: { cache, api }
  };
});
```


The deploy creates a database in the Upstash region closest to your stack's region (Upstash offers us-east-1,
us-west-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1, eu-central-1, ap-southeast-1, ap-southeast-2 and sa-east-1). `connectTo` gives the
function the connection variables listed in [Connecting from workloads](#connecting-from-workloads).

## Eviction

By default, Upstash keeps every key, and writes fail when the database is full. For a cache, set `enableEviction: true`
so Upstash removes keys to make room, starting with keys that have a TTL.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UpstashRedis } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const cache = new UpstashRedis({
    enableEviction: true
  });

  return {
    providerConfig: {
      upstash: {
        accountEmail: 'you@company.com',
        apiKey: "$Secret('upstash-api-key')"
      }
    },
    resources: { cache }
  };
});
```


Leave it off when every key matters, for example for sessions you can't lose or counters.

## Connecting from workloads

Add the database to a workload's [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources). For a database named `cache`, the
workload gets:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `STP_CACHE_REST_URL` | REST API URL |
| `STP_CACHE_REST_TOKEN` | REST token with full access |
| `STP_CACHE_READ_ONLY_REST_TOKEN` | REST token that can only read |
| `STP_CACHE_REDIS_URL` | Redis protocol URL, with the password |
| `STP_CACHE_HOST`, `STP_CACHE_PORT`, `STP_CACHE_PASSWORD` | Redis protocol parts |

Give code that only reads the read-only token.

### Using the REST API

The REST API needs no client library and no open connection, which suits Lambda functions:

```typescript
export const handler = async () => {
  const restUrl = process.env.STP_CACHE_REST_URL;
  const restToken = process.env.STP_CACHE_REST_TOKEN;

  await fetch(`${restUrl}/set/greeting/hello`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${restToken}` }
  });

  const response = await fetch(`${restUrl}/get/greeting`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${restToken}` }
  });
  const data = await response.json();

  return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify(data) };
};
```

The `@upstash/redis` package wraps it in a Redis-like client:

```typescript
import { Redis } from '@upstash/redis';

const redis = new Redis({
  url: process.env.STP_CACHE_REST_URL!,
  token: process.env.STP_CACHE_REST_TOKEN!
});

export const handler = async () => {
  await redis.set('greeting', 'hello');
  const value = await redis.get('greeting');
  return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ value }) };
};
```

### Using the Redis protocol

Long-running containers can use any Redis client with `STP_CACHE_REDIS_URL`:

```typescript
import { Redis } from 'ioredis';

const redis = new Redis(process.env.STP_CACHE_REDIS_URL!);

await redis.set('key', 'value');
const result = await redis.get('key');
```

In Lambda functions, each concurrent invocation opens its own TCP connection, which can exhaust the database's
connection limit. Use the REST API there.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `UpstashRedisProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/upstash-redis` with definition name `UpstashRedisProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enableEviction` | no | `boolean` | `false` |


## Referenceable parameters

Use [`$ResourceParam()`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) to reference Upstash Redis parameters in other parts of your config, for example to pass the host or REST URL as an environment variable to a resource that doesn't support `connectTo`.


## Referenceable Parameters: `upstash-redis`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | Hostname (address) of the Upstash Redis database. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "host")` |
| `port` | Port of the Upstash Redis database. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "port")` |
| `password` | Autogenerated password that can be used to authenticate towards the database. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "password")` |
| `restToken` | Rest token which can be used when reading/writing from/to the database using the REST API | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "restToken")` |
| `readOnlyRestToken` | Rest token which can be used only for reading from the database using the REST API | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "readOnlyRestToken")` |
| `restUrl` | Rest URL which can be used when communicating with the database using the REST API | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "restUrl")` |
| `redisUrl` | Standard redis url (including password) which can be used for connecting using cli. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "redisUrl")` |

# Astro

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/astro.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/astro`

An `astro-web` deploys an Astro app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a fully static Astro site (no `output: 'server'`), [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) with `hostingContentType: 'astro-static-website'` is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run Astro as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

Stacktape runs Astro through its Node adapter in middleware mode. Install it and configure the app:

```bash
npm install @astrojs/node
```

```js title="astro.config.mjs"
import node from '@astrojs/node';
import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config';

export default defineConfig({
  output: 'server',
  adapter: node({ mode: 'middleware' })
});
```

Without `@astrojs/node` in `package.json`, packaging stops with an error that says what to change.

Astro's image service uses `sharp`, which needs a Linux build for Lambda. On macOS, Windows or an ARM machine,
Stacktape builds it in Docker, so Docker must be running there. On x64 Linux, such as most CI runners, it usually isn't
needed.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AstroWeb } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const site = new AstroWeb({
    appDirectory: '.'
  });

  return {
    resources: { site }
  };
});
```


`appDirectory` is the folder with `astro.config.mjs`, relative to the Stacktape config. `.` (the default) fits an app at the
repository root; in a monorepo, point it at the app's folder, such as `./apps/web`.

Run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. The deploy builds the app and prints its URL, a CloudFront address until you add a
custom domain. Open it and check a server-rendered page and a static asset.

## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `astro build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `astro dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints.
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

## Connect to resources

`connectTo` gives the server code access to other resources and injects their parameters as environment variables:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, AstroWeb, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres, $Secret } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('main-database-password') }
  });

  const site = new AstroWeb({
    appDirectory: '.',
    connectTo: [mainDatabase],
    serverLambda: { joinDefaultVpc: true }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, site }
  };
});
```


The server code reads `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource injects. Set other values with
`environment`, and secrets with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives). `environment` applies to the build and to
the server function, so variables the framework inlines into browser code at build time work too. A value from this
stack that isn't deployed yet, such as the URL of a new custom domain, is left out of the build with a warning; the next
deploy includes it. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add `iamRoleStatements`.

To run database migrations on each deploy, set `releaseCommand`, for example `npx prisma migrate deploy`. It runs once
in the VPC before the new code goes live; see [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).

## Custom domain

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new AstroWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

## Caching

The defaults cache static assets on the CDN and send page requests to the function. To cache server-rendered pages
that change rarely, and save function runs, add rules per path:

```typescript
new AstroWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  cdn: {
    pathCachingOverrides: [{ path: '/blog/*', cachingOptions: { defaultTTL: 300 } }]
  }
})
```

Don't cache pages that depend on cookies or the signed-in user; every visitor would get the cached copy.

- `cdn.defaultCachingOptions` sets caching (`minTTL`, `defaultTTL`, `maxTTL`) for all server responses.
- `fileOptions` sets headers such as `Cache-Control` on static files matching an `includePattern`.
- Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy; `cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AstroWebProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/astro-web` with definition name `AstroWebProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `appDirectory` | no | `string` | `.` |
| `buildCommand` | no | `string` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `SsrWebCdnConfig` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `dev` | no | `AstroWebDevConfig` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `fileOptions` | no | `Array<DirectoryUploadFilter>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `releaseCommand` | no | `ReleaseCommand \| option-2` | - |
| `serverLambda` | no | `AstroWebServerLambdaConfig` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `astro-web`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | Website URL | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "url")` |


## Next steps

- [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains): put the app on your own domain.
- [Release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands): run migrations before new code goes live.
- [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview): run the app locally against your stack.

# Next.js

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/nextjs.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/nextjs`

A `nextjs-web` deploys a Next.js app on AWS. Stacktape builds it with OpenNext, runs server rendering in a Lambda
function, puts static assets in S3, serves both through a CloudFront CDN, and creates what ISR and image optimization
need. Nothing runs while nobody visits: you pay per request and for traffic, plus a little storage.

For a site exported with `output: 'export'`, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) is simpler. To run
Next.js as a long-running Node server instead, use a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NextjsWeb } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const web = new NextjsWeb({
    appDirectory: '.'
  });

  return {
    resources: { web }
  };
});
```


`appDirectory` is required: the folder with `next.config.js` (or `.ts`/`.mjs`), relative to the Stacktape config. `.`
fits an app at the repository root; in a monorepo, point it at the app's folder, such as `./apps/web`.

Next.js image optimization uses `sharp`, which needs a Linux build for Lambda. On macOS, Windows or an ARM machine,
Stacktape builds it in Docker, so Docker must be running there. On x64 Linux, such as most CI runners, it usually isn't
needed.

Run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. The deploy builds the app and prints its URL, a CloudFront address until you add a
custom domain. Open it and check a server-rendered page, a static asset and an optimized image (`/_next/image`).

What Stacktape creates:

- a Lambda function for server rendering, API routes and middleware;
- a Lambda function for image optimization;
- an S3 bucket for static assets;
- an SQS queue, a Lambda function and a DynamoDB table for ISR revalidation;
- a CloudFront distribution in front of all of it.

## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `next build` in `appDirectory`. If the app has `prisma/schema.prisma`, it runs `prisma generate` first.
Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for example `pnpm --filter web build`. [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) runs `next dev` locally;
change it with `dev.command`. Neither changes the other.

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints, but the ISR revalidation queue (SQS) doesn't.
  See [Connect to resources](#connect-to-resources).
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

### Cold starts

`warmServerInstances` keeps that many server function instances warm with a scheduled warmer function, so the first
request after a quiet period doesn't wait for a cold start. It's 0 by default. Use it for production apps where cold
starts are visible to users; each warm instance adds a small number of invocations.

### Streaming

`streamingEnabled: true` streams server-rendered responses, so the browser gets the first bytes before the page is
finished, and responses can be larger than the 6 MB limit of a buffered Lambda response.

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({ appDirectory: '.', streamingEnabled: true, warmServerInstances: 2 })
```

### Edge rendering

`useEdgeLambda: true` renders pages in Lambda@Edge, close to each visitor. Deploys get slower, and it can't be combined
with `warmServerInstances` or `streamingEnabled`. Keep regional rendering unless measured latency for distant users
says otherwise.

## Connect to resources

`connectTo` gives the server code access to other resources and injects their parameters as environment variables:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NextjsWeb, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres, $Secret } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('main-database-password') }
  });

  const web = new NextjsWeb({
    appDirectory: '.',
    connectTo: [mainDatabase],
    serverLambda: { joinDefaultVpc: true }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, web }
  };
});
```


The server code reads `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. A DynamoDB table or bucket works without
`joinDefaultVpc`.

With `joinDefaultVpc`, the server function can't reach SQS, where it queues ISR revalidation. If the app uses ISR, set
[`stackConfig.nat`](/configuration/connecting-resources#nat-internet-access-from-private-subnets), or add an SQS
interface endpoint to the VPC yourself; otherwise background revalidation fails. The same goes for
external APIs the server calls. See [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource injects.

Set other values with `environment`, and secrets with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives). `environment` applies
to the build and to the server function, so `NEXT_PUBLIC_*` variables, which `next build` inlines into browser code,
work too. A value from this stack that isn't deployed yet, such as the URL of a new custom domain, is left out of the
build with a warning; the next deploy includes it. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add
`iamRoleStatements`.

To run database migrations on each deploy, set `releaseCommand`, for example `npx prisma migrate deploy`. It runs once
in the VPC before the new code goes live; see [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).

## Custom domain

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new NextjsWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

## Caching

Next.js sets cache headers itself, and the CDN follows them: static assets are cached, dynamic pages are not, and ISR
pages are served from the cache and revalidated in the background. Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy;
`cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.

`cdn.defaultCachingOptions`, `cdn.pathCachingOverrides` and `fileOptions` change CDN caching and static file headers,
as on the other [framework resources](/resources/frontend/astro#caching). Most Next.js apps don't need them.

## Cost

A quiet app costs little: Lambda bills per request and duration, S3 per GB stored and per request, CloudFront per GB
and per request, and the DynamoDB table that tracks ISR per GB stored (with point-in-time recovery) and per request.
Warm instances add their scheduled invocations, whether or not anyone visits. After a deploy, the
[cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards) show the real spend per stack.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `NextjsWebProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/nextjs-web` with definition name `NextjsWebProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `appDirectory` | yes | `string` | - |
| `buildCommand` | no | `string` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `SsrWebCdnConfig` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `dev` | no | `unknown` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `fileOptions` | no | `Array<DirectoryUploadFilter>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `releaseCommand` | no | `ReleaseCommand \| option-2` | - |
| `serverLambda` | no | `NextjsServerLambdaProperties` | - |
| `streamingEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `useEdgeLambda` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |
| `warmServerInstances` | no | `number` | `0` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `nextjs-web`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | Website URL | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "url")` |


## Next steps

- [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains): put the app on your own domain.
- [Release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands): run migrations before new code goes live.
- [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview): run the app locally against your stack.

# Nuxt

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/nuxt.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/nuxt`

A `nuxt-web` deploys a Nuxt app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a Nuxt site you generate fully with `nuxt generate`, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) with `hostingContentType: 'nuxt-static-website'` is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run Nuxt as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

No adapter to install: Stacktape builds with Nitro's `aws-lambda` preset (it sets `NITRO_PRESET=aws-lambda`
for the build). Nuxt server routes are deployed with the pages and served by the same function.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NuxtWeb } from 'stacktape';
```

# Remix

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/remix.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/remix`

A `remix-web` deploys a Remix app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a site with no server rendering, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run Remix as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

Stacktape expects a Vite-based Remix app (`vite.config.ts` with the Remix plugin) and deploys the
`build/server` and `build/client` output. No adapter to install.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RemixWeb } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const web = new RemixWeb({
    appDirectory: '.'
  });

  return {
    resources: { web }
  };
});
```


`appDirectory` is the folder with `vite.config.ts`, relative to the Stacktape config. `.` (the default) fits an app at the
repository root; in a monorepo, point it at the app's folder, such as `./apps/web`.

Run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. The deploy builds the app and prints its URL, a CloudFront address until you add a
custom domain. Open it and check a server-rendered page and a static asset.

## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `remix vite:build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `remix vite:dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new RemixWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints.
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

## Connect to resources

`connectTo` gives the server code access to other resources and injects their parameters as environment variables:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, RemixWeb, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres, $Secret } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('main-database-password') }
  });

  const web = new RemixWeb({
    appDirectory: '.',
    connectTo: [mainDatabase],
    serverLambda: { joinDefaultVpc: true }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, web }
  };
});
```


The server code reads `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource injects. Set other values with
`environment`, and secrets with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives). `environment` applies to the build and to
the server function, so variables the framework inlines into browser code at build time work too. A value from this
stack that isn't deployed yet, such as the URL of a new custom domain, is left out of the build with a warning; the next
deploy includes it. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add `iamRoleStatements`.

To run database migrations on each deploy, set `releaseCommand`, for example `npx prisma migrate deploy`. It runs once
in the VPC before the new code goes live; see [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).

## Custom domain

```typescript
new RemixWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new RemixWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

## Caching

The defaults cache static assets on the CDN and send page requests to the function. To cache server-rendered pages
that change rarely, and save function runs, add rules per path:

```typescript
new RemixWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  cdn: {
    pathCachingOverrides: [{ path: '/blog/*', cachingOptions: { defaultTTL: 300 } }]
  }
})
```

Don't cache pages that depend on cookies or the signed-in user; every visitor would get the cached copy.

- `cdn.defaultCachingOptions` sets caching (`minTTL`, `defaultTTL`, `maxTTL`) for all server responses.
- `fileOptions` sets headers such as `Cache-Control` on static files matching an `includePattern`.
- Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy; `cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `RemixWebProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/remix-web` with definition name `RemixWebProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `appDirectory` | no | `string` | `.` |
| `buildCommand` | no | `string` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `SsrWebCdnConfig` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `dev` | no | `SsrWebDevConfig` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `fileOptions` | no | `Array<DirectoryUploadFilter>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `releaseCommand` | no | `ReleaseCommand \| option-2` | - |
| `serverLambda` | no | `SsrWebServerLambdaConfig` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `remix-web`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | Website URL | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "url")` |


## Next steps

- [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains): put the app on your own domain.
- [Release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands): run migrations before new code goes live.
- [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview): run the app locally against your stack.

# SolidStart

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/solidstart.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/solidstart`

A `solidstart-web` deploys a SolidStart app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a

[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

for the build).

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SolidStartWeb } from 'stacktape';
```

# Static hosting

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/static-hosting.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/static-hosting`

A `hosting-bucket` hosts a static site: Stacktape builds it, uploads the output to S3 and serves it through a CloudFront
CDN. Use it for single-page apps (React, Vue, Angular, Vite) and for static sites and fully pre-rendered framework
output. You pay for storage, requests and traffic, which for most sites is a few dollars a month or less.

For server rendering, use the framework resource instead: [Next.js](/resources/frontend/nextjs),
[Astro](/resources/frontend/astro), [Nuxt](/resources/frontend/nuxt), [SvelteKit](/resources/frontend/sveltekit),
[SolidStart](/resources/frontend/solidstart), [TanStack Start](/resources/frontend/tanstack-start) or
[Remix](/resources/frontend/remix). For files that aren't a website, use an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket).

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HostingBucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const website = new HostingBucket({
    uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
    build: { command: 'npm run build' },
    dev: { command: 'npm run dev' },
    hostingContentType: 'single-page-app'
  });

  return {
    resources: { website }
  };
});
```


On `stacktape deploy`, Stacktape runs `build.command`, uploads `uploadDirectoryPath` (here `./dist`) and prints the
site's URL, a CloudFront address until you add a custom domain. Open it and reload a client-side route such as `/about`
to check that routing works. `dev.command` is what [`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) runs.

## Build

`build.command` runs through the shell, so `npm ci && npm run build` works. `workingDirectory` (relative to the project
root, which is the default) sets where it runs; if that folder has its own `package.json`, Stacktape installs its
dependencies first. Point `uploadDirectoryPath` at the build output, not the sources.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './apps/site/dist',
  build: { command: 'npm run build', workingDirectory: './apps/site' },
  dev: { command: 'npm run dev', workingDirectory: './apps/site' }
})
```

Leave out `build` when another CI step already produced the files. `excludeFilesPatterns`, such as
`['**/*.map', '**/.DS_Store']`, keeps files out of the upload. Everything uploaded is public, so never put secrets in
the output folder.

## Caching and routing presets

`hostingContentType` sets browser caching, CDN caching and routing for the kind of site you have:

| Preset | For | What it does |
|--------|-----|--------------|
| `static-website` (default) | Multi-page static sites | CDN caches files; browsers revalidate, so visitors see a new deploy right away |
| `single-page-app` | React, Vue, Angular, Vite and other client-routed apps | Serves `index.html` for client-side routes; caches hashed `.js` and `.css` forever |
| `astro-static-website` | Static Astro builds | Caches hashed `_astro/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `sveltekit-static-website` | Static SvelteKit builds | Caches hashed `_app/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `nuxt-static-website` | Static Nuxt builds | Caches hashed `_nuxt/` assets forever; keeps HTML fresh |
| `gatsby-static-website` | Gatsby builds | Follows Gatsby's caching recommendations |

`fileOptions` adds headers, such as `Cache-Control`, to files matching an `includePattern` when a preset is close but
not exact.

`indexDocument` (default `/index.html`) is served for `/`, and `errorDocument` for missing pages, for example
`/404.html`. URLs are normalized so `/about` serves `/about.html`; `disableUrlNormalization: true` turns that off.

## Deploy-time values

A static site can't ask your stack for values such as the API URL. `injectEnvironment` puts them into the page: on each
deploy, Stacktape writes them into the uploaded HTML files, where your code reads `window.STP_INJECTED_ENV.API_URL`.
Your build doesn't change.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  build: { command: 'npm run build' },
  injectEnvironment: { API_URL: $ResourceParam('api', 'url') }
})
```

These values end up in the browser, so use them for public settings, not secrets. `writeDotenvFilesTo` also writes
them to `.env.<stage>` in the given folder after each deploy, merged with what's there, for local scripts and tools.

In dev mode, `stacktape dev` passes the `injectEnvironment` values to the `dev.command` server as environment variables.
A `$ResourceParam` of a function or container resolves to the URL dev mode runs it at. The values are also written to
`.env.local` in the dev `workingDirectory`, inside a block between `# >>> stacktape dev` and `# <<< stacktape dev <<<`
lines; your own lines in that file stay. Bundlers expose only prefixed variables to browser code, so name them
accordingly, for example `VITE_API_URL`, and read `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`.

## Custom domain

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

## API routes on the same domain

`routeRewrites` sends matching paths to another origin, for example `/api/*` to an HTTP API Gateway, so the site and its
API share one domain and need no CORS. Rules are checked in order; anything unmatched goes to the bucket.

```typescript
new HostingBucket({
  uploadDirectoryPath: './dist',
  hostingContentType: 'single-page-app',
  routeRewrites: [{ path: '/api/*', routeTo: { type: 'http-api-gateway', properties: { httpApiGatewayName: 'api' } } }]
})
```

The [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) page lists all origin types and caching options for rewrites.

## Edge functions and firewall

`edgeFunctions` runs an [edge function](/resources/compute/edge-function) on each request (`onRequest`, before the
cache lookup) or response (`onResponse`), for example for redirects, basic auth or headers. Keep application logic in a
normal backend.

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) with `scope: 'cdn'` in
front of the site.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `HostingBucketProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/hosting-bucket` with definition name `HostingBucketProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `uploadDirectoryPath` | yes | `string` | - |
| `build` | no | `HostingBucketBuild` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `dev` | no | `HostingBucketBuild` | - |
| `disableUrlNormalization` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `edgeFunctions` | no | `EdgeFunctionsConfig` | - |
| `errorDocument` | no | `string` | - |
| `excludeFilesPatterns` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `fileOptions` | no | `Array<DirectoryUploadFilter>` | - |
| `hostingContentType` | no | `string: "astro-static-website" \| "gatsby-static-website" \| "nuxt-static-website" \| "single-page-app" \| "static-website" \| "sveltekit-static-website"` | `static-website` |
| `indexDocument` | no | `string` | `/index.html` |
| `injectEnvironment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `routeRewrites` | no | `Array<CdnRouteRewrite>` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |
| `writeDotenvFilesTo` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `hosting-bucket`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | AWS (physical) name of the bucket | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "name")` |
| `arn` | Arn of the bucket | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `cdnDomain` | Default domain of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnDomain")` |
| `cdnUrl` | Default url of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnUrl")` |
| `cdnCustomDomains` | Comma-separated list of custom domain names assigned to the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomains")` |
| `cdnCustomDomainUrls` | Comma-separated list of custom domain name URLs of the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomainUrls")` |


## Next steps

- [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains): put the site on your own domain.
- [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn): route more paths and origins through one distribution.
- [Starter projects](/getting-started/starter-projects): start from a working frontend setup.

# SvelteKit

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/sveltekit.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/sveltekit`

A `sveltekit-web` deploys a SvelteKit app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a SvelteKit site built with `adapter-static`, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) with `hostingContentType: 'sveltekit-static-website'` is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run SvelteKit as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

Stacktape needs SvelteKit's Node adapter; `adapter-auto` from the default template doesn't produce the server
output it deploys. Install it and select it:

```bash
npm install -D @sveltejs/adapter-node
```

```js title="svelte.config.js"
import adapter from '@sveltejs/adapter-node';

export default {
  kit: {
    adapter: adapter()
  }
};
```

Without `@sveltejs/adapter-node` in `package.json`, packaging stops with an error that says what to change.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SvelteKitWeb } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const web = new SvelteKitWeb({
    appDirectory: '.'
  });

  return {
    resources: { web }
  };
});
```


`appDirectory` is the folder with `svelte.config.js`, relative to the Stacktape config. `.` (the default) fits an app at the
repository root; in a monorepo, point it at the app's folder, such as `./apps/web`.

Run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. The deploy builds the app and prints its URL, a CloudFront address until you add a
custom domain. Open it and check a server-rendered page and a static asset.

## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `vite build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `vite dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new SvelteKitWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```

## Server function

`serverLambda` tunes the function that renders pages:

- `memory`: 1024 MB by default, 128 to 10,240. More memory also means more CPU; 1,769 MB is one vCPU.
- `timeout`: 30 seconds by default, which is also the maximum.
- `joinDefaultVpc: true`: needed to reach a relational database or Redis. The function then has no direct internet
  access; S3 and DynamoDB stay reachable through VPC endpoints.
- `logging`: retention and forwarding of its CloudWatch logs.

## Connect to resources

`connectTo` gives the server code access to other resources and injects their parameters as environment variables:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SvelteKitWeb, RelationalDatabase, RdsEnginePostgres, $Secret } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mainDatabase = new RelationalDatabase({
    engine: new RdsEnginePostgres({ version: '16', primaryInstance: { instanceSize: 'db.t4g.micro' } }),
    credentials: { masterUserPassword: $Secret('main-database-password') }
  });

  const web = new SvelteKitWeb({
    appDirectory: '.',
    connectTo: [mainDatabase],
    serverLambda: { joinDefaultVpc: true }
  });

  return {
    resources: { mainDatabase, web }
  };
});
```


The server code reads `STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING`. See
[Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources) for what each resource injects. Set other values with
`environment`, and secrets with [`$Secret()`](/configuration/directives). `environment` applies to the build and to
the server function, so variables the framework inlines into browser code at build time work too. A value from this
stack that isn't deployed yet, such as the URL of a new custom domain, is left out of the build with a warning; the next
deploy includes it. For AWS services that `connectTo` doesn't cover, add `iamRoleStatements`.

To run database migrations on each deploy, set `releaseCommand`, for example `npx prisma migrate deploy`. It runs once
in the VPC before the new code goes live; see [release commands](/deployment-and-lifecycle/release-commands).

## Custom domain

```typescript
new SvelteKitWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'www.example.com' }]
})
```

Set the domain up once before the first deploy that uses it: run `stacktape domain add --region <your region>` for the
root domain, point your registrar at the Route 53 hosted zone it creates, and run it again until the certificates are
issued. The CDN needs a certificate in `us-east-1`, which the command requests too. Without an issued certificate, the
deploy stops with an error. Stacktape then creates the DNS record and renews the certificate.

To keep DNS at another provider, request an ACM certificate in `us-east-1` yourself, set `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and point a CNAME at the CloudFront domain. [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers both paths.

## Firewall

`useFirewall` puts a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) in front of the CDN. The
firewall resource needs `scope: 'cdn'`.

```typescript
new SvelteKitWeb({ appDirectory: '.', useFirewall: 'firewall' })
```

## Caching

The defaults cache static assets on the CDN and send page requests to the function. To cache server-rendered pages
that change rarely, and save function runs, add rules per path:

```typescript
new SvelteKitWeb({
  appDirectory: '.',
  cdn: {
    pathCachingOverrides: [{ path: '/blog/*', cachingOptions: { defaultTTL: 300 } }]
  }
})
```

Don't cache pages that depend on cookies or the signed-in user; every visitor would get the cached copy.

- `cdn.defaultCachingOptions` sets caching (`minTTL`, `defaultTTL`, `maxTTL`) for all server responses.
- `fileOptions` sets headers such as `Cache-Control` on static files matching an `includePattern`.
- Stacktape clears the CDN cache after each deploy; `cdn.disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` turns that off.

| `buildCommand` | no | `string` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `SsrWebCdnConfig` | - |
| `connectTo` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `dev` | no | `SsrWebDevConfig` | - |
| `environment` | no | `Array<EnvironmentVar>` | - |
| `fileOptions` | no | `Array<DirectoryUploadFilter>` | - |
| `iamRoleStatements` | no | `Array<StpIamRoleStatement>` | - |
| `releaseCommand` | no | `ReleaseCommand \| option-2` | - |
| `serverLambda` | no | `SsrWebServerLambdaConfig` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |

# TanStack Start

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/frontend/tanstack-start.mdx`
Route: `/resources/frontend/tanstack-start`

A `tanstack-web` deploys a TanStack Start app with server rendering on AWS. Stacktape builds the app, runs the server code in a
Lambda function, puts static assets in S3 and serves both through a CloudFront CDN. You pay per request and for traffic.
No server runs while nobody visits; the stored assets still cost a little.

For a site with no server rendering, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) is simpler and has no function to pay for. To run TanStack Start as a long-running Node server instead, use a
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service).

## Basic example

No adapter to install: Stacktape builds with Nitro's `aws-lambda` preset (it sets `NITRO_PRESET=aws-lambda`
for the build). The default commands are the Vinxi ones; if your app builds with plain Vite, set `buildCommand` and
`dev.command` to your package scripts.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, TanStackWeb } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const web = new TanStackWeb({
    appDirectory: '.'
  });

  return {
    resources: { web }
  };
});
```


`appDirectory` is the folder with `app.config.ts`, relative to the Stacktape config. `.` (the default) fits an app at the
repository root; in a monorepo, point it at the app's folder, such as `./apps/web`.

Run `stacktape deploy --stage dev`. The deploy builds the app and prints its URL, a CloudFront address until you add a
custom domain. Open it and check a server-rendered page and a static asset.

## Build and dev mode

Stacktape runs `vinxi build` in `appDirectory`. Set `buildCommand` when your repository builds through a script, for
example `pnpm --filter web build`.

[`stacktape dev`](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) starts `vinxi dev` locally. Change it with `dev.command`, and
with `dev.workingDirectory` (relative to the project root) when the command must run from another folder. Neither
changes the deployed build.

```typescript
new TanStackWeb({
  appDirectory: './apps/web',
  buildCommand: 'pnpm --filter web build',
  dev: { command: 'pnpm --filter web dev' }
})
```
