# Email sender

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/email-sender.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/email-sender`

An `email-sender` gives your workloads a verified Amazon SES identity to send email from: a domain or one email
address. Stacktape verifies the identity, sets up DKIM and bounce handling, and grants connected workloads permission
to send from it and nothing more.

## Basic example

```yaml
resources:
  mail:
    type: email-sender
    properties:
      identity: example.com

  sendWelcomeEmail:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/send-welcome-email.ts
      connectTo:
        - mail
```

```ts
import { SESv2Client, SendEmailCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sesv2';

const ses = new SESv2Client({ region: process.env.STP_MAIL_REGION });

export const handler = async () => {
  await ses.send(new SendEmailCommand({
    FromEmailAddress: `hello@${process.env.STP_MAIL_IDENTITY}`,
    Destination: { ToAddresses: ['customer@example.net'] },
    ConfigurationSetName: process.env.STP_MAIL_CONFIGURATION_SET_NAME,
    Content: {
      Simple: {
        Subject: { Data: 'Welcome' },
        Body: { Text: { Data: 'Thanks for joining us.' } }
      }
    }
  }));
};
```

`connectTo` injects `IDENTITY`, `IDENTITY_ARN`, `REGION`, `CONFIGURATION_SET_NAME` and `FEEDBACK_TOPIC_ARN` (here
`STP_MAIL_IDENTITY` and so on). It grants `ses:SendEmail` and `ses:SendRawEmail` on that identity and configuration set
only, and no SES administration.

## Verification and DNS

For a domain, Stacktape sets up 2048-bit Easy DKIM. If the domain has a public Route 53 hosted zone that the domain is
actually delegated to, Stacktape creates the three DKIM CNAME records. A hosted zone that exists but isn't delegated
doesn't count.

With DNS elsewhere, the deploy succeeds while verification is pending and prints the three CNAME names and values. Add
them at your DNS provider. For a single email address, SES sends a verification link to that mailbox instead.


> **Warning:** SES identities and the SES sandbox are per region. In the sandbox you can send only to verified recipients, with low
daily limits. Stacktape warns and links to the production access request, but doesn't block the deploy. Request
production access before you send to customers.


## Shared identity

An SES identity belongs to the AWS account and region, not to one project or stage. Stacktape creates it in a separate
shared CloudFormation stack with termination protection, one per identity. Every project and stage in that account and
region that uses `example.com` shares it; `billing@example.com` is a different identity.

Deleting a project's stack doesn't delete the shared stack, and the delete output lists it as retained. Stacktape
doesn't remove unused shared identities for you.

The shared stack also has:

- a configuration set that suppresses addresses that bounced or complained;
- an SNS topic for feedback;
- a destination that publishes `BOUNCE` and `COMPLAINT` events to that topic.

Because they're shared, a feedback subscriber sees the feedback for every send from that identity, including other
projects and stages. Make feedback processing idempotent.

## Handle bounces and complaints

Subscribe a function to the feedback topic with an [SNS event](/resources/triggers/sns-events):

```yaml
resources:
  mail:
    type: email-sender
    properties:
      identity: example.com

  processEmailFeedback:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/process-email-feedback.ts
      events:
        - type: sns
          properties:
            snsTopicArn: $ResourceParam('mail', 'feedbackTopicArn')
```

## Use an identity managed elsewhere

Set `manageIdentity: false` to use an identity that another tool created. Stacktape checks that the exact identity
exists, but never takes it over, changes it or widens it to a parent domain.

```yaml
resources:
  mail:
    type: email-sender
    properties:
      identity: billing@example.com
      manageIdentity: false
      configurationSetName: centrally-managed-mail
```

`configurationSetName` is optional. When you set it, Stacktape checks that it exists and limits the send permission to
it. External identities don't get Stacktape's feedback topic; set up feedback where the identity is managed.

## What it doesn't set up

Custom MAIL FROM domains, DMARC records, your own DKIM keys, SES templates, bulk sending, inbound email, dedicated IPs,
Virtual Deliverability Manager and multi-region identities. Add those with
[raw CloudFormation resources](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources) and `iamRoleStatements`.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `EmailSenderProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/email-senders` with definition name `EmailSenderProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `identity` | yes | `string` | - |
| `configurationSetName` | no | `string` | - |
| `manageIdentity` | no | `boolean` | `true` |


## Next steps

- [SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events): process bounce and complaint events.
- [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources): what `connectTo` injects and grants.
- [Secrets](/configuration/secrets): keep API keys of other email providers out of your config.

# Event bus

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/event-bus.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/event-bus`

An `event-bus` is an Amazon EventBridge event bus. Services publish events such as `OrderPlaced` to the bus, and rules
deliver each event to the consumers whose pattern matches it: [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function),
[batch jobs](/resources/compute/batch-job) or [SQS queues](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue). The producer doesn't know
who listens, and a new consumer doesn't need a change to the producer. You pay $1.00 per million published events in US
East.

For one consumer working through jobs, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) is simpler. When every subscriber
needs every message, an [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) is enough.

## Basic example

A bus needs no properties. Consumers subscribe with an [event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events), and
producers get access with `connectTo`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EventBus, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderBus = new EventBus({});

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    connectTo: [orderBus]
  });

  const orderProcessor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/order-processor.ts' }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'event-bus',
        properties: {
          eventBusName: 'orderBus',
          eventPattern: { source: ['order-service'], 'detail-type': ['OrderPlaced'] }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { orderBus, api, orderProcessor }
  };
});
```


Every consumer whose pattern matches gets the event; there are no competing consumers as with SQS. Patterns, payload
transformation and failure handling are on [Event bus events](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).

## Publish events

`connectTo` gives a workload permission to publish and injects the bus ARN. For a bus named `orderBus`, the variable is
`STP_ORDER_BUS_ARN`.

`PutEvents` can succeed as a request while individual entries fail, for example when AWS throttles them. Check
`FailedEntryCount` and retry only the failed entries:

```typescript
import { EventBridgeClient, PutEventsCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-eventbridge';

const eventBridge = new EventBridgeClient({});

const result = await eventBridge.send(
  new PutEventsCommand({
    Entries: [
      {
        EventBusName: process.env.STP_ORDER_BUS_ARN,
        Source: 'order-service',
        DetailType: 'OrderPlaced',
        Detail: JSON.stringify({ orderId: '12345', amount: 99.99 })
      }
    ]
  })
);

if (result.FailedEntryCount) {
  const failed = result.Entries?.filter((entry) => entry.ErrorCode);
  throw new Error(`EventBridge rejected ${result.FailedEntryCount} events: ${JSON.stringify(failed)}`);
}
```

One request takes up to 10 entries, and AWS limits the total size of a request (see
[PutEvents](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-putevents.html)). For large payloads, upload the
data to an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) and put the object key in `Detail`.

The consumer receives the whole event. Your data is in `detail`:

```typescript
export default async (event: { source: string; 'detail-type': string; detail: { orderId: string; amount: number } }) => {
  console.info(`Order ${event.detail.orderId} for $${event.detail.amount}`);
};
```

## Archive and replay

`archivation` stores the events published to the bus so you can replay them later, for example to debug an incident
or to fill a new consumer with past events. Replayed events go through the bus again and the current rules route them.

```typescript
new EventBus({ archivation: { enabled: true, retentionDays: 30 } })
```

Without `retentionDays`, archived events are kept forever. Archive storage and replays are billed separately. Setting
`enabled` back to `false` deletes the archive. The archive's ARN is the bus's `archiveArn` parameter.

## AWS and partner events

You don't need a bus for events from AWS services: they arrive on the account's default bus. Subscribe with
`useDefaultBus: true` on the [event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).

For a SaaS provider that sends events through EventBridge (Zendesk, Auth0, Datadog and others), set `eventSourceName`
to the partner event source name the provider gave you:

```typescript
new EventBus({ eventSourceName: 'aws.partner/example.com/1234567890/my-integration' })
```

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `EventBusProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/event-bus` with definition name `EventBusProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `archivation` | no | `EventBusArchivation` | - |
| `eventSourceName` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `event-bus`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arn` | Arn of the event bus | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `archiveArn` | Arn of the event bus archive (available only if the archivation is enabled) | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "archiveArn")` |


## Event bus FAQ

### Can a container consume events?

Not as a trigger. Deliver the events to an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue#deliver-eventbridge-events-to-the-queue)
with the queue's `events` property, and let a [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) poll that queue.

## Next steps

- [Event bus events](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events): subscribe consumers with patterns.
- [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue): buffer events for one consumer.
- [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic): fan out without content routing.

# Kafka cluster

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/kafka-cluster`

A `kafka-cluster` is an Amazon MSK Serverless cluster with IAM authentication in the stack's VPC. There are no broker
sizes, capacity units or network settings to choose; Stacktape sets secure defaults and a dedicated security group. Use
it only when you need Kafka itself, for example for existing Kafka clients or tools.


> **Warning:** An MSK Serverless cluster costs about $0.75 per cluster-hour in AWS's US East (Ohio) example, or about $558 for a
31-day month, before partition, data and storage charges. Every stage gets its own cluster. For queues and streams
without Kafka, use an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) or a [Kinesis stream](/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream).


## Basic example

```yaml
resources:
  events:
    type: kafka-cluster

  api:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/api.ts
      joinDefaultVpc: true
      connectTo:
        - events
```

`connectTo` injects `ARN`, `NAME` and a comma-separated `BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS` (here `STP_EVENTS_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`). It
grants IAM Kafka connect, topic and consumer group actions on this cluster, including `CreateTopic`, but not
`AlterTopic` or `DeleteTopic`.

A Lambda function that connects as a Kafka client needs `joinDefaultVpc: true`. Containers already run in the VPC. To
consume a topic with a Lambda trigger instead, use a [Kafka topic event](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics); its poller
has its own networking and the function doesn't join the VPC.

## Create topics

Topics aren't infrastructure here: MSK Serverless doesn't create them automatically, and CloudFormation can't declare
them for Serverless clusters. Create them with a Kafka admin client, from setup code or a
[deployment script](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts). For Node.js:

```bash
pnpm add kafkajs aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-js
```

```ts
import { Kafka } from 'kafkajs';
import { generateAuthToken } from 'aws-msk-iam-sasl-signer-js';

const region = process.env.AWS_REGION!;
const kafka = new Kafka({
  clientId: 'topic-setup',
  brokers: process.env.STP_EVENTS_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS!.split(','),
  ssl: true,
  sasl: {
    mechanism: 'oauthbearer',
    oauthBearerProvider: async () => ({ value: (await generateAuthToken({ region })).token })
  }
});

const admin = kafka.admin();
await admin.connect();
await admin.createTopics({ topics: [{ topic: 'orders', numPartitions: 3 }] });
await admin.disconnect();
```

`createTopics` skips topics that already exist, so the setup can run on every deploy. Choose the partition count on
purpose: MSK Serverless charges per partition-hour, and partitions also set how many consumers can read in parallel.

## Lambda triggers and VPC endpoints

A [Kafka topic event](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics) on a cluster in the stack makes Stacktape create Lambda and STS
interface endpoints in the VPC for Lambda's poller. They add hourly and per-GB charges in every availability zone.

## Dev mode

Stacktape doesn't emulate Kafka locally, and `stacktape dev` doesn't deploy the cluster unless you ask for it:

```yaml
events:
  type: kafka-cluster
  properties:
    dev:
      remote: true
```

`--remote-resources events` does the same for one session. Either way the real cluster is deployed and billed.
Containers running on your machine can't reach the private cluster by themselves; use a deployed workload or set up
private access to the VPC.

## Regions and deletion

Stacktape checks that MSK Serverless is available before deploying. Supported regions: US East (N. Virginia and Ohio),
US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul, Frankfurt, Stockholm, Ireland, London and
Paris. Other regions fail with the list of valid ones.

Deleting the stage deletes the cluster and all topic data; Stacktape doesn't keep it, because a forgotten cluster costs
around $558 a month. Back up or replicate data before you delete.

Every property of an MSK Serverless cluster requires a replacement, and AWS needs a fixed cluster name, so a
replacement may delete the old cluster before creating the new one. Stacktape's change preview marks this as
destructive. To keep it from happening by accident, the resource has no capacity, network, authentication, tag or
override settings.

In a reused VPC, Stacktape picks one public subnet per supported availability zone and needs at least two. MSK doesn't
support the `use1-az3` zone, and zone names map to physical zones differently in each account. So in `us-east-1` the
cluster requires `stackConfig.vpc.reuseVpc`, and Stacktape leaves out `use1-az3` when it picks subnets. In other regions
Stacktape can create the VPC itself.

Prices: [Amazon MSK pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/msk/pricing/) and
[AWS PrivateLink pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/privatelink/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `KafkaClusterProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/kafka-clusters` with definition name `KafkaClusterProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dev` | no | `DevModeConfig` | - |


## Next steps

- [Kafka topic events](/resources/triggers/kafka-topics): run a Lambda function on records from a topic.
- [Deployment scripts](/resources/advanced/deployment-scripts): create topics during the deploy.

# Kinesis stream

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/kinesis-stream`

A `kinesis-stream` is an Amazon Kinesis data stream: producers write records, and consumers read them in order per
partition key and can read them again later. Use it for high-volume, ordered data such as clickstreams, telemetry or
change events that several consumers read independently.

A stream costs money while idle. The default on-demand mode charges $0.04 per stream-hour in US East (about $29 for a
30-day month) before any data. For background jobs, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) has no idle charge.
For events that several services react to, an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) is cheaper at low volume.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, KinesisStream, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const clickStream = new KinesisStream({});

  const collector = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/collect.ts' }),
    connectTo: [clickStream]
  });

  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/process.ts' }),
    events: [{ type: 'kinesis-stream', properties: { kinesisStreamName: 'clickStream' } }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { clickStream, collector, processor }
  };
});
```


The stream is on-demand and keeps records for 24 hours. `collector` writes to it; `processor` runs on batches of new
records. Batching, retries and failure handling for consumers are on [Kinesis events](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events).

## Write records

`connectTo` gives a workload permission to read and write the stream and injects its `ARN` and `NAME`. For a stream
named `clickStream`, the variables are `STP_CLICK_STREAM_ARN` and `STP_CLICK_STREAM_NAME`:

```typescript
import { KinesisClient, PutRecordCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-kinesis';

const kinesis = new KinesisClient({});

await kinesis.send(
  new PutRecordCommand({
    StreamName: process.env.STP_CLICK_STREAM_NAME,
    PartitionKey: 'user-42',
    Data: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ userId: '42', page: '/pricing' }))
  })
);
```

Records with the same `PartitionKey` go to the same shard and are read in order. Pick a key with many values, such as
a user or device ID, so the load spreads across shards.

## Capacity mode

|  | On-demand (default) | Provisioned |
|---|---|---|
| Scaling | AWS adds capacity as traffic grows | You set `shardCount` |
| Throughput | Scales with traffic | Per shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s in, 2 MB/s out |
| Idle cost in US East | $0.04 per stream-hour | $0.015 per shard-hour |
| Traffic cost | Per GB written and read | Per million PUT units ($0.014) |

On-demand needs no planning and suits uneven traffic. For steady traffic, provisioned is cheaper: one shard costs about
$11 a month in US East before PUT units. See [Kinesis pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/kinesis/data-streams/pricing/).

```typescript
new KinesisStream({ capacityMode: 'PROVISIONED', shardCount: 2 })
```

## Retention

Records stay for 24 hours by default. `retentionPeriodHours` keeps them up to 8,760 hours (365 days), so consumers can
reprocess after a bug fix or a new consumer can read history. Retention beyond 24 hours costs extra.

```typescript
new KinesisStream({ retentionPeriodHours: 168 })
```

## Encryption

`encryption: { enabled: true }` encrypts records at rest with the AWS-managed Kinesis key, which needs no extra
permissions. Set `kmsKeyArn` to use your own KMS key. `connectTo` doesn't grant access to that key, so add
`kms:GenerateDataKey` for producers and `kms:Decrypt` for consumers with `iamRoleStatements`.

## Enhanced fan-out

Consumers share each shard's 2 MB/s read throughput. When several consumers read the same stream and latency matters,
give a Lambda consumer its own throughput with `autoCreateConsumer: true` on its
[Kinesis event](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events#enhanced-fan-out). AWS charges per consumer-shard hour and per GB
read.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `KinesisStreamProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/kinesis-stream` with definition name `KinesisStreamProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `capacityMode` | no | `string: "ON_DEMAND" \| "PROVISIONED"` | `ON_DEMAND` |
| `enableEnhancedFanOut` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `encryption` | no | `KinesisStreamEncryption` | - |
| `retentionPeriodHours` | no | `number` | `24` |
| `shardCount` | no | `number` | `1` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `kinesis-stream`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arn` | Arn of the Kinesis stream. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `name` | AWS (physical) name of the Kinesis stream. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "name")` |


## Next steps

- [Kinesis events](/resources/triggers/kinesis-events): consume the stream with a Lambda function.
- [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue): a cheaper choice for background jobs.
- [Event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus): route events between services.

# SNS topic

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/sns-topic.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/sns-topic`

An `sns-topic` is an Amazon SNS topic: you publish a message once and every subscriber gets its own copy. Use it when
one event needs several independent reactions, such as an order that triggers a receipt, an inventory update and
analytics. A standard topic costs $0.50 per million publishes in US East after the first million each month, and
delivery to Lambda and SQS is free.

SNS doesn't store messages. With one consumer, an [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) is simpler and keeps
messages until they're processed. To route on fields inside the message, use an
[event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus).

## Basic example

A topic needs no properties. Subscribers are Lambda functions with an [SNS event](/resources/triggers/sns-events):


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SnsTopic, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderEvents = new SnsTopic({});

  const sendReceipt = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/send-receipt.ts' }),
    events: [{ type: 'sns', properties: { snsTopicName: 'orderEvents' } }]
  });

  const recordAnalytics = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/record-analytics.ts' }),
    events: [{ type: 'sns', properties: { snsTopicName: 'orderEvents' } }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { orderEvents, sendReceipt, recordAnalytics }
  };
});
```


Each published message runs both functions. Filters, retries and the event shape are on
[SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events).

## Publish messages

`connectTo` gives a workload permission to publish and injects the topic's `ARN` and `NAME`:

```typescript
const api = new LambdaFunction({
  packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
  connectTo: [orderEvents]
});
```

```typescript
import { SNSClient, PublishCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sns';

const sns = new SNSClient({});

await sns.send(
  new PublishCommand({
    TopicArn: process.env.STP_ORDER_EVENTS_ARN,
    Message: JSON.stringify({ type: 'order-placed', orderId: '456' })
  })
);
```

For a topic named `orderEvents`, the variables are `STP_ORDER_EVENTS_ARN` and `STP_ORDER_EVENTS_NAME`. Containers
publish the same way. See [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

## Fan out to SQS queues

A Lambda subscriber loses a message after Lambda's retries run out. When each consumer needs a buffer, its own retries
and a dead-letter queue, subscribe an SQS queue per consumer. Stacktape has no property for this subscription, so add it
as a [raw CloudFormation resource](/resources/advanced/raw-cloudformation-resources), and allow the topic to send to
the queue:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SnsTopic, SqsQueue, $ResourceParam } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderEvents = new SnsTopic({});

  const billingQueue = new SqsQueue({
    policyStatements: [
      {
        Effect: 'Allow',
        Principal: { Service: 'sns.amazonaws.com' },
        Action: ['sqs:SendMessage'],
        Condition: { ArnEquals: { 'aws:SourceArn': $ResourceParam('orderEvents', 'arn') } }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { orderEvents, billingQueue },
    cloudformationResources: {
      BillingQueueSubscription: {
        Type: 'AWS::SNS::Subscription',
        Properties: {
          TopicArn: $ResourceParam('orderEvents', 'arn'),
          Protocol: 'sqs',
          Endpoint: $ResourceParam('billingQueue', 'arn'),
          RawMessageDelivery: true
        }
      }
    }
  };
});
```


`RawMessageDelivery: true` puts the published message in the SQS body as is, without the SNS envelope. Consume each
queue with an [SQS event](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) or a worker.

## Standard or FIFO

|  | Standard | FIFO |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Best effort | Kept within each message group |
| Duplicates | A message is sometimes delivered twice | Duplicate publishes within 5 minutes are dropped |
| Subscribers | Lambda, SQS, HTTP, email, SMS | SQS queues only |
| Throughput | Practically unlimited | Limited per topic, see the [AWS quotas](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/general/latest/gr/sns.html) |

Use a standard topic unless the order matters. `fifoEnabled: true` creates a FIFO topic. Each publish then needs a
`MessageGroupId` and a deduplication ID, or set `contentBasedDeduplication: true` to use a hash of the body.

```typescript
new SnsTopic({ fifoEnabled: true, contentBasedDeduplication: true })
```

A FIFO topic can't invoke Lambda. Subscribe FIFO queues and consume them with [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events)
to keep the order. It can also deliver to standard queues, but those don't keep the order or drop duplicates.

## SMS sender name

`smsDisplayName` (up to 11 characters) is the sender name on SMS messages sent through the topic. SMS has its own price
per message by country, and new AWS accounts start in an SMS sandbox that only sends to verified numbers.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `SnsTopicProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/sns-topic` with definition name `SnsTopicProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `contentBasedDeduplication` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `fifoEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `smsDisplayName` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `sns-topic`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |


## SNS topic FAQ

### What does a topic cost?

A standard topic costs $0.50 per million publish requests in US East after the first million each month. Each 64 KB of
a message counts as one request. Delivery to Lambda and SQS is free; HTTP, email and SMS deliveries are charged. A FIFO
topic is billed per published and delivered message and per GB of payload, so each extra subscriber adds cost. See
[SNS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/sns/pricing/).

### What is the largest message?

256 KB, for both topic types. For larger payloads, upload the data to an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) and
publish the object key.

- [SNS events](/resources/triggers/sns-events): subscribe functions, filter messages and handle failures.
- [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue): buffer messages for one consumer.
- [Event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus): route events by their content.

# SQS queue

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/messaging/sqs-queue.mdx`
Route: `/resources/messaging/sqs-queue`

An `sqs-queue` is an Amazon SQS message queue. One part of your app puts a job on the queue and returns; a consumer
processes it at its own pace, and a burst of jobs waits in the queue instead of overloading the consumer. You pay per
request: the first million each month are free, then $0.40 per million for standard queues in US East.

A queue delivers each message to one consumer. When several services need the same message, publish it to an
[SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic) or an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) and give each consumer its
own queue.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SqsQueue } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const taskQueue = new SqsQueue({});

  return {
    resources: { taskQueue }
  };
});
```


This creates a standard queue with the AWS defaults: messages up to 1 MiB, kept for 4 days, hidden for 30 seconds after
a consumer receives them. The queue alone does nothing; add a producer and a consumer.

## Send messages

`connectTo` gives a workload permission to send, receive and delete messages, and injects the queue's `ARN`, `NAME` and
`URL` as environment variables:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SqsQueue, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const taskQueue = new SqsQueue({});
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    connectTo: [taskQueue]
  });

  return {
    resources: { taskQueue, api }
  };
});
```


```typescript
import { SQSClient, SendMessageCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sqs';

const sqs = new SQSClient({});

await sqs.send(
  new SendMessageCommand({
    QueueUrl: process.env.STP_TASK_QUEUE_URL,
    MessageBody: JSON.stringify({ task: 'resize-image', imageId: '123' })
  })
);
```

For a queue named `taskQueue`, the variables are `STP_TASK_QUEUE_ARN`, `STP_TASK_QUEUE_NAME` and `STP_TASK_QUEUE_URL`.
See [Connecting resources](/configuration/connecting-resources).

## Consume messages

Pick the consumer by how the work runs:

- **A Lambda function**, for jobs that finish within 15 minutes. Add an [SQS event](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) to
  the function. Lambda polls the queue, passes batches and deletes the messages that succeed. Most queues should start
  here.
- **A container**, for long jobs, a steady stream of work or code that needs a long-lived process. Use a
  [worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service) with `connectTo` and poll the queue in your code.

A container consumer receives a message, processes it, then deletes it. If it crashes before the delete, the message
becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and another receive picks it up:

```typescript
import { SQSClient, ReceiveMessageCommand, DeleteMessageCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sqs';

const sqs = new SQSClient({});
const QueueUrl = process.env.STP_TASK_QUEUE_URL;

while (true) {
  const { Messages = [] } = await sqs.send(
    new ReceiveMessageCommand({ QueueUrl, MaxNumberOfMessages: 10, WaitTimeSeconds: 20 })
  );
  for (const message of Messages) {
    await processTask(JSON.parse(message.Body!));
    await sqs.send(new DeleteMessageCommand({ QueueUrl, ReceiptHandle: message.ReceiptHandle }));
  }
}
```

Test either consumer by sending one message after `stacktape deploy`:

```bash
aws sqs send-message --queue-url "<queue-url>" --message-body '{"task":"resize-image","imageId":"123"}'
```

`stacktape param get taskQueue url --stage dev --region eu-west-1` prints the queue URL.

## Visibility timeout and polling

After a consumer receives a message, the queue hides it for `visibilityTimeoutSeconds` (30 by default). If the consumer
doesn't delete it in time, the message comes back and runs again. Set it above your longest processing time; for a
Lambda consumer, at least the function's `timeout`. Stacktape refuses to deploy a Lambda trigger whose function timeout
is longer than the queue's visibility timeout.

`longPollingSeconds` makes a receive call wait up to that many seconds for messages instead of returning empty at once.
Set it to 20 for container consumers: fewer empty calls, lower cost. Lambda triggers poll on their own and ignore it.

```typescript
new SqsQueue({ visibilityTimeoutSeconds: 300, longPollingSeconds: 20 })
```

## Dead-letter queue

A message that always fails comes back after every visibility timeout until the retention period ends, and each attempt
costs a run of your consumer. A `redrivePolicy` moves it to a second queue after `maxReceiveCount` receives:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SqsQueue } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const deadLetterQueue = new SqsQueue({
    alarms: [{ trigger: { type: 'sqs-queue-not-empty' } }]
  });
  const taskQueue = new SqsQueue({
    redrivePolicy: {
      targetSqsQueueName: 'deadLetterQueue',
      maxReceiveCount: 3
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { taskQueue, deadLetterQueue }
  };
});
```


The `sqs-queue-not-empty` alarm tells you when a message lands in the dead-letter queue. `targetSqsQueueArn` points at
a queue outside the stack. A FIFO queue needs a FIFO dead-letter queue.

## Standard or FIFO

|  | Standard | FIFO |
|---|---|---|
| Order | Best effort | Kept within each message group |
| Duplicates | A message is sometimes delivered twice | Duplicate sends within 5 minutes are dropped |
| Throughput | Practically unlimited | 300 calls per second, 3,000 messages with batching |
| Price in US East | $0.40 per million requests | $0.50 per million requests |

Use a standard queue unless the order of messages matters. FIFO stops duplicate *sends*, but a consumer can still get
a message again when it fails or runs past the visibility timeout. Write consumers to be idempotent with either type.

`fifoEnabled: true` creates a FIFO queue. Each message then needs a deduplication ID, or set
`contentBasedDeduplication: true` to use a hash of the body. Every message also needs a `MessageGroupId`; messages with
the same group ID are processed in order.

```typescript
new SqsQueue({ fifoEnabled: true, contentBasedDeduplication: true })
```

`fifoHighThroughput: true` raises the FIFO limit to thousands of calls per second (up to 70,000 in the largest regions).
Order then holds only within each message group, which is already the rule for consumers.

## Deliver EventBridge events to the queue

The queue's `events` property sends matching events from an event bus into the queue, with no producer code. Set one
of `eventBusName`, `eventBusArn` or `useDefaultBus`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, SqsQueue, EventBus } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderBus = new EventBus({});
  const orderQueue = new SqsQueue({
    events: [
      {
        type: 'event-bus',
        properties: {
          eventBusName: 'orderBus',
          eventPattern: {
            source: ['order-service'],
            'detail-type': ['OrderPlaced']
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { orderBus, orderQueue }
  };
});
```


A FIFO queue also needs `messageGroupId` on the integration. `input`, `inputPath`, `inputTransformer` and
`onDeliveryFailure` work as on [event bus triggers](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).

## Other settings

- `delayMessagesSecond` (0 to 900) keeps new messages hidden for that long before consumers can receive them.
- `messageRetentionPeriodSeconds` sets how long unprocessed messages stay, from 60 seconds to 14 days. The default is
  4 days.
- `maxMessageSizeBytes` lowers the size limit below 1 MiB. For larger payloads, upload the data to an
  [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) and send the object key.
- `policyStatements` adds statements to the queue policy, for another account or an AWS service principal. Workloads in
  the stack use `connectTo` instead.

## Alarms

Two alarm triggers watch a queue:

- `sqs-queue-not-empty` goes off when the queue has visible, in-flight, received or sent messages. Use it on a
  dead-letter queue, or on a queue that should be drained.
- `sqs-queue-received-messages-count` goes off when received messages cross `thresholdCount` (average per period by
  default), for unexpected traffic.

See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) and [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `SqsQueueProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/sqs-queue` with definition name `SqsQueueProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alarms` | no | `Array<SqsQueueAlarm>` | - |
| `contentBasedDeduplication` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `delayMessagesSecond` | no | `number` | `0` |
| `disabledGlobalAlarms` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `events` | no | `Array<SqsQueueEventBusIntegration>` | - |
| `fifoEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `fifoHighThroughput` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `longPollingSeconds` | no | `number` | `0` |
| `maxMessageSizeBytes` | no | `number` | `1048576` |
| `messageRetentionPeriodSeconds` | no | `number` | `345600` |
| `policyStatements` | no | `Array<SqsQueuePolicyStatement>` | - |
| `redrivePolicy` | no | `SqsQueueRedrivePolicy` | - |
| `visibilityTimeoutSeconds` | no | `number` | `30` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `sqs-queue`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |


## Next steps

- [SQS events](/resources/triggers/sqs-events): consume the queue with a Lambda function.
- [Worker service](/resources/compute/worker-service): consume the queue with a container.
- [SNS topic](/resources/messaging/sns-topic): fan a message out to several queues.

# Application Load Balancer

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/application-load-balancer.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/application-load-balancer`

An Application Load Balancer (AWS ALB) receives HTTP and HTTPS traffic and routes it to container workloads and
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) by path, host, header, query string or source IP. It keeps
WebSocket connections open to containers, takes a [firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) directly and
is required for [gradual deployments](/deployment-and-lifecycle/gradual-deployments) of containers.

It costs $0.0225 an hour (about $16 a month in us-east-1) even with no traffic, plus capacity units as traffic grows.
For Lambda APIs with modest traffic, an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) costs less; see
[the cost comparison](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway#choosing-between-http-api-gateway-and-a-load-balancer).

## Basic example

The load balancer holds listeners and domains. Routes live on the functions and containers that use it.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'app.example.com' }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


By default the load balancer listens on HTTPS (443) and redirects HTTP (80) to HTTPS. The certificate comes from the
custom domain, so [set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) before the first deploy.
Without `customDomains`, the load balancer is served on a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain that the
[Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) provides; without the Console connected, the deploy stops and
asks for a custom domain.

Functions attach with an `ApplicationLoadBalancerIntegration` event. Containers use an `application-load-balancer`
event with a `containerPort`, or a [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) creates its own load balancer.

## Routing

Each integration has a `priority` and conditions. Rules are checked from the lowest priority up, and the first match
wins:

| Condition | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| `paths` | `['/api/*', '/health']` | URL path, with `*` and `?` wildcards, case-sensitive |
| `methods` | `['GET', 'POST']` | HTTP method |
| `hosts` | `['api.example.com', '*.myapp.com']` | `Host` header, with wildcards |
| `headers` | `[{ headerName: 'X-Tenant', values: ['acme'] }]` | Header value |
| `queryParams` | `[{ paramName: 'version', values: ['v2'] }]` | Query parameter value |
| `sourceIps` | `['10.0.0.0/8']` | Client IP range |

All conditions of one integration must match; any value in a list matches. Leave gaps between priorities (10, 20,
30) so you can add rules later. See [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) for the integration options.

### Several services behind one load balancer


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  ApplicationLoadBalancer,
  LambdaFunction,
  ApplicationLoadBalancerIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({});

  const usersApi = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/users.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new ApplicationLoadBalancerIntegration({
        loadBalancerName: 'myAlb',
        priority: 10,
        paths: ['/users', '/users/*']
      })
    ]
  });

  const ordersApi = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/orders.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new ApplicationLoadBalancerIntegration({
        loadBalancerName: 'myAlb',
        priority: 20,
        paths: ['/orders', '/orders/*']
      })
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb, usersApi, ordersApi }
  };
});
```


`/users/123` goes to `usersApi` (priority 10) and `/orders/456` to `ordersApi` (priority 20).

## Listeners

Set `listeners` to change ports, allow only some IP addresses or redirect unmatched requests. Each listener needs a
`protocol` (`HTTP` or `HTTPS`) and a `port`. An HTTPS listener uses the certificates of `customDomains`, or the ACM
certificates in its `customCertificateArns`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }],
    listeners: [
      {
        protocol: 'HTTPS',
        port: 443,
        whitelistIps: ['10.0.0.0/8', '192.168.1.0/24']
      },
      {
        protocol: 'HTTP',
        port: 80
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


`whitelistIps` rejects requests from other addresses at the load balancer. `defaultAction` redirects requests that
match no rule, with `HTTP_301` or `HTTP_302`, and can reuse parts of the URL with `#{protocol}`, `#{host}`, `#{port}`,
`#{path}` and `#{query}`.

## Custom domains


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }, { domainName: 'api-v2.example.com' }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


Each domain needs an issued certificate in the stack's region; [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
covers the setup and DNS hosted elsewhere. The object form takes the certificate and DNS options; the plain list of
names (`['api.example.com']`) also works.

## CDN

`cdn.enabled: true` puts CloudFront in front of the load balancer. It helps with cacheable public content and users far
from your region; for personalized responses it only adds cost. With custom listeners, `listenerPort` tells CloudFront
which one to use. See [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) for cache rules.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }],
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cloudfrontPriceClass: 'PriceClass_100'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


## Firewall

`useFirewall` names a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) resource with
`scope: 'regional'` and attaches it to the load balancer.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const apiFirewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional'
  });

  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    useFirewall: 'apiFirewall'
  });

  return {
    resources: { apiFirewall, myAlb }
  };
});
```


With a CDN in front, attach the firewall to the CDN instead (`cdn.useFirewall`, a firewall with `cdn` scope), so bad
requests stop at CloudFront.

## Internal load balancer

`interface: 'internal'` makes the load balancer reachable only from inside the VPC, for HTTP services your other
services call.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const internalAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    interface: 'internal'
  });

  return {
    resources: { internalAlb }
  };
});
```


## WebSockets and health checks

The load balancer keeps WebSocket connections open after the HTTP upgrade, which suits Socket.IO or `ws` servers in
containers. For WebSocket routes on Lambda, use a [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway).

Health checks belong to the targets: set them on the [web service](/resources/compute/web-service#health-checks) or
container workload behind the load balancer.

## Alarms

Load balancer alarms use the `application-load-balancer-error-rate` (share of 4xx and 5xx responses),
`application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets` and `application-load-balancer-custom` triggers.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    alarms: [
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'application-load-balancer-error-rate',
          properties: { thresholdPercent: 5 }
        }
      },
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets',
          properties: { thresholdPercent: 50 }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


The unhealthy-targets alarm fires when any target group passes the threshold; `onlyIncludeTargets` narrows it to some
services. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) for `evaluation` settings, comparison operators and channels.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `ApplicationLoadBalancerProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/application-load-balancer` with definition name `ApplicationLoadBalancerProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alarms` | no | `Array<ApplicationLoadBalancerAlarm>` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `ApplicationLoadBalancerCdnConfiguration` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `option-1 \| option-2` | - |
| `disabledGlobalAlarms` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `interface` | no | `string: "internal" \| "internet"` | `internet` |
| `listeners` | no | `Array<ApplicationLoadBalancerListener>` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |

| `cdnCustomDomainUrls` | Comma-separated list of custom domain name URLs of the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomainUrls")` |

# AppSync API

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/appsync-api.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/appsync-api`

An AppSync API is a GraphQL endpoint run by AWS AppSync. You write the schema and attach a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) to each field you want to resolve. Stacktape creates the API, the
resolvers, the roles that let AppSync call your functions, and the logs. It costs $4 per million queries and mutations
in us-east-1 and nothing while idle ([AppSync pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/appsync/pricing/)).

Each field has one Lambda resolver; there are no VTL or JavaScript resolvers and no pipelines.

## Basic example

Create `schema.graphql` in the project root:

```graphql
type Query {
  user(id: ID!): User
}

type User {
  id: ID!
  name: String!
}
```

Then configure the API and field handler:

```yaml
resources:
  graphql:
    type: appsync-api
    properties:
      authentication:
        type: aws-iam

  getUser:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/get-user.ts
      events:
        - type: appsync-api
          properties:
            appsyncApiName: graphql
            field: Query.user
```

The resolver gets the standard AppSync event: `arguments`, `identity`, `source` and field information. It returns
the value of the field:

```ts
export const handler = async (event: { arguments: { id: string } }) => {
  return { id: event.arguments.id, name: 'Ada' };
};
```

Stacktape reads `schema.graphql` (or `schemaFilePath`) before deploying and stops if a configured `Type.field` isn't in
it. AppSync directives and custom scalars are allowed.

After the deploy, run a query in the AWS console under **AppSync → your API → Queries**, which signs requests with
your IAM identity:

```graphql
query {
  user(id: "1") {
    id
    name
  }
}
```

It returns `{"data":{"user":{"id":"1","name":"Ada"}}}`. From your own code, call the `url` parameter with
SigV4-signed requests.

## Authentication

`authentication` is required and takes one mode:

- **`aws-iam`**: for calls from your AWS workloads. A workload that lists the API in `connectTo` gets permission to
  query this API's fields.
- **`user-auth-pool`**: signed-in users of a Stacktape [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool).
- **`api-key`**: for deliberately public or short-lived access. `expiresAt` is a fixed RFC 3339 time 1 to 365 days in
  the future; Stacktape never extends it, so the key stops working on that date until you set a new one. The key is a
  sensitive parameter and isn't printed in the deploy output.

## Operational defaults

By default the API logs errors without request content and keeps logs for 30 days, limits queries to a depth of 10 and
1,000 resolver calls, allows introspection and leaves X-Ray off. Each setting can be changed. Verbose logging can
record headers, variables and personal data, so turn it on only while debugging.

The Infrequent Access log class works only without log forwarding, because AWS can't forward from it.

## Custom domains

`customDomain` serves the API at your own hostname. The certificate must be in `us-east-1`, even when the API runs in
another region; `stacktape domain add` creates one there (see
[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain)). Stacktape creates the DNS record unless
you turn that off.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AppSyncApiProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/appsync-apis` with definition name `AppSyncApiProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `authentication` | yes | `aws-iam \| user-auth-pool \| api-key` | - |
| `customDomain` | no | `DomainConfiguration` | - |
| `introspectionEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `true` |
| `logging` | no | `AppSyncApiLogging` | - |
| `queryDepthLimit` | no | `number` | `10` |
| `resolverCountLimit` | no | `number` | `1000` |
| `schemaFilePath` | no | `string` | `schema.graphql` |
| `xrayEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `false` |


## Referenceable parameters

`url`, `realtimeUrl`, `apiId` and `arn`, plus the sensitive `apiKey` with API key authentication.

# CDN

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/cdn.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/cdn`

A CDN puts an Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of a [bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), an
[HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway), an
[Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) or a
[Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function). It's not a resource of its own: you turn it on with the `cdn`
property of that resource. CloudFront serves cached responses from locations near your users, routes paths to several
backends from one domain, runs [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function) and takes a
[firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall).

It has no monthly fee. The first 1 TB of transfer and 10 million requests each month are free, then North America costs
$0.085 per GB and $0.01 per 10,000 HTTPS requests
([CloudFront pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudfront/pricing/pay-as-you-go/)). A CDN in front of an API whose
responses are all personalized adds cost without caching anything.

## Basic example

Set `cdn.enabled: true` on the parent resource. By default CloudFront serves from all its locations, compresses
responses with Gzip and Brotli, and Stacktape clears the cache on every deploy.

### API-backed CDN


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


CloudFront caches API Gateway and load balancer responses only when your API sends `Cache-Control` headers or you set
`cachingOptions.defaultTTL`. The deploy prints the distribution URL (`cdnUrl`).

### Bucket-backed CDN

Static files from a [bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket) are the most common case. Files without a `Cache-Control`
header stay cached for six months, and each deploy clears the cache.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const staticAssets = new Bucket({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cloudfrontPriceClass: 'PriceClass_100'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { staticAssets }
  };
});
```


`PriceClass_100` limits CloudFront to its North American and European locations, the cheapest option; see
[Price class](#price-class). `$ResourceParam('staticAssets', 'cdnUrl')` gives the URL, using the parent resource's name.

## Examples

### Static site with custom domain

A bucket behind a CDN with your own domain, for a static site or single-page app:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const frontend = new Bucket({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cloudfrontPriceClass: 'PriceClass_100',
      customDomains: [{ domainName: 'app.example.com' }]
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { frontend },
    stackConfig: {
      outputs: [{ name: 'siteUrl', value: "$ResourceParam('frontend', 'cdnCanonicalUrl')" }]
    }
  };
});
```


CloudFront needs the certificate in `us-east-1`. `stacktape domain add` creates it there, so
[set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) before the first deploy.

### Multi-origin API with WAF

One domain for an API and its static assets, with a firewall in front of both:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway, Bucket, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const assets = new Bucket({});

  const waf = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'cdn'
  });

  const api = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      useFirewall: 'waf',
      routeRewrites: [
        {
          path: '/assets/*',
          routeTo: {
            type: 'bucket',
            properties: { bucketName: 'assets' }
          },
          cachingOptions: { defaultTTL: 86400 }
        }
      ]
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { assets, waf, api }
  };
});
```


`/assets/*` comes from the bucket and is cached for 24 hours; every other path goes to the API uncached. `useFirewall`
names a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) with `scope: 'cdn'`.

## Caching

CDN caching controls how long CloudFront stores responses at edge locations before requesting fresh content from your origin. Proper caching reduces latency, lowers origin load, and saves on data transfer costs.

The default caching behavior depends on the origin type:

- **Bucket origins**: cached for 6 months when the origin has no `Cache-Control` header. Stacktape automatically invalidates all cached content on each deploy.
- **API Gateway / ALB origins**: not cached by default. Responses are only cached if your origin sends `Cache-Control` headers or you set a `defaultTTL`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cachingOptions: {
        defaultTTL: 300,
        maxTTL: 86400,
        minTTL: 60,
        cacheMethods: ['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS']
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


The `defaultTTL` (in seconds) is used when the origin response has no `Cache-Control` or `Expires` header — here, 300 seconds (5 minutes). The `maxTTL` caps how long CloudFront caches content even if the origin sends a higher `max-age`. The `minTTL` overrides the origin's `max-age` if the origin sets a lower value. Adding `OPTIONS` to `cacheMethods` is useful when your API serves CORS preflight requests.

Automatic Gzip and Brotli compression is enabled by default, reducing transfer size and cost. Set `disableCompression: true` to turn it off — rarely needed unless your origin handles compression itself.

If you have a pre-existing CloudFront cache policy, pass its ID via `cachePolicyId` instead of configuring TTL and cache key options manually.

### Cache key

The cache key determines what makes each cached response unique. By default, bucket origins use the URL path only, while API/ALB origins use the URL path plus query string. You can include specific headers, cookies, and query parameters in the cache key — different values produce different cached entries. Values included in the cache key are always forwarded to the origin.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cachingOptions: {
        defaultTTL: 600,
        cacheKeyParameters: {
          queryString: { whitelist: ['page', 'limit'] },
          headers: { whitelist: ['Accept-Language'] },
          cookies: { none: true }
        }
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


In this example, only the `page` and `limit` query parameters and the `Accept-Language` header affect the cache key. No cookies are included. Requests with different values for these produce different cached responses.

For cookies, the options are `none` (no cookies), `all` (all cookies), `whitelist` (specific cookies), or `allExcept` (all except listed). For headers: `none` or `whitelist`. For query strings: `none`, `all`, or `whitelist`.


> **Tip:** Keep the cache key as narrow as possible. Including all cookies or headers effectively disables caching for most APIs since every request has unique cookie values.


## Route rewrites

Route rewrites let a single CDN distribution serve requests from multiple backends. Each rewrite matches a URL path pattern and routes matching requests to a different origin. Unmatched requests go to the default origin (the parent resource the CDN is attached to). Rewrites are evaluated in order — the first match wins.

Path patterns support wildcards, for example `/api/*`, `*.jpg`, and `/docs/v2/*`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const assetsBucket = new Bucket({});

  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      routeRewrites: [
        {
          path: '/assets/*',
          routeTo: {
            type: 'bucket',
            properties: { bucketName: 'assetsBucket' }
          },
          cachingOptions: {
            defaultTTL: 86400
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { assetsBucket, myApi }
  };
});
```


Requests to `/assets/*` are served from the `assetsBucket` bucket with a 24-hour default cache TTL, while all other requests go to the API gateway. This is a common pattern for SPAs: serve static assets from a bucket and proxy API calls to a backend through the same domain.

In `routeTo.properties`, the names `bucketName`, `httpApiGatewayName`, `loadBalancerName`, and `functionName` refer to Stacktape resource names defined in `resources`, not generated AWS physical names. The name must match the key used when returning the resource from `defineConfig`.

Each route rewrite can independently override `cachingOptions`, `forwardingOptions`, and `edgeFunctions`, so you can cache static assets aggressively while passing API requests through uncached.

Route rewrites support five origin types:

| Origin type | `type` value | Routes to |
|---|---|---|
| S3 bucket | `bucket` | A `bucket` resource in your stack |
| HTTP API Gateway | `http-api-gateway` | An `http-api-gateway` resource |
| Application Load Balancer | `application-load-balancer` | An `application-load-balancer` resource |
| Lambda function | `function` | A `function` resource (must have `url.enabled: true`) |
| External domain | `custom-origin` | Any external domain (e.g., `api.example.com`) |

For the `custom-origin` type, you specify a `domainName`, optional `protocol` (`HTTP` or `HTTPS`, default `HTTPS`), and optional `port`. This is useful for routing part of your traffic to a legacy API or third-party service while keeping everything behind one CDN domain.

Bucket route targets support `disableUrlNormalization` (disables clean URL normalization like `/about` to `/about.html`, defaults to `false`). ALB route targets support `listenerPort` (for custom listener setups) and `originDomainName` (when the ALB has no custom domains and uses `customCertificateArns`).

### Route prefixes

A `routePrefix` on a rewrite prepends a path prefix before forwarding to the origin. For example, with `routePrefix: '/v2'`, a request for `/users` is forwarded to the origin as `/v2/users`.

The top-level `defaultRoutePrefix` prepends a path prefix to all requests forwarded to the default origin. This is useful for versioned APIs or when your origin serves content from a sub-path. For example, setting `defaultRoutePrefix: '/v2'` on the CDN forwards all unmatched requests with `/v2` prepended to the path.

## Forwarding

Forwarding options control which headers, cookies, and query parameters the CDN passes through to your origin. By default, all headers, cookies, and query parameters are forwarded. Restricting forwarding strips unnecessary data from reaching your backend. Cache hit rate is primarily controlled by `cachingOptions.cacheKeyParameters`; forwarded values only affect cache variants when they are also included in the cache key.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      forwardingOptions: {
        cookies: { none: true },
        headers: { whitelist: ['Accept', 'Accept-Language'] },
        queryString: { all: true },
        customRequestHeaders: [{ headerName: 'X-Forwarded-By', value: 'cdn' }]
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


This configuration strips all cookies, forwards only the `Accept` and `Accept-Language` headers, passes all query parameters, and injects a custom `X-Forwarded-By` header on every request sent to the origin. The `customRequestHeaders` property is useful for identifying CDN-routed traffic, injecting API keys, or passing custom identifiers.


> **Warning:** The `Authorization` header requires special handling. To forward it, you must add it to `cachingOptions.cacheKeyParameters.headers` — forwarding options alone do not cover `Authorization`.


For cookie forwarding, the supported modes are `none` (strip all cookies), `whitelist` (forward specific cookies), and `all` (forward all cookies). For query string forwarding: `all`, `none`, and `whitelist`. For header forwarding, several strategies are available: `none` (strip all), `whitelist` (specific headers), `allViewer` (all viewer headers), `allViewerAndWhitelistCloudFront` (viewer headers plus specific CloudFront headers like `CloudFront-Viewer-Country`), and `allExcept` (all viewer headers except listed ones). The CloudFront-specific headers are useful for geo-based routing or content localization. Keep forwarded values narrow — unnecessary cookies or query parameters add overhead, and if they are also part of the cache key, they reduce cache hit rates.

By default, all HTTP methods are forwarded. Use `allowedMethods` to restrict which methods reach the origin, for example `['GET', 'HEAD']` for read-only bucket content or `['GET', 'HEAD', 'OPTIONS', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'POST', 'DELETE']` to explicitly allow all methods.

If you have a pre-existing CloudFront origin request policy, pass its ID via `originRequestPolicyId` instead of configuring forwarding options manually.

## Custom domains

[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add`, which also
creates the `us-east-1` certificate CloudFront needs. The deploy then attaches the certificate and creates the DNS
record. Without a custom domain, a CDN on a bucket, API Gateway or function uses its `*.cloudfront.net` URL. A CDN on
an Application Load Balancer needs a custom domain, or a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain from the
[Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console); without the Console connected, the deploy stops and asks for one.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }]
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


`disableDnsRecordCreation: true` skips the DNS record when DNS is elsewhere. A `customCertificateArn` must be in
`us-east-1`. `$ResourceParam('myApi', 'cdnCustomDomainUrls')` gives the domain URLs. See
[Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

## Edge functions

`edgeFunctions` runs [edge functions](/resources/compute/edge-function), defined as their own resources, at four points
of a request:

| Hook | Runs | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `onRequest` | When CloudFront receives the request, before the cache | Auth checks, redirects, URL rewrites, A/B tests |
| `onResponse` | Before the response goes to the client (not after an origin error of 400 or more, or when `onRequest` answered) | Security headers, cookies |
| `onOriginRequest` | Before a cache miss goes to the origin | Change the origin path or headers |
| `onOriginResponse` | After the origin answers, before caching | Change the response that gets cached |

`onRequest` can answer by itself, for example with a 401, so the request never reaches the cache or the origin. Keep
business logic and database access in the origin: edge functions deploy to every location and are harder to debug.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  HttpApiGateway,
  EdgeLambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const authAtEdge = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge/auth.ts'
    })
  });

  const securityHeaders = new EdgeLambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/edge/headers.ts'
    })
  });

  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      edgeFunctions: {
        onRequest: 'authAtEdge',
        onResponse: 'securityHeaders'
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { authAtEdge, securityHeaders, myApi }
  };
});
```


> **Warning:** Stacktape uses `onOriginRequest` itself for bucket and API Gateway origins. Setting your own can break that
behavior.


Each route rewrite can run its own edge functions.

## Price class

`cloudfrontPriceClass` picks the CloudFront locations that serve your users. Fewer locations cost less per request and
are slower for users far from them.

| Price class | Locations |
|---|---|
| `PriceClass_100` | North America and Europe |
| `PriceClass_200` | Also Asia, the Middle East and Africa |
| `PriceClass_All` (default) | Everywhere, including South America and Oceania |

For users in North America and Europe, `PriceClass_100` is the cheapest with no latency cost for them.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cloudfrontPriceClass: 'PriceClass_100'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


## Firewall

`useFirewall` names a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) with `scope: 'cdn'` and
attaches it to the distribution, so blocked requests stop at CloudFront. A firewall costs about $7 a month with the
default rules plus $0.60 per million requests.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myFirewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'cdn'
  });

  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      useFirewall: 'myFirewall'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myFirewall, myApi }
  };
});
```


## Cache invalidation

Stacktape clears the whole CDN cache on every deploy, so users see the new version at once. If your file names contain
a content hash, set `disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true` to keep old files cached between deploys.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      disableInvalidationAfterDeploy: true
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


## Document defaults

The `indexDocument` and `errorDocument` properties control which files are served for root requests and error responses. The `indexDocument` defaults to `/index.html` — requests to `/` serve this file. The `errorDocument` defaults to `/404.html` — requests for missing paths return this page. These defaults are most relevant for bucket-backed CDN distributions serving static sites and SPAs.

## Configuration reference
Because CDN is configured as a nested property on a parent resource, the API reference below documents `CdnConfiguration`, not a standalone resource props type. The full configuration reference for `CdnConfiguration` and all nested types is below.


### Definition: `CdnConfiguration`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/cdn` with definition name `CdnConfiguration`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | yes | `boolean` | `false` |
| `cachingOptions` | no | `CdnCachingOptions` | - |
| `cloudfrontPriceClass` | no | `string: "PriceClass_100" \| "PriceClass_200" \| "PriceClass_All"` | `PriceClass_All` |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `defaultRoutePrefix` | no | `string` | - |
| `disableInvalidationAfterDeploy` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `edgeFunctions` | no | `EdgeFunctionsConfig` | - |
| `errorDocument` | no | `string` | `/404.html` |
| `forwardingOptions` | no | `CdnForwardingOptions` | - |
| `indexDocument` | no | `string` | `/index.html` |
| `routeRewrites` | no | `Array<CdnRouteRewrite>` | - |
| `useFirewall` | no | `string` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

CDN parameters are accessed through the parent resource using `$ResourceParam()`. Since CDN is a sub-property (not a standalone resource), you reference CDN values using the parent resource name. For example, if your HTTP API Gateway is named `myApi`, use `$ResourceParam('myApi', 'cdnUrl')` to get the CDN URL.

Available CDN parameters:

| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| `cdnDomain` | The CloudFront distribution domain name |
| `cdnUrl` | The CloudFront distribution URL |
| `cdnCustomDomains` | Custom domain value(s) for the CDN |
| `cdnCustomDomainUrls` | Custom domain URL value(s) for the CDN |
| `cdnCanonicalDomain` | The primary domain for the CDN |
| `cdnCanonicalUrl` | The primary URL for the CDN |
