# Custom domains

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/custom-domains.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/custom-domains`

A custom domain serves a resource at your own address, such as `api.example.com`, instead of the hostname AWS
generates. You need a domain you already own. With its DNS in Route 53, Stacktape finds the certificate and creates the
DNS record on every deploy. You can also [keep DNS at your current provider](#external-dns).

Without a custom domain, API Gateways, CDNs and the frontends still get an HTTPS URL from AWS, which is enough for
development stages. Load balancers don't. Stacktape serves an application load balancer, or a network load balancer's
TLS listener, on a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain that the [Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console)
provides. Without the Console, give it a custom domain or your own certificate, or the deploy stops and asks for one. A
network load balancer's TCP listeners use the AWS hostname without TLS.

## Set up the domain

Do this once per root domain and AWS region, before the first deploy that uses the domain.

1. Run `stacktape domain add` with the region you deploy to and enter the domain when it asks:

   ```bash
   stacktape domain add --region eu-west-1
   ```

   If the domain's DNS isn't in Route 53 yet, the command offers to create a hosted zone for the root domain and prints
   its name servers.

2. If the domain already serves traffic, copy its existing DNS records into the new hosted zone first (see the
   [AWS migration steps](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/migrate-dns-domain-in-use.html)).
   Then set the printed name servers at your registrar. Your registrar keeps the registration.
3. When the name servers have changed, run `stacktape domain add` again. It requests free ACM certificates in your
   region and in `us-east-1` (CDNs and AppSync use `us-east-1`) and adds their validation records to the zone.
4. Wait until the certificates show **Issued** in ACM, usually a few minutes after the validation records exist.

For a two-part root domain such as `example.com`, the certificates cover `example.com` and `*.example.com`. A wildcard
covers one level only, so for `api.dev.example.com` enter that full name in `stacktape domain add` to get a certificate
for it. The command still uses the `example.com` zone. For a longer root domain, such as `example.co.uk`, the command
requests no wildcard, so enter each hostname you use, such as `api.example.co.uk`. Check the names a certificate covers
in ACM before you deploy.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


The deploy attaches the issued certificate that covers `api.example.com` and creates the DNS record in the
`example.com` zone. Open `https://api.example.com` after the deploy finishes. If no issued certificate covers the name,
the deploy stops before changing anything and says which certificate is missing.

Write `domainName` without a protocol: `api.example.com`, not `https://api.example.com`.

To give each stage its own hostname, build the name from the stage, for example `api-staging.example.com` for staging
and `api.example.com` for production. Every hostname must be covered by a certificate.

## Supported resources

These resources take a `customDomains` list with the same three fields: `domainName`, `customCertificateArn` and
`disableDnsRecordCreation`.

| Resource | Typical hostname |
|---|---|
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `api.example.com` for Lambda APIs |
| [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway) | `realtime.example.com` |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | `app.example.com` for containers |
| [Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer) | TCP or TLS services |
| [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) | `www.example.com` in front of a bucket, a load balancer, an API or a function |

[Web services](/resources/compute/web-service), [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) and the SSR
frontends accept `customDomains` on the resource itself. [AppSync APIs](/resources/networking/appsync-api) and
[user auth pools](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) take a single `customDomain`.

One API Gateway hostname can't serve both a WebSocket API and an HTTP API. Use two names, such as `api.example.com` and
`realtime.example.com`; Stacktape rejects the config before deploying.

## TLS certificates

Leave out `customCertificateArn` and Stacktape picks the most specific certificate that covers the hostname, issued or
still pending validation: an exact match first, then a wildcard. If it picks a pending certificate, the deploy stops
until that certificate is issued, even when an issued wildcard also covers the name. Wait for validation to finish, or
set `customCertificateArn` to the issued certificate. Set `customCertificateArn` also to use a certificate you manage
yourself, for example one from a certificate authority your company requires.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    customDomains: [
      {
        domainName: 'api.example.com',
        customCertificateArn: 'arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abc-def-123'
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


The certificate must be in ACM in your AWS account and cover `domainName`. CDNs, AppSync and user pool domains need it
in `us-east-1`. API gateways and load balancers need it in the stack's region.

ACM renews DNS-validated certificates on its own while they're in use, as long as the validation records stay in DNS.
Imported certificates you renew yourself. See
[ACM renewal](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/acm/latest/userguide/dns-renewal-validation.html).

## External DNS

Keep DNS at your current provider, such as Cloudflare, when you want to keep managing records there or keep its proxy
and firewall. With `customCertificateArn` and `disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, Stacktape doesn't look for a Route 53
zone for that hostname.

1. Request a public certificate in ACM, in the region the resource needs. Include every hostname you'll serve: a
   certificate for `example.com` alone doesn't cover `app.example.com`.
2. Add the validation CNAME records that ACM shows at your DNS provider, and wait for **Issued**.
3. Set `customCertificateArn` and `disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, then deploy.
4. At your DNS provider, add a CNAME from your hostname to the AWS hostname:
   - **Load balancer**: **DNS name** in EC2 → Load Balancers.
   - **API Gateway**: **API Gateway domain name** in API Gateway → Custom domain names.
   - **CDN**: the CloudFront distribution's domain name.

A plain CNAME doesn't work on the bare `example.com`. Use your provider's ALIAS record or CNAME flattening there.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, ApplicationLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myAlb = new ApplicationLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [
      {
        domainName: 'app.example.com',
        customCertificateArn: 'arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abc-def-123',
        disableDnsRecordCreation: true
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myAlb }
  };
});
```


For a user pool domain, the parent domain needs an
[A record](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/cognito-user-pools-add-custom-domain.html) before
the deploy; point the CNAME at the alias target Cognito shows. For AppSync, use the target AppSync shows.

If you bought the domain through Cloudflare Registrar, its DNS must stay at Cloudflare, so use this external DNS path.

## Multiple domains

A resource can serve several hostnames. Each entry has its own certificate and DNS settings:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    customDomains: [
      { domainName: 'api.example.com' },
      { domainName: 'api.mycompany.io' },
      {
        domainName: 'api-legacy.example.com',
        customCertificateArn: 'arn:aws:acm:eu-west-1:123456789012:certificate/abc-def-456',
        disableDnsRecordCreation: true
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


Stacktape uses one hosted zone per root domain. Here `api.example.com` uses the `example.com` zone, and
`api.mycompany.io` needs a `mycompany.io` zone with its own `stacktape domain add` setup. `api-legacy.example.com` uses
external DNS, so Stacktape creates no record for it.

To send different paths of one hostname to different backends, attach the domain to one
[Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) or
[HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) and route by path there.

## Cost

A Route 53 hosted zone costs $0.50 a month, plus $0.40 per million DNS queries. Queries for alias records that point
at AWS resources are free. ACM public certificates are free. See
[Route 53 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/route53/pricing/).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `DomainConfiguration`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/helpers` with definition name `DomainConfiguration`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `domainName` | yes | `string` | - |
| `customCertificateArn` | no | `string` | - |
| `disableDnsRecordCreation` | no | `boolean` | `false` |

---

# HTTP API Gateway

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/http-api-gateway.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/http-api-gateway`

An HTTP API Gateway is a public HTTPS endpoint, run by AWS API Gateway (HTTP API), that routes requests to
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) and container workloads. It costs $1 per million requests in
us-east-1 and nothing when idle, which makes it the default entry point for APIs. [Web services](/resources/compute/web-service)
use one by default too.

An integration must answer within 30 seconds and a request or response can be at most 10 MB. For long-lived
connections use a [WebSocket API Gateway](/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway), and for TCP use a
[Network Load Balancer](/resources/networking/network-load-balancer).

## Basic example

The gateway itself holds no routes. Each function or container declares the method and path it serves, with an
[HTTP trigger](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) that names the gateway.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  HttpApiGateway,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const getUsers = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handlers/users.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new HttpApiIntegration({
        httpApiGatewayName: 'myApi',
        method: 'GET',
        path: '/users'
      })
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi, getUsers }
  };
});
```


The deploy prints the gateway URL (`https://<api-id>.execute-api.<region>.amazonaws.com`). `GET /users` on it now
invokes `getUsers`. In the config, `$ResourceParam('myApi', 'url')` gives the same URL.

## Routing

A gateway serves routes from any number of functions and containers. Each integration sets a `method` (`GET`, `POST`,
`PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS` or `*` for any) and a `path`:

| Pattern | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Exact | `/users` | Only `/users` |
| Parameter | `/users/{id}` | `/users/123`, with `id` in `event.pathParameters` |
| Greedy | `/api/{proxy+}` | Everything under `/api/` |

The most specific route wins, so exact paths beat greedy ones. A container integration also needs `containerPort`.
Each integration can have its own authorizer (a Cognito user pool, a Lambda function or IAM), which runs before your code. See
[HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) for integration and authorizer options.

### One function for all routes

When a framework such as Hono, Express or FastAPI does the routing, send every request to one function:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  HttpApiGateway,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/api.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new HttpApiIntegration({
        httpApiGatewayName: 'myApi',
        method: '*',
        path: '/{proxy+}'
      })
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi, api }
  };
});
```


## Choosing between HTTP API Gateway and a load balancer

An [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) costs a fixed $0.0225 an hour (about
$16 a month) plus load balancer capacity units (LCUs, $0.008 each per hour) that grow with new connections, active
connections, traffic and rule evaluations. An HTTP API Gateway costs $1 per million requests. Monthly cost in
us-east-1 for small (2 KB) requests at a steady rate, each on a new connection
([API Gateway pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/pricing/),
[Elastic Load Balancing pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing/)):

| Requests per month | HTTP API Gateway | Application Load Balancer |
|---|---|---|
| 1 million | $1 | about $17 |
| 10 million | $10 | about $17 |
| 50 million | $50 | about $21 |
| 200 million | $200 | about $34 |

The load balancer gets cheaper from about 20 million requests a month. Bursty traffic and large responses add LCUs, and
connections that clients reuse remove them. Cost isn't the only difference: a load balancer also routes by header,
query string and source IP, keeps WebSocket connections to containers and has no 30-second limit, while the gateway
has per-route authorizers and scales to zero cost.

## CORS

CORS lets a browser app on another origin call your API. With CORS on, the gateway answers preflight `OPTIONS`
requests itself and replaces any CORS headers your code sets.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cors: {
      enabled: true,
      allowedOrigins: ['https://myapp.com', 'https://staging.myapp.com'],
      allowCredentials: true,
      maxAge: 86400
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


`enabled: true` alone allows every origin. Allowed methods come from the routes on the gateway, so you rarely set them.
`allowCredentials: true` is needed when the browser sends cookies or an `Authorization` header, and then you must list
the origins instead of using `*`. `maxAge` sets how long browsers cache the preflight answer, in seconds.

Server-side callers, mobile apps and same-origin frontends don't need CORS.

## Custom domains

After you [set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add`,
attach it to the gateway:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'api.example.com' }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


The deploy uses the issued certificate that covers `api.example.com` and creates the DNS record. To keep DNS at
another provider, see [External DNS](/resources/networking/custom-domains#external-dns).

## CDN

`cdn.enabled: true` puts a CloudFront distribution in front of the gateway. It helps when the API returns cacheable
public data or users are far from your region. For personalized responses it only adds CloudFront charges.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      cloudfrontPriceClass: 'PriceClass_100'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


`cloudfrontPriceClass` picks the CloudFront locations: `PriceClass_100` (North America and Europe, the cheapest),
`PriceClass_200` or `PriceClass_All`. See [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn) for caching and routing options.

## Firewall

The gateway has no firewall setting of its own. Enable `cdn` and attach a
[web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) to the CDN, or use an Application Load
Balancer with `useFirewall`.

## Access logging

The gateway logs every request (request ID, client IP, method, path, status, response size) and keeps the logs for 30
days. Read them with [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    logging: {
      format: 'JSON',
      retentionDays: 90
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


`format` is `JSON` by default; `CLF`, `XML` and `CSV` are also accepted. `retentionDays` takes the CloudWatch values (1,
3, 5, 7, 14, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180, 365, 400, 545, 731, 1827 or 3653). `logging.disabled: true` turns logging off,
and [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding) sends logs to another service.

## Payload format

The payload format is the shape of the event a function receives. Integrations use `1.0` unless you set `payloadFormat`
on the gateway or on the integration. `2.0` has a flatter event and is what AWS recommends for new code; Hono's Lambda
adapter handles both. All HTTP events of one function must use the same format.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    payloadFormat: '2.0'
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


## Alarms

Gateway alarms use the `http-api-gateway-error-rate` (share of 4xx and 5xx responses) and `http-api-gateway-latency`
triggers.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, HttpApiGateway } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const myApi = new HttpApiGateway({
    alarms: [
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'http-api-gateway-error-rate',
          properties: { thresholdPercent: 5 }
        }
      },
      {
        trigger: {
          type: 'http-api-gateway-latency',
          properties: {
            thresholdMilliseconds: 3000,
            statistic: 'p95'
          }
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { myApi }
  };
});
```


The error-rate alarm fires above 5%, the latency alarm when p95 latency is above 3,000 ms. `statistic` applies to
latency only (`avg` by default). See [Alarms](/observability/alarms) for `evaluation` settings, comparison operators
and notification channels.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `HttpApiGatewayProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/http-api-gateway` with definition name `HttpApiGatewayProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alarms` | no | `Array<HttpApiGatewayAlarm>` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `CdnConfiguration` | - |
| `cors` | no | `HttpApiCorsConfig` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `Array<DomainConfiguration>` | - |
| `disabledGlobalAlarms` | no | `Array<string>` | - |
| `logging` | no | `HttpApiAccessLogsConfig` | - |
| `payloadFormat` | no | `string: "1.0" \| "2.0"` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `http-api-gateway`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `domain` | Default domain name | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "domain")` |
| `url` | Default URL | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "url")` |
| `customDomains` | Comma-separated list of custom domain names assigned to the HTTP Api Gateway (only available if you use [custom domain names](/resources/networking/custom-domains/)) | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "customDomains")` |
| `customDomainUrls` | Comma-separated list of custom domain name URLs (only available if you use [custom domain names](/resources/networking/custom-domains/)) | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "customDomainUrls")` |
| `customDomainUrl` | URL of the first custom domain name connected to this resource (only available if you use [custom domain names](/resources/networking/custom-domains/)) | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "customDomainUrl")` |
| `cdnDomain` | Default domain of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnDomain")` |
| `cdnUrl` | Default url of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnUrl")` |

| `cdnCustomDomainUrls` | Comma-separated list of custom domain name URLs of the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomainUrls")` |

# Network Load Balancer

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/network-load-balancer.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/network-load-balancer`

A Network Load Balancer (AWS NLB) accepts TCP or TLS connections on the ports you list and passes them to container
workloads, without looking at HTTP. Use it for MQTT brokers, game servers, database proxies, gRPC with your own TLS or
any other non-HTTP protocol.

It costs $0.0225 an hour (about $16 a month in us-east-1) even with no traffic, plus $0.006 per capacity unit-hour as
connections and traffic grow ([Elastic Load Balancing pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing/)).
For HTTP, an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) routes by path and host and
takes a CDN and a firewall, which a Network Load Balancer can't.

## Basic example

A Network Load Balancer needs at least one listener; there is no default.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const tcpLb = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    listeners: [{ protocol: 'TCP', port: 5432 }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { tcpLb }
  };
});
```


This load balancer is reachable from the internet (`interface: 'internet'` is the default) and accepts TCP on port
5432. A container receives the connections with a `network-load-balancer` event that names the load balancer
(`loadBalancerName`), the listener (`listenerPort`) and its own port (`containerPort`). A
[web service](/resources/compute/web-service) with `loadBalancing.type: 'network-load-balancer'` creates its own.

## Listeners

Each listener has a `protocol` and a `port`:

- **TCP** passes connections through as they are. Use it when your app handles TLS itself, including mutual TLS or
  when it needs the client certificate.
- **TLS** decrypts at the load balancer and passes plain traffic to the container, so your app needs no certificate.
  The certificate comes from `customDomains` or from the listener's `customCertificateArns`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const mqttBroker = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'mqtt.example.com' }],
    listeners: [
      { protocol: 'TCP', port: 1883 },
      { protocol: 'TLS', port: 8883 }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { mqttBroker }
  };
});
```


This load balancer takes plain MQTT on 1883 and MQTT over TLS on 8883. Each listener can have its own certificates and
IP allowlist.

Without `customDomains`, give a TLS listener your own ACM certificate:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const grpcLb = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    listeners: [
      {
        protocol: 'TLS',
        port: 443,
        customCertificateArns: ['arn:aws:acm:us-east-1:123456789:certificate/abc-123']
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { grpcLb }
  };
});
```


A TLS listener with neither gets a `*.stacktape-app.com` domain from the
[Stacktape Console](/getting-started/add-the-console); without the Console connected, the deploy stops and asks for a
domain or certificate.

## Custom domains

[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add`, then list it.
The deploy uses the issued certificate for the TLS listeners and creates the DNS record.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const tcpLb = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    customDomains: [{ domainName: 'tcp.example.com' }, { domainName: 'mqtt.example.com' }],
    listeners: [{ protocol: 'TLS', port: 8883 }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { tcpLb }
  };
});
```


To keep DNS at another provider, set `disableDnsRecordCreation: true` and `customCertificateArn`; see
[External DNS](/resources/networking/custom-domains#external-dns).

## Access control

### Internet vs internal

`interface: 'internal'` makes the load balancer reachable only from inside the VPC, for example for an internal gRPC
service.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const internalLb = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    interface: 'internal',
    listeners: [{ protocol: 'TCP', port: 50051 }]
  });

  return {
    resources: { internalLb }
  };
});
```


### IP whitelisting

`whitelistIps` on a listener accepts connections only from the listed addresses and ranges. Each listener has its own
list.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, NetworkLoadBalancer } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const dbProxy = new NetworkLoadBalancer({
    listeners: [
      {
        protocol: 'TCP',
        port: 5432,
        whitelistIps: ['203.0.113.0/24', '198.51.100.42/32']
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { dbProxy }
  };
});
```


A Network Load Balancer can't take a [firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall), so this allowlist is
the only filter at the load balancer. For rate limits or geo-blocking, use an Application Load Balancer.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `NetworkLoadBalancerProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/network-load-balancer` with definition name `NetworkLoadBalancerProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `listeners` | yes | `Array<NetworkLoadBalancerListener>` | - |
| `customDomains` | no | `option-1 \| option-2` | - |
| `interface` | no | `string: "internal" \| "internet"` | `internet` |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `network-load-balancer`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `domain` | default domain name of load balancer | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "domain")` |
| `customDomains` | Comma-separated list of custom domain names assigned to the Load balancer (only available if you use [custom domain names](/resources/networking/custom-domains/)) | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "customDomains")` |

# WebSocket API Gateway

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway.mdx`
Route: `/resources/networking/websocket-api-gateway`

A WebSocket API Gateway is a `wss://` endpoint, run by AWS API Gateway, whose routes are Lambda functions: `$connect`,
`$disconnect`, `$default` and your own, such as `sendMessage`. It suits chat, live notifications, job progress and
presence without an always-on server. Stacktape creates the API, the routes, the permissions to send to connections,
and the access logs.

You pay $1 per million messages (32 KB each) and $0.25 per million connection-minutes in us-east-1, and nothing while
idle ([API Gateway pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/pricing/)). If you already run a WebSocket server such
as Socket.IO in a container, put it behind an [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer)
instead.

Clients pick a route with the `action` field of a JSON message: `{ "action": "sendMessage", "text": "hello" }` invokes
the function that owns `sendMessage`.

## Basic example

Routes live on the functions, not on the gateway. Route handlers get the gateway's variables and permission to send to
its connections without `connectTo`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  WebSocketApiGateway,
  WebSocketApiIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const realtime = new WebSocketApiGateway({});

  const connections = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/connections.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new WebSocketApiIntegration({
        websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
        routeKey: '$connect'
      }),
      new WebSocketApiIntegration({
        websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
        routeKey: '$disconnect'
      })
    ]
  });

  const messages = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/messages.ts'
    }),
    events: [
      new WebSocketApiIntegration({
        websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
        routeKey: 'sendMessage'
      }),
      new WebSocketApiIntegration({
        websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
        routeKey: '$default'
      })
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { realtime, connections, messages } };
});
```


Example (YAML):

```yaml
resources:
  realtime:
    type: websocket-api-gateway

  connections:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/connections.ts
      events:
        - type: websocket-api-gateway
          properties:
            websocketApiGatewayName: realtime
            routeKey: $connect
        - type: websocket-api-gateway
          properties:
            websocketApiGatewayName: realtime
            routeKey: $disconnect

  messages:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: ./src/messages.ts
      events:
        - type: websocket-api-gateway
          properties:
            websocketApiGatewayName: realtime
            routeKey: sendMessage
        - type: websocket-api-gateway
          properties:
            websocketApiGatewayName: realtime
            routeKey: $default
```


The deploy prints the `wss://` URL. Connect to it with any WebSocket client, for example `npx wscat -c <url>`, and send
`{"action":"sendMessage","text":"hello"}`. Route changes deploy with the stack; there is no API Gateway stage to manage.

## Route behavior

| Route | When it runs |
|---|---|
| `$connect` | During the opening handshake. Returning an error rejects the connection. |
| `$disconnect` | After a connection closes. Delivery is best-effort and is not guaranteed. |
| `$default` | When no custom route matches, including messages that cannot be selected. |
| Custom key | When the route selection expression resolves to that key. |

Only JSON messages can be selected by `$request.body.action`. Non-JSON messages and JSON without a matching action go to `$default` when that route exists.

Route handler return bodies are not sent to the client by default. Use `returnResponse: true` for a simple reply to the calling client, as described below. Use the API Gateway Management API when the application should send later, broadcast, or target a different connection.

## Sending a message to a connection

For a gateway named `realtime`, every route handler receives:

- `STP_REALTIME_URL`: the public `wss://` client URL
- `STP_REALTIME_MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT`: the HTTPS endpoint for `ApiGatewayManagementApiClient`
- `STP_REALTIME_API_ID`: the API ID
- `STP_REALTIME_CANONICAL_DOMAIN`: the AWS DNS target

The handler also gets connection-management permission scoped to this gateway and Stacktape's managed stage.

```ts
import {
  ApiGatewayManagementApiClient,
  PostToConnectionCommand
} from '@aws-sdk/client-apigatewaymanagementapi';

const client = new ApiGatewayManagementApiClient({
  endpoint: process.env.STP_REALTIME_MANAGEMENT_ENDPOINT
});

export default async (event) => {
  await client.send(
    new PostToConnectionCommand({
      ConnectionId: event.requestContext.connectionId,
      Data: Buffer.from(JSON.stringify({ type: 'ack' }))
    })
  );

  return { statusCode: 200 };
};
```

Do not post to the connection from `$connect`: the connection does not exist until that handler succeeds. Handle `GoneException` when a connection has already closed.

Other producers can send to clients too. Add `connectTo: [realtime]` to a different Lambda, container workload, batch job, or script to receive the same scoped permission and environment variables. The permission covers `PostToConnection`, `GetConnection` and `DeleteConnection` on every connection of the gateway's stage.

## Connection storage and broadcasts

Stacktape does not create a DynamoDB connection registry automatically. A direct reply needs only the `connectionId` in the current event, while broadcast, rooms, and user-to-connection lookup each need different application data. An automatic table would impose the wrong schema on many applications.

When you need lookup or broadcast:

1. Add a normal [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb) for the fields your application needs.
2. Connect the `$connect`, `$disconnect`, and broadcasting workloads to that table with `connectTo`.
3. Store connection IDs with a TTL.
4. Delete stale records when a Management API send returns `GoneException`.

TTL and failed-send cleanup matter because `$disconnect` is best-effort and may not run.

## Authorization

Authorization is optional and belongs on the `$connect` route because API Gateway authorizes a WebSocket connection only while opening it. Later messages use the identity established at connection time and any checks in your application code.

For application-specific authentication, use a Lambda REQUEST authorizer:

```ts
const connect = new LambdaFunction({
  packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
    entryfilePath: './src/connect.ts'
  }),
  events: [
    new WebSocketApiIntegration({
      websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
      routeKey: '$connect',
      authorizer: {
        type: 'lambda',
        properties: {
          functionName: authorizeConnection
        }
      }
    })
  ]
});
```

The default identity source is `route.request.header.Authorization`. You can explicitly use header or query-string sources such as `route.request.querystring.token`. A WebSocket Lambda authorizer returns an IAM policy response; the HTTP API simple-response and JWT/Cognito authorizer settings do not apply.

Use `{ type: 'aws-iam' }` only for clients that can sign the opening request with AWS Signature Version 4. It is usually unsuitable for ordinary browser clients.

## Return a response to the calling client

WebSocket routes are one-way by default. For a simple request-response interaction on `$default` or a custom message route, set `returnResponse: true` and return a `body` from the Lambda handler:

```ts
new WebSocketApiIntegration({
  websocketApiGatewayName: realtime,
  routeKey: 'getStatus',
  returnResponse: true
});
```

```ts
export default async () => ({
  statusCode: 200,
  body: JSON.stringify({ status: 'ready' })
});
```

Stacktape configures the API Gateway route response, and only the client that invoked the route receives the returned body. Lifecycle routes (`$connect` and `$disconnect`) cannot use `returnResponse`, because no established calling connection is available for that reply. Keep the default for broadcasts, delayed responses, and messages sent to a different connection; use the management endpoint for those cases.

## Custom domains

Add `customDomains` when clients should connect through your own hostname:

```ts
const realtime = new WebSocketApiGateway({
  customDomains: [{ domainName: 'realtime.example.com' }]
});
```

[Set up the domain](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) with `stacktape domain add` first, so an
issued certificate for the hostname exists in the stack's region. The deploy then creates the domain mapping and the
Route 53 record. For DNS or certificates you manage elsewhere, use `disableDnsRecordCreation` or
`customCertificateArn`; see [Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains#external-dns).

One API Gateway hostname can't serve both a WebSocket API and an HTTP API, so give each its own name. Stacktape rejects
the config before deploying.

## Logs

JSON access logs are enabled by default with connection ID, event type, route, status, source IP, request time, and integration error context. Payload data is not logged by default. Configure retention or forwarding through `logging`, or set `logging.disabled: true`.

API Gateway needs a CloudWatch Logs role in the account's API Gateway settings to write these logs, and new accounts
have none. Before the deploy, Stacktape checks the region's setting. If no role is set, it creates the IAM role
`stacktape-api-gateway-cloudwatch-logs` (one per account, with the AWS managed policy
`AmazonAPIGatewayPushToCloudWatchLogs`), registers it and says so. It never replaces a role that is already set; if
that role was deleted, the deploy stops and says so.

Restricted deployer roles need `apigateway:GET` on `/account` for the check (without it, Stacktape warns and deploys),
and `iam:GetRole`, `iam:CreateRole`, `iam:AttachRolePolicy`, `iam:PassRole` on the role and `apigateway:PATCH` on
`/account` to register it.

`logging.logClass: 'infrequent-access'` lowers the ingestion price for new log groups. Those logs can be read only with
Logs Insights and can't be forwarded.

## Dev mode

`stacktape dev` keeps the WebSocket gateway deployed and hot-swaps its Lambda handlers. Dev stages have no access logs. The dev UI shows the deployed `wss://` URL. Stacktape does not emulate API Gateway's connection lifecycle locally, so test clients continue to use the deployed endpoint while code changes are updated quickly.

## AWS limits to design around

API Gateway currently limits a connection to 2 hours with a 10-minute idle timeout. Frames are limited to 32 KB, messages to 128 KB, binary frames are unsupported, and integrations can run for at most 29 seconds. Split large payloads and design clients to reconnect.

### Definition: `WebSocketApiGatewayProps`

| Property | Required | Type | Default |

# State machine

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/orchestration/state-machine.mdx`
Route: `/resources/orchestration/state-machine`

A state machine is an AWS Step Functions workflow: steps that call your Lambda functions and other AWS services, with
branching, retries, parallel branches and loops defined in [Amazon States Language](https://states-language.net/spec.html)
(ASL) instead of code. Each execution has a visible history, and a standard workflow can run for up to a year.

Standard workflows cost $0.025 per 1,000 state transitions in us-east-1, with 4,000 free each month
([Step Functions pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/pricing/)), and nothing while idle. For one step after
another without branching or retries, a Lambda function with an [SQS trigger](/resources/triggers/sqs-events) is
simpler and cheaper.

## Basic example

Two [Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function) in one workflow: it validates an order, branches on the
result, and either processes the order or fails.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  StateMachine,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  $ResourceParam
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const validateOrder = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/validate-order.ts' })
  });

  const processOrder = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/process-order.ts' }),
    timeout: 60
  });

  const orderWorkflow = new StateMachine({
    definition: {
      Comment: 'Order processing workflow',
      StartAt: 'ValidateOrder',
      States: {
        ValidateOrder: {
          Type: 'Task',
          Resource: $ResourceParam('validateOrder', 'arn'),
          Next: 'CheckValidity',
          Catch: [{ ErrorEquals: ['States.ALL'], Next: 'OrderFailed' }]
        },
        CheckValidity: {
          Type: 'Choice',
          Choices: [{ Variable: '$.valid', BooleanEquals: true, Next: 'ProcessOrder' }],
          Default: 'OrderFailed'
        },
        ProcessOrder: {
          Type: 'Task',
          Resource: $ResourceParam('processOrder', 'arn'),
          Retry: [
            {
              ErrorEquals: ['States.TaskFailed'],
              IntervalSeconds: 3,
              MaxAttempts: 2,
              BackoffRate: 2
            }
          ],
          End: true
        },
        OrderFailed: {
          Type: 'Fail',
          Error: 'OrderProcessingFailed',
          Cause: 'Validation or processing failed'
        }
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { validateOrder, processOrder, orderWorkflow }
  };
});
```


`StartAt` names the first state and `States` lists them. Each state has a `Type` and moves on with `Next` or ends with
`End: true`; `Succeed` and `Fail` end the execution by themselves. A Task state names its function with
`$ResourceParam('validateOrder', 'arn')`, which becomes the function's ARN at deploy time.

After the deploy, start an execution in the AWS console (**Step Functions → your state machine → Start execution**)
with input such as `{"orderId": "42"}`, and watch each step's input and output in the execution graph.

## Workflow definition

`definition` is an ASL workflow: `StartAt`, `States`, and optionally `Comment`, `Version` and `TimeoutSeconds`.

### State types

Stacktape checks eight ASL state types:

| State type | Purpose | Key properties |
|---|---|---|
| **Task** | Invokes a Lambda function or another supported ASL task target | `Resource`, `Retry`, `Catch`, `TimeoutSeconds`, `HeartbeatSeconds`, `Parameters` |
| **Choice** | Branches based on input conditions | `Choices` (condition rules), `Default` (fallback state) |
| **Parallel** | Runs multiple branches concurrently, waits for all to complete | `Branches` (each a `StartAt`/`States` workflow), `Retry`, `Catch` |
| **Map** | Iterates over an array, running a sub-workflow per item | `ItemProcessor` (or the older `Iterator`), `ItemsPath`, `MaxConcurrency` |
| **Wait** | Pauses execution for a duration or until a timestamp | `Seconds`, `Timestamp`, `SecondsPath`, `TimestampPath` |
| **Pass** | Passes input to output, optionally injecting or transforming data | `Result`, `Parameters`, `ResultPath` |
| **Succeed** | Marks successful completion — terminates the workflow | — |
| **Fail** | Terminates execution with an error | `Error`, `Cause` |

Stacktape checks the state types and the fields listed above. Other ASL fields, such as `QueryLanguage`, `Arguments` or `Assign`, are passed to AWS unchanged, and a path set to `null` (for example `OutputPath: null`) is kept.

### Permissions of the workflow

The workflow runs with one IAM role that Stacktape creates for all state machines in the stack. It can:

- invoke Lambda functions of this stack,
- read and write DynamoDB items, publish to SNS, send to SQS,
- run ECS tasks, submit AWS Batch jobs and run Glue jobs.

A Task that calls another service, for example S3, Bedrock or another state machine, fails at run time with an access
error. Call that service from a Lambda function task instead, and give the function the permission with
`iamRoleStatements`. This role is separate from the role of the code that starts executions; see
[Starting executions](#starting-executions).

### Referencing Lambda functions

Task states use the `Resource` property to identify a Lambda function or another supported ASL task target. For a function in the same config, use the [`$ResourceParam` directive](/configuration/directives) with the function's resource name and its `arn` parameter. Stacktape resolves it to the function's ARN at deploy time.

```yaml
resources:
  scoreReceipt:
    type: function
    properties:
      packaging:
        type: js-bundle
        properties:
          entryfilePath: src/score-receipt.ts
  approvalWorkflow:
    type: state-machine
    properties:
      definition:
        StartAt: ScoreReceipt
        States:
          ScoreReceipt:
            Type: Task
            Resource: $ResourceParam('scoreReceipt', 'arn')
            End: true
```

Use a plain string when you already have a concrete Task `Resource` value, such as the ARN of a function outside this config or an [ASL service integration](https://states-language.net/spec.html) URI. An object with a CloudFormation intrinsic function, such as `Fn::GetAtt`, also works when you need one.

### Workflow timeout

A standard workflow can run for up to a year and bills every transition. Set `TimeoutSeconds` at the top of the
definition for any workflow that should finish in minutes or hours, and on Task states to bound one step.
`HeartbeatSeconds` makes a long task report progress.

## Error handling

AWS Step Functions provides built-in error handling through `Retry` and `Catch` blocks on Task, Parallel, and Map states. This replaces the need for custom retry logic in your Lambda function code and gives you a declarative way to handle failures at the orchestration layer.

**Retry** accepts an array of rules, each specifying which errors to match (`ErrorEquals`), the initial delay (`IntervalSeconds`), maximum attempts (`MaxAttempts`), and backoff multiplier (`BackoffRate`). Multiple retry rules are evaluated in order — the first matching rule is used.

**Catch** routes to a fallback state when all retries are exhausted or for errors not covered by retry rules. Each catch rule matches error types (`ErrorEquals`) and redirects to a named state (`Next`). This lets you build graceful degradation paths, for example notifying a support team when payment processing fails after retries.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  StateMachine,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  $ResourceParam
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const chargePayment = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/charge.ts' }),
    timeout: 60
  });

  const notifySupport = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/notify-support.ts' })
  });
  const paymentWorkflow = new StateMachine({
    definition: {
      StartAt: 'ChargePayment',
      States: {
        ChargePayment: {
          Type: 'Task',
          Resource: $ResourceParam('chargePayment', 'arn'),
          Retry: [
            {
              ErrorEquals: ['States.TaskFailed'],
              IntervalSeconds: 5,
              MaxAttempts: 3,
              BackoffRate: 2
            }
          ],
          Catch: [
            {
              ErrorEquals: ['States.ALL'],
              Next: 'NotifySupport'
            }
          ],
          Next: 'PaymentComplete'
        },
        NotifySupport: {
          Type: 'Task',
          Resource: $ResourceParam('notifySupport', 'arn'),
          Next: 'PaymentFailed'
        },
        PaymentFailed: {
          Type: 'Fail',
          Error: 'PaymentError',
          Cause: 'Payment failed after 3 retries'
        },
        PaymentComplete: {
          Type: 'Succeed'
        }
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { chargePayment, notifySupport, paymentWorkflow }
  };
});
```


In this example, `ChargePayment` retries up to 3 times on failure with exponential backoff (5s, 10s, 20s). If all retries fail, `Catch` redirects to `NotifySupport`, which alerts the support team before the workflow terminates with a `Fail` state. Without the retry block, any transient error would immediately fail the workflow.

Retry and Catch match error strings in `ErrorEquals`. Common ASL error names include `States.ALL`, `States.TaskFailed`, `States.Timeout`, and `States.HeartbeatTimeout`. You can also match custom error strings thrown by your Lambda functions. See the [ASL specification](https://states-language.net/spec.html) for the complete list and matching rules.

## Starting executions

To start executions from your code, add the state machine to the workload's
[`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources). The workload's role can then start, stop and describe executions,
and it gets `STP_ORDER_WORKFLOW_ARN` and `STP_ORDER_WORKFLOW_NAME`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  StateMachine,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging,
  $ResourceParam
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const processOrder = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/process-order.ts' })
  });

  const orderWorkflow = new StateMachine({
    definition: {
      StartAt: 'ProcessOrder',
      States: {
        ProcessOrder: {
          Type: 'Task',
          Resource: $ResourceParam('processOrder', 'arn'),
          End: true
        }
      }
    }
  });
  const startOrder = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/start-order.ts' }),
    connectTo: [orderWorkflow]
  });

  return {
    resources: { processOrder, orderWorkflow, startOrder }
  };
});
```


Use the ARN in your handler to start executions:

```typescript
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { handle } from 'hono/aws-lambda';
import { SFNClient, StartExecutionCommand, DescribeExecutionCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-sfn';

const sfn = new SFNClient({});
const stateMachineArn = process.env.STP_ORDER_WORKFLOW_ARN!;

const app = new Hono();

app.post('/orders', async (c) => {
  const input = await c.req.text() || '{}';
  const result = await sfn.send(
    new StartExecutionCommand({ stateMachineArn, input })
  );
  return c.json({ executionArn: result.executionArn }, 202);
});

app.get('/orders/status/:executionArn{.+}', async (c) => {
  const executionArn = decodeURIComponent(c.req.param('executionArn'));
  const result = await sfn.send(new DescribeExecutionCommand({ executionArn }));
  return c.json({
    status: result.status,
    output: result.output ? JSON.parse(result.output) : null
  });
});

export default handle(app);
```

The `POST` route starts an execution and returns its ARN; the `GET` route reports its status and output. Attach
`startOrder` to an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) to call them.

## Express workflows and other settings

The resource exposes only `definition`. Set anything else, such as the workflow type or logging, with
[overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches) of the `AWS::StepFunctions::StateMachine` child resource.

An Express workflow suits high-volume, short work: it runs for at most five minutes and bills per request and duration
instead of per transition. [`stacktape synth`](/cli/synth) shows the child resource's logical name; the example assumes
`OrderWorkflowStateMachine`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, StateMachine } from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const orderWorkflow = new StateMachine({
    definition: {
      StartAt: 'Process',
      States: {
        Process: { Type: 'Pass', End: true }
      }
    },
    overrides: {
      OrderWorkflowStateMachine: {
        StateMachineType: 'EXPRESS'
      }
    }
  });

  return { resources: { orderWorkflow } };
});
```

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/state-machine` with definition name `StateMachineProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `definition` | yes | `StateMachineDefinition` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `state-machine`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arn` | Arn of the state machine. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `name` | AWS (physical) name of the state machine. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "name")` |
