# Bastion host

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/security/bastion-host.mdx`
Route: `/resources/security/bastion-host`

A bastion host is a small EC2 instance in your stack's VPC that lets you reach private resources from your machine:
[relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis) and other
services that accept VPC connections only. You connect through AWS Systems Manager, so there are no SSH keys and no
open SSH port.

It runs all the time. In us-east-1 the default `t3.micro` costs about $7.60 a month, plus about $3.65 for its public
IPv4 address and a few cents for its disk ([EC2 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/on-demand/)). For a
database that's open to the internet, you don't need one.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bastion } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const bastion = new Bastion({});

  return {
    resources: { bastion }
  };
});
```


The deploy starts one Amazon Linux 2023 instance in a public subnet. Nothing on the internet can connect to it; Systems Manager
sessions go out from the instance.

Open a tunnel from your machine to a private database:

```bash
stacktape bastion tunnel mainDatabase --stage production
```

The command prints a `localhost` address for each endpoint of the resource. Point `psql`, DBeaver, TablePlus or your
ORM at it and keep the command running while you work. A Redis cache with a reader endpoint gets two local ports.

## Connecting to private resources

[`bastion tunnel`](/cli/bastion-tunnel) forwards local ports to one resource. It works with
[relational databases](/resources/databases/relational-database), [Redis caches](/resources/databases/redis),
[MongoDB Atlas clusters](/resources/databases/mongodb-atlas),
[application load balancers](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) and
[private services](/resources/compute/private-service) behind a load balancer.

[`bastion shell`](/cli/bastion-session) opens a shell on the instance itself:

```bash
stacktape bastion shell --stage production
```

With several bastions in one stack, pick one with `--bastion-resource`. For a one-off query, `stacktape query sql` and
`stacktape query redis` take `--bastion-resource` too and need no tunnel.

## Scripts

Two [script](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) types use a bastion, for example to run migrations from a hook against a
private database:

- **`local-script-with-bastion-tunneling`** runs on your machine and routes its connections through the bastion. The
  `connectTo` variables it gets point at the tunnel, so the script needs no changes.
- **`bastion-script`** runs the commands on the bastion instance and streams the output to your terminal.

Both take `bastionResource` when the stack has more than one bastion.

## Instance size

`instanceSize` is `t3.micro` by default, which is enough for tunnels and admin work. Pick a larger size only if you run
heavy scripts on the bastion.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bastion } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const bastion = new Bastion({
    instanceSize: 't3.small'
  });

  return {
    resources: { bastion }
  };
});
```


## Startup commands

`runCommandsAtLaunch` runs commands as root when the instance starts, for example to install database clients. The
instance runs Amazon Linux 2023, so use `dnf` or `yum`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bastion } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const bastion = new Bastion({
    runCommandsAtLaunch: ['yum install -y postgresql15', 'yum install -y redis6']
  });

  return {
    resources: { bastion }
  };
});
```


> **Warning:** Changing `runCommandsAtLaunch` replaces the instance on the next deploy, and files on the old one are lost. Don't keep
anything on the bastion you can't recreate.


## Logging

The bastion sends three system logs to CloudWatch, each with its own retention:

| Log type | Source | Default retention | Contains |
|---|---|---|---|
| `messages` | `/var/log/messages` | 30 days | Startup, kernel and service messages |
| `secure` | `/var/log/secure` | 180 days | Sign-ins and authentication events |
| `audit` | `/var/log/audit/audit.log` | 365 days | Linux audit events |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bastion } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const bastion = new Bastion({
    logging: {
      messages: { retentionDays: 14 },
      secure: { retentionDays: 365 },
      audit: { disabled: true }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { bastion }
  };
});
```


Keep `secure` and `audit` longer when you need an audit trail, and shorten or turn them off for development stacks.
Each log type also supports [log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `BastionProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/bastion` with definition name `BastionProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `instanceSize` | no | `string` | `t3.micro` |
| `logging` | no | `BastionLoggingConfig` | - |
| `runCommandsAtLaunch` | no | `Array<string>` | - |

---

# User authentication pool

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/security/user-auth-pool.mdx`
Route: `/resources/security/user-auth-pool`

A user authentication pool is an Amazon Cognito user pool: sign-up, sign-in, password reset, email or phone
verification, MFA, social and enterprise sign-in (Google, Facebook, Apple, SAML, OIDC) and OAuth 2.0. It issues JWTs
that an [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) can check on every request, so your code gets only
signed-in users.

New pools use Cognito's Essentials tier: the first 10,000 monthly active users are free, then $0.015 per user in
us-east-1. Users who sign in through SAML or OIDC have a separate free allowance of 50
([Cognito pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/cognito/pricing/)).

Stacktape configures password, email or phone, MFA, social and enterprise sign-in. Passkeys and other passwordless
sign-in that Cognito offers aren't Stacktape settings; set them with [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches)
or pick a provider such as Auth0 or Clerk. For service-to-service calls without users, IAM is simpler.

## Basic example

A pool needs no properties; Stacktape creates the Cognito user pool and an app client. Most apps set at least how new
users verify their email or phone:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code'
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


New users verify their email with a one-time code. They can sign in with their email or phone number
(`allowEmailAsUserName` and `allowPhoneNumberAsUserName` are `true` by default). The deploy prints nothing to open; your
app uses the pool through `connectTo` or the [Hosted UI](#hosted-ui).

### Admin-only accounts

For internal tools, B2B dashboards, or any app where you do not want public sign-ups, set `allowOnlyAdminsToCreateAccount: true`. Accounts must then be created through an admin flow (using the Cognito `AdminCreateUser` API from your backend).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    allowOnlyAdminsToCreateAccount: true,
    unusedAccountValidityDays: 7
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


Use `unusedAccountValidityDays` to control how long an unused admin-created account stays valid if the user never signs in. Setting it to `7` means the temporary password and account expire after 7 days. The default is 31 days. This is separate from `passwordPolicy.temporaryPasswordValidityDays`, which controls how long a temporary password is valid before it must be changed on first sign-in.

## Connecting to resources

To use the user pool from a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service), or any other compute resource, add it to the resource's [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) list. For a `UserAuthPool`, `connectTo` grants full-control permissions and injects `ID`, `CLIENT_ID`, and `ARN` environment variables.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  UserAuthPool,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiGateway,
  HttpApiIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code'
  });

  const gateway = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    }),
    connectTo: [auth],
    events: [
      new HttpApiIntegration({
        httpApiGatewayName: 'gateway',
        method: '*',
        path: '/{proxy+}'
      })
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth, gateway, api }
  };
});
```


For a resource named `auth`, the following environment variables are injected by `connectTo`:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `STP_AUTH_ID` | Cognito User Pool ID |
| `STP_AUTH_CLIENT_ID` | User Pool Client ID |
| `STP_AUTH_ARN` | User Pool ARN |

`$ResourceParam('auth', 'domain')` gives the Hosted UI domain.

Your application code can pass the injected pool ID, client ID, and ARN to AWS SDKs or Cognito-compatible libraries. For example, backend code commonly uses Cognito APIs for admin user creation or authentication flows. Libraries like `amazon-cognito-identity-js` or `@aws-sdk/client-cognito-identity-provider` accept the pool ID and client ID directly.

## Protecting API routes

A Stacktape user authentication pool integrates with [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) to protect routes using JWT validation. With a `cognito` authorizer on an HTTP trigger, API Gateway checks the bearer token on every request before your code
runs, and answers `401` when it's missing or invalid.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  UserAuthPool,
  LambdaFunction,
  HttpApiGateway,
  HttpApiIntegration,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code'
  });

  const gateway = new HttpApiGateway({});

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    }),
    connectTo: [auth],
    events: [
      new HttpApiIntegration({
        httpApiGatewayName: 'gateway',
        method: 'GET',
        path: '/me',
        authorizer: {
          type: 'cognito',
          properties: {
            userPoolName: 'auth'
          }
        }
      })
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth, gateway, api }
  };
});
```


The `cognito` authorizer type validates JWTs issued by the referenced user pool. Stacktape uses `userPoolName` to set the expected audience to the user pool client ID and build the issuer URL from the user pool and AWS region. By default, the token is read from the `Authorization` header. You can customize this with the `identitySources` property on the authorizer to read from a different header, query parameter, or stage variable using the `$request.*` syntax.

Stacktape also supports a `lambda` authorizer type, where a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) runs custom authorization logic for each request. Use it for checks beyond the JWT, for example API keys, permissions from a database or another identity provider. See [HTTP triggers](/resources/triggers/http-triggers) for details on both authorizer types.

## Verification

Stacktape user authentication pools support four verification strategies that control how new users prove ownership of their contact information. Set `userVerificationType` to choose the strategy:

| Strategy | Behavior |
|---|---|
| `email-code` | Cognito emails a short numeric code the user enters during sign-up |
| `email-link` | Cognito emails a clickable verification link |
| `sms` | Cognito sends a verification code via SMS to the user's phone number |
| `none` | No email or phone verification is required during sign-up |

For most web apps, `email-code` is the best default: it needs nothing else and users know it. Use `email-link` for a smoother UX where users just click a link instead of copying a code. Use `sms` when phone numbers are the primary identifier (ride-sharing, delivery apps). Use `none` only for internal tools where you trust all users.

You can customize the email subject and body text for both code and link verification using `userVerificationMessageConfig`. To fully customize the email sender and message format, configure `emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn` with a verified SES identity. Without SES configuration, Cognito sends emails through its built-in sender, which works for standard verification flows but has lower daily sending limits.


> **Warning:** `requireEmailVerification` and `requirePhoneNumberVerification` have no effect yet; `userVerificationType` decides
verification.


## Identity providers

A Stacktape user authentication pool supports six types of external identity providers, allowing users to sign in with existing accounts instead of creating new credentials:

| Provider type | Use case |
|---|---|
| `Google` | Consumer and business apps |
| `Facebook` | Consumer apps, especially social or e-commerce |
| `SignInWithApple` | Required for iOS apps that offer other social logins |
| `LoginWithAmazon` | E-commerce or Alexa-integrated apps |
| `OIDC` | Any OpenID Connect provider (Okta, Azure AD, etc.) |
| `SAML` | Enterprise SSO (Active Directory, Ping Identity, etc.) |

Every provider needs a `clientId` and a `clientSecret`. For social and OIDC providers, obtain them from the provider's developer console. For SAML and OIDC providers, advanced provider-specific options can be passed through `providerDetails` as Cognito `ProviderDetails` values. Store secrets using the [`$Secret` directive](/configuration/directives) to avoid exposing them in your config. See [secrets](/configuration/secrets) or [`stacktape secret set`](/cli/secret-set) for setup.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    enableHostedUi: true,
    hostedUiDomainPrefix: 'myapp-login',
    identityProviders: [
      {
        type: 'Google',
        clientId: "$Secret('google-credentials', 'clientId')",
        clientSecret: "$Secret('google-credentials', 'clientSecret')"
      }
    ],
    callbackURLs: ['https://myapp.com/auth/callback'],
    logoutURLs: ['https://myapp.com/logged-out']
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


When you add an identity provider, Stacktape creates separate `AWS::Cognito::UserPoolIdentityProvider` resources and registers them in the user pool client's `SupportedIdentityProviders`. If you do not specify `attributeMapping`, Stacktape defaults to mapping `email` from the provider to the Cognito `email` attribute. You can override this with the `attributeMapping` property to map additional attributes like `given_name` or `picture`.

If you omit `authorizeScopes`, Stacktape uses a reasonable default per provider. Set `authorizeScopes` explicitly when your app needs specific provider scopes, for example requesting access to a user's Google Calendar or Facebook friend list.

Set `allowOnlyExternalIdentityProviders: true` only after configuring at least one `identityProviders` entry. Stacktape then removes `COGNITO` from the user pool client's `SupportedIdentityProviders`, so users must sign in through the configured external providers.

## Lambda hooks

Cognito triggers let you run custom logic at key points in the authentication lifecycle. The `hooks` property connects [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) ARNs to specific trigger points. Use [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) to reference a Lambda function from your stack:

| Hook | When it runs | Common use case |
|---|---|---|
| `preSignUp` | Before a new user is created | Validate input, auto-confirm trusted domains, block sign-ups |
| `postConfirmation` | After account confirmation | Create records in your database, provision resources |
| `preAuthentication` | Before credential validation | Block sign-in by IP, device, or user state |
| `postAuthentication` | After successful sign-in | Update last-login timestamps, record analytics |
| `preTokenGeneration` | Before tokens are issued | Add custom claims (roles, permissions) to JWTs |
| `customMessage` | Before sending email/SMS | Customize message content, localize text |
| `userMigration` | When an unknown user signs in | Import users on-the-fly from a legacy system |
| `createAuthChallenge` | During custom auth flow | Generate a custom challenge (e.g., OTP) |
| `defineAuthChallenge` | During custom auth flow | Decide whether a challenge is needed |
| `verifyAuthChallengeResponse` | During custom auth flow | Validate the user's challenge response |

Each hook value must be a Lambda function ARN. Stacktape maps the configured hooks to the Cognito user pool `LambdaConfig`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  UserAuthPool,
  LambdaFunction,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const createProfile = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/create-profile.ts'
    })
  });

  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    hooks: {
      postConfirmation: "$ResourceParam('createProfile', 'arn')"
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { createProfile, auth }
  };
});
```


Here `createProfile` runs after each user confirms their account, for example to add the user to your own database. The `$ResourceParam('createProfile', 'arn')` directive resolves to the Lambda ARN at deploy time.

## Multi-factor authentication

MFA adds a second verification step during sign-in, making it harder for attackers to access accounts even if they know a user's password. Stacktape supports three MFA factor types:

| Factor | How it works | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| `SOFTWARE_TOKEN` | Time-based one-time codes from an authenticator app (Google Authenticator, Authy) | None |
| `SMS` | One-time codes sent via text message | Requires an SNS role so Cognito can send SMS |
| `EMAIL_OTP` | One-time codes sent via email | Requires `emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn` with a verified SES identity |

The `mfaConfiguration.status` property controls enforcement: `ON` requires MFA for all users, `OPTIONAL` lets users opt in, and `OFF` disables MFA entirely. For most apps, start with `OPTIONAL` and move to `ON` once your users have enrolled their second factor.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    mfaConfiguration: {
      status: 'OPTIONAL',
      enabledTypes: ['SOFTWARE_TOKEN']
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


`SOFTWARE_TOKEN` is the best default: no per-message cost, works everywhere and needs no SES or SNS setup. Use `SMS` only when your users might not have access to authenticator apps, keeping in mind the per-message SMS cost. Use `EMAIL_OTP` when you already have SES configured and want a low-friction second factor that does not require a separate authenticator app.

## Hosted UI

Cognito provides a pre-built, hosted login and registration page so you do not have to build your own auth screens. Enable it with `enableHostedUi: true`. The Hosted UI is useful when you want authentication screens outside your main app. If you use OAuth redirects, configure `callbackURLs` and `logoutURLs` explicitly.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    enableHostedUi: true,
    hostedUiDomainPrefix: 'myapp-auth',
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    callbackURLs: ['https://myapp.com/auth/callback'],
    logoutURLs: ['https://myapp.com/logged-out'],
    allowedOAuthFlows: ['code'],
    allowedOAuthScopes: ['email', 'openid', 'profile']
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


The `hostedUiDomainPrefix` sets the first part of the Hosted UI URL: `https://<prefix>.auth.<region>.amazoncognito.com`. Choose a prefix that matches your project name. Cognito accepts 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting and ending with a letter or digit, and rejects a prefix that contains `aws`, `amazon` or `cognito`; Stacktape checks this before deploying. Without `hostedUiDomainPrefix`, the prefix is `<stack name>-<pool name>`. When Cognito would reject that, for example for a pool named `cognitoPool`, a new pool gets the same name without the rejected parts and with a short hash. A deployed pool keeps the prefix it has. Use `hostedUiCSS` to provide custom CSS for the Hosted UI, applied via Cognito's `AWS::Cognito::UserPoolUICustomizationAttachment` resource.

**When to enable the Hosted UI:** Use it when you want to ship authentication quickly without building custom UI. It is especially useful with social login providers, since the Hosted UI handles the OAuth redirect flow for you. **When to skip it:** For full control of the sign-in screens, build your own UI on the Cognito SDK against the same pool.

### Custom domain

By default, the Hosted UI is served from a Cognito-managed subdomain. To use your own domain (e.g., `auth.example.com`), configure `customDomain`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    enableHostedUi: true,
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    customDomain: {
      domainName: 'auth.example.com'
    },
    callbackURLs: ['https://example.com/auth/callback'],
    logoutURLs: ['https://example.com/logged-out']
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


Use your own domain when users see the sign-in URL, for example in login redirects. Otherwise the Cognito subdomain
from `hostedUiDomainPrefix` needs no DNS or certificate.

Cognito serves custom domains through CloudFront, so the certificate must be in `us-east-1`. Run
[`stacktape domain add`](/resources/networking/custom-domains#set-up-the-domain) before the first deploy; it creates one
there. Cognito also requires the parent domain (`example.com` for `auth.example.com`) to have an A record. Stacktape
creates the DNS record for `customDomain` unless you set `disableDnsRecordCreation: true`, and `customCertificateArn`
picks a specific certificate.

## OAuth

The user pool client's OAuth configuration controls which flows, scopes, and redirect URLs are allowed. Configure these explicitly when using the Hosted UI or integrating with external identity providers:

- **`allowedOAuthFlows`**: which OAuth 2.0 flows the client can use: `code` (Authorization Code, recommended for web apps), `implicit` (legacy browser-only flow), or `client_credentials` (server-to-server with no end user). For most web applications, use `['code']`.
- **`allowedOAuthScopes`**: a string list of scopes the user pool client can request. Common values are `email`, `openid`, and `profile`. These are passed to the Cognito user pool client as `AllowedOAuthScopes`. For scopes requested from an external provider (e.g., Google Calendar access or Facebook friend list), set `authorizeScopes` on that provider's `identityProviders` entry instead.
- **`callbackURLs`**: URLs where Cognito redirects users after authentication. Must exactly match the URLs configured in your application. Include `http://localhost:3000/...` during development and your production URL for deployed environments.
- **`logoutURLs`**: URLs where Cognito redirects after sign-out. Must also be explicitly configured.
- **`generateClientSecret`**: set to `true` when your backend can safely store a client secret (server-side apps, not SPAs). Defaults to `false`.

For server-rendered web apps or backend-mediated OAuth flows, use the `code` flow with `generateClientSecret: true`. For single-page applications that call Cognito directly from the browser, use the `code` flow without a client secret (PKCE is handled automatically by the Cognito SDK).

## Password policy

Stacktape lets you configure password strength requirements through the `passwordPolicy` property. You can set `minimumLength` and require specific character classes (`requireLowercase`, `requireUppercase`, `requireNumbers`, `requireSymbols`).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    passwordPolicy: {
      minimumLength: 12,
      requireNumbers: true,
      requireUppercase: true,
      requireLowercase: true,
      temporaryPasswordValidityDays: 3
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


The `temporaryPasswordValidityDays` inside `passwordPolicy` controls how long a temporary password issued to a new user is valid before it must be changed on first sign-in. This is distinct from the top-level `unusedAccountValidityDays`, which controls when the entire unused admin-created account expires if the user never signs in at all.

Without `passwordPolicy`, Cognito's own defaults apply. For production, set at least `minimumLength: 12` with
`requireNumbers` and `requireUppercase`.

## Client restrictions

The pool's app client accepts every sign-in flow and can read and write every user attribute unless you limit it:

| Property | Limits |
|---|---|
| `allowedAuthFlows` | Which sign-in flows the client accepts, for example `ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH` and `ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH` only |
| `readAttributes` | Which user attributes tokens and `GetUser` return through the client |
| `writeAttributes` | Which attributes users can set through the client, for example to keep `custom:role` admin-only |

```typescript
new UserAuthPool({
  allowedAuthFlows: ['ALLOW_USER_SRP_AUTH', 'ALLOW_REFRESH_TOKEN_AUTH'],
  readAttributes: ['email', 'name'],
  writeAttributes: ['name']
});
```

## Token lifetimes

Stacktape lets you control how long tokens issued by the user pool remain valid:

| Property | Controls | Allowed values | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `accessTokenValiditySeconds` | How long access tokens (used for API authorization) are valid | 300 to 86400 seconds | 3600 (1 hour) |
| `idTokenValiditySeconds` | How long ID tokens (containing user profile claims) are valid | 300 to 86400 seconds | 3600 (1 hour) |
| `refreshTokenValidityDays` | How long refresh tokens can obtain new access/ID tokens | 1 to 3650 days | 30 |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600,
    idTokenValiditySeconds: 3600,
    refreshTokenValidityDays: 30
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


Shorter access token lifetimes reduce the window for token theft at the cost of more frequent refresh calls. Longer refresh token lifetimes keep users signed in longer but extend the window for session hijacking. The defaults, 1 hour for access and ID tokens and 30 days for refresh tokens, are a common starting point.

Before Stacktape v4, Cognito read `accessTokenValiditySeconds` and `idTokenValiditySeconds` in hours, so only values from 1 to 24 deployed. Such a value still means that many hours, and the CLI warns you to write it in seconds instead: `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 1` becomes `accessTokenValiditySeconds: 3600`.

The client's `TokenValidityUnits` are seconds for access and ID tokens and days for refresh tokens. An `overrides` entry that sets `AccessTokenValidity` or `IdTokenValidity` on the client is read in seconds too, so a value written in hours before v4 fails to deploy. Set the unit you mean in the same override; the other units stay as they are:

```yaml
resources:
  auth:
    type: user-auth-pool
    properties:
      userVerificationType: email-code
    overrides:
      AuthUserPoolClient:
        AccessTokenValidity: 2
        TokenValidityUnits:
          AccessToken: hours
```

## Custom attributes

The `schema` property lets you define custom attributes stored on each user record. These are useful for data like `role`, `plan`, `tenantId`, or `companyName` that you want attached to the user profile and optionally included in JWT claims (via the `preTokenGeneration` hook).


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    schema: [
      {
        name: 'role',
        attributeDataType: 'String',
        mutable: true,
        stringMinLength: 1,
        stringMaxLength: 50
      },
      {
        name: 'tenantId',
        attributeDataType: 'String',
        required: true,
        mutable: false,
        stringMinLength: 1,
        stringMaxLength: 128
      },
      {
        name: 'loginCount',
        attributeDataType: 'Number',
        mutable: true
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { auth }
  };
});
```


Each attribute specifies a `name`, `attributeDataType` (e.g., `String`, `Number`), and optional constraints like `required`, `mutable`, `stringMinLength`, and `stringMaxLength`. Attributes with `developerOnlyAttribute: true` are readable only from your backend, not by users.


> **Warning:** Cognito user pool custom attribute schemas are difficult to change after creation. Plan the schema carefully before deploying to production.


## Firewall

Stacktape user authentication pools can be protected by a [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) that inspects requests to the Hosted UI and Cognito token endpoints. `useFirewall` is the Stacktape resource name of a `web-app-firewall` resource; it is not an inline WAF rule definition. Set it to the name of a `WebAppFirewall` resource in your stack.

`useFirewall` creates a `WebACLAssociation` between the user pool and the referenced firewall. AWS requires a regional WAF web ACL for Cognito user pool associations, so the referenced `WebAppFirewall` resource must use `scope: 'regional'`. A CDN-scoped firewall targets CloudFront and cannot be associated with a Cognito user pool. See the [web application firewall](/resources/security/web-application-firewall) page for firewall scope configuration.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, UserAuthPool, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional'
  });

  const auth = new UserAuthPool({
    userVerificationType: 'email-code',
    useFirewall: 'firewall'
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall, auth }
  };
});
```


**When to enable a firewall:** Use it when your Hosted UI is publicly accessible and you want to protect against credential stuffing, bot traffic, or IP-based attacks. A firewall costs about $7 a month with the default rules, plus $0.60 per million requests. **When to skip it:** For internal-only apps or apps that use custom UI with backend-only Cognito API calls, the firewall adds cost without significant benefit.

## Email configuration

By default, Cognito sends emails (verification codes, password resets, admin invitations) through its built-in email service. This works for development but has low daily sending limits. For production, configure `emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn` with a verified SES identity to use your own sender address and get higher throughput:

- **`sesAddressArn`**: ARN of a verified SES email or domain. `EMAIL_OTP` MFA requires it.
- **`from`**: the sender address recipients see. It must be verified in SES.
- **`replyToEmailAddress`**: where replies go; by default the `from` address.

The `inviteMessageConfig` property customizes the email and SMS sent when an administrator creates a user account. Use `{username}` and `{####}` placeholders in the message body for the username and temporary password.

# Web application firewall

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/security/web-application-firewall.mdx`
Route: `/resources/security/web-application-firewall`

A web application firewall (AWS WAF) inspects HTTP requests before they reach your app and blocks common attacks:
SQL injection, cross-site scripting, known bad inputs and floods from one IP address. You define it as its own
resource and attach it to a load balancer, a CDN, a website or a user pool.

A firewall with the two default rule groups costs about $7 a month ($5 for the firewall and $1 per rule group) plus
$0.60 per million requests ([AWS WAF pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/waf/pricing/)). Bot Control and other paid rule
groups add their own fees.

## Basic example


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional'
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall }
  };
});
```


With no `rules`, the firewall uses two AWS-managed rule groups, `AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet` and
`AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet`, and lets through every request they don't block. Attach it by name from the
resource it protects:

| Scope | Attach it with | To |
|---|---|---|
| `regional` | `useFirewall` | [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer), [web service](/resources/compute/web-service) with an Application Load Balancer, [user auth pool](/resources/security/user-auth-pool) |
| `cdn` | `cdn.useFirewall` or `useFirewall` | [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn), the CDN of a load balancer, HTTP API Gateway, function or bucket, [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) and the SSR frontends |

`scope` is required. A `cdn` firewall works at CloudFront locations and stops bad requests before they reach your
region; Stacktape creates it in `us-east-1`, where AWS keeps CloudFront firewalls. A firewall can't change scope after
its first deploy, so create a new one instead.

HTTP API Gateways and Network Load Balancers can't take a firewall directly. Put a CDN in front of an HTTP API Gateway
and attach a `cdn` firewall to it.

## Rules

Three rule types: managed rule groups, rate-based rules and custom rule groups. Each rule has a `name` and a unique
`priority`; lower priorities run first. Setting `rules` replaces the defaults, so list the default groups again if you
want to keep them.

### Managed rule groups

Managed rule groups are rule sets maintained by AWS or by vendors on AWS Marketplace. For AWS groups, set
`vendorName: 'AWS'`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional',
    rules: [
      {
        type: 'managed-rule-group',
        properties: {
          name: 'AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet',
          vendorName: 'AWS',
          priority: 1
        }
      },
      {
        type: 'managed-rule-group',
        properties: {
          name: 'AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet',
          vendorName: 'AWS',
          priority: 2
        }
      },
      {
        type: 'managed-rule-group',
        properties: {
          name: 'AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet',
          vendorName: 'AWS',
          priority: 3
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall }
  };
});
```


| Rule group | Blocks |
|---|---|
| `AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet` | Cross-site scripting, path traversal, file inclusion, oversized requests |
| `AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet` | Known exploit payloads |
| `AWSManagedRulesSQLiRuleSet` | SQL injection in the query, body, cookies and headers |
| `AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList` | IP addresses Amazon threat intelligence flags |
| `AWSManagedRulesBotControlRuleSet` | Bots, by category (extra monthly and per-request fees) |

AWS changes the rules inside these groups over time; see the
[AWS list of managed rule groups](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/waf/latest/developerguide/aws-managed-rule-groups-list.html).

To try a group without blocking anything, set `overrideAction: 'Count'`: matching requests are only counted. `'None'`
enforces the group. If one rule of a group blocks legitimate requests, list it in `excludedRules`; you find its name in
the sampled requests in the AWS WAF console.

### Rate-based rules

A rate-based rule limits how many requests one IP address can send in a rolling five-minute window.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional',
    rules: [
      {
        type: 'managed-rule-group',
        properties: {
          name: 'AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet',
          vendorName: 'AWS',
          priority: 1
        }
      },
      {
        type: 'rate-based-rule',
        properties: {
          name: 'rateLimiter',
          priority: 10,
          limit: 2000,
          action: 'Block'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall }
  };
});
```


`limit` takes 100 to 20,000,000. 2,000 means about 6 to 7 requests per second, sustained. `action` is `'Block'` (a 403
response) by default; `'Count'` only counts, which helps you find the right limit, and `'Captcha'` or `'Challenge'`
make the client prove it's a browser.

Behind a proxy or CDN, every request comes from the proxy's address. Set `aggregateBasedOn: 'FORWARDED_IP'` and
`forwardedIPConfig` with the header (usually `X-Forwarded-For`) and a `fallbackBehavior` for requests without it
(`'MATCH'` or `'NO_MATCH'`).

### Custom rule groups

A custom rule group uses a WAF rule group that already exists in your account, by ARN, for example one another team
maintains. It takes `overrideAction` like a managed group.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional',
    rules: [
      {
        type: 'custom-rule-group',
        properties: {
          name: 'teamSharedRules',
          priority: 5,
          arn: 'arn:aws:wafv2:eu-west-1:123456789012:regional/rulegroup/my-shared-rules/abc123'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall }
  };
});
```


## Default action

`defaultAction` decides what happens to requests no rule matched. `'Allow'` (default) makes your rules a blocklist.
`'Block'` returns 403 for everything your rules don't allow, which suits only APIs with a small, known set of allowed
requests.

## Custom response bodies

A blocked request gets a plain 403 by default. `customResponseBodies` defines named bodies, for example a JSON error
for an API or an HTML page for a website. `contentType` is `application/json`, `text/plain` or `text/html`.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, WebAppFirewall } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const firewall = new WebAppFirewall({
    scope: 'regional',
    customResponseBodies: {
      blockedResponse: {
        contentType: 'application/json',
        content: '{"error": "Request blocked by firewall", "code": "WAF_BLOCKED"}'
      }
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { firewall }
  };
});
```


The rule types here don't select a body per rule. For that and other WAF settings Stacktape doesn't expose, use
[overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches).

## CAPTCHA and challenge immunity

After a client solves a `'Captcha'` or `'Challenge'`, it isn't asked again for `captchaImmunityTime` or
`challengeImmunityTime` seconds (300 by default). `tokenDomains` lets several of your domains accept the same token.

## Metrics and request sampling

Each firewall and rule publishes CloudWatch metrics unless `disableMetrics: true`. `sampledRequestsEnabled: true`
keeps samples of matched requests to inspect in the AWS WAF console, which is how you find false positives. Both can
be set on the firewall and on each rule.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `WebAppFirewallProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/web-app-firewall` with definition name `WebAppFirewallProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `scope` | yes | `string: "cdn" \| "regional"` | - |
| `captchaImmunityTime` | no | `number` | `300` |
| `challengeImmunityTime` | no | `number` | `300` |
| `customResponseBodies` | no | `CustomResponseBodies` | - |
| `defaultAction` | no | `string: "Allow" \| "Block"` | `Allow` |
| `disableMetrics` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `rules` | no | `Array<managed-rule-group \| custom-rule-group \| rate-based-rule>` | - |
| `sampledRequestsEnabled` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `tokenDomains` | no | `Array<string>` | - |


## Referenceable parameters


## Referenceable Parameters: `web-app-firewall`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `arn` | Arn of the `web-app-firewall`. | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `scope` | Scope of the `web-app-firewall` (`regional` or `cdn`). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "scope")` |

# EFS file system

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/storage/efs-filesystem.mdx`
Route: `/resources/storage/efs-filesystem`

An EFS file system is shared, persistent file storage on Amazon Elastic File System. Containers and Lambda functions
mount it as a directory and read and write it with normal file calls, several at once. It grows and shrinks with the
data. Use it for apps that need a real directory: CMS uploads, model files shared between containers, state that must
survive container replacement.

In us-east-1, Standard storage costs $0.30 per GB-month, and in the default elastic throughput mode reads cost $0.03 and
writes $0.06 per GB transferred ([EFS pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/efs/pricing/)). Files your code uploads and
downloads through an API belong in an [S3 bucket](/resources/storage/s3-bucket), which stores a GB for about $0.023.

## Basic example

A file system needs no properties:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EfsFilesystem } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const sharedStorage = new EfsFilesystem({});

  return {
    resources: { sharedStorage }
  };
});
```


It uses elastic throughput. Mount it into a workload with `volumeMounts`:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  WorkerService,
  EfsFilesystem,
  JsBundleImagePackaging
} from 'stacktape';

export default defineConfig(() => {
  const sharedData = new EfsFilesystem({});

  const worker = new WorkerService({
    packaging: new JsBundleImagePackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/worker.ts' }),
    resources: { cpu: 0.5, memory: 1024 },
    connectTo: [sharedData],
    volumeMounts: [
      {
        type: 'efs',
        properties: {
          efsFilesystemName: 'sharedData',
          mountPath: '/mnt/shared',
          rootDirectory: '/workers'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return { resources: { sharedData, worker } };
});
```


The worker sees the file system at `/mnt/shared`, limited to its `/workers` directory. Every container that mounts it
sees the same files. Web services, private services, multi-container workloads and
[Lambda functions](/resources/compute/lambda-function#storage) (with `joinDefaultVpc: true`) mount it the same way.
`stacktape dev` doesn't mount EFS, so test file access on a deployed stage.

## Throughput modes

`throughputMode` decides how read and write speed scales and what you pay for it:

| Mode | Speed | You pay | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `elastic` (default) | Scales with demand | Per GB read and written | Most workloads, spiky access |
| `provisioned` | Fixed `provisionedThroughputInMibps` | Per MiB/s provisioned, used or not | Steady heavy throughput |
| `bursting` | 50 KiB/s per GiB stored, plus burst credits | Included in storage | Large file systems with light access |

### Elastic (default)

Throughput follows your workloads up and down, and you pay for the data they move. Keep it unless you measured a need
it can't meet.

### Provisioned

A fixed rate regardless of how much data is stored, for example `provisionedThroughputInMibps: 100` for 100 MiB/s. It
suits video pipelines or analytics that move a lot of data all the time. You pay for the provisioned rate even when
idle. You can change it any time.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EfsFilesystem } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const videoStorage = new EfsFilesystem({
    throughputMode: 'provisioned',
    provisionedThroughputInMibps: 100
  });

  return {
    resources: { videoStorage }
  };
});
```


### Bursting

Throughput is 50 KiB/s per GiB stored, with short bursts above that from credits. A small file system runs out of
credits quickly and slows down, so use it only for large file systems with light access.

## Backups

`backupEnabled: true` turns on daily AWS Backup backups kept for 35 days. They are incremental, so you pay for the
changed data. Turn it on for data you can't recreate, such as user uploads. The schedule and retention can't be
changed here.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, EfsFilesystem } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const sharedStorage = new EfsFilesystem({
    backupEnabled: true
  });

  return {
    resources: { sharedStorage }
  };
});
```


## Configuration reference


### Definition: `EfsFilesystemProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/efs-filesystem` with definition name `EfsFilesystemProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `backupEnabled` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `provisionedThroughputInMibps` | no | `number` | - |
| `throughputMode` | no | `string: "bursting" \| "elastic" \| "provisioned"` | `elastic` |


## Referenceable parameters

EFS filesystems expose the following parameter for use with [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters):

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
|---|---|---|
| `arn` | ARN of the EFS filesystem | `$ResourceParam('myEfs', 'arn')` |

---

# S3 bucket

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/storage/s3-bucket.mdx`
Route: `/resources/storage/s3-bucket`

A bucket is an Amazon S3 bucket for files: user uploads, images, PDFs, exports, backups, data for pipelines. S3 keeps
your files with eleven nines of durability and scales without limits.

You pay for what you store, the requests you make and the data you send out to the internet. In us-east-1, S3 Standard
costs $0.023 per GB-month, uploads $0.005 per 1,000 and downloads $0.0004 per 1,000 requests
([S3 pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/s3/pricing/)). Many small, frequently read files cost more in requests than in
storage. For a website, use [static hosting](/resources/frontend/static-hosting); for a directory that containers
mount, an [EFS file system](/resources/storage/efs-filesystem).

## Basic example

A bucket needs no properties:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const uploads = new Bucket({});

  return {
    resources: { uploads }
  };
});
```


The bucket is private: only workloads you connect with [`connectTo`](#connecting-to-a-bucket) and IAM identities with
permission can read or write it.

## Uploading files on deploy

The `directoryUpload` property syncs a local directory to the bucket on every deployment. Stacktape mirrors the directory exactly — files in the bucket that are not in the local directory get deleted.


> **Warning:** Directory upload replaces all existing bucket contents. Do not use this for buckets that store user-uploaded or application-generated files. It is designed for deploying build output, static assets, or configuration files.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const assets = new Bucket({
    directoryUpload: {
      directoryPath: './dist',
      headersPreset: 'single-page-app'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { assets }
  };
});
```


The `headersPreset` property sets optimized HTTP caching headers for your framework. Available presets:

| Preset | Behavior | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| `single-page-app` | HTML never cached, hashed assets cached forever | React, Vue, Angular SPAs |
| `static-website` | CDN-cached, never browser-cached | Generic static sites |
| `astro-static-website` | Hashed build assets cached forever, HTML always fresh | Astro static builds |
| `sveltekit-static-website` | Hashed build assets cached forever, HTML always fresh | SvelteKit static builds |
| `nuxt-static-website` | Hashed build assets cached forever, HTML always fresh | Nuxt static builds |
| `gatsby-static-website` | Supported Gatsby preset | Gatsby builds |

For more control, use `fileOptions` to set custom HTTP headers and tags on files matching specific glob patterns. For example, set a long `Cache-Control` header on image files while keeping HTML files uncached. Use `excludeFilesPatterns` to skip specific files during upload.

S3 Transfer Acceleration is enabled by default for faster uploads from distant locations. Disable it with `disableS3TransferAcceleration: true` to avoid the small per-GB surcharge.

## Access control

Bucket access control determines who can read from and write to the bucket. The `accessibility.accessibilityMode` property supports three modes:

| Mode | Who can read | Who can write | Default |
|---|---|---|---|
| `private` | Only resources with IAM permissions | Only resources with IAM permissions | Yes |
| `public-read` | Anyone on the internet | Only resources with IAM permissions | No |
| `public-read-write` | Anyone on the internet | Anyone on the internet | No |

Most buckets should stay `private`. Use [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) to grant your compute resources access — `connectTo` grants bucket read, write, and delete object permissions automatically. Use `public-read` only when you need to serve files directly to browsers without signed URLs. Avoid `public-read-write` unless you have a specific reason — it allows anyone on the internet to write to your bucket.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const publicAssets = new Bucket({
    accessibility: {
      accessibilityMode: 'public-read'
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { publicAssets }
  };
});
```


For fine-grained access control, use `accessibility.accessPolicyStatements` for advanced access configuration with bucket policy IAM role statements.

## CORS

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) configuration is needed when browsers make requests directly to your S3 bucket, for example uploading files via presigned URLs from a frontend app. If your application only accesses the bucket from server-side code (Lambda functions, containers), you don't need CORS.

Set `cors.enabled: true` without `corsRules` to use permissive defaults (`*` origins, all methods). Add `corsRules` to replace those defaults with explicit browser access rules for production.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const uploads = new Bucket({
    cors: {
      enabled: true,
      corsRules: [
        {
          allowedOrigins: ['https://myapp.com'],
          allowedMethods: ['GET', 'PUT'],
          allowedHeaders: ['*'],
          maxAge: 3600
        }
      ]
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { uploads }
  };
});
```


When `corsRules` are provided, they define the explicit browser access rules for your bucket. Each rule specifies `allowedOrigins`, `allowedMethods`, `allowedHeaders`, optional `exposedResponseHeaders` (headers accessible to browser JavaScript), and `maxAge` (how long in seconds browsers can cache preflight responses). Rules are evaluated in order; the first matching rule wins for each preflight request. Allowed methods can be `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, or `*` for any.

## CDN

Placing a CDN (Amazon CloudFront) in front of a bucket reduces download latency for global users, lowers bandwidth costs (CloudFront data transfer is cheaper than direct S3 transfer), and enables edge caching for frequently accessed files. Configure it with the `cdn` property.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const spa = new Bucket({
    directoryUpload: {
      directoryPath: './dist',
      headersPreset: 'single-page-app'
    },
    cdn: {
      enabled: true,
      rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp: true
    }
  });

  return {
    resources: { spa }
  };
});
```


The `rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp` option routes requests without a file extension (e.g., `/about`, `/dashboard`) to `index.html`, letting your SPA handle client-side routing. Requests with extensions (`.js`, `.css`, `.png`) serve the actual file. Enable `rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp` only for browser-routed SPAs where URLs like `/dashboard` should load `index.html`. Leave it disabled for ordinary file buckets or assets where extensionless keys should be looked up as stored objects.

Bucket CDN URL normalization is enabled by default for clean HTML URLs. Disable it with `disableUrlNormalization: true` only when your bucket object keys intentionally rely on exact URL paths.

Enable it when browsers download files from the bucket, especially users far from your region. Buckets that only your
backend reads don't need it. To serve the files at your own domain, set `cdn.customDomains`; see
[Custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

The bucket `cdn` property adds bucket-specific options `rewriteRoutesForSinglePageApp` and `disableUrlNormalization` on top of the shared CDN configuration. See the [CDN resource page](/resources/networking/cdn) for shared CDN options.


> **Tip:** If you're building a static website or SPA with CDN, client-side routing, and custom domains, a [HostingBucket](/resources/frontend/static-hosting) bundles all of this in a single resource type.


## Lifecycle rules

Lifecycle rules automate storage cost management by expiring objects, transitioning them to cheaper storage classes, or cleaning up incomplete uploads. Configure them with the `lifecycleRules` array.

Stacktape supports five lifecycle rule types:

| Rule type | What it does |
|---|---|
| `expiration` | Delete objects after a set number of days since upload |
| `non-current-version-expiration` | Delete old object versions after a set number of days (requires `versioning: true`) |
| `class-transition` | Move objects to a cheaper storage class after a set number of days |
| `non-current-version-class-transition` | Move old versions to a cheaper storage class after they become non-current; use with `versioning: true` |
| `abort-incomplete-multipart-upload` | Clean up incomplete multipart uploads after a set number of days |


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const dataLake = new Bucket({
    lifecycleRules: [
      {
        type: 'class-transition',
        properties: {
          daysAfterUpload: 30,
          storageClass: 'STANDARD_IA',
          prefix: 'logs/'
        }
      },
      {
        type: 'expiration',
        properties: {
          daysAfterUpload: 365,
          prefix: 'logs/'
        }
      },
      {
        type: 'abort-incomplete-multipart-upload',
        properties: {
          daysAfterInitiation: 7
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { dataLake }
  };
});
```


This example moves log files to cheaper storage after 30 days, deletes them after a year, and cleans up failed multipart uploads after 7 days. Each rule supports optional `prefix` and `tags` filters to target specific objects.

### Storage classes

The `storageClass` property in transition rules determines where objects move. Cheaper classes have higher retrieval costs or latency:

| Storage class | Access pattern | Retrieval speed | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `STANDARD_IA` | Infrequent access | Instant | Backups, older data you still query occasionally |
| `ONEZONE_IA` | Infrequent, single AZ | Instant (less durable than multi-AZ) | Reproducible data like thumbnails or transcoded media |
| `INTELLIGENT_TIERING` | Unknown or changing | Instant (auto-tiered by AWS) | Data with unpredictable access patterns |
| `GLACIER` | Archive | Minutes to hours | Compliance archives, old logs |
| `DEEP_ARCHIVE` | Long-term archive | 12+ hours | Data you rarely need but must retain for years |


> **Tip:** Add an `abort-incomplete-multipart-upload` rule to every bucket. Large file uploads that fail midway leave invisible partial objects that accumulate storage charges. A 7-day cleanup rule prevents this waste.


## Versioning and encryption

**Versioning** keeps previous versions of overwritten or deleted objects, letting you recover from accidental changes. Enable it with `versioning: true`. Versioning is a prerequisite for `non-current-version-expiration` and `non-current-version-class-transition` lifecycle rules. Enable versioning for buckets where accidental overwrites would be costly — user uploads, application data, configuration files. Skip it for ephemeral data like logs or build caches where old versions have no value. Note that versioning increases storage costs since all object versions are retained until explicitly expired by a lifecycle rule.

**Encryption** sets `encryption: true` to configure AES-256 server-side encryption at rest on the bucket. The source JSDoc describes this as "Encrypt stored objects at rest (AES-256)." If you need different encryption (e.g., AWS KMS customer-managed keys), use [overrides](/configuration/overrides-and-escape-hatches) on the underlying CloudFormation resource.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const secureBucket = new Bucket({
    versioning: true,
    encryption: true,
    lifecycleRules: [
      {
        type: 'non-current-version-expiration',
        properties: {
          daysAfterVersioned: 30
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { secureBucket }
  };
});
```


When versioning is enabled, pair it with a `non-current-version-expiration` rule to automatically clean up old versions and avoid unbounded storage growth. In this example, old versions are deleted 30 days after they become non-current (i.e., after a newer version replaces them).

## Event-driven workflows

Stacktape buckets support two approaches for reacting to object changes:

**S3 event triggers** invoke a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) directly for configured S3 event types — commonly object-created, object-removed, and object-restore events. The trigger type also supports replication-related and reduced-redundancy lost-object events through the [S3 trigger configuration](/resources/triggers/s3-events). This is the simplest approach for processing uploads, for example resizing images or parsing CSV files. Configure S3 triggers on the Lambda function side.

**EventBridge notifications** send bucket events to [EventBridge](/resources/messaging/event-bus), where multiple consumers can react to the same event independently. Enable with `enableEventBusNotifications: true` (defaults to `false`). Use EventBridge notifications when bucket events should be available on EventBridge for other parts of your architecture. For direct upload processing, an S3 trigger on a Lambda function is usually simpler.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const uploads = new Bucket({
    enableEventBusNotifications: true
  });

  return {
    resources: { uploads }
  };
});
```


For most use cases, an S3 event trigger on a Lambda function is simpler and sufficient. Choose EventBridge when you need fan-out to multiple consumers or complex event routing rules.

## Connecting to a bucket

Add the bucket to a workload's [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources). The workload can then read, write and
delete objects and gets the bucket's name and ARN as environment variables.


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, Bucket, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const uploads = new Bucket({});

  const processor = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/processor.ts'
    }),
    connectTo: [uploads]
  });

  return {
    resources: { uploads, processor }
  };
});
```


The `processor` function receives these environment variables at runtime:

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `STP_UPLOADS_NAME` | The S3 bucket name |
| `STP_UPLOADS_ARN` | The S3 bucket ARN |

Use the bucket name with any AWS S3 SDK to read and write objects:

```typescript
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from '@aws-sdk/client-s3';

const s3 = new S3Client({});

export default async () => {
  await s3.send(new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.STP_UPLOADS_NAME,
    Key: 'example.txt',
    Body: 'Hello from Stacktape'
  }));

  return { statusCode: 200, body: JSON.stringify({ message: 'Uploaded' }) };
};
```

For uploads from a browser, generate a presigned URL in your backend and let the browser upload straight to S3, so large
files don't pass through your API. That needs [CORS](#cors) on the bucket. To run code when a file arrives, see
[Event-driven workflows](#event-driven-workflows).

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `BucketProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/bucket` with definition name `BucketProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `accessibility` | no | `BucketAccessibility` | - |
| `cdn` | no | `BucketCdnConfiguration` | - |
| `cors` | no | `BucketCorsConfig` | - |
| `directoryUpload` | no | `DirectoryUpload` | - |
| `enableEventBusNotifications` | no | `boolean` | `false` |
| `encryption` | no | `boolean` | - |
| `lifecycleRules` | no | `Array<expiration \| non-current-version-expiration \| class-transition \| non-current-version-class-transition \| abort-incomplete-multipart-upload>` | - |
| `versioning` | no | `boolean` | - |


## Referenceable parameters

Use [`$ResourceParam`](/configuration/referenceable-parameters) to reference bucket properties in other parts of your config, for example passing the bucket name as an environment variable or using the ARN in a custom IAM policy.


## Referenceable Parameters: `bucket`
These values can be referenced with `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "<<parameter-name>>")`.

| Parameter | Description | Usage |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | AWS (physical) name of the bucket | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "name")` |
| `arn` | Arn of the bucket | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "arn")` |
| `cdnDomain` | Default domain of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnDomain")` |
| `cdnUrl` | Default url of the [CDN distribution](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you DO NOT configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnUrl")` |
| `cdnCustomDomains` | Comma-separated list of custom domain names assigned to the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomains")` |
| `cdnCustomDomainUrls` | Comma-separated list of custom domain name URLs of the [CDN](/resources/networking/cdn/) (only available if you configure custom domain names for the CDN). | `$ResourceParam("<<resource-name>>", "cdnCustomDomainUrls")` |

# Alarms as triggers

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers.mdx`
Route: `/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers`

A `cloudwatch-alarm` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) when one of your
[alarms](/observability/alarms) goes into the `ALARM` state. Use it when the response needs code: restart something,
open a ticket, page an on-call tool the alarm can't notify directly.

If a person only needs to see the alert, skip the function and add `notificationChannels` to the alarm. Alarms notify
Slack, Microsoft Teams, email, Discord and webhooks without code; see [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels).

## Basic example

The alarm lives on the resource it watches. The trigger names it by the resource's name, `alarms` and the alarm's
position in that list:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' }),
    alarms: [
      {
        description: 'API error rate above 5%',
        trigger: { type: 'lambda-error-rate', properties: { thresholdPercent: 5 } }
      }
    ]
  });

  const onApiErrors = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/on-api-errors.ts' }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'cloudwatch-alarm',
        properties: { alarmName: 'api.alarms.0' }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { api, onApiErrors }
  };
});
```


`api.alarms.0` is the first alarm in the `alarms` list of the `api` resource. An alarm that you defined in the Console
for a resource is `<resource>.alarms.<alarm name>`. The alarm must be in the same stack.

Several functions can reference the same alarm. Each one gets its own EventBridge rule and runs independently.

## Handling the event

The function receives the CloudWatch "Alarm State Change" event from EventBridge. It runs only when the alarm moves
into `ALARM`, not when it recovers.

```typescript
type AlarmEvent = {
  detail: {
    alarmName: string;
    state: { value: string; reason: string; timestamp: string };
    previousState: { value: string };
  };
};

export default async (event: AlarmEvent) => {
  const { alarmName, state } = event.detail;
  console.info(`${alarmName} is ${state.value}: ${state.reason}`);
  // remediation or paging logic
};
```

The [AWS event reference](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch-and-eventbridge.html)
lists every field.

The event arrives asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice, so make side effects idempotent: an
alarm that pages twice for one incident is noise. To keep events that still fail, set
[`destinations.onFailure`](/resources/compute/lambda-function#api-ref_lambda-function-props--destinations) on the
function.

## Alarm types

The referenced alarm can use any trigger type its resource supports:

| Resource | Alarm trigger types |
|---|---|
| [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) | `lambda-error-rate`, `lambda-duration` |
| [Relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) | `database-read-latency`, `database-write-latency`, `database-cpu-utilization`, `database-free-storage`, `database-free-memory`, `database-connection-count` |
| [HTTP API Gateway](/resources/networking/http-api-gateway) | `http-api-gateway-error-rate`, `http-api-gateway-latency` |
| [Application Load Balancer](/resources/networking/application-load-balancer) | `application-load-balancer-error-rate`, `application-load-balancer-unhealthy-targets`, `application-load-balancer-custom` |
| [SQS queue](/resources/messaging/sqs-queue) | `sqs-queue-received-messages-count`, `sqs-queue-not-empty` |

Thresholds, evaluation windows and notifications are covered in [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

## Limits

- Only Lambda functions accept `cloudwatch-alarm` events.
- `alarmName` is the only property. You can't reshape the event or reference an alarm in another stack or account.
  For those, send the alarm's events to an [event bus](/resources/messaging/event-bus) and use an
  [event bus trigger](/resources/triggers/event-bus-events).
- Dev mode doesn't create alarms, so the trigger doesn't fire in a dev stack.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `AlarmIntegrationProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/events` with definition name `AlarmIntegrationProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alarmName` | yes | `string` | - |


## Next steps

- [Alarms](/observability/alarms): define alarms and their thresholds.
- [Alert channels](/observability/alert-channels): notify people without code.
- [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function): logs and permissions of the handler.

# CloudWatch Logs

Source: `apps/docs/content/resources/triggers/cloudwatch-logs.mdx`
Route: `/resources/triggers/cloudwatch-logs`

A `cloudwatch-log` event runs a [Lambda function](/resources/compute/lambda-function) or a
[batch job](/resources/compute/batch-job) when new records arrive in a CloudWatch log group. Use it to act on log
content: extract errors, enrich and forward records, or watch CloudTrail or VPC flow logs.

To read logs, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs). To send logs to Datadog or another service without code, use
[log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding). To react when a metric crosses a threshold, use an
[alarm trigger](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers).

## Basic example

This function receives the `ERROR` lines of another function in the stack:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import { defineConfig, LambdaFunction, JsBundleLambdaPackaging, $ResourceParam } from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/api.ts' })
  });

  const errorWatcher = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({ entryfilePath: './src/error-watcher.ts' }),
    events: [
      {
        type: 'cloudwatch-log',
        properties: {
          logGroupArn: $ResourceParam('api', 'logGroupArn'),
          filter: 'ERROR'
        }
      }
    ]
  });

  return {
    resources: { api, errorWatcher }
  };
});
```


`logGroupArn` takes the ARN of any log group. Lambda functions in the stack expose theirs as the `logGroupArn`
[parameter](/configuration/referenceable-parameters). For a log group outside the stack, paste its ARN.

The payload arrives base64-encoded and gzipped. Decode it before you read it:

```typescript
import { gunzipSync } from 'node:zlib';

export default async (event: { awslogs: { data: string } }) => {
  const logData = JSON.parse(gunzipSync(Buffer.from(event.awslogs.data, 'base64')).toString());
  // logData.logGroup, logData.logStream
  for (const logEvent of logData.logEvents) {
    console.info(logEvent.id, new Date(logEvent.timestamp).toISOString(), logEvent.message);
  }
};
```

One invocation carries a batch of log events. CloudWatch decides the batch size; the trigger has no setting for it.
Always loop over `logEvents`.

## Filter patterns

`filter` uses the
[CloudWatch filter pattern syntax](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html).
Without it, every record invokes the function.

| Pattern | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `ERROR` | Lines that contain `ERROR` |
| `ERROR -DEBUG` | Lines with `ERROR` but not `DEBUG` |
| `{ $.level = "error" }` | JSON lines whose `level` is `error` |
| `{ $.statusCode >= 500 }` | JSON lines whose `statusCode` is 500 or more |

## Limits

- A log group accepts at most two subscriptions, and each trigger uses one. Stacktape may already use one on a
  function's log group for error tracking or log forwarding. When you hit the limit, have one function forward the
  records to an SQS queue, an SNS topic or an event bus.
- Log groups with `logging.logClass: infrequent-access` don't support subscriptions. Stacktape stops the deploy if a
  trigger points at one.

## Failures and retries

CloudWatch Logs invokes the function asynchronously. If the function throws, Lambda retries it twice. The same records
can arrive more than once, so deduplicate on each log event's `id` when it matters.

## Configuration reference


### Definition: `CloudwatchLogIntegrationProps`

The complete property-level reference is included in `llms-api-reference.txt` and indexed under route `/config-reference/events` with definition name `CloudwatchLogIntegrationProps`.

| Property | Required | Type | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `logGroupArn` | yes | `string` | - |
| `filter` | no | `string` | - |


## Next steps

- [Logs](/observability/logs): read and search logs from the CLI and the Console.
- [Log forwarding](/observability/log-forwarding): send logs to another service without code.
- [Alarms as triggers](/resources/triggers/alarms-as-triggers): run code when a metric crosses a threshold.
