# API keys

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/api-keys.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/api-keys`

An API key signs the Stacktape CLI in to the Console where nobody can open a browser: a CI pipeline, a server or a script. Keys live on **Organization → API keys**, and there are two kinds:

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| A pipeline or tool your team shares | An **organization key**. It belongs to the organization and keeps working when people leave. Owners and Admins create it. |
| Your own script or server | A **personal key**. It acts as you, with your role and access, and stops working if you leave the organization. |
| The CLI on your own machine | No key: run [`stacktape login`](/cli/login). |

A personal organization has only personal keys. CI that a team shares belongs in a team organization, with an organization key.

## Create an organization key

1. Open **Organization → API keys** and click **New organization key**.
2. Name it after where it runs, for example `github-actions`.
3. Pick its role: **Developer** with the projects and AWS accounts the pipeline deploys, or **Admin** for everything.
4. Pick when it expires, from 30 days to a year.
5. Copy the key from the next dialog. It is shown only once.

Store it as the `STACKTAPE_API_KEY` secret of your CI. When the organization has more than one connected AWS account, pass `--aws-account <name>` on the CLI commands, so a pipeline never has to guess. See [Custom CI/CD](/ci-cd-and-gitops/custom-ci-cd).

The table shows each key's access, status, when it was last used, when it expires and who created it. Organization keys can't create organizations or connect AI subscriptions, which belong to people.

## Create a personal key

Click **New personal key** (in a personal organization, **New API key**), give it a name and an expiry, and copy the key from the next dialog. The dialog says whose access the key uses: yours, in the organization that is open, with your role and, for a Developer, your projects and AWS accounts. Viewers have no API keys page and can't create keys.

`stacktape login` creates a key for this machine too. It is listed as a **CLI session**, and [`stacktape logout`](/cli/logout) revokes it.

## What a key can reach

A key never does more than its role. A Developer key reaches only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for it; asking it for credentials in another AWS account fails with "Your access does not include the AWS account". See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for the roles.

A key is a password. Keep it in your CI's secret store, never in code, chat, issue trackers or shell history.

## Rotate and revoke keys

A key can't be shown again, reactivated or extended. To replace one, create the new key, put it in your CI secret, check that a pipeline run works, then revoke the old key.

**Revoke key** stops every CLI session and pipeline that uses the key at once. Expired and revoked keys stay in the list with their status.

Owners and Admins can also revoke a member's personal keys from the Members page, and removing a member revokes theirs. The removal dialog warns when one of their keys was used in the last 7 days, because a pipeline may depend on it.

# Audit log

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/audit-log.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/audit-log`

The **Audit log** page answers "who changed what" for your organization. It shows three kinds of rows in one table,
newest first:

- **Stacktape events**: changes made through Stacktape, such as a member invited, an API key revoked or an AWS account
  connected.
- **Stack operations**: deploys, deletes and the other CLI operations that the Activity page lists, with who ran them.
- **AWS events**: what AWS CloudTrail recorded in your connected AWS accounts, read live from those accounts.

Open it from **Audit log** in the Organization group of the sidebar. It is available on every plan.

## Who can see it

Owners and Admins. Developers and Viewers do not see the page in the sidebar, and opening its address tells them that
only Owners and Admins can see the audit log.

## What Stacktape records

Stacktape records an event for every change that affects access, credentials, integrations or settings, including:

- members invited, removed, or given another role or other projects and AWS accounts
- API keys created or revoked, deployment tokens created, and CLI logins (`stacktape login`) and logouts
- AWS accounts connected and disconnected
- projects, stages, secrets and SSM parameters created, changed or deleted (names only, never values)
- Git, Slack and AI provider connections
- runner settings and runner terminal sessions
- guardrails, budgets, alert channels and notification rules
- organization settings, such as the two-factor requirement, and single sign-on and SCIM changes
- exports of the audit log itself

Changes people make to their own sign-in appear in every organization they belong to: password changed, authenticator
app turned on or off, passkey added or removed, Google or GitHub connected or disconnected, and sessions ended.
Sign-ins themselves are not recorded.

Refused attempts to change members, API keys, AWS connections, the two-factor requirement and single sign-on are
recorded too, with the outcome **Denied**.

## Reading the table

| Column | What it shows |
|---|---|
| Time | When it happened. Hover for the exact time. |
| Source | **Stacktape** or **AWS** |
| Actor | Who did it, and how: in the Console, from the CLI, with an API key, or through Stacktape in AWS |
| Action | For example `member.removed` or an AWS API call such as `DeleteBucket` |
| Target | What it changed |
| AWS account · region | Where it happened, when it happened in AWS |
| Outcome | **Succeeded**, **Denied**, **Failed**, **In progress** or **Unknown** |

Click a row to see all its fields. For an AWS event, the panel also shows the event record as CloudTrail returned it and
links to the event in the AWS console.

The table shows 50 rows at a time. **Load more** continues further back.

## Filters

- **Time range**: from **Last 24 hours** to **Last 400 days**. The default is **Last 7 days**.
- **Source**: **All sources**, **Stacktape** or **AWS**.
- **Person**: everyone, or one member. Organization keys are listed with "(organization key)".
- **AWS account**: one connected account. It keeps that account's AWS events, the stack operations in it, and the
  Stacktape events that changed it.
- **Read-only AWS events**: off by default, so AWS rows show only changes. Turn it on to include reads, such as
  `Describe*` and `List*` calls.

The filters are part of the page address, so you can share a filtered view by copying the link.

## AWS events are read live

Stacktape does not copy your CloudTrail events into its own storage. When you open or filter the page, Stacktape reads
them from your AWS accounts through each account's connection role.

Stacktape reads:

- every connected AWS account, or the one you filtered on;
- the regions where your organization has run Stacktape operations in that account, plus `us-east-1`, where AWS records
  global services such as IAM, CloudFront and Route 53;
- management events only. Data events, such as S3 object reads or Lambda invocations, are not available here.

For an event in another region, use CloudTrail in the AWS console.

The line above the table says which accounts and regions were read and which time they cover. AWS limits how fast
CloudTrail can be read, so on a busy account the line can say "Complete back to" a time; **Load more** reads further.
When an account cannot be read, the line names it and the reason: access denied, region not enabled, throttled by AWS,
or could not be read.

The **Person** filter works on AWS events after they are read. The line above the table says so when it applies.

## Who did it in AWS

For an AWS event, the **Actor** column names the person when Stacktape can tell:

- **"through Stacktape (purpose)"**: a member caused Stacktape to act in AWS, for example by creating a budget or
  deleting a project in the Console. The purpose says what for, such as "budget" or "project delete".
- **Stacktape, "background work (purpose)"**: Stacktape's own scheduled or background work.
- **"with their own AWS credentials"**: the event used AWS access keys that a member's recorded Stacktape operation also
  used, for example when they ran `stacktape deploy` with their own AWS profile.
- Otherwise the AWS principal as AWS reports it, such as a role or an IAM user.

AWS events name only current members. Someone who has left shows as an unknown Stacktape user there. Stacktape events
keep naming the person after they leave.

### Older AWS account connections

AWS account connections created from an older connection template need an update so that AWS records the person
behind each action everywhere. Until then, Stacktape names the person only for actions the connection role makes directly; actions made
through further roles show the AWS principal instead.

Owners and Admins see an **Update** button next to these accounts on **Configuration → AWS accounts**. It opens a
dialog with the steps and a link that updates the connection stack in AWS CloudFormation. See
[AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions#who-can-use-the-role) for how the person is recorded.

## How long events are kept

| Rows | Kept for | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Stacktape events | 400 days, also after the organization is deleted | Stacktape |
| AWS events | 90 days, CloudTrail's event history | Your AWS account |

The page shows at most the last 400 days. When a time range reaches further back than 90 days, AWS events cover only the
last 90 days and older rows are Stacktape events only; the line above the table says so. To keep AWS events longer, set
up a CloudTrail trail that delivers them to an S3 bucket in your AWS account.

## Export

Click **Export** and choose **Stacktape events as CSV** or **Stacktape events as JSON**.

- The file has the Stacktape events and stack operations of the selected time range, narrowed by the **Person** and
  **AWS account** filters. The **Source** and **Read-only AWS events** filters do not apply.
- AWS events are not exported: you already have them in your AWS account.
- One export holds at most 50,000 rows, the newest ones. When there are more, the Console says so; narrow the time range
  to export the rest.
- The columns are `time`, `type` (`event` or `stack operation`), `actor`, `actorEmail`, `action`, `targetType`,
  `target`, `awsAccountId`, `region`, `outcome`, `details` and `id`. In the CSV file, `details` is a JSON object.
- In the CSV file, a value that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` gets a leading apostrophe, so a spreadsheet does not run
  it as a formula.

Each export is itself recorded in the audit log, with its format, time range and filters.

## Troubleshooting

### There are no AWS events

Check that the **Source** filter is not **Stacktape**, that the time range ends within the last 90 days, and that the
organization has a connected AWS account. Events from regions where your organization never ran a Stacktape operation
are not read, except `us-east-1`.

### An account shows "access denied"

Stacktape could not use the account's connection role. Check the account's state on the **AWS accounts** page.

### An account shows "throttled by AWS"

AWS limited the reads. Try again in a minute.

### An AWS event shows a role instead of a person

The action did not go through Stacktape, or it went through further roles in an account whose connection has not been
updated. See [Older AWS account connections](#older-aws-account-connections).

## Related features

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): members, roles and organization keys
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): SSO and SCIM changes appear in the audit log
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): the connection role the AWS events are
  read through

# AWS permissions

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/aws-permissions.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/aws-permissions`

Connecting an AWS account to the Console creates one CloudFormation stack in it. The stack holds an IAM role that the Console assumes to deploy your stacks and read their logs, metrics and costs. This page says exactly what the stack creates, who can use the role and how to limit or remove it. [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) covers the steps.

The CLI without an account doesn't use any of this: it deploys with your own AWS credentials.

## What the connection stack creates

The stack is created in `eu-west-1`, whatever regions you deploy to. It holds:

- **The role Stacktape assumes.** Only Stacktape's AWS account can assume it, and only with an external ID unique to this connection. Sessions last at most 12 hours.
- **A cost report bucket**, `stacktape-cur-<connection ID>`. AWS writes the account's Cost and Usage Reports there, and Stacktape reads them for the [cost pages](/managing-costs/dashboards). Reports are deleted after 30 days, and the bucket blocks public access.
- **A reporting policy** that lets the role manage the cost report definition, read the bucket, list CloudFormation stacks and turn on cost allocation tags.

Connecting is free, and the role costs nothing in AWS. The cost report bucket is billed as normal S3 storage and holds at most 30 days of reports.

## Deploy access or read-only

The role gets one of two AWS managed policies:

| Access | AWS policy | Stacktape can |
|---|---|---|
| **Can deploy** | `AdministratorAccess` | Deploy, update and delete your stacks, and read their logs, metrics and costs |
| **Read-only** | `ReadOnlyAccess` | Read logs, metrics and costs. Deploys, budgets and other writes fail. |

A connection made in the Console or with `stacktape connect` can deploy. The **Status** column of the AWS accounts page shows **Can deploy** or **Read-only** next to **Connected**. An Owner or Admin can switch a read-only account with **Allow deploys**.

Deploy access is administrator access because a stack can contain almost any AWS service: functions, containers, databases, networking, IAM roles for your workloads and more. A policy limited to some services would fail on the next resource you add. Your workloads don't get these permissions: each one runs with its own role that allows only what its config declares.

## Who can use the role

The role's trust policy names Stacktape's AWS account. Inside Stacktape, the Console decides who may use the account:

- Owners and Admins reach every connected account.
- Developers and Viewers reach only the AWS accounts chosen for them on the Members page. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#project-and-aws-account-access).
- Only Owners and Admins can connect, update or disconnect an account.

When a person causes an AWS call, Stacktape names them in it: the source identity `stp-<user ID>` and a role session name that starts with `stp-`. Background work uses session names that start with `stacktape-`. The Console's [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) turns these into names. A connection created before source identities were supported shows an update link on the AWS accounts page.

## Supported regions

The role works in every region, but Stacktape deploys only to the regions it supports. The allowed values of [`--region`](/cli/deploy#option-deploy-region) list them. An AWS service can still be missing in a supported region, and an SCP or organization guardrail can block a region.

## Restrict what Stacktape can do

**Service control policies.** An SCP in AWS Organizations limits every role in the account, Stacktape's included, whatever its own policy allows. Use it to block regions, protect resources with a tag, or deny actions you never want. A deploy that an SCP blocks fails with `AccessDenied`; the CloudFormation event names the action.

**Separate accounts.** The usual setup is one AWS account for production with stricter SCPs and one for development and previews. Each account has its own connection and its own role, and members can get access to one without the other.

**Read-only.** Keep an account read-only when you only want logs, metrics and costs in the Console, for example an account another tool deploys.

**Guardrails.** Console [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) refuse deploys that break your rules, such as oversized instances or a region you don't use, before anything reaches AWS.

## Revoke access

1. Open **Configuration → AWS accounts** and choose **Disconnect account** in the account's menu. The Console blocks this while [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) target the account and lists the projects to change first.
2. Delete the connection stack in the AWS CloudFormation console, in `eu-west-1`. That removes the role and the cost report bucket.

Deleting only the stack leaves the account in the Console as **No access**. Your deployed stacks are separate CloudFormation stacks and keep running either way; manage or delete them with the CLI and your own credentials.

## Audit Stacktape's activity

Filter AWS CloudTrail by the role's ARN to see each call Stacktape made. The `stp-` source identity and session names say which person caused it, and the Console's [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) shows the same events with names.

# Billing and subscription

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription`

The Stacktape CLI is open source and free, and it works without a Stacktape account; see [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli). This page covers the plans of the Stacktape Console: Free, Flexible and Enterprise. AWS bills you for your infrastructure as before; the Stacktape fee is a separate invoice from Stacktape.

You compare and change plans on **Subscription plans**, and see the fee estimate and invoices on **Organization → Billing**. Owners and Admins can change the plan. Developers can compare plans but don't see Billing, and Viewers see neither.

## Plans

Stacktape charges a share of the AWS costs of the stacks it manages, not per seat, deployment or request.


## Feature Comparison

| Feature | Free | Flexible | Enterprise |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | $0 | 19–25% of managed AWS spend | Custom |
| Managed AWS spend | Up to $200/mo | No limit | No limit |
| Team members | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Deployments and stacks | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Single sign-on and SCIM | no | yes | yes |
| Shared Slack channel with the founders | no | yes | yes |
| Your feature requests come first | no | yes | yes |
| Single-tenant Console in your AWS account | no | no | yes |
| Support | — | Shared Slack channel | Up to 24x7 premium |


### Free plan

The Free plan is the whole Console except single sign-on and SCIM provisioning. It costs $0, needs no credit card and has no member limit. It covers managed AWS spend up to $200 a calendar month (UTC). When an organization passes $200, deploys keep working for 7 days the first time, then pause until it upgrades or the next month starts. See [Free plan cost limit](#free-plan-cost-limit).

### Flexible plan

The Flexible plan has no spend limit. Its fee is one rate applied to the whole month's managed AWS spend. The rate depends on how large that spend is:

| Monthly managed AWS spend | Rate |
|---|---|
| Up to $2,000 | 25% |
| $2,000 to $5,000 | 23% |
| $5,000 to $10,000 | 21% |
| $10,000 to $25,000 | 20% |
| Above $25,000 | 19% |

For example:

| Managed AWS spend in a month | Stacktape fee |
|---|---|
| $500 | $125 (25%) |
| $1,000 | $250 (25%) |
| $3,000 | $690 (23%) |
| $8,000 | $1,680 (21%) |

Managed spend is what the resources in Stacktape stacks cost, summed over all AWS accounts connected to the organization. Everything else in those accounts doesn't count. Say your two accounts cost $1,400 in a month: $1,000 for your Stacktape stacks and $400 for AWS Support and an old EC2 instance. You pay AWS $1,400 and Stacktape $250 (25% of $1,000), plus tax where it applies. The [Costs](/managing-costs/dashboards) page shows the same split: your projects, and costs outside projects.

The fee for a month is charged on the 7th of the next month (UTC), after AWS finishes the month's cost reports. The Subscription plans page shows what Flexible would cost your organization, in dollars, from its own costs.

On top of the Free plan, Flexible adds [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on) (SAML or OIDC) with SCIM provisioning, a shared Slack channel with the founders, and priority for your feature requests. Priority means your requests are worked on first; it comes with no SLA or delivery dates.

### Enterprise plan

The Enterprise plan runs a single-tenant Console in your own AWS account and region, for data residency. It includes single sign-on and SCIM and up to 24x7 premium support, and its price is agreed with you. Click **Schedule a meeting** on the Subscription plans page to talk to the Stacktape team.

## Free plan cost limit

A Free organization can deploy while its managed AWS spend for the current calendar month (UTC) is $200 or less.

- **What counts.** The same managed spend the Flexible fee is based on, from the AWS billing data Stacktape reads.
- **Grace, once per organization.** The first time the organization is over the limit, Stacktape emails its Owners and Admins and starts a 7-day grace period. Deploys keep working during it, but only within the calendar month (UTC) it started in: a grace period that starts on November 29 doesn't cover December. In any later month, deploys pause as soon as the organization passes the limit, with no new grace period.
- **What pauses.** After the grace period, every new deploy: `stacktape deploy`, including code-only (fast) deploys, remote and runner deploys, deploys after a Git push and deploys started from the Console. `stacktape dev` does not start either, because it deploys a dev stack. A deploy that already started finishes normally.
- **What keeps working.** Your running infrastructure is never touched. Deleting stages, rolling back, running scripts and the rest of the Console keep working.
- **How it lifts.** Upgrading to Flexible lifts it immediately. Without an upgrade, deploys resume when the next calendar month starts.
- **Missing cost data.** AWS delivers billing data a few times a day, and a new connection has none at first. Until Stacktape has this month's costs, deploys are not limited.

The Console shows where you are. The sidebar shows this month's managed spend against the limit, and from $150 on it adds what Flexible would cost this month. During the grace period every page has a banner, for example "Day 3 of 7 over the Free limit. Flexible would cost about $53 this month." While deploys are paused, every page opens with an upgrade notice, which you can close to keep reading. Members who can't change the plan see which Owners and Admins can.

The CLI tells you too. From $150 on, and during the grace period, a successful deploy prints one line with the month's spend or the days left and what Flexible would cost. A refused deploy or dev session stops before it changes anything in AWS. [`deploy`](/cli/deploy#free-plan-cost-limit) shows both messages.

The limit applies to the Console only. The open-source CLI without an account has no limit.

## Change your plan

1. Open **Subscription plans**. From Billing, click **Compare plans**. The card of your plan says **Current plan**.
2. Click **Upgrade to Flexible**. Paddle's checkout opens; enter your payment details there.
3. When Paddle accepts the payment, the page shows **Confirming your Flexible plan** until Paddle confirms it to Stacktape, usually within seconds. Don't start the checkout again. If the confirmation takes more than a minute, the page shows **Not confirmed yet** with a **Check again** button.

To go back, click **Downgrade to Free** on the Free card. If this month's managed spend is already above $200, the [Free plan cost limit](#free-plan-cost-limit) applies right after the downgrade. An Enterprise plan is changed through your agreement.

The buttons are disabled, with the reason, for members who can't change the plan.

## Billing page

**Organization → Billing** shows:

- **Next charge, estimated**: the Flexible fee so far for this month, or for last month until it is charged on the 7th, with the managed spend it is based on. A fee is estimated only when your AWS cost reports are in US dollars, because the rates are set on dollar amounts. On Free, this tile shows this month's spend against the $200 limit instead.
- **Plan and payment**: the plan, who is billed, the invoice email and currency, and the Paddle subscription ID to quote when you contact support. Paddle stores the card, address and tax ID. **Update payment details** opens Paddle.
- **Invoices**: one row per charged month with the fee, tax and total, and **View invoice**.

The estimate uses the cost reports Stacktape has so far, and AWS keeps finishing a month's reports for a few days after it ends. The invoice charges the final amount.

## Billing FAQ

### Why is my plan still Free after paying?

Paddle confirms the payment to Stacktape separately, usually within seconds. While it does, Subscription plans shows **Confirming your Flexible plan**. If it says **Not confirmed yet**, click **Check again**, and contact support if it stays that way.

### Can I calculate the fee before connecting anything?

Yes, from the table above and your expected AWS bill for the stacks Stacktape would manage. For a stack you haven't deployed yet, [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) shows a monthly AWS estimate before the first deploy. See [Costs overview](/managing-costs/overview) for what drives an AWS bill.

# Connecting your AWS account

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account`

The Stacktape Console works with your AWS accounts through a connection: an IAM role in your account that Stacktape
assumes with short-lived credentials. With it, the Console deploys from Git, shows logs, metrics and costs, and runs
deploys for the CLI when it is signed in. You connect each AWS account once.

The open-source CLI doesn't need a connection. Without a Stacktape account, it deploys with your own AWS credentials.
See [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli).

There are two ways to connect an account:

- **From the terminal**, if you already deploy with the CLI: [`stacktape connect`](/getting-started/add-the-console#connect-from-the-terminal)
  signs you in, creates the connection with your local AWS credentials and adds the Stacktape stacks already in the
  account as projects and stages. Nothing is redeployed.
- **In the Console**, on the **AWS accounts** page, as described below.

Connecting costs nothing by itself. The Console is free while the AWS spend it manages for your organization stays at
or under $200 a month; see [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription). AWS bills your
account for the resources.

## Connect an account in the Console

You need to be an Owner or Admin of the organization.

1. Open **AWS accounts**. With no account connected yet, the page shows **Connect an AWS account**. To add another
   account later, click **Connect AWS account**.
2. Fill in **Account name**, a name your team recognizes, such as `production`. You use it in the CLI as
   `--aws-account production`.
3. Click **Open AWS CloudFormation**. AWS opens in a new tab with everything filled in.
4. At the bottom of the AWS page, check the box that lets CloudFormation create IAM resources, then choose **Create
   stack**.
5. Come back to the Console. Setup takes about a minute after you choose **Create stack**. The page shows
   **Connected** when it's done.

The role has administrator access, so Stacktape can create and update everything your configurations declare. See
[AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) for what it can do and how to restrict it.

The connection stack is always created in `eu-west-1`. That doesn't limit where you deploy: your projects can deploy
to any region Stacktape supports.

To bring in stacks that were deployed before the account was connected, open the account's menu and choose **Find
existing stacks**.

## Account status

The **Status** column on the AWS accounts page says what Stacktape can do with each account:

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|-------|---------|---------------|
| **Connected**, Can deploy | Stacktape deploys your projects here and shows their logs, metrics and costs. | Nothing. |
| **Connected**, Read-only | Stacktape shows logs, metrics and costs but can't deploy. | An Owner or Admin can click **Allow deploys**. |
| **Connecting** | The role is being created in AWS. | Wait; the page updates by itself. |
| **Setup not finished** | Someone started connecting, and AWS hasn't confirmed it. | Click **Finish setup** to see what to check. |
| **Could not connect** | The CloudFormation stack in AWS failed. | Click **Finish setup** to see what to do. |
| **No access** | The role was deleted in AWS, or Stacktape can't reach the account. | Disconnect the account, then connect it again. |

## Common tasks

### Connecting multiple AWS accounts

Organizations commonly connect separate AWS accounts for different purposes, such as a production account with stricter controls and a development account for experimentation. Click **Connect AWS account** and repeat the steps for each additional account.

### Choosing the account for a CLI command

CLI commands that work with a deployed stack, such as `deploy`, `delete` and `rollback`, run in one connected account. The CLI picks it in this order:

1. `--aws-account <name>`, the account's name in the Console.
2. The account your local AWS credentials belong to: `--profile`, then `AWS_PROFILE`, then `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` in the environment. The CLI reads the account ID from the profile's `sso_account_id` or `role_arn` when it can, and otherwise asks AWS STS.
3. The default saved with [`stacktape defaults set`](/cli/defaults-configure).
4. Your organization's only connected account.

If the local credentials belong to an account that is not connected, the command stops before it changes anything and lists the connected accounts. It also stops when their account cannot be determined, for example when an SSO session has expired, and when a profile and environment keys point to different accounts. To deploy anyway, pass `--aws-account`, unset the profile, or connect the account.

`--aws-account` takes precedence over a profile; the CLI prints a line saying the profile is ignored. AWS credentials in environment variables are still used for the deployment when they are set, so they must belong to the selected account.

Each of these commands prints the account it uses, for example `AWS credentials loaded via Stacktape for account production (222222222222)`.

### Revoking access

Revoking stops Console deploys to the account. Your deployed stacks keep running. You can revoke access in two ways:

- **Disconnect the account in the Stacktape Console**: open the account's menu on the AWS accounts page and choose **Disconnect account**. This removes the connection from Stacktape's side.
- **Delete the CloudFormation connection stack in the AWS Console**: this removes the IAM role from your AWS account. The Console then shows the account as **No access**.

### Updating an older connection

A connection made from an older template shows an **Update** button next to it. It opens a dialog with the steps and a
link that updates the connection stack in AWS CloudFormation, so the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log) can name the
person behind each AWS action.

### Checking which regions an account uses

The **Regions** column of the AWS accounts page shows the regions each account has deployments in. Stacktape checks them once the account is connected.

## Troubleshooting

### Account stuck in Connecting or Setup not finished

1. Click **Finish setup**. If you closed AWS before creating the stack, choose **Open AWS again**. If AWS reports a stack creation failure, the Console shows why.
2. Check that the stack is created in the **eu-west-1** region. The link the Console opens targets it automatically.
3. If you can't complete the AWS side, an Owner or Admin can remove the account from its menu and start a new connection.

### Cannot delete a connected AWS account

Stacktape prevents deletion when projects reference the account in their GitOps deployment configurations. The error message lists the affected projects. Delete the GitOps deployment configurations from the listed projects, then retry the deletion.

### Account shows No access

The connection is no longer usable: someone deleted Stacktape's role in AWS, or Stacktape can't reach the account. Deploys to it fail and its logs can't be shown. Disconnect the account, then connect it again.

### "You do not have permission to manage AWS accounts"

Connecting and disconnecting accounts is for Owners and Admins. Ask one of them, or ask for that role. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for details.

## Related features

- [AWS permissions](/stacktape-console/aws-permissions) — details on what the cross-account role can do
- [Organizations, projects, and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) — how connected accounts relate to your project structure
- [GitOps with Console](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) — auto-deploy to connected accounts on push
- [Add the Console](/getting-started/add-the-console) — connect the Console to stacks you deployed with the CLI

## FAQ

### Do I need to create AWS access keys for Stacktape?

No. Stacktape uses cross-account IAM role assumption, not static access keys. The connection CloudFormation stack creates an IAM role that Stacktape assumes with temporary credentials. You never need to generate, rotate, or store AWS access keys for Stacktape to work.

### Can I deploy to any AWS region after connecting?

Yes, to any region Stacktape supports. The connection stack is always created in `eu-west-1`, but that only controls where the connection's CloudFormation stack lives.

### Is connecting my AWS account free?

Connecting has no fee. The Console itself is free while the AWS spend it manages stays at or under $200 a month, and the Flexible plan charges a percentage above that; see [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription). AWS bills your account for the resources.

# Console overview

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/console-overview.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/console-overview`

The Stacktape Console is the web app for the stacks you deploy with Stacktape. It shows your projects and stages with their deployments, logs, metrics, errors, incidents and AWS costs. It also manages team access, Git deployments, alert channels, budgets, secrets and AWS account connections.

The Console is optional. The [CLI](/cli) is open source and deploys without it; see [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli) for what needs the Console and why. The Console is free while your organization's managed AWS spend is up to $200 a month. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).

## Get your stacks into the Console

- **You already deploy with the CLI.** Run [`stacktape connect`](/cli/connect). It signs you in and connects the AWS account of your current AWS credentials. The stacks already in that account appear as projects and stages, without a redeploy.
- **You start in the Console.** Sign in, open **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group and click **Connect AWS account**. [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) walks through it. Then deploy with [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy), or connect a repository for [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console).

## Find your stack and its logs

1. Open **Projects** at the top of the sidebar and select your project. A project is usually one repository, with stages such as `production` and `dev`. [Organizations, projects and stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages) explains how they relate.
2. Select the stage in the row of stages in the project header. Its page has the tabs **Overview**, **Activity**, **Costs**, **Configuration**, **Diagram** and **Danger zone**. Overview lists the stage's endpoints and resources.
3. Click a resource. Its details show **Logs**, **Logs live tail**, **Metrics**, its **Configuration** and the **AWS resources** behind it. Containers also offer a **Remote session**.

The **Logs** page in the Observability group searches the logs of the whole organization. From the terminal, [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs) reads the same logs. See [Logs](/observability/logs).

## The Projects home

**Projects** opens after you sign in. Before your first deploy, it shows how to make one and a search for stacks that are already in your connected AWS accounts. After that, **Your app** shows the stage you deployed most recently with its URL, its state and its recent deploys. The home also lists recent deployments of other projects, **Costs this month** with any budget that is over its limit, and the deploys of the last 30 days.

## What you can do in the Console

- Review deployments and AWS costs across projects and stages
- Respond to [incidents](/observability/incidents), which group signals such as a failing uptime check, a firing alarm or a new error in a production stage
- Read [logs](/observability/logs), [metrics](/observability/metrics) and [traces](/observability/tracing), and see the state of [uptime checks](/observability/uptime-checks) and [synthetic tests](/observability/synthetic-tests)
- Triage runtime errors on the [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking) page
- Review [security findings and vulnerable packages](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) from each deployment, and set [guardrails](/guardrails/overview) that every deployment must pass
- Create [alert channels](/observability/alert-channels), [notification rules](/observability/notifications) and [budgets](/managing-costs/budgets), and check delivery in [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history)
- Manage secrets in AWS Secrets Manager and values in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
- Connect [AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), [Git repositories](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) and [custom domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains)
- Manage [members and roles](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control), sign in through your identity provider with [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on), and review the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log)

Alarms, uptime checks and synthetic tests are defined in the Stacktape configuration and go live when the stack is deployed. The Console shows their state.

## Console navigation

The sidebar starts with **Projects** and **Incidents**, followed by five groups. Some items appear only when your role has the required permission; see [Permission-gated navigation](#permission-gated-navigation). Incidents, Error tracking, Security Overview and Alarms show a count when there is something to look at.

- **Organization**: Activity (the CLI operations of every project), [Costs](/managing-costs/dashboards), [Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control), [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys), [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log), [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on) and [Billing](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).
- **Observability**: [Logs](/observability/logs), [Metrics](/observability/metrics), [Traces](/observability/tracing), [Uptime](/observability/uptime-checks), [Synthetics](/observability/synthetic-tests) and [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).
- **Security**: [Overview](/stacktape-console/security-scanning) (findings and scores), Exposure (what the internet can reach), [Guardrails](/guardrails/overview) and Settings.
- **Alerting**: [Channels](/observability/alert-channels) with their [notification rules](/observability/notifications), [Sent alerts](/observability/alert-history), [Alarms](/observability/alarms) and [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).
- **Configuration**: [Secrets](/configuration/secrets), SSM parameters, [AWS accounts](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account), [Git connections](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console), [Runners](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners), Third-party providers and [Domains](/resources/networking/custom-domains).

The account menu in the header has **Account** (your [account settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings)) and **Sign out**. **Subscription plans** opens from Billing.

## Common tasks

### Viewing deployment activity

Open **Activity** in the Organization group. The page lists Stacktape CLI operations across your organization, so you can see who ran deploys, deletes, scripts, bucket syncs and other recorded commands. The **Activity** tab of a stage lists the operations of that stage.

For each recorded operation, the CLI sends the command, the project, stage, region and AWS account, the Git branch, commit and repository URL, the Stacktape version, timing and the result. It also sends the flags that name the target and change how the command runs, such as `--stage`, `--region`, `--config`, `--full`, `--auto-rollback`, `--no-cache`, `--target-version`, `--script-name`, `--resource-name` and `--bucket-id`. Flags whose value is free-form input are never sent: `--docker-args`, script `--env` values, commands, SDK inputs, secret values and API keys stay on your machine or CI runner.

### Managing secrets

Open **Secrets** in the Configuration group to manage sensitive values stored in AWS Secrets Manager. Secrets created here can be referenced in your Stacktape configuration. The page requires the `secrets:view` permission. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets).

### Managing SSM parameters

Open **SSM parameters** in the Configuration group to manage values stored in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. Use parameters for non-sensitive configuration your workloads need at runtime, such as feature flags or endpoint URLs. Click **New parameter** to add one. The page requires the `ssm-params:view` permission.

### Setting up alarms

Alarms are defined in the Stacktape configuration, in the `alarms` list of a resource, and are created when the stack is deployed. The **Alarms** page in the Alerting group shows the current state of the CloudWatch alarms in your connected AWS accounts. See [Alarms](/observability/alarms).

Alarm rules created in the Console earlier are legacy. They are listed under **Legacy alarm rules** on the Alarms page and keep applying to matching deployments until the stack's configuration defines its alarms. Run `stacktape alarm export` to move them into your configuration.

### Tracking runtime errors

The **Error tracking** page in the Observability group is an error inbox for your deployed workloads. Stacktape reads runtime errors from your logs and groups repeated occurrences into one entry per distinct error and resource. Error tracking is on for every stage by default; a stack turns it off or limits it to some stages with `deploymentConfig.errorTracking`. The page requires the `issues:view` permission. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

### Inviting members

Open **Members** in the Organization group and click **Invite members**. Each member has a role that determines what they can view and change. The page requires the `members:view` permission. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

### Setting budgets

Open **Budgets** in the Alerting group and click **New budget**. Each budget monitors one connected AWS account for the calendar month. Stacktape creates the AWS budget when you save it and removes it when you delete the budget. The **Alerts sent** section on the same page lists the budget alerts that were sent. See [Budgets](/managing-costs/budgets).

### Configuring alert channels and notification rules

Channels are the destinations where alerts are delivered, such as a Slack channel, an email address or a webhook. Open **Channels** in the Alerting group and click **New channel**. The new channel's page opens; click **New rule** there to choose which events (for example a failed deployment, an opened incident or a changed secret) it receives. Adding rules requires the `org:manage-notifications` permission. **Sent alerts** lists every alert that was sent and its delivery status per channel.

## Permission-gated navigation

The Console uses role-based access control. Sidebar items are hidden when your role lacks the required permission:

| Navigation item | Required permission |
|---|---|
| Incidents | `incidents:view` |
| Members | `members:view` |
| API keys | `api-keys:manage-own` (not Viewers) |
| Audit log | `audit-log:view` (Owners and Admins) |
| Single sign-on | `sso:manage` (Owners only) |
| Costs, Billing | `org:view-billing` (Owners and Admins) |
| Error tracking | `issues:view` |
| Security group | `security:view` |
| Alarms | `org:manage-alarms` |
| Budgets | `org:manage-budgets` |
| Secrets | `secrets:view` |
| SSM parameters, Third-party providers | `ssm-params:view` |
| Git connections | Not Viewers |
| Domains | `domains:manage` |

Projects, Activity, Logs, Metrics, Traces, Uptime, Synthetics, Channels, Sent alerts, AWS accounts and Runners are shown to every role. Every role that sees the Security group can read Guardrails; only owners and admins (`org:manage-guardrails`) can change them.


> **Warning:** If a sidebar item is missing, your role may not include the required permission. Ask your organization's owner or admin to adjust your access. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control) for role details.


## Troubleshooting

### Cost data is not appearing

Cost reports are generated daily from AWS Cost and Usage Reports and may take up to a day to appear. If the Costs page shows no data, check that you have a connected [AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) and allow up to 24 hours for data to arrive.

### An alarm does not exist in AWS

Alarms are created when the stack is deployed. After you add an alarm to a resource's `alarms` list, run [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) for the target stage. Legacy Console alarm rules also take effect only on the next deployment of each matching stage.

### The Error tracking page is empty despite errors in logs

A stack reports errors only after it has been deployed with Stacktape v4 while signed in to the Console, because the log subscriptions are added during that deployment. Stacks you deployed without an account and brought in with `stacktape connect` need one signed-in deploy. Click **Settings** on the Error tracking page to open **Error tracking settings**: it shows whether error tracking is on for the organization and lists each deployed stack with whether its last deployment wired error tracking. Also check that the stack's `deploymentConfig.errorTracking` does not turn it off for that stage, and that the resource does not use `logging.logClass: infrequent-access`. See [Error tracking](/observability/error-tracking).

### Sidebar items are missing

Some sidebar items are permission-gated. If you don't see an item (for example, Costs or Alarms), your role may not include the required permission. See the [permission-gated navigation](#permission-gated-navigation) table or ask your organization admin.

## FAQ

### Do I need the Console to use Stacktape?

No. The CLI deploys with your own AWS credentials and needs no account. See [Use the CLI without an account](/getting-started/open-source-cli). The Console adds team access, Git deployments, cost visibility, incidents, error tracking, security findings, budgets and guardrails. Most teams use both: the CLI, directly or in CI, for deploying, and the Console for visibility and operations.

### Does Stacktape deploy into my own AWS account?

Yes. Stacktape uses a cross-account IAM role to manage resources in your AWS account, so you never hand over long-lived AWS credentials. Connect more accounts from **AWS accounts** in the Configuration group. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account) for the required role.

# Organizations, projects and stages

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages`

The Console organizes your work in three levels. An **organization** holds members, connected AWS accounts and projects. A **project** is one application, usually one Git repository. A **stage** is one deployment of that project, such as `production`, `staging` or `dev-alice`, with its own copy of every resource.

## Organizations

Everything in the Console belongs to the organization you have open: projects, costs, alarms, members and billing. Switch organizations in the header.

Most teams need one organization. Create another for a separate boundary, such as each client of an agency, a business unit, or work that must not share members and AWS accounts. Each organization has its own plan and bill. Your personal organization has only you; to work with others, create a team organization. From the CLI, use [`stacktape org create`](/cli/org-create) and [`stacktape org list`](/cli/org-list).

An organization is not an AWS account. You connect one or more AWS accounts to it, and its stages deploy into them. See [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account).

## Projects

A project appears in the Console with its first deploy, from the CLI or from a Git push. There's no separate setup: [`stacktape init`](/cli/init) writes a config with `projectName`, and a signed-in deploy creates the project. Stacks you deployed before you had an account appear as projects when you run [`stacktape connect`](/cli/connect). **New project** in the Console shows the commands to run, and [`stacktape project create`](/cli/project-create) creates an empty project.

Projects are listed on the **Projects** home, the most recently deployed first.

## Stages

A stage is a complete, isolated set of AWS resources, with its own CloudFormation stack, databases, functions and URLs. Stages don't share resources unless you [reference one on purpose](/configuration/stages-and-environments). Most teams deploy the same config to every stage and change sizes per stage in the config.

Each stage costs money for its always-on resources. Delete stages you no longer use.

### Find a stage

Open a project. Its stages are a row of buttons in the project header, each with a dot for its state, so you see every stage's health on every page of the project. `production` and `staging` come first. Past five stages, the rest are in the menu at the end of the row, which has a **Find a stage** search and lists pull request previews under **Pull-request previews**. The AWS account and region of the open stage are at the right of the row.

Click a stage to open its overview: what is deployed, the resources and their URLs, recent deploys, logs, metrics and costs.

### Create a stage

From the CLI, deploy with a new stage name:

```bash
stacktape deploy --stage staging
```

In the Console, click **New stage** in the project header. Name the stage and pick the AWS account and region. A project with a connected Git repository also asks for the branch, commit and config, and **Deploy** starts the deploy on your runner. Without a repository, the page shows the CLI command to run. The new stage gets its own copy of every resource, and existing stages don't change.

### Redeploy, roll back or delete a stage

- **Redeploy** a stage from its overview. The Console asks you to confirm the commit, then shows the deploy's logs.
- **Roll back** with **Roll back to previous** on the stage's latest deploy, **Roll back to this** on an earlier deploy in its activity, or [`stacktape rollback`](/cli/rollback).
- **Delete** a deployed stage with [`stacktape delete`](/cli/delete). It deletes the stack and its data. A Developer can delete only stages that are not production.

A failed first deploy shows as a failed stage until you deploy it again or dismiss it. Dismissing removes its deploy history from the Console; it doesn't touch AWS.

### Project settings

The gear icon next to the project name opens the settings, for members with the `projects:update-settings` permission:

| Setting | Shown when | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Configure Git deployments** | A repository is connected | Opens [Git deployments](/ci-cd-and-gitops/gitops-with-console) for the project |
| **Configure Runner** | Always | Sets the project's [build runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/build-runners) |
| **Configure GitHub Actions runner** | A repository is connected | Sets up a [self-hosted GitHub Actions runner](/ci-cd-and-gitops/self-hosted-github-actions-runners) |
| **Delete project** | You also have `projects:delete` | Removes the project from the Console |

A project created by a CLI deploy has no repository until you click **Connect** on its page, or accept the CLI's offer to deploy on push after a deploy.

Deleting a project in the Console removes it from the Console only. Its deployed stages keep running in AWS, so delete them first with `stacktape delete`. [`stacktape project delete`](/cli/project-delete) refuses while stages exist and prints the commands to delete them.

## Who can do what

Owners and Admins can do everything here. Developers deploy, roll back and delete non-production stages in the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them. Viewers see their projects, deploys, logs and metrics. See [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

## Organizations, projects and stages FAQ

### Why does a new stage show $0?

AWS reports costs about a day after they occur, so a stage deployed today shows its costs tomorrow. See [Cost dashboards](/managing-costs/dashboards#when-numbers-are-missing).

---

# Security scanning

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/security-scanning.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/security-scanning`

Every deploy checks the stack for risky settings and records which packages it uses. The **Security** section of the
Stacktape Console then shows, for each deployed stack, what should change, which packages have known vulnerabilities
and what the internet can reach.

Scanning only reports. It never stops a deploy, even for a critical finding. To block deploys that break a rule, use
[guardrails](/guardrails/overview). An owner or admin can turn on a finding's matching guardrail from the finding's
page (see [Blocking deploys with a guardrail](#blocking-deploys-with-a-guardrail)).

Scanning is on by default. It adds no AWS resources to your stack.

## What is checked

Each AWS account runs two kinds of checks, both on unless an organization owner or admin turns them off.

### Configuration checks

While you deploy, the Stacktape CLI evaluates the stack's resolved configuration against the rules below. It adds no
noticeable time to the deploy.

| Finding | Severity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Database reachable from the internet | High; low outside production | Guardrail: **Keep SQL and OpenSearch private** |
| Production database without deletion protection | Medium | Production only. Guardrail: **Protect databases from deletion** |
| Production data store without backups | Medium | Production only. Guardrail: **Require recoverable data stores** |
| Public load balancer without a web application firewall | Medium; low outside production | Guardrail: **Require WAF on application load balancers** |
| Bucket readable or writable by anyone | Medium | |
| IAM statement allows every action | High | |
| IAM statement grants a whole service on every resource | Medium | For example `s3:*` on `*` |
| Production stack without termination protection | Low | Production only. Guardrail: **Protect stacks from deletion** |
| Production container service runs a single instance | Low | Production only. Guardrail: **Require two container instances** |
| Queue without a dead-letter queue | Low; info outside production | Guardrail: **Require dead-letter queue** |
| Secret stored as a plain environment variable | Critical | A value in `environment` that looks like a credential |

### Dependency checks

The CLI also lists the packages the deployment uses: the packages in your lockfiles and the operating-system and
language packages inside every container image the deploy rebuilt. Images that were not rebuilt keep the packages from
the previous list. The CLI uses the Trivy scanner for this, which it downloads once (about 50 MB).

The list is a CycloneDX file stored in the stack's deployment bucket in your AWS account. After the deploy, the Console
reads it through your AWS account connection, checks every package against the [OSV.dev](https://osv.dev)
vulnerability database, and keeps only the vulnerabilities it finds. It checks every stack's latest list again every
night, so a vulnerability published after your deploy shows up without a new deploy.

Dependency checks run only when configuration checks run.

## The Security pages

The sidebar's **Security** group has four pages: **Overview**, **Exposure**, **Guardrails** and **Settings**.

**Overview** is where you start. Its summary counts the open findings to **Fix now** (critical and high) and to **Fix
when you can** (medium and lower), and how many of your stacks were scanned. Below it, the list of findings has the
severity, what to fix, the stack, when it was last seen and its status, and you can search it. It holds both kinds of
finding: configuration findings, including secrets found in environment variables, and vulnerable packages, with the
versions in use and the version that fixes them (**Fixed in**) or **No fix yet**.

Each stack also has a **Score**: it starts at 100 and loses 25 points for each open critical finding, 10 for each high,
3 for each medium and 1 for each low. Ignored findings don't count. A stack that was deployed but never reported shows
**Not scanned**, so a quiet row is not mistaken for a clean one. Click a stack's counts to see only its findings.

**Exposure** lists what the internet can reach in each stack: public endpoints and whether a web application firewall
protects them, how databases can be reached, and buckets that anyone can read or write. Being reachable is not a
finding by itself; the findings on Overview say what should change.

Click a finding to open its page. It shows **What was found** and **How to fix it**. A configuration finding also
explains **Why it matters**, and a vulnerability shows its **Advisory**: the advisory ID with a link to OSV.dev, other
IDs such as the CVE, the affected and fixed versions, the CVSS rating and references.

## When results appear

The CLI prints a one-line summary and the most severe findings in the output of `stacktape deploy` and
`stacktape validate`. `validate` also lists the findings that only apply to production.

The Console receives the findings after the deploy succeeds:

- **Configuration findings** appear right after the deploy.
- **Vulnerabilities** appear a few minutes later, once the Console has checked the package list. Until then the
  Overview shows **Checking…**. If the check fails, it shows **Check failed**; hover it for the reason. A failed check
  is retried automatically.

A stack is scanned only when it is deployed with Stacktape 4 or newer. Run `stacktape upgrade`, then deploy.

### How a finding changes over time

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Open | The last deploy (or, for a vulnerability, the last check) found the problem. |
| Resolved | A later deploy or check no longer found it. It reopens on its own if the problem returns. |
| Ignored | Someone accepted the risk. It no longer counts as open, also after later deploys, until someone reopens it. |

An ignored finding reopens on its own when it comes back after being resolved, or when its severity rises to high or
critical, for example because the stage became a production stage. The earlier decision to ignore it does not carry
over.

## Production and non-production stages

Some rules matter only once real users depend on the stack, so their findings are reported for production stages only.
Others are reported at a lower severity outside production: a password-protected database that the internet can reach
is a reasonable default for a dev or preview stage, but a real exposure in production. The table in
[Configuration checks](#configuration-checks) shows both.

A stage counts as production when:

1. its `stackConfig.stageType` is `production`; otherwise,
2. it was created as a production stage in the Stacktape Console; otherwise,
3. its name is `prod`, `production`, `prd` or `live`, also with a number such as `prod2`.

The deploy output says which of these decided, for example ``stage `dev` is non-production by its name``. When a
non-production deploy skips production-only findings, it says how many there are; `stacktape validate` lists them.

## Choosing what is scanned

### For an AWS account

Click **Settings** on the Security overview to open **Security settings**. The **AWS accounts** section has two
switches per connected account:

- **Configuration** turns the configuration checks on or off. Off means the account's stacks are not scanned at all.
- **Dependencies** turns the dependency checks on or off. It can be on only while **Configuration** is on.

A newly connected account runs both checks. Only organization owners and admins can change the switches. A change
to the configuration checks applies from each stack's next deploy. Turning **Dependencies** off also stops the
vulnerability checks of packages already listed, including the nightly re-check, and turning it back on resumes them
within about an hour, without a deploy. Findings already reported stay visible.

### For a stack or some stages

Use `deploymentConfig.securityScanning` in the stack's configuration:

```yaml
deploymentConfig:
  securityScanning:
    enabled: true        # default; false turns scanning off for this stack
    stages: [production] # omitted or empty means every stage; names must match exactly
```

```ts
export default defineConfig(() => ({
  deploymentConfig: { securityScanning: { stages: ['production'] } },
  resources: { /* ... */ }
}));
```

When scanning is off for a stack or stage, nothing is evaluated, recorded or sent for it.

### Which setting wins

The AWS account's setting in the Console wins over the configuration:

1. If the account has **Configuration** off, the stack is not scanned, whatever its configuration says.
2. Otherwise, `enabled: false` turns scanning off for the stack.
3. Otherwise, a stage that is missing from `stages` is not scanned.
4. Otherwise, the stack is scanned. Its dependencies are checked unless the account has **Dependencies** off.

The deploy output names the reason, for example
``Security scanning: off (turned off for AWS account `Production` in the Stacktape Console).``

## Ignoring and reopening a finding

Open the finding and click **Ignore**. You can add a reason, which everyone in the organization sees on the finding.
Click **Reopen** on an ignored finding to count it as open again in the lists, the score and the sidebar badge.
Ignoring and reopening need the `security:manage` permission.

A finding resolves on its own when you fix the problem; you do not need to mark it.

## Fixing a finding

- **Configuration findings:** **How to fix it** lists the steps and the configuration change, in TypeScript or YAML
  (it starts with the format the stack was last deployed from). Change your configuration and deploy. The finding
  resolves after the next deploy that no longer has the problem.
- **Secrets in environment variables:** store the value with `stacktape secret set`, reference it with
  `$Secret('...')`, and rotate the credential. The old value stays in your Git history and in earlier deployments, and
  it stays valid until you revoke it. See [Secrets](/configuration/secrets).
- **Vulnerabilities:** upgrade the package to a version listed under **Fixed in**, in your lockfile or in the container
  image, and deploy. The vulnerability resolves after the next check that no longer finds it.

### Blocking deploys with a guardrail

When a finding's rule has a matching guardrail, its page has a **Guardrail** section. It lists the stacks that the
guardrail would block, because they have the same finding open or ignored. An organization owner or admin can click
**Enforce as guardrail** to turn it on for the whole organization.

Once the guardrail is on, the next deploy of a stack that breaks the rule is blocked until the problem is fixed.
Ignoring the finding does not lift the block. Guardrails apply to every stage, including the non-production stages
where a production-only finding is not reported. See [Security and data protection
guardrails](/guardrails/security-and-data-protection).

## Notifications

To hear about new findings, add a rule with the event **New critical or high security findings** to an
[alert channel](/observability/alert-channels). A new Slack (Stacktape app) channel has this rule by default. A channel
receives one message per deploy or nightly check that opens new critical or high findings in a stack. It lists the
first ten and links to the Console. The **When something is found** section of Security settings lists the channels
that receive these messages.

## Permissions

| Action | Permission | Roles |
|---|---|---|
| See the Security pages | `security:view` | Owner, Admin, Developer, Viewer |
| Ignore and reopen findings | `security:manage` | Owner, Admin, Developer |
| Change an AWS account's checks, enforce a finding as a guardrail | `org:manage-guardrails` | Owner, Admin |

Members limited to some projects see only the stacks of those projects. See
[Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control).

## What leaves your AWS account

The CLI sends one report per deploy to the Stacktape Console. It contains:

- **Each configuration finding:** the rule ID, severity, title, message, fix description, resource name and type, an
  identifier that keeps the finding stable across deploys, and a few details: the database's accessibility mode, the
  index and actions of an IAM statement, or, for a secret, the kind of credential it looks like, the variable name and
  where it is set. **The value of a secret is never sent.**
- **Each exposure entry:** the resource name and type, how it can be reached, and whether a firewall protects it.
- **The package list's location:** the bucket, object key, SHA-256 hash, size, format and package count, the scanner
  name and version, and for each workload its name, how its packages were read, its package count and its image digest.
- **About the report:** the deployment it belongs to, the rule catalog version and the Stacktape version.

The package list itself stays in your deployment bucket. To check it, the Console reads the file through your AWS
account connection, keeps it in memory only, and sends each package's identifier (name and version) to OSV.dev. It
stores only the vulnerabilities it finds: the package, the versions in use, the workloads that run them, and the
advisory's IDs, summary, affected and fixed versions, rating and references.

## Related pages

- [Guardrails overview](/guardrails/overview): rules that block deploys
- [Stages and environments](/configuration/stages-and-environments): `stackConfig.stageType`
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account)
- [Console overview](/stacktape-console/console-overview)
