# Single sign-on

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/single-sign-on.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/single-sign-on`

Single sign-on lets your team sign in to Stacktape through your company's identity provider: Okta, Microsoft Entra ID,
Google Workspace, or any SAML 2.0 or OIDC provider. With SCIM, your directory also adds and removes members, so
disabling someone in the directory removes them from your Stacktape organization.

An organization Owner sets it up on the **Single sign-on** page in the Organization group of the sidebar. The page has
five steps, in this order: email domains, identity provider, test sign-in, access, and SCIM.

## Before you start

- **Plan.** Single sign-on and SCIM are part of the Flexible and Enterprise plans. On the Free plan the page shows an
  upgrade prompt. See [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription).
- **Role.** Only Owners can see and change the page. Admins do not see it.
- **Access you need.** You must be able to add a DNS record for your company's email domain, and to create an
  application in your identity provider.

## What your members will see

After setup, people sign in like this:

1. On the Stacktape sign-in page, they click **Sign in with SSO** and enter their work email.
2. Stacktape sends them to your identity provider, and they sign in there.
3. They return to the Console, signed in.

Starting from the identity provider also works, for example from a Stacktape tile in the Okta dashboard.

The first SSO sign-in links the person to the Stacktape account with the same email address, or creates one. If they
are not a member of your organization yet, they join it with the [role for new people](#role-of-new-people). Existing members keep
their role.

An SSO sign-in counts as two-factor sign-in, because your provider enforces its own factors. `stacktape login` works
with SSO too: the CLI opens a browser page where the person signs in with SSO and approves the login.


> **Warning:** Anyone with an address in a verified domain whom your identity provider lets sign in to the Stacktape application
joins your organization. If you remove a
member on the Members page, they join again at their next SSO sign-in. To remove someone for good, remove them from the
Stacktape application in your identity provider, and remove them on the Members page or let [SCIM](#5-scim-provisioning)
do it.


## 1. Verify your email domains

People can sign in through your provider only with an address in a verified domain. You prove that your organization
owns a domain with a DNS record.

1. Under **1. Email domains**, enter the part after @ in your team's addresses, such as `acme.com`, and click
   **Add domain**.
2. The domain appears as **Not verified**, with a TXT record to create. Copy its **Name** and **Value** and add the
   record at your DNS provider. The name has the form `_stacktape-verification.acme.com`.
3. Click **Verify**. DNS changes can take up to an hour to appear. If Stacktape does not find the record yet, try again
   later.

The domain then shows **Verified**.

Keep the TXT record in place. Stacktape checks it daily. If the record is missing, the domain shows **Record missing**
with the date sign-ins will stop. After 7 days without the record, the domain is no longer verified, and people with
addresses in it can no longer sign in through your provider.

A few rules apply to domains:

- Public email providers, such as gmail.com or outlook.com, are refused.
- A subdomain is a separate domain. Add `eu.acme.com` on its own if your team uses it.
- A verified domain belongs to one Stacktape organization. An organization can claim at most 20 domains.

Removing a verified domain stops sign-ins through your provider for addresses in it, and SCIM can no longer add them.
Their Stacktape accounts and memberships stay.

## 2. Connect your identity provider

An organization has one connection. Under **2. Identity provider**, choose the **Protocol**: **SAML 2.0** suits Okta,
Entra ID and Google Workspace; **OIDC** suits providers that offer it.

### SAML 2.0

1. In your identity provider, create a SAML application for Stacktape.
2. Copy these values from the Stacktape page into the application:
   - **ACS URL**, also called the single sign-on URL or reply URL.
   - **Entity ID**, also called the audience URI or identifier.

   If your provider can import service provider metadata, click **Download metadata** instead.
3. Configure the application to send the person's email address as the Name ID, in the `emailAddress` format. The
   attributes `email`, `givenName`, `surname` and `groups` are optional. Microsoft Entra ID's default claims also work.
4. Make sure the provider signs its assertions with SHA-256 or stronger, and that it does not require signed
   authentication requests. Stacktape does not sign its requests.
5. Back in Stacktape, enter the application's **Metadata URL**, or paste the downloaded file into **Metadata XML** when
   the provider has no metadata URL.
6. Click **Save connection**.

Stacktape downloads a metadata URL once, when you save. When your provider changes its signing certificate, save the
connection again.

### OIDC

1. In your identity provider, create an OIDC web application for Stacktape. Set its redirect URI to the
   **Redirect URI** shown on the Stacktape page.
2. Allow client-secret authentication for the application (`client_secret_basic` or `client_secret_post`).
3. In Stacktape, enter the provider's **Issuer URL**, such as `https://acme.okta.com`, and the application's
   **Client ID** and **Client secret**.
4. Click **Save connection**.

Stacktape stores the client secret encrypted and never shows it again. When you edit the connection later, leave
**Client secret** empty to keep the saved one.

### Change or delete the connection

Saving a changed connection asks for a new successful test sign-in before you can turn enforcement on again. If
enforcement is already on, it stays on.

**Delete connection** stops all sign-ins through your provider and turns enforcement off. People keep their Stacktape
accounts and memberships and sign in another way.

## 3. Test the sign-in

**Test sign-in** checks the connection without signing anyone in. It needs a saved connection and at least one verified
domain.

1. Under **3. Test sign-in**, click **Test sign-in**.
2. Sign in at your identity provider as any person from a verified domain. Finish within 10 minutes.
3. You return to the Single sign-on page, still signed in as yourself.

**Last test** shows **Succeeded** or **Failed**. It shows what the provider sent (name, email, groups and attribute
names) or the exact error. You cannot require single sign-on until a test has succeeded.

## 4. Access

### Role of new people

**Role of new people** is the role a person gets when they first sign in through your provider or your directory adds
them: **Viewer** (the default), **Developer** or **Admin**. Owners and Admins can change anyone's role later on the
Members page.


> **Info:** A Developer or Viewer who joins through SSO or SCIM starts without projects or AWS accounts. An Owner or Admin gives
them access with **Edit access** on the [Members](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control#project-and-aws-account-access)
page. An Admin reaches everything from the start.


### Require single sign-on

**Require single sign-on** makes your provider the only way into the organization for members whose address is in a
verified domain. It is off until you turn it on, and it needs a successful test sign-in first. Turn it on and confirm
with **Require SSO**.

While it is on:

- Members in your verified domains who signed in another way (password, passkey, Google or GitHub) see a
  **Sign in with SSO** screen instead of the organization. Their other organizations keep working.
- The password form refuses their address and tells them to use SSO.
- `stacktape login` for this organization works only when the login is approved from an SSO sign-in.
- API keys and CLI logins created before you turned it on keep working until they expire or are revoked.
- Members whose address is outside your verified domains, such as contractors, are not affected.


> **Tip:** Owners are exempt from the requirement, so a broken identity provider cannot lock the organization out. An Owner can
still sign in another way and fix or delete the connection.


## 5. SCIM provisioning

SCIM is optional. It lets your directory add and remove members, so that leaving the company also removes Stacktape
access.

1. Under **5. SCIM provisioning (optional)**, copy the **SCIM base URL** into your directory's provisioning settings.
2. Click **Create SCIM token**. Copy the token from the **Your SCIM token** dialog into your directory as the bearer
   token or secret token, then click **Done**. Stacktape keeps only a digest of the token and cannot show it again.
3. Assign people to the Stacktape application in your directory.

What the directory's changes do:

- **Assigning a person** adds them as a member with the [role for new people](#role-of-new-people). Only addresses in
  verified domains are accepted. If Stacktape already has an account with that address, the directory uses it and does
  not change its name or address.
- **Unassigning, deactivating or deleting a person** removes their membership, exactly as an Owner removing them on the
  Members page. Their CLI logins and personal API keys for the organization stop working. Stacks they deployed keep
  running. When no directory keeps them active any more, they are also signed out of every Console session.
- **Groups** are stored and shown in the test result, but they do not change roles yet.

The last Owner of an organization is never removed this way; the directory gets an error instead.

The **Bearer token** row shows when the token was created and last used.

- **Rotate token** creates a new token that replaces the old one at once. Update your directory immediately, or its
  next changes fail.
- **Revoke** stops your directory from adding or removing people. Everyone it added stays a member.

## If the organization moves to the Free plan

The connection keeps working, so nobody is locked out. You cannot change it until you upgrade again, but you can still
remove domains, delete the connection, revoke the SCIM token and turn enforcement off.

## Audit log

Every change on this page is recorded in the [audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log), including refused attempts.
Members that SSO or SCIM add or remove appear as `member.provisioned` and `member.deprovisioned`, with Stacktape as the
actor and SSO or SCIM as the source.

## Troubleshooting

### Verify says no TXT record holds the value

The record is not visible yet, or its name or value differs. DNS changes can take up to an hour. Some DNS providers add
your domain to the name automatically: then enter only `_stacktape-verification` as the name.

### "is verified by another Stacktape organization"

Another Stacktape organization verified the domain first. A domain belongs to one organization. Use that organization,
or ask its Owner to remove the domain.

### The test sign-in fails with "is not a verified domain"

The provider sent an address outside your verified domains. Check which address it sent in **Last test**. With
Microsoft Entra ID, make sure the address is the person's email address and not a sign-in name from another domain.
Otherwise, add and verify that domain.

### The test sign-in fails at the provider

Check the error under **Last test**. Common causes are unsigned assertions, SHA-1 signatures, a provider that requires
signed authentication requests, or an ACS URL or entity ID copied incorrectly.

### A member sees "requires single sign-on"

They signed in another way. They sign out, click **Sign in with SSO** on the sign-in page and enter their work email.

### A removed member is back

Your identity provider still lets them sign in to the Stacktape application. Remove them there.

## Related features

- [Team and access control](/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control): roles, project and AWS account access
- [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log): who changed what in your organization
- [Account settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings): each person's own ways to sign in
- [Billing and subscription](/stacktape-console/billing-and-subscription): plans that include single sign-on

# Team and access control

Source: `apps/docs/content/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control.mdx`
Route: `/stacktape-console/team-and-access-control`

The **Members** page in the Organization group of the Stacktape Console controls who can use your organization and
what they reach. Invite people, choose their role, projects and AWS accounts, require two-factor sign-in, and see what
stops working before you remove someone. Keys for CI are on the [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys) page.

## Overview

The page has up to three parts:

- **Sign-in rules** (Owners and Admins): whether members who sign in with a password must also use an authenticator
  app.
- **People**: everyone who has joined, with their role, what a Developer or Viewer reaches, two-factor status, when
  they were last active and when they joined. Search by name or email, filter by role, or show only members without
  two-factor or inactive for 30 days or more.
- **Pending invitations**: invitations that have not been accepted yet, who sent them, and when they expire.

Click a member's name to open their page. Owners and Admins can open anyone's page; Developers and Viewers can open
their own.

## Roles

| Role | Can do | Reaches |
|------|--------|---------|
| Owner | Everything, including deleting the organization, billing and appointing other Owners | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Admin | Everything except deleting the organization, setting up single sign-on and changing Owners | Every project and every connected AWS account |
| Developer | Deploy, delete non-production stages, manage secrets and parameters | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |
| Viewer | Read projects, deployments, logs, incidents and members | Only the projects and AWS accounts chosen for them |

## Project and AWS account access

A Developer or Viewer has two lists, set when you invite them and changed with **Edit access**:

- **Projects** decide which projects they see in the Console and which projects the CLI lets them deploy.
- **AWS accounts** decide where Stacktape gives them AWS access: CLI credentials for deploys, scripts and stack
  commands, deployments started from the Console, and the Console pages that read AWS directly (logs, metrics,
  secrets, parameters, debug sessions, redeploys and rollbacks, Investigate and Fix with AI).


> **Warning:** AWS access always covers the whole account. A Developer given the account `production` for the project `shop` can,
with the credentials the CLI receives, also reach other projects' stacks in `production`. Give a person an account
only if they may act in all of it. Agencies with one AWS account per client get a clean boundary by giving each
person only their clients' accounts.


A Developer with no AWS accounts can still see their projects in the Console, but the CLI refuses to deploy, and the
pages that read AWS say that their access does not include the account. Owners and Admins always reach every account.

## Inviting members

1. Open **Members** and click **Invite members**.
2. Enter one or more email addresses, separated by commas or new lines (up to 20 at once).
3. Choose a role. For a Developer or Viewer, choose their projects and AWS accounts.
4. Click **Send invitations**.

Someone who already has a Stacktape account becomes a member at once. Anyone else gets an email and appears under
**Pending invitations** until they sign up. An address that is already a member, or that could not be invited, stays in the
field with the reason, so the rest are not lost.

An invitation works for 14 days after its email last went out. **Resend invitation** sends it again and starts the
14 days again; an expired invitation can be resent the same way. **Copy invite link** copies the sign-up link to
share another way; it only works for the invited address. **Cancel invitation** stops the link from working.

Personal organizations have exactly one member. To work with others, create a team organization; team organizations
have no member limit.

With [single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on), people from your company's email domains can also join
without an invitation, by signing in through your identity provider or being added by your directory.

## Organization keys for CI

A personal API key acts as the person who created it and stops working when they leave the organization, so CI that
uses one breaks when that person is removed. Give CI an organization key instead: it belongs to the organization and
has a role of its own. Owners and Admins create it on **Organization → API keys**; see
[Create an organization key](/stacktape-console/api-keys#create-an-organization-key).

## Requiring two-factor sign-in

Owners and Admins can require two-factor sign-in with **Require** in **Sign-in rules**. Members must then sign
in with a passkey, Google, GitHub, single sign-on, or a password with an authenticator app; a password alone is not
enough. The confirmation lists the members who sign in with a password only. After that, those members see only a
screen that sends them to [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings) to add an authenticator app or a
passkey; the rest of the organization opens again as soon as they sign in that way. API keys, including the CLI and CI,
keep working.

You need two-factor sign-in on your own account before you can require it.

## Removing a member

Open the member's row menu, or their page, and choose **Remove**. The dialog lists what stops working with them:

- their personal API keys, with when each was last used,
- their own AI subscriptions for incident runs,
- their Slack link.

If one of their keys was used in the last 7 days, the dialog says so, because CI may depend on it, and offers to
create an organization key first. Stacks they deployed keep running, their deployments stay in the history, and
organization keys keep working, including ones they created.

**Revoke API keys** in the row menu revokes a member's personal keys without removing them.

## Last active

The Last active column shows the most recent of three times, listed separately when you hover it and on the member's
page:

- **Console**: their last visit, recorded at most once an hour.
- **CLI**: the last request with one of their personal API keys.
- **Last deploy**: the last deploy they started.

## Troubleshooting

### "Your access does not include the AWS account"

The member is a Developer or Viewer and the account is not in their AWS accounts. An Owner or Admin adds it with
**Edit access** on the Members page. The CLI shows the same reason, and `stacktape` lists only the accounts the member
can use.

### The CLI stopped deploying for a Developer after an upgrade

Developers and Viewers reach only the AWS accounts chosen for them. When this was introduced, each of them was given
the accounts their projects had deployed to; an account their projects never used must be added with **Edit access**.

### Invite members is disabled

Either your role cannot invite (only Owners and Admins can), or this is a personal organization.

### An invitation shows Expired

Its 14 days passed. Choose **Resend invitation**; the person can sign up for 14 more days.

## Related features

- [Account Settings](/stacktape-console/account-settings): password and two-factor authentication
- [Single sign-on](/stacktape-console/single-sign-on): sign-in through your identity provider, and SCIM
- [Audit log](/stacktape-console/audit-log): member, key and access changes, and AWS events
- [API keys](/stacktape-console/api-keys): organization keys for CI and personal keys
- [Connecting your AWS account](/stacktape-console/connecting-your-aws-account): what Stacktape can do in an account
- [Organizations, Projects, and Stages](/stacktape-console/organizations-projects-and-stages)

# Agent mode in dev

Source: `apps/docs/content/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev.mdx`
Route: `/using-with-ai/agent-mode-in-dev`

Stacktape [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) can start an HTTP API next to your local workloads and databases. This **agent mode** lets a coding agent, or any HTTP client, check workload status, trigger rebuilds, read logs, query local databases and call read-only AWS operations, so it can edit, test and fix code in a loop. Agent mode is in preview: `GET /` on the running agent lists the endpoints it has.

## When to use

Agent mode is designed for workflows where an AI coding assistant drives the edit-test-fix loop. Enable it when:

- **AI-driven development** — You're using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Windsurf, or another AI coding assistant to build your application. The assistant starts `stacktape dev --agent` as a shell command, then uses the HTTP API to check status, rebuild workloads, read the log file path, query local databases, call AWS SDK commands, and stop dev mode.
- **Automated test harnesses** — You want a script to verify application behavior during development by hitting the status, env, or database endpoints.
- **Database inspection without client tools** — You need to run SQL queries, check Redis keys, scan DynamoDB items, or search OpenSearch indices against local dev databases without installing separate database clients.

## When NOT to use

- **Manual development** — If you're editing code yourself and checking results in a browser, standard [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) without `--agent` is simpler. The TUI output is optimized for human reading.
- **Production observability** — Agent mode runs locally. For deployed stacks, use [`stacktape logs`](/cli/logs), [`stacktape metrics`](/cli/metrics), or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview).
- **CI/CD pipelines** — Use [`stacktape deploy`](/cli/deploy) directly in your pipeline. Agent mode is a development-time feature.

## Starting agent mode

Add the `--agent` flag to the [`stacktape dev`](/cli/dev) command to start the HTTP API server alongside your workloads. Agent mode is dev mode, so it changes your AWS account the same way: the first start deploys the stage's dev stack, and the account's dev network when deployed functions need it. Lambda functions run in AWS; containers and databases run on your machine. [Dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) explains what runs where and what it costs.

```bash
stacktape dev --agent --agent-port 9900 --stage dev --region eu-west-1
```

| Flag            | Description                                                                              |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--agent`       | Enables the agent HTTP API server alongside dev mode                                     |
| `--agent-port`   | Port for the agent HTTP server                                                           |
| `--stage`       | Stage used for dev mode and the `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` directory                 |
| `--region`      | Session AWS region; `/aws/sdk` rejects any different region   |
| `--resources`   | Which workloads to run (`all` or comma-separated names)                                  |
| `--fresh-db`     | Reset local database data on startup                                                     |
| `--yes`         | Confirms creating a project that does not exist yet. `--agent` never confirms it; without `--yes` the start fails with `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` |

Once ready, Stacktape prints the agent URL and a summary of available endpoints. Local database data persists in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` between runs — see [reset scope](/local-development/local-databases#resetting-local-data) before using `--fresh-db`. It resets prepared databases, including relay dependencies, and DynamoDB Local tables share storage.

### Startup progress

A first start creates the account's dev network and the stage's dev stack and takes several minutes; a warm start takes seconds. While the agent starts, the command prints one JSONL `event` line per step with `"phase": "DEV_STARTUP"`, so an assistant can tell a long start from a hung one:

| `eventType`    | Reports                                                                                         |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DEV_SESSION`  | The agent's port and token file first (`detail.kind: "dev-agent"`), the project, stage, region and config file the session resolved (`detail.kind: "dev-target"`), a heartbeat every 20 s, and "Dev session ready" |
| `DEV_NETWORK`  | Creating, updating or reusing the dev network                                                   |
| `DEV_BOX`      | Starting the dev box and connecting to it                                                       |
| `DEV_STACK`    | Creating or updating the dev stack; CloudFormation `UPDATE_STACK` events carry resource counts  |
| `DEV_WORKLOAD` | Each workload starting and running, or its error (`instanceId` is the workload name)            |
| `DEV_DATABASE` | Each local database starting and running, or its error                                          |

If the start fails, the final `result` line carries the failure's own code and hints, for example `CLI_DEV_STACK_CONFLICT` with how to resolve it. Dev mode never updates or deletes a stack it did not create. A dev stack in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` requires explicit deletion before another start; `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` permits another start. A stack still rolling back or in `UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED` must finish or recover before an update can proceed. A Lambda build/deploy failure may leave the agent running with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES` and `ready: false`; inspect status and rebuild it.

## Authentication

The agent listens on `127.0.0.1` only and accepts a request only when it carries the session's token. Each `stacktape dev --agent` run creates a new random token and stores it in `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token` in your home directory (`%USERPROFILE%\.stacktape\dev-agent-tokens\{port}.token` on Windows). Because the file is named after the agent's port, any of your tools can find it from any directory. Only your user can read the file. Stacktape deletes it when the agent stops, and an agent that starts later removes the files of agents that were killed. The startup message and the `AGENT_READY` result print the file path, never the token.

Every request must send the token in an `Authorization: Bearer` header. POST requests must also send `content-type: application/json`. The examples on this page use these shell variables:

```bash
AGENT=http://127.0.0.1:9900
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/9900.token)"
JSON='content-type: application/json'

curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

The agent refuses requests that a web page or another machine could send:

| Request                                                              | Response                     |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| No token or a wrong token                                            | `401 UNAUTHORIZED`           |
| A `Host` header other than `127.0.0.1:{port}` or `localhost:{port}`  | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| Any request with an `Origin` header (sent by browsers)               | `403 FORBIDDEN`              |
| A POST without `content-type: application/json`                      | `415 UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` |

The 401 response names the token file, so a coding assistant that forgot the header can recover on its own. [`stacktape dev stop`](/cli/dev-stop) and the [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) read the token file themselves. `dev stop` stops the agent of the project in the current directory; pass `--cwd <directory>` for another project directory and `--stage <stage>` when several stages run.


> **Tip:** AI coding assistants can call `GET /` on the agent server to receive a full endpoint listing dynamically. Use `GET /?compact=true` for a shorter LLM-oriented response — it includes the current phase, workload names, available local resources with their primary query/schema endpoints, core action templates (rebuild, logs, env, aws, stop), and a pointer to `GET /` for full docs.


## Response format

Every agent endpoint wraps its result in a consistent JSON envelope so clients can handle success and error uniformly.

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "message": "OK",
  "data": {}
}
```

| Field     | Description                                                                          |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `v`       | Envelope version (currently `"1.0"`)                                                 |
| `ok`      | `true` on success, `false` on error                                                  |
| `code`    | Machine-readable status. Common values include `OK`, `NOT_FOUND`, `VALIDATION_ERROR`, `INTERNAL_ERROR`, `ALREADY_EXISTS`, `AUTH_ERROR`, and `READ_ONLY_VIOLATION` |
| `message` | Human-readable description (optional — most responses include it, but not all)       |
| `data`    | Endpoint-specific payload (optional — present when the endpoint returns structured data) |

Many not-found and validation errors include contextual hints in `data`, such as an `available` array of valid resource names or a `hint` string describing expected input. For example, referencing a non-existent workload returns the list of available workloads in `data.available` and a usage hint in `data.hint`. This makes it easy for AI agents to self-correct without extra calls.

Agent endpoints return a JSON envelope with `v`, `ok`, and `code` on every response; most successful responses also include `message` and endpoint-specific `data`. Response examples throughout this page may omit envelope fields like `v` for brevity.

## Core endpoints

### Status

The `/status` endpoint reports the current agent phase and a map of workload names to their local URLs (if running) or status strings. AI agents should poll this endpoint after starting dev mode and wait for `"ready"` before testing workload URLs.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/status
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "phase": "ready",
    "ready": true,
    "failedWorkloads": [],
    "workloads": {
      "api": "http://localhost:3000",
      "worker": "running"
    },
    "sessionId": "0b6c…",
    "projectDirectory": "/home/me/my-app",
    "projectName": "my-app",
    "stage": "dev",
    "region": "eu-west-1",
    "pid": 12345
  }
}
```

`sessionId`, `projectDirectory`, `projectName`, `stage` and `region` identify the session; `dev stop` and the MCP server use them to find the agent of a project.

The `phase` value is one of `starting`, `ready`, `rebuilding`, `stopping`, or `stopped`. Phase becomes `ready` once dev mode has started every selected workload and local resource, and `/stop` moves it to `stopping`. The `ready` field is `true` only when the phase is `ready`, every workload is `running`, and the configuration file still matches the one the session started with. A container workload with a port is `running` once that port accepts connections, after a start and after a rebuild; one that does not within 120 seconds gets the status `error`. A workload that failed, crashed or failed to rebuild makes `ready` false and appears in `failedWorkloads` with its error, so an assistant waiting for `ready` never tests against a workload that is down or runs outdated code. When the configuration file changed, `ready` is false and `restartRequired` explains that dev mode has to restart (see [Rebuild](#rebuild)). A frontend whose running dev server printed an error, such as a request that failed in the app's code with its cause, stays `running` and keeps the session ready, because its server still serves: the error is in `requestErrors` (and the workload's `requestError` in verbose mode) until the next successful request, compile or code update.

If a workload fails while `stacktape dev --agent` is starting, the command stops the session, prints each failed workload with its error and the log file path, and exits with a non-zero code.

For detailed information including uptime, per-workload type/port/error data, local resource status, and the log file path, use verbose mode.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" "$AGENT/status?verbose=true"
```

The verbose response replaces the workload string map with an array of objects containing `name`, `type`, `status`, `url`, `port`, and `error` fields, plus a `localResources` array, `uptime` in seconds, and the `logFile` path. Workload `status` is one of `pending`, `starting`, `running`, `error`, or `stopped`. Local resource status uses the same values.

### Logs

The `/logs` endpoint returns the path to the JSONL log file on disk. Logs are **not** streamed through the HTTP response — AI agents should read the file directly using standard tools like `tail`, `grep`, or `jq`.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/logs
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt",
    "format": "jsonl",
    "hint": "Use standard tools: tail -n 50 <logFile> | jq ."
  }
}
```

Each line in the log file is a JSON object with these fields:

| Field    | Example                      | Description                           |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| `ts`     | `"2025-03-15T14:30:15Z"`    | When the line was produced. For a deployed function, the CloudWatch event time, not the time it was fetched |
| `source` | `"api"`, `"dev"`             | Workload or database that produced the line, or `dev` for dev mode itself |
| `level`  | `"info"`, `"warn"`, `"error"` | Severity level                      |
| `msg`    | `"Server started on :3000"`  | Log message content, without terminal colors |

Lines with `"source":"dev"` record dev mode's own lifecycle: startup steps, file changes, rebuilds started, finished or failed with the error, dev stack updates and dev box state. Grep them to see what dev mode did, for example whether a rebuild failed:

```bash
grep '"source":"dev"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

A restart keeps the previous session's lines. Each session appends to the file and starts with a `"msg":"Dev session started"` line whose `session` field names its session ID, project directory and stage. A file over 10 MB moves to `<file>.1` when the next session starts.

Deployed dev functions keep their source maps and run with `--enable-source-maps`, so stack traces in the log point at your source files rather than the bundle.

View the last 50 lines:

```bash
tail -n 50 .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter for errors only:

```bash
grep '"level":"error"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

Filter by a specific workload:

```bash
grep '"source":"api"' .stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt
```

This file-based approach is intentional — AI coding assistants already have file-reading tools, and `tail -f` provides real-time streaming without polling overhead.

### Environment variables

The `/env/{workload}` endpoint returns the environment variables available to a specific workload. For Lambda functions, variables are fetched from the deployed AWS function configuration. A function that uses a local database shows that database's `STP_*` variables with the address of the [dev box](/local-development/debugging-lambda-functions#connecting-to-local-databases), through which the function reaches it. For containers and frontends, variables are read from the local runner state. A container whose image failed to build still shows the environment it would get. A workload that failed before dev mode prepared its environment, for example because the dev stack did not deploy, returns `WORKLOAD_NOT_STARTED` with its error.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/env/api
```

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": true,
  "code": "OK",
  "data": {
    "workload": "api",
    "type": "function",
    "source": "aws",
    "envVars": {
      "STP_NOTES_TABLE_TABLE_NAME": "my-project-dev-notesTable",
      "AWS_REGION": "eu-west-1"
    },
    "count": 2
  }
}
```

Secret values are masked. The agent replaces the values of variables read from `$Secret` or `$SsmParam`, of variables whose names mark them as secret (such as `PASSWORD`, `TOKEN`, `KEY`, `SECRET` or `AUTHORIZATION`, which includes the AWS credentials of container workloads), and the password inside connection strings, for example `postgresql://[redacted:credentials]@localhost:5432/app`. Host names, private IP addresses, ports, database names and plain settings stay readable. A deployed dev function reaches a local database at the private address of the dev box, such as `10.230.4.17`, so its `/env` shows that address. Public IP addresses are masked as `[redacted:ip]`. Your workloads still receive the real values.

Local databases never use the deployed database's secret. When the configured password is a directive such as `$Secret('db', 'password')`, dev mode generates a local password, keeps it in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/{resource}/password`, and gives that same password to the container, the deployed dev functions and local workloads.

This endpoint is useful for debugging [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) wiring. If an expected `STP_*` variable is missing, the workload's `connectTo` array likely doesn't reference the target resource. The response also includes the `source` field — `"aws"` for Lambda functions (fetched from the deployed function configuration) or `"local"` for other tracked workload types (currently container, hosting-bucket, and nextjs-web workloads, read from the local runner state).

### Rebuild

After editing application code, trigger a workload rebuild to pick up the changes. Rebuilding a specific workload is faster than rebuilding all of them — AI agents should target only the workload whose code changed.

Rebuild a specific workload:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/rebuild/api
```

Rebuild all workloads at once:

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/rebuild/all
```

The request answers after the workload has been rebuilt and, for a Lambda function, its new code deployed. A rebuild that fails, for example because of a syntax error, answers with `ok: false`, the code `REBUILD_FAILED`, the build error, the failed workloads and the log file path:

```json
{
  "v": "1.0",
  "ok": false,
  "code": "REBUILD_FAILED",
  "message": "Rebuild failed. api: Build failed: Unexpected ;",
  "data": {
    "failedWorkloads": [{ "name": "api", "error": "Build failed: Unexpected ;" }],
    "logFile": ".stacktape/dev-agent/9900-logs.txt",
    "hint": "The failed workloads keep the status error. A failed function keeps its deployed code, and a container's error says whether its previous build still serves requests. Fix the error and rebuild again."
  }
}
```

The workload then has the status `error` and `/status` reports `ready: false` until a rebuild of it succeeds. Its previous code may still answer requests, so a test that passes while the workload is in `error` does not test your change.

When the rebuilt workload's files are also used by other workloads, such as a shared package in a monorepo, and changed after those workloads were last built, the result names them in `staleWorkloads` with the changed files, and the message says so: `Rebuilt api. quote, report also use changed files (packages/shared/src/index.ts) and still run the previous build; rebuild them or rebuild all.` With `--watch`, a change rebuilds every workload that uses the file.

A batch job runs in AWS from the image dev mode built when it started, and no rebuild builds it again. When that image also uses the changed files, the result names the job in `staleRemoteImages` and the message says to restart dev mode, which builds and pushes the image again. Images built from a Dockerfile or with Railpack report their files; a job whose image reports none is not named.

`/rebuild/all` leaves running frontends (Next.js, other SSR frameworks and static sites with a dev command) alone, because their dev servers load changed code themselves; the result lists them in `leftRunning`. A frontend whose server failed is restarted, and `/rebuild/{name}` restarts a frontend's server.

A rebuild deploys code only. When the Stacktape configuration file changed since dev mode started, the rebuild does nothing and answers with the code `CONFIG_CHANGED_RESTART_REQUIRED`. A change to the `scripts` section alone does not count: scripts run only on request, and the seed endpoint reads them from the file each time. It still counts when another part of the configuration reads the scripts with `$This()`. Stop dev mode and start it again: the start updates the dev stack with the new configuration. Formatting and comments do not count as a change. The refused workloads keep their status and their previous build keeps serving; `ready` stays false and `restartRequired` explains why. If you revert the configuration instead, the next rebuild, or with `--watch` the configuration check, rebuilds them.

With `--watch`, dev mode rebuilds a workload when one of its source files changes, through the same path, so a failed build sets the same `error` status and writes the error to the log file. It also watches the configuration file and sets `restartRequired` when it changes. `stacktape dev --agent --watch` reports the session started only after the watcher is running, so an edit made right after the start is rebuilt.

A workload builds one rebuild at a time. A request for a workload that is rebuilding waits for that build and then builds the current files, and further requests made meanwhile join it. Only the last build sets the workload's status, so the status always reflects the newest files.

Running `stacktape dev --agent` again while the session runs reports the same workloads, URLs and database ports as the start did. When the session waits for a restart, the command fails with `CLI_DEV_RESTART_REQUIRED`. When a workload in it failed, the command fails with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES`, and while it still starts, with `DEV_SESSION_NOT_READY`; the session keeps running and the result's `data` carries it with `ready: false` and `failedWorkloads`.

### Liveness check

`GET /health` returns the current agent phase and can be used as a simple liveness check. Unlike `/status`, `/health` does not include workloads or local resources — it only returns `ok` and the current agent `phase` inside the standard envelope. Use `/status` for full workload details.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/health
```

### Resource health checks

Check the health of a specific local resource (database, cache). The agent monitors local resources automatically, but this endpoint triggers an immediate check and returns the result.

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/health/myDb
```

The response includes `name`, `type`, `port`, `host`, and the `status` value returned by the local health monitor. If the resource name doesn't match any running local resource, the error response includes an `available` array listing valid resource names.

### Stop

Gracefully shut down dev mode, all workloads, and all local resources.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" -d '{}' $AGENT/stop
```

Calling stop when the agent is already stopping or stopped returns success without side effects.

## Database endpoints

Agent mode exposes database endpoints for PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB and OpenSearch. Most operate on local instances. DynamoDB `query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` can also read a table deployed by the dev stack and mark responses `deployed: true`; `get`, `put`, `delete` and `reset` require a local table. `GET /` lists endpoint groups for running local resources. Errors include available resource names where applicable.

The `{name}` path parameter in every database endpoint matches the resource name in your Stacktape configuration. If you reference a name that doesn't exist, the error response includes an `available` array listing the valid resource names.


> **Warning:** The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis command/query endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` in the request body — without it, the request is rejected. The DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields shown below.


### PostgreSQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a PostgreSQL engine in your Stacktape configuration.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/postgres/myDb/query \
  -d '{"sql": "SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 10"}'
```

| Endpoint                          | Method | Description                    | Parameters                            |
| --------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------- |
| `/postgres/{name}/query`          | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`   |
| `/postgres/{name}/schema`         | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)     |
| `/postgres/{name}/tables`         | GET    | List all tables                |                                       |
| `/postgres/{name}/explain`        | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, analyze?}`                     |
| `/postgres/{name}/indexes`        | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/stats`          | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)       |
| `/postgres/{name}/sample`         | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                 |

### MySQL

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [relational database](/resources/databases/relational-database) with a MySQL or MariaDB engine in your Stacktape configuration. The endpoint path uses `/mysql/` for both MySQL and MariaDB resources.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/mysql/myDb/query \
  -d '{"sql": "SHOW TABLES"}'
```

| Endpoint                        | Method | Description                    | Parameters                                             |
| ------------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `/mysql/{name}/query`           | POST   | Execute SQL                    | `{sql, limit?, timeout?, confirm?}`                    |
| `/mysql/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Column types and constraints   | `?tables=t1,t2` (optional filter)                      |
| `/mysql/{name}/tables`          | GET    | List all tables                |                                                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/explain`         | POST   | Query execution plan           | `{sql, format?}` (format: `"traditional"`, `"json"`, or `"tree"`) |
| `/mysql/{name}/indexes`         | GET    | Index definitions              | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/stats`           | GET    | Table statistics               | `?table=name` (optional filter)                        |
| `/mysql/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample rows from a table       | `?table=name&limit=5`                                  |

A PostgreSQL or MySQL query that writes rows (`INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`) returns the number of rows it changed in `affectedRows`, as the database driver reports it. `rowCount` is the number of rows returned, or the number of changed rows when the statement returns none.

### Redis

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for a [Redis cache](/resources/databases/redis) in your Stacktape configuration. The `cmd` field accepts a Redis command as a single string (e.g. `"GET mykey"`, `"SET user:1 '{\"name\":\"Alice\"}'"`).

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/redis/myCache/command \
  -d '{"cmd": "GET session:user123"}'
```

| Endpoint                       | Method | Description                  | Parameters                       |
| ------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
| `/redis/{name}/command`        | POST   | Execute any Redis command    | `{cmd, confirm?}`               |
| `/redis/{name}/keys`           | GET    | List keys matching pattern   | `?pattern=*&limit=100`          |
| `/redis/{name}/get`            | GET    | Get value by key             | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/ttl`            | GET    | Get TTL for a key            | `?key=name`                     |
| `/redis/{name}/info`           | GET    | Server info                  | `?section=memory` (optional)    |
| `/redis/{name}/type`           | GET    | Get type of a key            | `?key=name`                     |

### DynamoDB

`query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` support both local tables and tables deployed by the dev stack (responses include `deployed: true`). `get`, `put`, `delete` and `reset` require a local [DynamoDB table](/resources/databases/dynamodb). Key parameters (`pk`, `sk`) are objects mapping attribute names to values — for example, `{"userId": "123"}`.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/dynamodb/notesTable/scan \
  -d '{"limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                           | Method | Description                  | Parameters                                    |
| ---------------------------------- | ------ | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/query`           | POST   | Query by partition/sort key  | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?, index?, limit?}`       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/scan`            | POST   | Full table scan              | `{filter?, limit?}`                           |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/get`             | POST   | Get single item              | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/put`             | POST   | Put an item                  | `{item: {...}}`                               |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete an item               | `{pk: {key: val}, sk?}`                       |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/schema`          | GET    | Table key schema and indexes |                                                |
| `/dynamodb/{name}/sample`          | GET    | Sample items                 | `?limit=5`                                    |

### OpenSearch

Available when dev mode is running a local instance for an [OpenSearch domain](/resources/databases/opensearch) in your Stacktape configuration. Query bodies follow standard OpenSearch query DSL.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/opensearch/searchDomain/search \
  -d '{"query": {"match": {"title": "serverless"}}, "limit": 10}'
```

| Endpoint                             | Method | Description                  | Parameters                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ------ | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| `/opensearch/{name}/search`          | POST   | Search documents             | `{query: {...}, index?, limit?}`     |
| `/opensearch/{name}/get`             | GET    | Get document by ID           | `?index=idx&id=docid`               |
| `/opensearch/{name}/put`             | POST   | Index a document             | `{index, id?, doc: {...}}`           |
| `/opensearch/{name}/delete`          | POST   | Delete a document            | `{index, id}`                        |
| `/opensearch/{name}/indices`         | GET    | List all indices             |                                      |
| `/opensearch/{name}/mapping`         | GET    | Get index mapping            | `?index=idx`                         |
| `/opensearch/{name}/analyze`         | POST   | Analyze text with tokenizer  | `{text, analyzer?, index?}`          |
| `/opensearch/{name}/count`           | GET    | Count documents              | `?index=idx` (optional)              |

## Reset and seed local databases

An end-to-end test needs a known database state. Resetting deletes the data of the local databases and keeps their schema, so a test can start from empty tables without restarting dev mode. A seed script then writes the rows the test expects.

```bash
# Every local database, keeping the settings table
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/reset/all -d '{"confirm": true, "keepTables": ["settings"]}'
# One database
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/reset/myDb -d '{"confirm": true}'
# Run the seed script from the config
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/scripts/seed/run -d '{}'
```

| Endpoint                  | Method | Description                                                         | Parameters                   |
| ------------------------- | ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `/reset/{name}`           | POST   | Delete the data of one local database, or of all with `/reset/all` | `{confirm: true, keepTables?}` |
| `/scripts/{script}/run`   | POST   | Run a `local-script` from the config against the local databases    | `{timeoutSeconds?}`          |

A reset requires `{"confirm": true}` and changes only databases that dev mode runs on your machine; any other name returns `NOT_FOUND`. What it does per database type:

- **PostgreSQL**: one `TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY` of every table in the database's own schemas, so identity columns start again at 1. Tables that extensions own, such as PostGIS's `spatial_ref_sys`, stay.
- **MySQL and MariaDB**: `TRUNCATE` of every table of the configured database, which also resets `AUTO_INCREMENT`. A database without `dbName` uses the MySQL system database `mysql`. The reset refuses it, like the other system databases `sys`, `performance_schema` and `information_schema`, because they hold the server's users and state; set `dbName` on the engine to reset the application's data.
- **Redis**: `FLUSHALL`.
- **DynamoDB**: deletes every item; the table and its indexes stay.
- **OpenSearch**: not supported. `/reset/all` skips it and names it in `skipped`; start dev mode with `--fresh-db` to delete its data.

Migration history tables stay in every SQL database, so the schema and the migration tool still agree after a reset: `_prisma_migrations`, `__drizzle_migrations`, `knex_migrations`, `kysely_migration`, `pgmigrations`, `migrations`, `mikro_orm_migrations`, `SequelizeMeta`, `schema_migrations`, `flyway_schema_history`, `databasechangelog`, `alembic_version`, `django_migrations`, `goose_db_version`, `__EFMigrationsHistory` and their lock tables. `keepTables` names more tables to keep. A kept table that references a reset table through a foreign key stops the reset with an error instead of being emptied with it.

The seed is a script from the `scripts` section of your config. It runs as a [`beforeDev` hook](/configuration/hooks-and-scripts) would: its `connectTo` resources resolve to the local databases of this session, and the response carries its output. It is stopped after `timeoutSeconds` (default 50, at most 280) and then returns `SCRIPT_TIMEOUT`. The seed reads the script from the config file as it is now, so a script added or edited after dev mode started runs without a restart; a config file that no longer loads returns `CONFIG_INVALID`.

The seed endpoint refuses scripts that reference a deployed resource it knows about. It checks every string of the script, including directives nested in `$Format` and directives inside commands: `connectTo` and `$ResourceParam` must name databases running locally, and `$CfResourceParam`, `$StackOutput`, `$CfStackOutput` and `$CfFormat` are refused. Bastion scripts and scripts that assume a workload's role are refused. After the directives resolve, a script whose environment or commands contain the host or endpoint of one of the stack's deployed databases is refused before it runs.


> **Warning:** A seed script is not a sandbox. It runs on your machine with your AWS credentials, so it can still reach deployed data in ways the check cannot see: a value read with `$Secret`, a URL written literally in the script or in an `.env` file it loads, or an AWS SDK call. Keep seed scripts pointed at the connection that dev mode gives them.


```typescript
scripts: {
  seed: {
    type: 'local-script',
    properties: {
      executeCommand: 'npx prisma db seed',
      // STP_MAIN_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING points at the local database
      connectTo: ['mainDatabase']
    }
  }
}
```

## Invoke a function with a test event

A function that no URL reaches, such as one triggered by a schedule, a queue, a topic or a stream, can be tested by invoking it with an event of that shape. `/functions/{name}/invoke` invokes a function of this session in AWS and returns what it returned.

```bash
# sessionId and stage from /status, the function's ARN from its deployedResources
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/functions/nightly-report/invoke \
  -d '{"event": {"source": "aws.events", "detail-type": "Scheduled Event"}, "confirm": true,
       "expectedSessionId": "<sessionId>", "expectedStage": "dev",
       "expectedFunctionArn": "arn:aws:lambda:eu-west-1:123456789012:function:my-app-dev-nightly-report"}'
```

The function runs its deployed code with its own role, so it can change data and call other services: without `"confirm": true` the endpoint returns `CONFIRMATION_REQUIRED` and invokes nothing. Only a function this session runs is invoked, and only while it is `running`: another name returns `NOT_FOUND` with the session's functions, a function the session leaves out returns `NOT_IN_SESSION`, and a function whose rebuild failed returns `WORKLOAD_NOT_RUNNING`. Before it invokes, the agent reads the function and its environment in AWS: the `payload` it returns is masked with that environment, values read with `$Secret` or `$SsmParam` included, and with every other environment the session knows, as the logs are. A JSON payload is masked value by value before it is serialized, so a secret with a quote or backslash in it is masked too. When the function cannot be read, or Lambda reports an environment error or returns no environment for a function whose configuration sets variables, the endpoint returns `MASKING_UNAVAILABLE` and invokes nothing. The response has the function's `functionArn`, `statusCode`, its `payload` (at most 16 KB) and `durationMs`. Every request must name the session it checked: `expectedSessionId` and `expectedStage` as `/status` reports them, and `expectedFunctionArn` from its `deployedResources`. A request without them returns `SESSION_BINDING_REQUIRED`; when the agent runs another session or the function has another ARN, it returns `DEV_SESSION_CHANGED`. Neither invokes anything.

Masking keeps secret values from reaching an assistant's transcript or the logs by accident: values read with `$Secret` or `$SsmParam` and values under names such as `PASSWORD`, `SECRET`, `TOKEN` or `KEY` are replaced wherever they appear as they are, trimmed, line by line or escaped in JSON. It is not a boundary against code the assistant writes itself, which can always print a secret in another form, such as base64, URL-encoded or split up; those forms are not matched. A handler that throws returns `FUNCTION_ERROR` with `functionError` and the error payload, and a failed call to Lambda returns `INVOKE_FAILED`. What the function logs arrives in the session's logs. The `/aws/sdk` endpoint below stays read-only and refuses `Invoke`.

## AWS SDK access

Agent mode provides access to read-only AWS SDK commands through the `/aws/sdk` endpoint. It sends only the reviewed read-only operations that [`aws call`](/cli/aws-call#safety-model) accepts; any other operation, including the Secrets Manager and SSM value reads, is rejected before a request is sent. Environment variable values and Cognito client secrets come back redacted, CloudFormation templates come back as their structure without any value, while other reads, such as log events and S3 objects, return application data as it is. The endpoint uses the dev agent IAM role. The role only reads, and only the resources of this dev stack in the session region: it identifies them by the stack-name tag CloudFormation puts on every resource, or by their identifiers in the template. CloudWatch metric and alarm reads cover the whole session region, because metrics belong to no stack. The HTTP endpoint accepts only reviewed read operations and adds resource filtering for Batch, whose read actions IAM cannot limit to the stack. If the role is missing or cannot be assumed after the IAM-propagation retry, the request fails; it never falls back to the developer's credentials. Restart dev mode to update the stack and role when needed.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "$AUTH" -H "$JSON" $AGENT/aws/sdk \
  -d '{"service": "lambda", "command": "GetFunctionConfiguration", "input": {"FunctionName": "my-app-dev-api"}}'
```

The request body accepts `service` (required), `command` (required), `input` (optional, defaults to `{}`), and `region` (optional, must equal the session region if supplied; another region is rejected). Use [`stacktape aws call`](/cli/aws-call) with an explicit target for a different region. If `service` or `command` is missing, the agent returns a validation error with a hint showing the expected request shape.

To list all supported services and example commands:

```bash
curl -H "$AUTH" $AGENT/aws/sdk/services
```

`GET /aws/sdk/services` returns a successful envelope whose payload lists the accepted operations for each supported service, nested under `data.data` in the response. Use the running endpoint response as the authoritative list of valid `service` and `command` values before constructing `/aws/sdk` calls. The service list in the startup message and on this page is a summary; the endpoint response is always up to date.

Common AWS SDK calls for AI agents:

| Use case                  | Service            | Command              | Example input                                                  |
| ------------------------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read Lambda logs          | `logs`             | `FilterLogEvents`    | `{"logGroupName": "/aws/lambda/fn", "filterPattern": "ERROR"}` |
| Scan a DynamoDB table     | `dynamodb`         | `Scan`               | `{"TableName": "tbl", "Limit": 10}`                           |
| List S3 objects           | `s3`               | `ListObjectsV2`      | `{"Bucket": "bkt", "Prefix": "uploads/"}`                     |
| Check a queue's backlog   | `sqs`              | `GetQueueAttributes` | `{"QueueUrl": "https://…/q", "AttributeNames": ["All"]}`       |
| Describe a stack          | `cloudformation`   | `DescribeStacks`     | `{"StackName": "my-stack"}`                                    |


> **Info:** The startup message lists supported `service` identifiers: `lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `cloudwatch`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, `eventbridge`, `secretsmanager`, `ssm`, `sts`, `iam`, `ec2`, `ecs`, `ecr`, `rds`, `ses`, `cognito`, `apigatewayv2`, `xray`, `kinesis`, `firehose`, and more. Call `GET /aws/sdk/services` on the running agent for the complete, up-to-date list.


## Typical AI agent workflow

The core value of agent mode is the **automated feedback loop**: an AI agent writes code, checks if it works, reads any errors, fixes them, and rebuilds — all without human intervention.


## Flow
1. **Write config**: AI writes or edits stacktape.ts based on your requirements
2. **Start agent mode**: AI runs stacktape dev --agent to boot workloads and databases
3. **Write application code**: AI implements handlers, services, and frontend code
4. **Rebuild and test**: AI calls POST /rebuild/{name}, checks status, reads logs, queries databases
5. **Fix and iterate**: AI reads error logs, fixes code, rebuilds — repeating until everything works
6. **Deploy**: When you ask for it, the agent deploys a real stage; through MCP the deploy waits for your go-ahead


### Example session

An AI coding assistant building a notes API would follow this sequence:

1. Write `stacktape.ts` with a Lambda function, DynamoDB table, and HTTP API Gateway trigger
2. Start agent mode: `stacktape dev --agent --agent-port 9900 --stage dev --region eu-west-1`
3. Poll `GET /status` until `phase` is `"ready"` and `ready` is `true`
4. Write the handler code in `src/handler.ts`
5. Call `POST /rebuild/api` to pick up the new code
6. Test the endpoint by calling the workload URL from the status response
7. If errors occur, get the log file path from `GET /logs`, then read it: `tail -n 50 <logFile>`
8. Check `GET /env/api` to verify that `STP_NOTES_TABLE_TABLE_NAME` is injected
9. Query the database directly via `POST /dynamodb/notesTable/scan` to verify stored data
10. Fix code, rebuild, and test again until everything works
11. When you ask for a deploy, run `stacktape deploy` to a stage other than the dev stage (through MCP, the deploy waits for your approval)

Here is a minimal Stacktape configuration that an AI agent might produce for this workflow:


Example (TypeScript):

```typescript
import {
  defineConfig,
  LambdaFunction,
  DynamoDbTable,
  HttpApiGateway,
  JsBundleLambdaPackaging
} from 'stacktape';
export default defineConfig(() => {
  const notesTable = new DynamoDbTable({
    primaryKey: { partitionKey: { name: 'noteId', type: 'string' } }
  });

  const api = new LambdaFunction({
    packaging: new JsBundleLambdaPackaging({
      entryfilePath: './src/handler.ts'
    }),
    connectTo: [notesTable],
    events: [
      {
        type: 'http-api-gateway',
        properties: { httpApiGatewayName: 'apiGw', path: '/{proxy+}', method: '*' }
      }
    ]
  });

  const apiGw = new HttpApiGateway({});

  return {
    resources: { notesTable, api, apiGw }
  };
});
```


### Tips for AI agent integrations

- **Poll status before testing** — Wait for `"phase": "ready"` before making requests to workload URLs. Workloads may still be compiling during the `starting` phase.
- **Use compact docs** — Call `GET /?compact=true` at the start of a session to discover available endpoints with minimal token usage. The full `GET /` listing is more detailed but token-heavy.
- **Rebuild selectively** — `POST /rebuild/{name}` rebuilds only the named workload. Use it instead of `/rebuild/all` when you changed code in a single workload.
- **Check env vars early** — `GET /env/{workload}` reveals whether [`connectTo`](/configuration/connecting-resources) is wired correctly before you start debugging application code.
- **Read logs from the file** — The `/logs` endpoint returns a file path. Use `tail`, `grep`, or `jq` to filter the JSONL log file. Use `tail -f` for real-time streaming.
- **Inspect schemas before writing queries** — Call the `/schema` or `/tables` endpoint to discover table and column names before writing SQL or DynamoDB queries.
- **Use database endpoints for verification** — After writing data through your API, query the database directly to confirm it was stored correctly.

## MCP server integration

For MCP-based assistant setup, see the [Stacktape MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) page. If your AI assistant supports the Model Context Protocol (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf), the MCP server provides a higher-level integration layer. Agent mode's HTTP API is the lower-level alternative that works with any tool capable of making HTTP requests. The MCP `stacktape_dev` tool calls this API for the assistant, so it never handles the token file: its `status`, `logs`, `rebuild`, `query`, `tables`, `reset_db`, `seed`, `invoke`, `env`, `aws` and `stop` actions map to the endpoints on this page. Without a session ID it acts only on sessions of its own project directories, so an assistant in one worktree cannot rebuild or reset another worktree's session by accident.

## Security

The agent can run SQL against your local databases, rebuild and stop workloads, and call AWS read operations with the dev agent's credentials. Only programs running as your user on this machine can call it:

- It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines on your network cannot connect.
- Every request needs the session token from `~/.stacktape/dev-agent-tokens/{port}.token`, which only your user can read.
- It refuses requests with an `Origin` header or a foreign `Host` header, so a web page cannot call it, even through DNS rebinding.
- POST requests must be JSON, which a web page cannot send to another site without the browser asking the agent first.

Do not forward the agent port to other machines, and do not paste the token into chats or logs.

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint fails closed when the dev agent role is missing or cannot be assumed; it never falls back to developer credentials. The role reads only this dev stack's resources in the session region; CloudWatch metric and alarm reads cover the whole session region. The endpoint accepts only reviewed read operations and adds resource filtering for Batch. See [AWS SDK access](#aws-sdk-access) for the boundary.

## FAQ

### Should I use agent mode or the Stacktape MCP server?

Both work with assistants like Claude Code, Cursor, and Windsurf. Agent mode is a plain HTTP API that any tool can call with `curl` or HTTP libraries — no protocol integration needed, so it suits custom tooling or any client that can make HTTP requests. The [MCP server](/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup) uses the Model Context Protocol standard that those assistants support natively, providing a more integrated, higher-level layer. If your AI tool supports MCP, prefer the MCP server; reach for agent mode when you need raw HTTP access.

### What databases can I query through the agent API?

Agent mode exposes typed HTTP endpoints for five local resource types started by dev mode — PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch — so agents can inspect schemas, run queries, and verify data without installing separate database client tools. Each type has its own endpoint group (SQL engines get `query`/`schema`/`tables`/`explain`/`indexes`/`stats`/`sample`, plus key-value and document operations for Redis, DynamoDB, and OpenSearch). `GET /` lists only the endpoint groups for resources currently running in the session.

### Is my data persisted between agent mode sessions?

Yes. The startup message confirms local database data is stored in `.stacktape/dev-data/{stage}/` and survives restarts. To empty the databases while dev mode runs, call [`/reset`](#reset-and-seed-local-databases); it keeps the schema. The `--fresh-db` flag deletes the data directories when dev mode starts, including the schema.

### Are destructive database operations safe during AI sessions?

The PostgreSQL, MySQL, and Redis query/command endpoints accept an optional `confirm` field. The startup documentation warns that destructive operations require `{"confirm": true}` — without it, the request is rejected. `/reset` always requires it. DynamoDB and OpenSearch delete handlers do not accept a `confirm` parameter; they require the key or document identifier fields directly. All of these endpoints reach only the databases dev mode runs locally, except that the DynamoDB `query`, `scan`, `schema` and `sample` endpoints also read a table the dev stack deploys (a remote resource). Their answer then has `deployed: true`, and the write endpoints refuse that table.

### What happens if a workload fails?

If a function fails to build or deploy while `stacktape dev --agent` starts, the session keeps running and the function keeps its previous code. The command exits with `DEV_STARTED_WITH_FAILURES`, names the function and its error, and its result carries the session with `ready: false`. Fix the code and call `POST /rebuild/{name}`. Any other workload that fails during the start stops the session, and the command exits with `CLI_DEV_WORKLOAD_FAILED`; fix the code and start again. After the start, a workload that crashes or fails to rebuild does not stop the session: `/status` reports it in `failedWorkloads` with its error, and `ready` stays false. Fix the code and call `POST /rebuild/{name}` to retry without restarting the session.

### Why does an `/aws/sdk` call fail or return access-denied?

The `/aws/sdk` endpoint uses the dev agent IAM role, which reads only this dev stack's resources in the session region. CloudWatch metric and alarm reads are the one exception: they cover the whole session region. See [AWS SDK access](#aws-sdk-access). A missing role or failed AssumeRole makes the call fail; it never falls back to your credentials. IAM can also deny a resource the role cannot read. Restart dev mode to update a missing or outdated role. A call is also rejected, without reaching AWS, when the operation is not a reviewed read-only one; the error lists the operations accepted for that service. The endpoint supports a broad set of services (`lambda`, `dynamodb`, `s3`, `logs`, `cloudformation`, `sqs`, `sns`, `sfn`, and more); call `GET /aws/sdk/services` for the authoritative, up-to-date list of valid `service` and `command` values before constructing a call.

---

# MCP server

Source: `apps/docs/content/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup.mdx`
Route: `/using-with-ai/mcp-server-setup`

The Stacktape MCP server gives coding agents structured access to Stacktape documentation, CLI commands, project inspection and dev mode. Instead of copying CLI output back and forth, your agent calls Stacktape tools directly and gets JSON answers. The server is in preview, so its tools can still change between releases.

## Quick start

```bash
stacktape mcp add
```

[`mcp add`](/cli/mcp-add) finds the coding agents on your machine and asks which ones to connect, with the installed ones preselected. For each agent you pick, it adds the Stacktape MCP server for your user, then starts the server once to check that it works. Start a new session (or reload the window) in your agent and ask: “Use Stacktape to show what this project deploys.”

A working integration exposes `stacktape_incident`, `stacktape_docs`, `stacktape_project`, `stacktape_cli`, and `stacktape_dev`. For an incident, the assistant starts with `stacktape_incident` and reads logs, metrics and other diagnostics through `stacktape_cli` directly. Mutating commands are planned with `action: "plan"` and run only after you approve them.

To undo the setup, run [`stacktape mcp remove`](/cli/mcp-remove).

## When to use

Use the MCP server when your AI coding assistant supports the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io). The structured tool interface is better than raw CLI output for several workflows:

- **Deploying or deleting stacks** — the assistant plans the command, validates arguments against CLI metadata, and executes with safety gates, all through tool calls.
- **Debugging** — query [logs](/cli/logs), [metrics](/cli/metrics), [alarms](/cli/alarms), [database contents](/cli/query-sql), or [DynamoDB items](/cli/query-dynamodb) during a conversation. The assistant gets structured JSON instead of parsing terminal output.
- **Configuration help** — the assistant searches Stacktape's bundled documentation index for resource types, config syntax, and deployment patterns without opening a browser.
- **Dev mode** — start, monitor, rebuild, and stop [dev mode](/local-development/dev-mode-overview) sessions from within your AI conversation.

## When NOT to use

Skip the MCP server if your AI client does not support the Model Context Protocol — use the [Stacktape CLI](/cli/deploy) directly or the [Stacktape Console](/stacktape-console/console-overview) instead. For long-running deployments, prefer the CLI when you want to watch the command directly in your own terminal. MCP command responses are consolidated and may be truncated. The MCP server runs CLI commands as subprocesses and returns a consolidated response; if an optional caller-specified timeout is exceeded, the subprocess is terminated and an error is returned.

## Supported agents

`mcp add` sets up these agents. Every agent starts `stacktape mcp` itself, as a local process on your machine.

| Agent | How `mcp add` adds the server |
|-------|-------------------------------|
| Claude Code | `claude mcp add --scope user` |
| Codex (CLI, IDE extension and app) | `codex mcp add`; edits `~/.codex/config.toml` when the `codex` command is missing |
| Cursor | Edits `~/.cursor/mcp.json` |
| VS Code (GitHub Copilot) | Edits the user `mcp.json` of your default profile |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | Edits `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json` |
| Windsurf (Devin Desktop) | Edits the existing `mcp_config.json`, or creates `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json` |
| OpenCode | Edits `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` or `opencode.json` |

An agent counts as installed when its command is on your PATH, or its app or settings folder exists. In a named VS Code profile, add the server from that profile with **MCP: Open User Configuration** (see [Manual setup](#manual-setup)). Any other MCP client that can start a local stdio server works too; see [Other MCP clients](#other-mcp-clients).


> **Info:** The server speaks the current MCP revision (`2026-07-28`) and the earlier 2025 revisions (`2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`), so it works with agents that have not moved to the new protocol yet. The confirmation form for destructive commands works in both: on older revisions it arrives as a standard elicitation request.


## What `mcp add` changes

- **User level only.** Entries go into your own agent configuration, never into the project, so nothing reaches your repository or your teammates. Claude Code and Codex are changed through their own `mcp add` commands; Claude Code's `~/.claude.json` is never edited directly.
- **Edits in place.** In JSON and JSONC files, `mcp add` changes only the `stacktape` entry. Your comments, other servers and formatting stay as they are, and the previous file is kept next to it as `<file>.bak.<timestamp>`. A file it cannot parse is left untouched and reported.
- **The command it writes.** When `stacktape` is on your PATH, the entry runs `stacktape mcp`, so upgrades keep working. When you installed Stacktape with the install script, the entry uses the binary's full path (`~/.stacktape/bin/stacktape`), because agents started from the Dock or Start menu often do not see your shell's PATH. Otherwise it writes the running binary's full path and tells you to run `mcp add` again if that file moves.
- **A check at the end.** `mcp add` starts the configured command, completes an MCP handshake and lists the tools. It reports a failure with the server's own error output.

Running `mcp add` again is safe: entries that already match are reported as already set up and left untouched.
